questions.answer: Water evaporates from seas and lakes and is lost from plants by transpiration. Water vapour cools and condenses to form clouds. Precipitation (rain) falls, providing fresh water for plants and animals, and runs off back into the sea.
ms: Evaporation from sea / transpiration from plants (1 mark)
Condensation forming clouds (1 mark)
Precipitation / rain returning water to land (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the three process names: evaporation, condensation, precipitation.

questions.q: Describe how a student could use random sampling with quadrats to estimate the population of buttercups in a field of 2000 m².
questions.answer: Lay two tape measures at right angles along edges of the field. Use a random number generator to give coordinates. Place a 1 m² quadrat at each coordinate and count buttercups. Repeat for at least 10 quadrats. Calculate the mean number per quadrat (per m²). Multiply by 2000 m² to estimate the total population.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear method with randomisation using coordinates from a random number generator, a stated quadrat size, a large enough number of quadrats, counting buttercups, calculating mean per m², and scaling up by the field area with a calculation shown.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Method including quadrats placed randomly and counting, with some idea of scaling up.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic: put quadrats down and count buttercups.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: Random sampling avoids bias. Never throw quadrats over your shoulder: say 'random coordinates'.

questions.q: A student places 15 quadrats, each 0.25 m², in a meadow of 600 m². The total number of daisies counted is 30. Estimate the daisy population.
questions.answer: Total area sampled = 15 × 0.25 = 3.75 m². Density = 30 ÷ 3.75 = 8 per m². Population = 8 × 600 = 4800.
ms: Area sampled 3.75 m² (or mean per quadrat 2) (1 mark)
Density 8 per m² (1 mark)
questions.tip: Convert from 'per quadrat' to 'per m²' before multiplying by the field area.

questions.q: Explain how animals living in hot deserts are adapted to survive, giving examples of structural, behavioural and functional adaptations.
questions.answer: Structural: large ears (fennec fox) or thin fur give large surface area to lose heat. Behavioural: nocturnal, burrow in daytime to avoid heat. Functional: produce very concentrated urine to conserve water. Extremophiles live in extreme conditions such as high temperature or salt.
ms: Structural adaptation with explanation (1 mark)
Behavioural adaptation with explanation (1 mark)
Functional adaptation with explanation (1 mark)
Clear link to conserving water or losing heat (1 mark)
questions.tip: Learn one example for each of structural, behavioural and functional.

questions.q: Explain why the sizes of a population of organisms can be affected by interdependence in a community.
questions.answer: Species depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal. If one species is removed, it can affect the whole community, e.g. predators decrease if prey decrease. A stable community has species and environmental factors in balance so population sizes remain fairly constant.
ms: Species depend on others for food / shelter / pollination / seed dispersal (1 mark)
Removal of one species affects others in the community (1 mark)
Example or stable community idea (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give a named example from a food web if you can.

questions.q: Which gas is mainly responsible for global warming from burning fossil fuels?
ms: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas.
questions.tip: Methane is also a greenhouse gas, from cattle and rice fields.

questions.q: Why does deforestation increase carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: Trees release CO₂ when they photosynthesise
Fewer trees take in CO₂ by photosynthesis, and burning the wood releases CO₂
ms: Less photosynthesis removes less CO₂; burning or decay of trees releases CO₂.
questions.tip: Give both effects: less removed AND more released.

questions.q: What does 'biodiversity' mean?
options: The number of producers in an area
The amount of biomass in a food chain
The number of individuals of one species
The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth or within an ecosystem
ms: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species in an ecosystem or on Earth.
questions.tip: High biodiversity makes an ecosystem more stable.

questions.q: Destroying peat bogs to produce garden compost has which effect?
options: Releases carbon dioxide as the peat is decayed or burned and reduces habitat biodiversity
Has no effect on the carbon cycle
Increases the area of peat bogs
Reduces carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
ms: Peat stores carbon; when used, microorganisms decay it and release CO₂; habitats are lost.
questions.tip: Peat-free compost is the alternative.

questions.q: Give two ways humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants.
questions.answer: Building, quarrying, farming, dumping waste.
ms: Any one, e.g. building / quarrying (1 mark)
Second, e.g. farming / landfill (1 mark)
questions.tip: Simple list questions: give distinct examples.

questions.q: Describe some of the biological consequences of global warming.
questions.answer: Loss of habitat from rising sea levels flooding low-lying areas; changes in distribution of species as temperature and rainfall change; changes in migration patterns; reduced biodiversity as some species cannot adapt; extinction.
ms: Loss of habitat (e.g. sea level rise flooding) (1 mark)
Changes in species distribution (1 mark)
Changes in migration patterns (1 mark)
Reduced biodiversity / extinction (1 mark)
questions.tip: The spec wants BIOLOGICAL consequences: focus on species, not weather.

questions.q: Evaluate the methods used to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity.
questions.answer: Breeding programmes for endangered species: preserve species, but small gene pool and expensive. Protection and regeneration of rare habitats: protect many species but limits land use. Reintroducing field margins and hedgerows in farms: increases biodiversity, but less land for crops, so lower profit. Reducing deforestation and CO₂ emissions: slows climate change, but conflicts with economic needs. Recycling: less waste to landfill. Conflicting pressures: farmers' income, food security, cost; judgement needed.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Several methods described with a clear evaluation of benefits and drawbacks, recognising conflicting pressures (economic, food security, development) and giving a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): At least two methods described with a benefit or drawback of each.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): One or two methods named, e.g. recycling, breeding programmes.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: Spec phrase: 'conflicting pressures'. Include the cost to farmers or industry.

questions.q: Explain why it is important to maintain high biodiversity.
questions.answer: High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable, because species depend on each other for food, shelter and maintaining the physical environment. Our future may depend on it, e.g. for food, medicines and materials.
ms: Ecosystem more stable / less affected by change (1 mark)
Species depend on each other / interdependence (1 mark)
Humans depend on biodiversity for food, medicines, materials (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Stability' is the key idea.

questions.q: Large-scale deforestation in tropical areas has been carried out to grow crops for biofuels and to provide land for cattle and rice. Explain how this affects the atmosphere.
questions.answer: Less photosynthesis so less CO₂ removed; burning trees releases CO₂; decay of wood by microorganisms releases CO₂; cattle and rice fields release methane; both are greenhouse gases contributing to global warming.
ms: Less CO₂ removed by photosynthesis (1 mark)
CO₂ released by burning / microbial decay (1 mark)
Cattle and rice fields release methane, a greenhouse gas (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention methane for the cattle and rice part.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes an electron?
options: Relative charge −1, relative mass very small
Relative charge +1, relative mass very small
ms: Electrons have a relative charge of −1 and a very small relative mass (about 1/2000 of a proton). Protons are +1, mass 1; neutrons are 0, mass 1.
questions.tip: Learn the three-row table (proton, neutron, electron) word for word. 'Mass 1' for an electron is the common slip.

questions.q: A potassium ion is written as ³⁹K⁺. Potassium has atomic number 19. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does this ion have?
ms: Protons = atomic number = 19. Neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20. A 1+ ion has lost one electron, so 19 − 1 = 18 electrons.
questions.tip: Positive ions have LOST electrons. Never change the number of protons when an ion forms.

questions.q: Chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine?
questions.tip: Weight by abundance. Simply averaging the two mass numbers (36.0) ignores the percentages.

questions.q: Why does reactivity increase going down Group 1?
options: The atoms have more electrons in their outer shell, so they lose them more easily
The atoms get smaller, so the outer electron is lost more easily
The nucleus has more protons, so it attracts the outer electron more strongly
The outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is less strongly attracted and lost more easily
ms: Down Group 1 atoms gain shells, so the single outer electron is further from the nucleus (and more shielded). Weaker attraction means it is lost more easily.
questions.tip: All Group 1 atoms have ONE outer electron. The explanation must be about distance/attraction, not number of outer electrons.

questions.q: Which mixture would react, producing a colour change?
options: Iodine solution added to potassium bromide solution
Iodine solution added to potassium chloride solution
Chlorine water added to potassium bromide solution
Bromine water added to potassium chloride solution
ms: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ (solution turns orange).
questions.tip: Reactivity in Group 7 DEcreases down the group: F > Cl > Br > I.

questions.q:
Sodium has atomic number 11.
Give the electronic structure of a sodium atom and explain how this shows which group sodium is in.
questions.answer: 2,8,1. It has 1 electron in its outer shell so it is in Group 1.
ms: Electronic structure 2,8,1 (1 mark)
One electron in outer shell, so Group 1 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Group number = number of outer shell electrons (for groups 1 to 7). Period number = number of shells.

questions.q:
In the alpha particle scattering experiment, positively charged alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil.
Describe the results of the experiment and explain how they led to the nuclear model of the atom replacing the plum pudding model.
questions.answer: Most alpha particles passed straight through, so most of the atom is empty space. Some were deflected, so the centre must be positively charged (repelling them). A very few bounced back, so the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus. The plum pudding model (ball of positive charge with embedded electrons) could not explain this.
ms: Most passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space (1 mark)
Some deflected, so the nucleus/centre is positively charged (1 mark)
A few bounced back, so mass is concentrated in a very small region (1 mark)
Plum pudding model had spread-out positive charge so could not explain large deflections (1 mark)
questions.tip: Pair each observation with its conclusion. Just listing observations caps you at about half marks.

questions.q:
A small piece of sodium is added to a trough of water.
Give two observations and write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction.
questions.answer: Fizzes/bubbles; floats and moves around; melts into a ball; gets smaller and disappears. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
ms: Any one observation: fizzing, floats, moves on surface, melts into a ball, disappears (1 mark)
Second different observation (1 mark)
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ correctly balanced (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Hydrogen is produced' is a conclusion, not an observation. Say what you would SEE.

questions.q:
Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution. The solution turns brown.
Explain why this happens and write a balanced symbol equation.
questions.answer: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine from potassium iodide. The iodine formed makes the solution brown. Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂
ms: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine (1 mark)
Chlorine displaces iodine / iodine is formed (1 mark)
Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Halogens are diatomic: Cl₂ and I₂, never Cl or I on their own.

questions.q: Explain why the noble gases are unreactive and why their boiling points increase down Group 0.
questions.answer: They have a full outer shell (stable arrangement; helium has 2), so they do not need to gain, lose or share electrons. Down the group the atoms get larger with greater relative atomic mass, so the intermolecular forces between atoms are stronger and need more energy to overcome.
ms: Full/stable outer shell of electrons (allow 8 outer electrons, helium 2) (1 mark)
So they do not easily gain, lose or share electrons (1 mark)
Boiling point rises because relative atomic mass/atom size increases, so forces between atoms are stronger (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not say noble gases have 'full shells' for all shells; it is the OUTER shell that matters.

questions.q:
Mendeleev placed tellurium (relative atomic mass 127.6) before iodine (relative atomic mass 126.9) in his periodic table, even though this broke his rule of ordering by atomic weight.
Explain why he did this and why the modern periodic table shows he was right.
questions.answer: He placed elements in groups with similar properties, so iodine went with other halogens. Elements are now ordered by atomic number (proton number); tellurium has fewer protons than iodine. Its higher mass is due to isotopes with more neutrons.
ms: Ordered to keep elements with similar properties in the same group (iodine with the halogens) (1 mark)
Modern table uses atomic/proton number; Te has fewer protons; difference in mass due to isotopes (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link knowledge of isotopes to explain why atomic weight order was sometimes 'wrong'.

questions.q:
Bromine has two isotopes: 50.7% bromine-79 and 49.3% bromine-81.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of bromine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
ms: 80.0 (must be to 1 decimal place; 79.986 or 80 alone scores the method mark only) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Read the rounding instruction. 80 alone does not show 1 decimal place.

questions.q:
The radius of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The radius of the nucleus is about 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom.
Calculate the radius of the nucleus in metres. Give your answer in standard form.
ms: Divides by 10 000 (1 × 10⁴) (1 mark)
1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dividing by 10⁴ makes the power MORE negative: −10 − 4 = −14.

questions.q:
Group 1 metals and Group 7 elements show opposite trends in reactivity.
Compare the trends in reactivity in Group 1 and Group 7 and explain each trend in terms of electronic structure.
questions.answer: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group; Group 7 reactivity decreases down the group. Both groups: atoms get larger with more shells, so outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so attraction to the nucleus is weaker. Group 1 atoms react by losing one outer electron: weaker attraction makes this easier, so more reactive. Group 7 atoms react by gaining one electron: weaker attraction from the nucleus for an incoming electron makes this harder, so less reactive.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: Group 1 more reactive down the group | Group 7 less reactive down the group | Group 1 have 1 outer electron, lose it to form 1+ ions | Group 7 have 7 outer electrons, gain one to form 1− ions | down both groups: more shells, outer shell further from nucleus, more shielding | weaker attraction between nucleus and outer electrons | Group 1: outer electron lost more easily | Group 7: harder to attract/gain an extra electron
questions.tip: Level 3 needs BOTH groups explained with the same reasoning (distance/attraction) and the opposite outcome (lose vs gain).

questions.q: Which substance has a giant covalent structure?
ms: Diamond is a giant covalent lattice of carbon atoms. Sodium chloride is giant ionic, copper is metallic, methane is simple molecular.
questions.tip: Giant covalent examples to know: diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide (and graphene).

questions.q: Why can graphite conduct electricity?
options: It contains ions that are free to move
Each carbon atom is bonded to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom
It has weak covalent bonds between atoms
Its layers can slide over each other
ms: Each carbon in graphite forms 3 covalent bonds, so one outer electron per atom is delocalised and can move through the structure carrying charge.
questions.tip: Sliding layers explains softness, not conductivity. Graphite has no ions.

questions.q: Aluminium forms Al³⁺ ions and oxygen forms O²⁻ ions. What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
ms: Charges must cancel: 2 × (+3) = +6 and 3 × (−2) = −6, so Al₂O₃.
questions.tip: Use the 'swap and drop' idea, then check the total charge is zero.

questions.q: Why are alloys harder than pure metals?
options: Different sized atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide over each other easily
Alloys contain ionic bonds between the different metals
ms: In a pure metal atoms are in regular layers that slide. Atoms of a different size in an alloy distort the layers, making sliding harder.
questions.tip: Mention 'layers' and 'distorted' - examiners look for both ideas.

questions.q: Bromine has a melting point of −7 °C and a boiling point of 59 °C. What is its state at 25 °C?
options: Liquid and gas in equal amounts
ms: 25 °C is above the melting point (−7 °C) but below the boiling point (59 °C), so bromine is a liquid.
questions.tip: Draw a quick number line: below mp = solid, between mp and bp = liquid, above bp = gas.

questions.q: Describe the structure and bonding in a metal.
questions.answer: A giant structure of positive metal ions arranged in a regular pattern (layers), surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons. Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
ms: Positive ions in a regular lattice/layers (1 mark)
Delocalised electrons with strong electrostatic attraction between ions and electrons (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'positive ions', not 'atoms', and 'delocalised electrons', not 'free electrons' alone (allow free electrons in some schemes, but delocalised is safest).

questions.q: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
questions.answer: Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice. There are strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions. A lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces.
ms: Giant (ionic) lattice/structure (1 mark)
Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (1 mark)
Lots of energy needed to overcome these forces/bonds (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do NOT mention molecules or intermolecular forces for an ionic compound. That scores zero for the explanation.

questions.q:
Magnesium (2,8,2) reacts with oxygen (2,6) to form magnesium oxide.
Describe, in terms of electrons, how magnesium oxide forms. Give the charge and electronic structure of each ion.
questions.answer: Each magnesium atom transfers 2 electrons to an oxygen atom. Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ with electronic structure 2,8. Oxygen forms O²⁻ with electronic structure 2,8.
ms: Magnesium loses/transfers 2 electrons to oxygen (1 mark)
Mg²⁺ [2,8] (1 mark)
O²⁻ [2,8] (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'transferred', not 'shared'. Sharing is covalent bonding.

questions.q: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.
questions.answer: In the solid the ions are fixed in place in the lattice and cannot move. When molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
ms: Solid: ions held in fixed positions/cannot move (1 mark)
Molten: ions free to move and carry charge (1 mark)
questions.tip: In ionic compounds it is IONS that move, not electrons. 'Electrons move' scores zero here.

questions.q:
Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon.
Explain why diamond is very hard and does not conduct electricity, but graphite is soft and does conduct.
questions.answer: Diamond: each carbon forms 4 strong covalent bonds in a rigid giant structure so it is very hard; all outer electrons are used in bonding so there are no delocalised electrons and it cannot conduct. Graphite: each carbon forms 3 covalent bonds in hexagonal layers with weak forces between layers, so layers slide and it is soft; one electron per carbon is delocalised and can move, so it conducts.
ms: Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others with strong covalent bonds/rigid structure, so hard (1 mark)
Diamond: no delocalised/free electrons, so no conduction (1 mark)
Graphite: layers with weak forces between them so layers slide, soft (1 mark)
Graphite: each C bonded to 3, one delocalised electron per atom that moves through the structure (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not say graphite has 'weak covalent bonds'. The covalent bonds are strong; the forces BETWEEN layers are weak.

questions.q:
Methane, CH₄, boils at −162 °C and does not conduct electricity.
Explain these properties.
questions.answer: Methane is made of small (simple) molecules. Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome to boil it (the covalent bonds do not break), so little energy is needed. The molecules have no overall charge and there are no free electrons or ions, so it cannot conduct.
ms: Small/simple molecules with weak intermolecular forces (1 mark)
Little energy needed to overcome them; covalent bonds not broken (1 mark)
Molecules have no overall charge / no delocalised electrons or ions (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Weak covalent bonds' is a classic zero-mark error. Covalent bonds are strong.

questions.q: The particle model shows particles as small solid spheres. Give two limitations of this model.
questions.answer: No forces between particles are shown; particles are not solid spheres (atoms are mostly empty space); particles are not all the same/not spherical; it does not show the movement or the spaces accurately.
ms: Any one: no forces shown / particles shown as solid / particles shown as spheres / particles are not all identical (1 mark)
A second different limitation (1 mark)
questions.tip: Keep limitations about the MODEL, not about the substance.

questions.q: Poly(ethene) is a polymer. Explain why poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature.
questions.answer: Polymer molecules are very large (long chains), so the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong and need a lot of energy to overcome.
ms: Very large molecules/long chains (1 mark)
Relatively strong intermolecular forces (allow forces between molecules) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Atoms within the chain are joined by covalent bonds; it is the forces BETWEEN chains that explain the state.

questions.q:
Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C, diamond sublimes at about 3600 °C and methane melts at −182 °C.
Compare the structure and bonding in these three substances and use this to explain the differences in their melting points.
questions.answer: Sodium chloride: giant ionic lattice, strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, lots of energy needed. Diamond: giant covalent, each carbon has four strong covalent bonds that must all be broken, so even more energy needed. Methane: simple covalent molecules with weak intermolecular forces; covalent bonds are not broken on melting, so very little energy needed.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: NaCl: giant ionic lattice | NaCl: strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions | diamond: giant covalent structure, each C bonded to 4 others | diamond: many strong covalent bonds must be broken | methane: small/simple molecules | methane: weak intermolecular forces | methane: covalent bonds NOT broken when it melts | more energy needed = higher melting point; links ordered: diamond > NaCl > methane
questions.tip: Every substance needs structure + the force overcome + energy link. Saying 'methane has weak bonds' caps you at Level 1.

questions.q: What is a covalent bond?
questions.answer: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms (usually non-metals).
ms: Shared pair of electrons (between atoms) (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Sharing electrons' is fine but 'a PAIR' is the precise wording that always earns the mark.

questions.q:
Graphene is a single layer of graphite.
Give two properties of graphene and explain one of them using its structure.
questions.answer: Very strong / conducts electricity / very thin (one atom thick). It conducts because each carbon has one delocalised electron; it is strong because of the strong covalent bonds in its hexagonal layer.
ms: Two correct properties (strong, conducts electricity, very thin/light) (1 mark)
Correct explanation linked to structure (delocalised electrons / strong covalent bonds) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Graphene and fullerenes are tested as 'new forms of carbon': know one property and one use of each.

questions.q:
What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂?
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1
questions.tip: The 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside it. 57 comes from ignoring the bracket.

questions.q: How many moles are in 4.4 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂? (Ar: C = 12, O = 16)
ms: Mr CO₂ = 12 + 32 = 44. Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 4.4 ÷ 44 = 0.1 mol
questions.tip: moles = mass ÷ Mr. Flipping it (Mr ÷ mass) gives 10.

questions.q: How many atoms are in 0.5 mol of water, H₂O? (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ per mole)
ms: Molecules = 0.5 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³. Each H₂O has 3 atoms, so atoms = 3 × 3.01 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³.
questions.tip: Read whether the question asks for molecules or atoms. 3.01 × 10²³ is molecules.

questions.q: 12.5 g of a salt is dissolved in water to make 250 cm³ of solution. What is the concentration in g/dm³?
ms: 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³. Concentration = 12.5 ÷ 0.25 = 50 g/dm³
questions.tip: Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000 BEFORE dividing.

questions.q:
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
2.4 g of magnesium (0.10 mol) is added to 0.15 mol of HCl. Which statement is correct?
options: HCl is the limiting reactant because 0.10 mol Mg needs 0.20 mol HCl
Magnesium is the limiting reactant because its Ar is smaller
Neither is limiting because both are in excess
Magnesium is the limiting reactant because there is less of it
ms: From the equation, 1 mol Mg needs 2 mol HCl. 0.10 mol Mg would need 0.20 mol HCl but only 0.15 mol is present, so HCl runs out first and is limiting.
questions.tip: Always use the ratio from the balanced equation. The reactant with fewer moles is NOT automatically limiting.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate is heated in an open crucible. The mass of the crucible and contents decreases. Why?
options: Carbon dioxide gas is produced and escapes
The calcium carbonate melts and evaporates
Mass is destroyed in the reaction
Oxygen from the air is added to the solid
ms: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The CO₂ gas escapes from the open container so the measured mass falls. Mass is still conserved overall.
questions.tip: Never say mass is lost or destroyed. Say a gas escapes.

questions.q:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of:
(a) sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄
(b) ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄
Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32
ms: (a) 98 (1 mark)
questions.tip: For brackets, work out the bracket (NH₄ = 18) then multiply.

questions.q:
Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
Calculate the mass of calcium oxide produced from 25 g of calcium carbonate.
Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16
questions.answer: Mr CaCO₃ = 100, moles = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol. Ratio 1:1 so 0.25 mol CaO. Mr CaO = 56, mass = 0.25 × 56 = 14 g
ms: Moles CaCO₃ = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 (1 mark)
Uses 1:1 ratio and Mr CaO = 56 (1 mark)
14 g (1 mark)
questions.tip: Show the moles step clearly. Correct answer with no working gets full marks, but a slip with no working gets zero.

questions.q:
Balance these equations:
(a) Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
(b) C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
questions.answer: (a) 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ (b) C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
ms: (a) 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ (1 mark)
(b) C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O (1 mark)
questions.tip: Only change the big numbers in front. Never change a formula's subscripts.

questions.q:
4.8 g of magnesium reacts completely with 3.2 g of oxygen, O₂, to produce 8.0 g of magnesium oxide, MgO.
Use these masses to work out the balanced equation for the reaction. Show your working.
Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16
ms: Moles of Mg = 0.2 (1 mark)
Moles of O₂ = 0.1 (Mr 32 used) (1 mark)
Moles of MgO = 0.2 (1 mark)
Divides by smallest to get 2:1:2 and writes 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO (1 mark)
questions.tip: Oxygen is O₂ so its Mr is 32, not 16. Using 16 ruins the ratio.

questions.q:
Iron reacts with sulfur: Fe + S → FeS
5.6 g of iron is heated with 4.0 g of sulfur.
(a) Identify the limiting reactant. Show your working.
(b) Calculate the maximum mass of iron sulfide produced.
Ar: Fe = 56, S = 32
questions.answer: (a) Fe: 5.6 ÷ 56 = 0.10 mol; S: 4.0 ÷ 32 = 0.125 mol. Ratio 1:1 so iron is limiting. (b) 0.10 mol FeS × 88 = 8.8 g
ms: Moles Fe = 0.10 and moles S = 0.125 (1 mark)
Iron is limiting (with reason: fewer moles in a 1:1 ratio) (1 mark)
Mr FeS = 88 (1 mark)
8.8 g (1 mark)
questions.tip: The maximum product always comes from the LIMITING reactant. Using the excess reactant here gives 11 g, which is wrong.

questions.q:
A solution of sodium chloride has a concentration of 8.0 g/dm³.
Calculate the mass of sodium chloride in 250 cm³ of this solution.
ms: Converts 250 cm³ to 0.25 dm³ (1 mark)
2.0 g (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mass = concentration × volume (in dm³). Rearranging the formula is a common 2-mark question.

questions.q:
A student timed a reaction three times. The results were 24.2 s, 24.6 s and 24.0 s.
(a) Calculate the mean time.
(b) Estimate the uncertainty in the mean.
ms: Mean calculated: 24.3 s (allow 24.27) (1 mark)
Range = 0.6 s used (1 mark)
Uncertainty = ± 0.3 s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Uncertainty = range ÷ 2, written with ±. Quote the mean to the same decimal places as the data.

questions.q:
Iron is extracted in the blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
Calculate the mass of iron that can be produced from 320 g of iron(III) oxide.
Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16
questions.answer: Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160. Moles = 320 ÷ 160 = 2 mol. Ratio Fe₂O₃ : Fe = 1 : 2, so 4 mol Fe. Mass = 4 × 56 = 224 g
ms: Mr = 160 and moles Fe₂O₃ = 2 (1 mark)
Uses 1:2 ratio to get 4 mol Fe (1 mark)
224 g (1 mark)
questions.tip: Forgetting the ratio gives 112 g. Always check the big numbers in the equation.

questions.q:
Calculate the number of molecules in 8.8 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂.
Ar: C = 12, O = 16. Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ per mole
ms: Moles = 0.2 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give the answer in standard form with the number between 1 and 10.

questions.q:
8.0 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH, is dissolved in water to make 250 cm³ of solution.
(a) Calculate the concentration of the solution in g/dm³.
(b) A student uses 50 cm³ of this solution. Calculate the mass of sodium hydroxide in 50 cm³.
ms: (a) Converts 250 cm³ to 0.25 dm³ (1 mark)
(a) 32 g/dm³ (1 mark)
(b) 1.6 g (allow 8.0 × 50/250 = 1.6 g; allow ecf: answer to (a) × 0.050) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always convert cm³ to dm³ (÷ 1000) first. Mass = concentration × volume, so the 50 cm³ sample holds one fifth of the 8.0 g.

questions.q:
When magnesium ribbon is burned in a crucible, the mass of the solid increases.
Explain why, using the idea of conservation of mass.
questions.answer: Magnesium reacts with oxygen from the air to form magnesium oxide. The mass of oxygen atoms that combine is added, so the product is heavier; no atoms are created or destroyed.
ms: Magnesium reacts with/gains oxygen from the air (1 mark)
Mass of oxygen added to the solid; total mass of atoms conserved (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mass changes in open systems are always due to a gas entering or leaving.

questions.q:
Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃.
Ar: N = 14, H = 1, O = 16
ms: Mr = 80 and mass of N = 28 (both N atoms counted) (1 mark)
35% (1 mark)
questions.tip: There are TWO nitrogen atoms in NH₄NO₃. Counting one gives 17.5%.

questions.q:
Aluminium reacts with oxygen: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃
Calculate the mass of aluminium oxide formed when 2.7 g of aluminium burns completely.
Ar: Al = 27, O = 16
questions.answer: Moles Al = 2.7 ÷ 27 = 0.1 mol. Ratio Al : Al₂O₃ = 4 : 2, so 0.05 mol Al₂O₃. Mr = 102. Mass = 0.05 × 102 = 5.1 g
ms: Moles Al = 0.1 (1 mark)
0.05 mol Al₂O₃ from 4:2 ratio (1 mark)
5.1 g (1 mark)
questions.tip: Ratio 4:2 means halve the moles. Ignoring it gives 10.2 g.

questions.q: What are the products when zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid?
ms: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, so zinc chloride + hydrogen.
questions.tip: Metal + acid gives hydrogen. Metal oxide/hydroxide + acid gives water.

questions.q: Which metal can be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon?
ms: Carbon can only reduce oxides of metals less reactive than carbon. Iron is below carbon in the reactivity series; the others are above it.
questions.tip: Metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium) need electrolysis.

questions.q: Which is the ionic equation for neutralisation of any acid by any alkali?
ms: Acids provide H⁺(aq) and alkalis provide OH⁻(aq). They combine to make water; the other ions are spectator ions.
questions.tip: Learn this one off by heart; it is worth an easy mark on Higher papers.

questions.q: The hydrogen ion concentration of an acid solution is increased by a factor of 100. What happens to the pH?
ms: Each decrease of 1 pH unit means 10 times more H⁺. 100 = 10 × 10, so the pH falls by 2.
questions.tip: pH is a log scale: factor 10 = 1 unit. More H⁺ means LOWER pH.

questions.q: What is meant by a strong acid?
options: An acid that only partially ionises in water
An acid with a pH of 7
An acid with a high concentration
An acid that is completely ionised in aqueous solution
ms: Strong acids (hydrochloric, nitric, sulfuric) fully ionise in water. 'Concentrated' is about the amount of acid per volume, not strength.
questions.tip: Strong/weak = how much it ionises. Concentrated/dilute = how much acid is dissolved.

questions.q:
Name the salt produced in each reaction:
(a) copper oxide + sulfuric acid
(b) potassium hydroxide + nitric acid
questions.answer: (a) copper sulfate (b) potassium nitrate
ms: (a) copper sulfate (allow copper(II) sulfate) (1 mark)
(b) potassium nitrate (1 mark)
questions.tip: Hydrochloric → chloride, sulfuric → sulfate, nitric → nitrate.

questions.q:
Magnesium is added to copper sulfate solution. A displacement reaction happens.
(a) Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
(b) State which species is oxidised and which is reduced. Explain your answer in terms of electrons.
questions.answer: (a) Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu (b) Magnesium is oxidised because it loses electrons; copper ions are reduced because they gain electrons.
ms: (a) Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu (sulfate ions omitted) (1 mark)
Mg oxidised, loses (2) electrons (1 mark)
Cu²⁺ reduced, gains (2) electrons (1 mark)
questions.tip: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). Sulfate ions are spectators.

questions.q:
Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid. The ionic equation is Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂
Write two half equations for this reaction and identify which is oxidation.
questions.answer: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation). 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (reduction).
ms: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (1 mark)
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (1 mark)
Zinc half equation identified as oxidation (loss of electrons) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Electrons must balance the charges on both sides. Check total charge left = total charge right.

questions.q: Describe how you would make a pure, dry sample of copper sulfate crystals from copper oxide (an insoluble solid) and dilute sulfuric acid.
questions.answer: Warm the sulfuric acid in a beaker. Add copper oxide a spatula at a time, stirring, until no more dissolves (excess). Filter to remove excess copper oxide. Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate some water until crystals start to form, then leave to cool and crystallise. Remove crystals by filtering and dry between filter paper or in a warm oven.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: measure acid into beaker | warm the acid (gently, not boiling) | add copper oxide a little at a time, stirring | until in excess / black solid remains | filter to remove excess copper oxide | pour filtrate into evaporating basin | heat to evaporate some of the water / until crystals start to form | leave to cool/crystallise slowly | pat crystals dry with filter paper / warm oven
questions.tip: Do NOT say 'evaporate all the water' or 'heat to dryness'. That gives a powder, not crystals.

questions.q:
In making copper sulfate, copper oxide is added to sulfuric acid until it is in excess.
Give one reason why excess copper oxide is used and state how you can tell it is in excess.
questions.answer: To make sure all the acid has reacted (so the product is not contaminated with acid). You can see black solid remaining that no longer dissolves.
ms: All the acid is used up/neutralised (1 mark)
Black solid remains / no more dissolves (1 mark)
questions.tip: The excess solid is easy to filter off; excess acid would not be.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid.
questions.answer: Strength is how much the acid ionises: a strong acid is completely ionised in water, a weak acid only partially ionises. Concentration is the amount of acid in a given volume: a dilute acid has a small amount of acid per dm³, a concentrated acid has a large amount per dm³.
ms: Strong = fully ionised; weak = partially ionised (1 mark)
Concentration = amount of acid (solute) per unit volume (1 mark)
Dilute = little acid per volume, concentrated = lots of acid per volume (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two different ideas. Using 'strong' to mean 'concentrated' loses the marks.

questions.q:
A student added three metals X, Y and Z to dilute acid.
X: fizzed rapidly. Y: no bubbles. Z: a few bubbles slowly.
Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first, and explain how you decided.
questions.answer: X, Z, Y. The faster the bubbles of hydrogen are produced, the more reactive the metal.
ms: Order X > Z > Y (1 mark)
More reactive metals react faster / produce gas (hydrogen) faster (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rate of bubbling or temperature rise are the usual measures of reactivity.

questions.q:
Iron oxide is reduced by carbon. Balance the equation and explain why carbon can be used.
Fe₂O₃ + C → Fe + CO₂
questions.answer: 2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂. Carbon is more reactive than iron, so it removes oxygen from iron oxide.
ms: 2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂ (1 mark)
Carbon more reactive than iron (so takes the oxygen) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Reduction here means loss of oxygen. Carbon is oxidised to CO₂.

questions.q:
Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid.
Complete and balance the equation: CaCO₃ + HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
Name the salt formed.
questions.answer: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Salt: calcium chloride.
ms: 2 in front of HCl (1 mark)
Calcium chloride (1 mark)
questions.tip: Carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Three products every time.

questions.q:
Sodium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid.
Give the formula of the salt and write the balanced symbol equation.
questions.answer: Na₂SO₄. 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
ms: Na₂SO₄ (1 mark)
2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O (1 mark)
questions.tip: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻, so you need two Na⁺ ions.

questions.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution, and what colour is universal indicator in a strong acid?
questions.answer: pH 7. Red.
ms: pH 7 (1 mark)
Red (1 mark)
questions.tip: pH 0 to 14: acids below 7, alkalis above 7.

questions.q: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. What forms at the cathode (negative electrode)?
ms: Positive Pb²⁺ ions are attracted to the negative cathode, gain electrons and form lead. In a molten compound there is no water, so no hydrogen.
questions.tip: Molten = only two ions, so metal at cathode, non-metal at anode.

questions.q: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?
ms: There is no halide ion, so hydroxide ions from water are discharged at the anode, forming oxygen.
questions.tip: Anode rule for solutions: halide present → halogen; otherwise → oxygen.

questions.q: Which half equation happens at the anode when sodium chloride solution (brine) is electrolysed?
ms: Chloride ions are attracted to the positive anode and lose electrons (oxidation) to form chlorine gas.
questions.tip: At the anode electrons are LOST, so e⁻ appears on the right-hand side.

questions.q: Why is aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite during extraction of aluminium?
options: Cryolite is a catalyst for the reaction
It lowers the melting point, saving energy
ms: Aluminium oxide melts above 2000 °C. Dissolving it in cryolite lowers the operating temperature, which reduces energy costs.
questions.tip: Link to energy/cost in your answer for the full explanation.

questions.q: Aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed. What forms at the cathode?
ms: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions (from water) are discharged instead of sodium ions.
questions.tip: Cathode rule for solutions: if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen forms.

questions.q: Explain why an ionic compound must be melted or dissolved in water before it can be electrolysed.
questions.answer: So that the ions are free to move. They can then move to the oppositely charged electrodes.
ms: Ions free to move (1 mark)
To the (oppositely charged) electrodes / to carry charge (1 mark)
questions.tip: In a solid, ions are fixed in the lattice.

questions.q:
In the extraction of aluminium, the positive electrodes are made of carbon and must be replaced regularly.
Explain why.
questions.answer: Oxygen is formed at the positive electrode. At the high temperature the oxygen reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the electrode burns away.
ms: Oxygen forms at the anode (1 mark)
Oxygen reacts with the carbon (1 mark)
Forming carbon dioxide so the anode wears away (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the product gas, CO₂, to secure the last mark.

questions.q:
Molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed.
Write the half equations at each electrode and state which is oxidation.
questions.answer: Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻. The anode reaction is oxidation (loss of electrons).
ms: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (1 mark)
2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (allow O²⁻ → ½O₂ + 2e⁻) (1 mark)
Anode/oxide ion reaction is oxidation (1 mark)
questions.tip: Count charges: 2 × (−2) = −4 on the left, so 4e⁻ on the right.

questions.q:
Describe a method to investigate what is produced at each electrode when an aqueous solution, such as copper chloride solution, is electrolysed.
Include how you would identify the products.
questions.answer: Pour copper chloride solution into a beaker. Place two inert (graphite) electrodes in the solution, not touching, connected to a low-voltage d.c. power supply. Switch on and observe each electrode. A brown/pink solid forming on the cathode is copper. Bubbles at the anode: hold damp blue litmus paper near the anode; if it turns red then bleaches white, the gas is chlorine. Do it in a well-ventilated area because chlorine is toxic. Repeat with other solutions.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: solution in beaker/cell | two inert (carbon/graphite) electrodes, not touching | connect to d.c. supply (low voltage, e.g. 4 V) | observe each electrode | metal coating at cathode e.g. copper (pink/brown) | gas collected in test tube over electrode | chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper | hydrogen: lit splint squeaky pop | oxygen: relights glowing splint | safety: ventilation, chlorine is toxic
questions.tip: Say which electrode is which and give the test with its positive result. Vague 'test the gas' answers stay in Level 1.

questions.q: Predict the products at each electrode when potassium bromide solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Explain each prediction.
questions.answer: Cathode: hydrogen, because potassium is more reactive than hydrogen so H⁺ ions are discharged. Anode: bromine, because bromide (a halide) ions are present and are discharged in preference to hydroxide ions.
ms: Hydrogen at cathode (1 mark)
Potassium more reactive than hydrogen (1 mark)
Bromine at anode (1 mark)
Halide ions discharged in preference to hydroxide (1 mark)
questions.tip: Each product needs its own reason for full marks.

questions.q:
During the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution, the solution left at the end is alkaline.
Explain why.
questions.answer: Hydrogen ions are removed (as hydrogen gas) and chloride ions are removed (as chlorine). Sodium ions and hydroxide ions remain, forming sodium hydroxide solution.
ms: H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are discharged/removed (1 mark)
Na⁺ and OH⁻ left so sodium hydroxide forms (1 mark)
questions.tip: Electrolysis of brine gives three products: hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide.

questions.q:
Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
Write the half equation at each electrode.
questions.answer: Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
ms: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (1 mark)
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ (allow 4OH⁻ − 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O) (1 mark)
questions.tip: The hydroxide half equation is a Higher favourite. Learn it exactly.

questions.q: Describe the test for chlorine gas and give the result.
questions.answer: Hold damp (blue) litmus paper in the gas. It is bleached white (blue litmus may turn red first).
ms: Damp litmus paper (1 mark)
Bleached / turns white (1 mark)
questions.tip: The paper must be DAMP.

questions.q: Define electrolysis.
questions.answer: The breaking down of an ionic compound (molten or in solution) using electricity.
ms: Decomposition of an ionic compound using electricity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention both 'ionic compound' and 'electricity'.

questions.q: Which type of reaction is endothermic?
options: Oxidation of iron in hand warmers
ms: Thermal decomposition takes in energy from the surroundings. Combustion, neutralisation and oxidation release energy.
questions.tip: Endothermic examples: thermal decomposition, citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate, sports injury packs.

questions.q: What is the activation energy of a reaction?
options: The overall energy change of the reaction
The energy released when a reaction happens
The minimum energy particles need when they collide in order to react
The energy stored in the products
ms: Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles must have to react. On a profile it is from reactants up to the peak.
questions.tip: Draw the arrow on profiles from reactant level to the top of the hump.

questions.q:
Use the bond energies to calculate the energy change for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
H–H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl = 243 kJ/mol, H–Cl = 432 kJ/mol
ms: Bonds broken = 436 + 243 = 679. Bonds made = 2 × 432 = 864. Change = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol (exothermic).
questions.tip: Energy change = broken − made. Forgetting the 2 in 2HCl gives +247.

questions.q: During a reaction the temperature of the solution falls from 22 °C to 15 °C. What does this show?
options: The reaction is endothermic, taking in energy from the surroundings
The reaction has a high activation energy
The reaction is exothermic, releasing energy
ms: The solution (surroundings) gets colder because the reaction absorbs thermal energy from it: endothermic.
questions.tip: Temperature drop = endothermic. The energy goes INTO the chemicals.

questions.q: Which is a use of an exothermic reaction?
ms: Self-heating cans and hand warmers use exothermic reactions to release heat.
questions.tip: Cold packs are endothermic.

questions.q: What is an exothermic reaction? Give one example.
questions.answer: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. Example: combustion / neutralisation / many oxidation reactions.
ms: Transfers energy to the surroundings (temperature rises) (1 mark)
Valid example (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Gives out heat' is accepted but 'transfers energy to the surroundings' is the spec wording.

questions.q:
A student measured the temperature change when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, using a glass beaker.
Suggest three improvements to make the results more accurate.
questions.answer: Use a polystyrene cup (insulator) instead of a glass beaker; put a lid on the cup to reduce heat loss; stand the cup in a beaker for stability; stir the mixture; record the highest temperature reached; use a thermometer with a higher resolution / data logger; repeat and take a mean.
ms: Polystyrene cup (insulation) (1 mark)
Lid to reduce energy loss (1 mark)
Any one: stir, record maximum temperature, more precise thermometer, repeat for mean (1 mark)
questions.tip: Each improvement should reduce energy loss or improve measurement. 'Be more careful' never scores.

questions.q:
Methane burns: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Use the bond energies to calculate the overall energy change.
C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 805, O–H = 464 (all kJ/mol)
ms: Energy to break bonds = 2648 (1 mark)
Energy released making bonds = 3466 (1 mark)
Uses broken − made (1 mark)
−818 kJ/mol with negative sign (1 mark)
questions.tip: CO₂ has TWO C=O bonds and each water has TWO O–H bonds. Draw out the molecules to count.

questions.q:
Ammonia is made: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
N≡N = 945, H–H = 436, N–H = 391 (all kJ/mol)
Calculate the energy change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
questions.answer: Broken: 945 + 3 × 436 = 2253. Made: 6 × 391 = 2346. Change = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol. Exothermic.
ms: Broken = 2253 and made = 2346 (1 mark)
−93 kJ/mol (1 mark)
Exothermic (because more energy released making bonds than used breaking them) (1 mark)
questions.tip: 2NH₃ contains 6 N–H bonds, not 3.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why a reaction is exothermic.
questions.answer: Breaking bonds needs (takes in) energy, which is endothermic. Making bonds releases energy, which is exothermic. In an exothermic reaction more energy is released making new bonds than is needed to break the old bonds.
ms: Bond breaking takes in/requires energy (1 mark)
Bond making releases energy (1 mark)
More energy released forming bonds than taken in breaking them (1 mark)
questions.tip: Never say breaking bonds releases energy. It always takes energy in.

questions.q: Describe the reaction profile for an endothermic reaction.
questions.answer: The products are at a higher energy level than the reactants. The line rises from reactants to a peak (the activation energy is the difference between reactants and the peak) then falls to the products. The overall energy change is the difference between reactants and products and is positive.
ms: Products higher in energy than reactants (1 mark)
Curve rises to a peak; activation energy from reactants to peak (1 mark)
Overall energy change shown as difference between reactants and products (energy taken in) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Label arrows carefully: activation energy starts at the REACTANT line.

questions.q: Plan an investigation to find how the mass of zinc powder added to copper sulfate solution affects the temperature change.
questions.answer: Measure 25 cm³ of copper sulfate solution with a measuring cylinder into a polystyrene cup inside a beaker. Record the starting temperature. Weigh 0.5 g zinc powder on a balance. Add the zinc, stir, put a lid on and record the highest temperature. Calculate the temperature change. Repeat with 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 g. Keep volume and concentration of copper sulfate and the particle size of zinc the same. Repeat each mass and calculate means. Plot mass against temperature change.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: fixed volume of copper sulfate solution measured with measuring cylinder | in polystyrene cup with lid | measure initial temperature | weigh zinc on balance | add zinc and stir | record maximum temperature | calculate temperature change | repeat with at least 5 different masses | control: volume, concentration, starting temperature, particle size | repeat for mean / plot graph
questions.tip: Level 3 plans name the independent, dependent and control variables and say how each is measured.

questions.q:
In a reaction the temperature started at 21.0 °C and the highest temperature reached was 28.5 °C.
Calculate the temperature change and state the type of reaction.
questions.answer: 28.5 − 21.0 = 7.5 °C rise. Exothermic.
ms: 7.5 °C (1 mark)
Exothermic (1 mark)
questions.tip: Temperature change = final − initial. A rise means exothermic.

questions.q:
H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr. The overall energy change is −103 kJ/mol.
H–H = 436 kJ/mol and Br–Br = 193 kJ/mol.
Calculate the bond energy of the H–Br bond.
questions.answer: Broken = 436 + 193 = 629. Change = broken − made, so −103 = 629 − made, made = 732. Two H–Br bonds, so H–Br = 732 ÷ 2 = 366 kJ/mol
ms: Energy to break bonds = 629 (1 mark)
Energy released making bonds = 732 (1 mark)
H–Br = 366 kJ/mol (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rearrange carefully. Then divide by the number of bonds of that type.

questions.q: Which change would NOT increase the rate of reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid?
options: Using a larger volume of the same acid
Using marble powder instead of chips
ms: A larger volume of the same concentration does not increase the frequency of collisions per unit volume, so the rate stays the same. The others all increase rate.
questions.tip: Volume is not concentration. Read the factor carefully.

questions.q: Why does increasing the temperature increase the rate of reaction?
options: It increases the surface area of the particles
It increases the concentration of the reactants
Particles move faster, so collide more often and more collisions have energy ≥ activation energy
ms: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy: more frequent collisions AND a greater proportion of collisions are successful.
questions.tip: Catalysts lower activation energy; temperature does not.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It increases the number of particles
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
It is used up and releases energy
It gives the particles more energy
ms: Catalysts provide a different pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful. They are not used up.
questions.tip: Catalysts are not 'reactants' and do not appear in the overall equation.

questions.q: A 1 cm cube is cut into eight 0.5 cm cubes. What happens to the total surface area?
options: It increases eight times to 48 cm²
It stays the same at 6 cm²
ms: Original: 6 × 1 × 1 = 6 cm². New: 8 cubes × 6 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm². Surface area doubles, so rate increases.
questions.tip: Smaller pieces = larger surface area to volume ratio = more frequent collisions.

questions.q:
48 cm³ of gas was collected in 30 s.
Calculate the mean rate of reaction. Give the unit.
ms: Unit cm³/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mean rate = quantity of product formed ÷ time taken.

questions.q: Explain, using collision theory, why increasing the concentration of an acid increases the rate of its reaction with magnesium.
questions.answer: There are more acid particles in the same volume. So collisions between acid particles and magnesium are more frequent. More successful collisions per second, so a faster rate.
ms: More particles in the same volume (1 mark)
More frequent collisions (allow more collisions per second; not just 'more collisions') (1 mark)
So more successful collisions per unit time (1 mark)
questions.tip: Write 'more FREQUENT collisions'. 'More collisions' on its own often fails the mark.

questions.q:
Volume of gas against time is plotted for a reaction. A tangent is drawn to the curve at 20 s. The tangent passes through (0 s, 10 cm³) and (40 s, 50 cm³).
Calculate the rate of reaction at 20 s.
ms: Uses change in y ÷ change in x for the tangent (1 mark)
1.0 cm³/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rate at a specific time = gradient of the TANGENT. Do not divide the reading by the time.

questions.q: Describe how you would investigate the effect of concentration of hydrochloric acid on the rate of reaction with magnesium ribbon, by measuring the volume of gas produced.
questions.answer: Measure 50 cm³ of hydrochloric acid into a conical flask using a measuring cylinder. Set up a gas syringe (or upturned measuring cylinder in a trough of water) connected with a bung and delivery tube. Add a 3 cm length of magnesium ribbon, quickly put in the bung and start a stopwatch. Record volume of gas every 10 s until the reaction stops. Repeat with different concentrations of acid (at least four different concentrations). Control length/mass of magnesium, volume of acid and temperature. Plot volume against time and compare initial gradients.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: measured volume of acid in conical flask | fixed length/mass of magnesium ribbon | gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder/burette over water | bung in quickly, start timer | record gas volume at regular intervals | repeat with at least 4-5 concentrations | control: volume of acid, mass/length of Mg, temperature | repeat and calculate mean | plot graph / compare rates
questions.tip: Name the equipment for collecting the gas. Missing control variables keeps answers in Level 2.

questions.q:
Sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid to form a cloudy precipitate of sulfur.
Describe how to use this reaction to investigate the effect of temperature on rate.
questions.answer: Draw a cross on paper and put the flask on it. Add a fixed volume of sodium thiosulfate solution warmed to a known temperature (water bath). Add a fixed volume of acid and start the timer. Time how long until the cross can no longer be seen. Repeat at different temperatures. Rate is proportional to 1/time.
ms: Cross under the flask, time until cross disappears (1 mark)
Heat thiosulfate to different temperatures using a water bath, measured with thermometer (1 mark)
Same volumes and concentrations each time (1 mark)
Shorter time = faster rate (allow rate = 1/time) (1 mark)
questions.tip: This method is subjective. A light sensor/data logger would be an improvement.

questions.q:
In the 'disappearing cross' experiment the cross disappeared after 45 s at 30 °C.
Calculate the relative rate (1/time) and explain one limitation of this method.
questions.answer: 1/45 = 0.022 s⁻¹. Limitation: deciding when the cross disappears is subjective (depends on the person's eyesight), so different people get different times.
ms: Endpoint is subjective / depends on observer (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give the answer to 2 significant figures.

questions.q:
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst for this reaction.
(a) Explain how the catalyst increases the rate.
(b) Describe how you could show that manganese(IV) oxide is not used up.
questions.answer: (a) It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react. (b) Weigh the catalyst before, filter it out after the reaction, dry it and reweigh: the mass is unchanged.
ms: (a) Alternative pathway / route (1 mark)
(a) Lower activation energy so more collisions are successful (1 mark)
(b) Weigh before and after, filtering and drying (1 mark)
(b) Same mass at the end (1 mark)
questions.tip: Catalysts do not appear in the balanced equation; write them over the arrow if needed.

questions.q:
The mass of a flask containing marble chips and acid fell by 0.24 g in 20 s.
Calculate the mean rate of reaction in g/s.
ms: 0.012 g/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mass decreases because CO₂ escapes. Rate is still a positive value.

questions.q: What does the symbol ⇌ show in an equation?
ms: ⇌ means the reaction can go both forwards and backwards.
questions.tip: Know the symbol: two half-arrows.

questions.q: Which statement about a system at equilibrium is correct?
options: The forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate
The forward and reverse reactions have stopped
The concentrations of reactants and products are always equal
ms: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant (not necessarily equal).
questions.tip: 'Constant' is not 'equal'. Do not say the reactions stop.

questions.q: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. Which change moves the equilibrium to the right?
ms: Left side has 3 molecules of gas, right side has 2. Increasing pressure shifts the position to the side with fewer gas molecules (the right).
questions.tip: For pressure, count gas molecules on each side. For temperature, find which direction is endothermic.

questions.q: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). The forward reaction is endothermic. The temperature is increased. What happens?
options: The rate of the forward reaction only decreases
The equilibrium shifts left; less NO₂
The equilibrium shifts right; more NO₂
No change, because the number of molecules changes
ms: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, here the forward reaction, so more NO₂ forms.
questions.tip: Raise temperature → endothermic direction favoured. Lower it → exothermic direction favoured.

questions.q:
Hydrated copper sulfate (blue) is heated to form anhydrous copper sulfate (white) and water.
hydrated copper sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate + water
What would you see when water is added to anhydrous copper sulfate, and what happens to the temperature?
questions.answer: It turns from white to blue. The temperature rises (the reverse reaction is exothermic).
ms: White to blue (1 mark)
Gets hot / exothermic (1 mark)
questions.tip: If a reaction is endothermic one way, it is exothermic by the same amount the other way.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by equilibrium in a closed system.
questions.answer: The forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate, so the amounts (concentrations) of reactants and products stay constant. A closed system means nothing can enter or leave.
ms: Forward and reverse reactions at the same rate (1 mark)
Concentrations/amounts stay constant (1 mark)
questions.tip: The word 'rate' must be in your answer.

questions.q:
Hydrogen and iodine react: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). The forward reaction is exothermic.
Predict and explain the effect on the equilibrium yield of HI of:
(a) increasing the temperature
(b) increasing the pressure
questions.answer: (a) Yield of HI decreases. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic reaction, which is the reverse reaction. (b) No change. There are 2 molecules of gas on each side, so pressure does not affect the position.
ms: (a) Yield decreases / moves left (1 mark)
(a) Endothermic (reverse) direction favoured by higher temperature (1 mark)
(b) No effect on yield (1 mark)
(b) Same number of gas molecules on each side (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always count molecules of GAS. Equal numbers means pressure has no effect.

questions.q:
Ethanol is made industrially: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g). The forward reaction is exothermic.
The concentration of steam is increased. Explain the effect on the equilibrium and the yield of ethanol using Le Chatelier's principle.
questions.answer: If a condition is changed, the system responds to counteract the change. Increasing steam concentration, the equilibrium shifts right to use up the extra steam. More ethanol is produced, so the yield increases.
ms: States system acts to oppose/counteract the change (1 mark)
Equilibrium shifts to the right (forward reaction) (1 mark)
More ethanol / yield increases (1 mark)
questions.tip: Le Chatelier: the system opposes the change. Then say which way and what happens to the product.

questions.q:
Methanol is made by: CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g). The forward reaction is exothermic.
Explain how changing the temperature and pressure affects the yield of methanol AND the rate of production. Suggest why a compromise temperature is used.
questions.answer: Pressure: 3 gas molecules on the left, 1 on the right. High pressure shifts equilibrium right, increasing yield; it also increases rate because particles are closer, so more frequent collisions. But high pressure is expensive and dangerous. Temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature increases yield. But low temperature gives a slow rate because fewer particles have enough energy. A compromise temperature gives a reasonable yield in a reasonable time. A catalyst can be used to increase rate without changing yield.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: 3 gas molecules on left, 1 on right | high pressure shifts equilibrium right, increases yield | high pressure increases rate (more frequent collisions) | high pressure costly/needs strong equipment/safety | forward reaction exothermic so low temperature gives higher yield | low temperature means slow rate | compromise: acceptable yield at a fast enough rate | catalyst increases rate but does not change yield/equilibrium position
questions.tip: Separate YIELD (equilibrium position) from RATE. Mixing them up is the most common way to drop to Level 1.

questions.q:
Ammonium chloride decomposes on heating: NH₄Cl ⇌ NH₃ + HCl
What would you observe when the products cool near the top of a test tube, and why?
questions.answer: A white solid forms again near the top of the tube. As the gases cool, the reverse reaction happens and ammonium chloride re-forms.
ms: White solid forms (1 mark)
Reverse reaction happens on cooling (1 mark)
questions.tip: This shows the reaction is reversible depending on conditions.

questions.q:
A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium. A catalyst is added.
State and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium.
questions.answer: No effect on the position. The catalyst increases the rate of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster.
ms: No change in position/yield (1 mark)
Speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally / equilibrium reached faster (1 mark)
questions.tip: Catalysts change how quickly equilibrium is reached, not where it lies.

questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
ms: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2 (e.g. CH₄, C₂H₆).
questions.tip: CnH2n is the alkenes.

questions.q: Which is the molecular formula of the fourth alkane, butane?
ms: n = 4, so H = 2 × 4 + 2 = 10. Butane is C₄H₁₀. (Mnemonic: meth, eth, prop, but.)
questions.tip: Use the general formula rather than guessing.

questions.q: As hydrocarbon chain length increases, which property decreases?
ms: Longer chains have higher boiling points and viscosity but are LESS flammable.
questions.tip: Short chains: low bp, runny, very flammable - better fuels.

questions.q: What is the test for an alkene?
ms: Alkenes have a C=C double bond, which reacts with bromine, so orange bromine water becomes colourless. Alkanes do not react.
questions.tip: Say 'colourless', NOT 'clear'. Clear means see-through and loses the mark.

questions.q: Decane, C₁₀H₂₂, is cracked to form octane, C₈H₁₈, and one other product. What is the other product?
ms: C: 10 − 8 = 2. H: 22 − 18 = 4. The other product is C₂H₄, ethene (an alkene).
questions.tip: Balance carbons and hydrogens separately. Cracking always produces at least one alkene.

questions.q:
Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation.
State where in the column the fractions with the lowest boiling points are collected, and why.
questions.answer: At the top. The column is cooler at the top, and these fractions have low boiling points so they only condense at low temperatures (they stay as gases until near the top).
ms: At the top (1 mark)
Column is cooler at top / they condense at lower temperatures (1 mark)
questions.tip: The column is hot at the bottom and cool at the top.

questions.q: Describe how crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.
questions.answer: Crude oil is heated until most of it evaporates (vaporises). The vapour enters the fractionating column, which has a temperature gradient: hot at the bottom, cooler at the top. The vapour rises. Hydrocarbons condense when they reach the level where the temperature is below their boiling point. Fractions are collected at different heights. Long-chain hydrocarbons have high boiling points and condense near the bottom (e.g. bitumen, fuel oil). Short chains have low boiling points and are collected near the top or leave as gases (e.g. petrol, LPG).
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: crude oil heated/vaporised | vapour fed into the column | temperature gradient: hot at bottom, cool at top | vapours rise | condense when they reach their boiling point | fractions collected at different levels | each fraction has molecules with similar numbers of carbon atoms | long chains/high bp near bottom | short chains/low bp at top as gases
questions.tip: Use 'evaporate' and 'condense' explicitly. Avoid saying 'the oil burns'.

questions.q:
Balance the equation for the complete combustion of ethane:
C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
questions.answer: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O
ms: Correct formulae with 4CO₂ and 6H₂O (1 mark)
7O₂ and 2C₂H₆ (allow C₂H₆ + 3½O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O) (1 mark)
questions.tip: If oxygen ends up as a half, double everything.

questions.q: Explain why cracking is carried out by oil companies.
questions.answer: There is more supply of long-chain hydrocarbons than demand, but more demand than supply for short-chain hydrocarbons (like petrol). Cracking breaks long chains into shorter, more useful alkanes for fuel. It also produces alkenes, which are used to make polymers and other chemicals.
ms: Supply of long chains exceeds demand / demand for short chains exceeds supply (1 mark)
Short chains are better fuels (more useful) (1 mark)
Alkenes produced to make polymers/chemicals (1 mark)
questions.tip: Data questions often give a supply vs demand table. Use the numbers to support your answer.

questions.q: Describe two ways of cracking hydrocarbons.
questions.answer: Catalytic cracking: heat to vaporise and pass over a hot catalyst (e.g. aluminium oxide/zeolite). Steam cracking: mix the vapour with steam at a very high temperature.
ms: Catalytic: vapour over hot catalyst (1 mark)
Steam: mixed with steam at very high temperature (1 mark)
questions.tip: Both methods vaporise the hydrocarbons first.

questions.q:
Write a balanced equation for cracking dodecane, C₁₂H₂₆, into hexane, C₆H₁₄, and propene, C₃H₆.
Explain why hexane is classed as saturated and propene as unsaturated.
questions.answer: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₆H₁₄ + 2C₃H₆. Hexane has only single C–C bonds (saturated). Propene has a C=C double bond (unsaturated).
ms: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₆H₁₄ + 2C₃H₆ (1 mark)
Hexane only single bonds (1 mark)
Propene contains a C=C double bond (1 mark)
questions.tip: Check atoms: C 12 = 6 + 6; H 26 = 14 + 12.

questions.q: What is a hydrocarbon? What are the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
questions.answer: A compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only. Carbon dioxide and water.
ms: Contains hydrogen and carbon ONLY (1 mark)
Carbon dioxide and water (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Only' is essential in the definition.

questions.q:
Pentane (C₅H₁₂) boils at 36 °C and decane (C₁₀H₂₂) boils at 174 °C.
Explain this difference.
questions.answer: Decane has longer molecules, so the intermolecular forces between them are stronger and need more energy to overcome.
ms: Decane has larger/longer molecules (1 mark)
Stronger intermolecular forces needing more energy to overcome (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not say that covalent bonds break when a hydrocarbon boils.

questions.q: Which gas test gives a 'squeaky pop'?
ms: Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is held at the mouth of the tube.
questions.tip: Lighted splint for hydrogen, GLOWING splint for oxygen.

questions.q: In chromatography a spot moves 3.6 cm and the solvent front moves 8.0 cm. What is the Rf value?
ms: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent = 3.6 ÷ 8.0 = 0.45
questions.tip: Rf is always less than 1. If you get more than 1 you divided the wrong way.

questions.q: A pure substance melts at 0 °C. A sample of it melts over the range −4 °C to −1 °C. What does this show?
options: The sample is impure; impurities lower and widen the melting range
ms: Pure substances melt at a sharp, specific temperature. Impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.
questions.tip: In chemistry, 'pure' means a single element or compound, not 'natural'.

questions.q: What is a formulation?
options: A substance made in a reversible reaction
A single compound with a fixed melting point
A mixture designed as a useful product, with components in measured quantities
ms: Formulations are mixtures made to a precise recipe, e.g. paints, medicines, fertilisers, alloys, fuels.
questions.tip: The phrase 'measured quantities' is what examiners look for.

questions.q: Describe the test for carbon dioxide and give the result.
questions.answer: Bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution). It turns milky/cloudy.
ms: Limewater (1 mark)
Turns milky/cloudy (1 mark)
questions.tip: Bubble THROUGH limewater; do not just 'add' it.

questions.q: Describe the test for oxygen and give the result.
questions.answer: Insert a glowing splint into the gas. It relights.
ms: Glowing splint (1 mark)
Relights (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Lit splint' for oxygen loses the mark.

questions.q: Describe how to use paper chromatography to find out whether a food colouring contains any of three known dyes, A, B and C.
questions.answer: Draw a start line in pencil about 1 cm from the bottom of the chromatography paper. Put small spots of the food colouring and of dyes A, B and C on the line, spaced apart. Place the paper in a beaker with solvent (e.g. water) below the pencil line. Put a lid on to stop the solvent evaporating. Leave until the solvent has nearly reached the top. Remove, mark the solvent front and let it dry. Compare: if a spot in the food colouring is at the same height (same Rf value) as a known dye, that dye is present. Calculate Rf = distance spot ÷ distance solvent.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: pencil start line (pencil does not dissolve/run) | small spots of colouring and known dyes on line | solvent level below the start line (so spots don't dissolve into it) | lid on beaker | leave until solvent near top | mark solvent front, dry paper | compare horizontal positions/heights | calculate Rf values and compare | same Rf in same solvent = same substance
questions.tip: Two reasons you MUST give: pencil line (ink would run) and solvent below the line.

questions.q: In a chromatogram, a pure substance gives one spot. Explain why a mixture separates into several spots.
questions.answer: Different substances have different solubilities in the solvent (mobile phase) and different attractions to the paper (stationary phase), so they move up the paper at different rates/distances.
ms: Different solubility in the solvent / mobile phase (1 mark)
Different attraction to the paper / stationary phase, so travel different distances (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the terms 'mobile phase' and 'stationary phase' for Higher.

questions.q:
A spot has an Rf value of 0.62 in a chromatogram where the solvent front moved 7.5 cm.
(a) Calculate how far the spot moved.
(b) Explain why the Rf value of a substance can be different in a different solvent.
