questions.answer: (a) 0.62 × 7.5 = 4.65 cm (4.7 cm) (b) The substance's solubility in the new solvent / its distribution between the mobile and stationary phases is different, so it moves a different proportion of the distance.
ms: (a) 4.65 cm (allow 4.7) (1 mark)
(b) Different solubility in different solvent / different balance between phases (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rf values are only comparable in the same solvent and conditions.

questions.q:
A student says 'orange juice is pure because nothing has been added to it'.
Explain why a chemist would disagree.
questions.answer: In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with anything else. Orange juice is a mixture of many substances (water, sugars, acids).
ms: Pure = single element or compound (1 mark)
Orange juice contains many substances / is a mixture (1 mark)
questions.tip: Contrast the everyday and the scientific meaning.

questions.q:
Three substances were tested. Results:
X: melts at 80 °C exactly
Y: melts between 75 °C and 79 °C
Z: chromatogram shows one spot in three different solvents
Which substances are likely to be pure? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: X is pure: it has a sharp, specific melting point. Y is impure: it melts over a range below the pure value. Z is likely pure: one spot in several solvents suggests a single substance.
ms: X pure - sharp/fixed melting point (1 mark)
Y impure - melts over a range / lower (1 mark)
Z pure - single spot in different solvents (1 mark)
questions.tip: One spot in one solvent is weaker evidence; several solvents is stronger.

questions.q: What are the approximate percentages of nitrogen and oxygen in today's atmosphere?
ms: Nitrogen about 4/5 (78%), oxygen about 1/5 (21%), with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
questions.tip: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.

questions.q: How did oxygen levels in the atmosphere increase?
options: Algae and plants produced it by photosynthesis
Oxygen was released from the oceans as they cooled
ms: Algae (about 2.7 billion years ago) and later plants photosynthesised: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
questions.tip: Learn the photosynthesis equation as part of this topic.

questions.q: Which pollutant is produced when fuels burn with too little oxygen?
ms: Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide (and soot/carbon particulates).
questions.tip: Sulfur dioxide comes from sulfur impurities; nitrogen oxides from high temperatures in engines.

questions.q: Why is carbon monoxide toxic?
options: It combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells, reducing the oxygen carried
ms: CO binds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen. It is colourless and odourless, so hard to detect.
questions.tip: Say 'reduces oxygen carried by the blood', not just 'stops breathing'.

questions.q: Explain how the greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm.
questions.answer: Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the Earth's surface. The Earth emits longer-wavelength (infrared) radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back to Earth, keeping it warm.
ms: Short wavelength radiation from Sun passes through atmosphere (1 mark)
Earth emits longer wavelength / infrared radiation (1 mark)
Greenhouse gases absorb (and re-emit) it, trapping heat (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do NOT mention the ozone layer or 'heat bouncing off'.

questions.q: Name two greenhouse gases and give one human activity that increases each.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide: burning fossil fuels / deforestation. Methane: cattle farming / rice fields / landfill.
ms: Carbon dioxide with valid activity (1 mark)
Methane with valid activity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Water vapour is a greenhouse gas but not usually linked to a human activity in mark schemes.

questions.q: Describe how the Earth's early atmosphere is thought to have changed to form today's atmosphere.
questions.answer: Early atmosphere (first billion years): intense volcanic activity released gases forming an atmosphere mainly of carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, like Mars/Venus today; also water vapour, nitrogen, and small amounts of methane and ammonia. As Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form oceans. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and formed carbonate precipitates (sediments). Algae and plants evolved and photosynthesised, using carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen. Carbon was locked up in sedimentary rocks (limestone) and fossil fuels (coal, crude oil, natural gas). Nitrogen built up to about 78%, oxygen to about 21%, carbon dioxide fell to about 0.04%.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: volcanoes released gases | early atmosphere mainly carbon dioxide, little/no oxygen | water vapour condensed to form oceans as Earth cooled | CO₂ dissolved in oceans, forming carbonate precipitates | algae/plants photosynthesised: CO₂ used, O₂ released | carbon locked in sedimentary rocks (limestone) and fossil fuels | nitrogen released by volcanoes built up | today: ~78% N₂, ~21% O₂, ~0.04% CO₂
questions.tip: Level 3 explains the mechanisms that REMOVED CO₂ and ADDED O₂, in time order.

questions.q: Give three possible effects of global climate change.
questions.answer: Sea level rise (flooding, coastal erosion); more frequent/severe storms; changes in rainfall amount and distribution; changes to food production capacity; changes to the distribution of wildlife species; temperature and water stress for humans and wildlife.
ms: Any three valid effects, 1 mark each (3 marks)
questions.tip: Be specific: 'sea levels rise causing flooding' beats 'the weather changes'.

questions.q: Give two ways of reducing the carbon footprint of a product or activity, and one problem with reducing it.
questions.answer: Ways: renewable energy / energy conservation / carbon capture and storage / carbon taxes / carbon off-setting (planting trees). Problems: scientific disagreement, economic cost, lack of public information, reluctance to change lifestyle, lack of international agreement.
ms: Two valid ways (1 mark)
One valid problem (1 mark)
questions.tip: Carbon footprint = total amount of CO₂ and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle.

questions.q: Explain how sulfur dioxide is formed when fuels burn and describe two problems it causes.
questions.answer: Some fossil fuels (e.g. coal) contain sulfur. When the fuel burns, the sulfur is oxidised to sulfur dioxide. It dissolves in rain to form acid rain (damaging buildings, trees and aquatic life) and causes respiratory problems.
ms: Sulfur impurities in fuel react with oxygen (1 mark)
Acid rain (1 mark)
Respiratory problems (1 mark)
questions.tip: SO₂ comes from the fuel; nitrogen oxides come from the air reacting at high temperature.

questions.q: Explain why it is difficult to model the effects of climate change accurately and why scientists still trust the conclusions.
questions.answer: The climate is a complex system with many factors (oceans, clouds, feedbacks), so models are simplified and predictions are uncertain. Data from the past is limited. Scientists trust conclusions because many independent studies/models agree, results are peer reviewed, and there is a strong correlation between rising CO₂ and rising global temperature.
ms: Complex system / many variables, so models are simplified (1 mark)
Speculation/uncertainty or limited past data (1 mark)
Peer review / many independent sources agree (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Peer review' is a key phrase in the spec for this topic.

questions.q: Explain how carbon particulates (soot) affect health and the environment.
questions.answer: They cause respiratory problems (lung damage) and global dimming (they reflect sunlight, reducing light reaching the surface).
ms: Respiratory problems (1 mark)
Global dimming (1 mark)
questions.tip: Global dimming is linked to particulates, not CO₂.

questions.q: What is potable water?
options: Pure water with nothing dissolved in it
Water that is safe to drink
ms: Potable water is safe to drink. It contains low levels of dissolved salts and microbes, so it is not chemically pure.
questions.tip: Potable ≠ pure. This is tested often.

questions.q: Which steps are used to treat fresh water in the UK to make it potable?
ms: UK fresh water from rivers/reservoirs is passed through filter beds, then sterilised with chlorine, ozone or UV light.
questions.tip: Desalination (distillation/reverse osmosis) is used for sea water, mainly in dry countries.

questions.q: What is phytomining?
options: Using bacteria to extract metals from low-grade ores
Growing plants that absorb metal compounds, then burning them to give ash containing the metal compounds
Mining metals from plants grown in sea water
Using electrolysis to extract metals from plants
ms: Plants absorb metal compounds from the soil; they are harvested and burned; the ash contains metal compounds from which the metal is extracted.
questions.tip: Bioleaching uses BACTERIA; phytomining uses PLANTS.

questions.q: What is the purpose of sterilising water with chlorine?
ms: Chlorine, ozone or UV light kill harmful microorganisms.
questions.tip: Filtration removes solids; sterilising kills microbes.

questions.q: What is meant by sustainable development? Give one example of how chemists help.
questions.answer: Using resources to meet the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Example: developing processes that use less energy, renewable resources, recycling, catalysts.
ms: Correct definition including future generations (1 mark)
Valid example (1 mark)
questions.tip: The phrase 'future generations' is key.

questions.q: Describe how you would analyse and purify a sample of salty water by distillation, and how you would show that the water collected is pure.
questions.answer: Test pH with universal indicator or a pH meter. To find dissolved solids mass, evaporate a known volume in a weighed evaporating basin and reweigh. Distil: heat the salty water in a flask; water boils, vapour passes into a condenser cooled by cold water; it condenses and is collected in a beaker. Salt stays in the flask. Test purity: check the boiling point is 100 °C; pH 7; evaporate a sample and see no residue remains.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): detailed, coherent answer covering the points below in a logical sequence, with correct scientific terms throughout.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): most key points given with some linking/explanation, but some steps missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): a few simple relevant statements, not linked, little use of scientific terms.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: test pH (universal indicator / pH meter) | measure dissolved solids by evaporating and weighing residue | heat salty water in flask (with anti-bumping granules) | water evaporates/boils | vapour cooled in condenser | condenses and is collected | salt left behind | pure water boils at exactly 100 °C | no residue on evaporation; pH 7
questions.tip: Describe the condenser with cold water. Use 'evaporate' and 'condense' accurately.

questions.q: Describe the stages in treating sewage (waste water).
questions.answer: Screening and grit removal; sedimentation to give sewage sludge and effluent; anaerobic digestion of sludge; aerobic biological treatment of effluent.
ms: Screening/grit removal (1 mark)
Sedimentation into sludge and effluent (1 mark)
Anaerobic digestion of sludge AND aerobic treatment of effluent (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not mix up which part is anaerobic (sludge) and which is aerobic (effluent).

questions.q: Copper-rich ores are running out. Describe how phytomining and bioleaching can be used to extract copper from low-grade ores, and give one advantage and one disadvantage.
questions.answer: Phytomining: plants grow on low-grade ore, absorb copper compounds, are harvested and burned; ash contains copper compounds. Bioleaching: bacteria produce leachate solutions containing copper compounds. Copper is then obtained by displacement with scrap iron or by electrolysis. Advantage: avoids digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock / uses low-grade ores. Disadvantage: very slow.
ms: Phytomining: plants absorb copper compounds, burned to ash (1 mark)
Bioleaching: bacteria produce leachate containing copper compounds (1 mark)
Copper extracted by displacement (scrap iron) or electrolysis (1 mark)
Advantage AND disadvantage (e.g. less mining waste / slow) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Higher tier only. Always finish with how the metal is obtained from the compound.

questions.q:
A life cycle assessment (LCA) compares plastic and paper shopping bags.
Name the four stages of an LCA and give one reason why LCAs can be biased.
questions.answer: Extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation during its lifetime; disposal at end of life (including transport/distribution at each stage). Bias: some values (e.g. pollutant effects) are value judgements, and selective/abbreviated LCAs can be used to support claims for advertising.
ms: Extracting/processing raw materials (1 mark)
Manufacturing and packaging (1 mark)
Use AND disposal (1 mark)
Valid reason for bias (value judgements / selective use for advertising) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Energy, water, resources and waste are quantified easily; pollution effects are not.

questions.q: Explain why recycling metals such as aluminium is better than extracting new metal.
questions.answer: Recycling uses less energy than extraction (electrolysis needs lots of energy). It conserves finite ores and reduces waste going to landfill / mining damage.
ms: Uses less energy (1 mark)
Conserves finite resources / less waste or environmental damage (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give a specific reason rather than 'better for the environment'.

questions.q: Explain why desalination of sea water is used in some countries but not widely in the UK.
questions.answer: Desalination (distillation or reverse osmosis using membranes) requires large amounts of energy, so it is expensive. The UK has plenty of fresh water from rain, rivers and reservoirs, which only needs filtering and sterilising. Dry countries with little fresh water need it.
ms: Desalination uses large amounts of energy / is expensive (1 mark)
UK has enough fresh water (rainfall, rivers, reservoirs/aquifers) (1 mark)
Countries with limited fresh water need it (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the two methods: distillation and reverse osmosis.

questions.q: Distinguish between finite and renewable resources, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: Finite resources will run out / cannot be replaced quickly (e.g. crude oil, metal ores). Renewable resources can be replaced as fast as they are used (e.g. timber, cotton, wool).
ms: Finite with example (1 mark)
Renewable with example (1 mark)
questions.tip: Fossil fuels are the classic finite example.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg trolley moves at 3.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
ms: Ek = ½mv² = 0.5 × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J. 18 J forgets the ½; 6.0 J forgets to square v.
questions.tip: Square the speed before multiplying, and don't drop the ½.

questions.q: A 1200 g ball is lifted through a height of 2.5 m. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. What is the increase in its gravitational potential energy store?
ms: Ep = mgh = 1.2 kg × 9.8 × 2.5 = 29.4 J. 29 400 J comes from using 1200 instead of 1.2 kg.
questions.tip: Mass must be in kg: divide grams by 1000.

questions.q: A car of mass 900 kg travels at 54 km/h. Calculate the kinetic energy of the car. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
ms: Converts speed: 54 ÷ 3.6 = 15 m/s (1 mark)
Substitutes into Ek = ½mv²: 0.5 × 900 × 15² (1 mark)
Answer 101 000 J to 3 s.f. (allow 1.01 × 10⁵ J) (1 mark). Using 54 m/s (1 312 200 J) scores max 1 for substitution method only.
questions.tip: km/h to m/s: divide by 3.6. Examiners love hiding this conversion.

questions.q:
A ball of mass 0.15 kg is dropped from a height of 3.2 m. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg.
(a) Assuming no air resistance, calculate the speed of the ball just before it hits the ground. (3 marks)
(b) The measured speed was lower than your answer. Explain why. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
(a) Ep = 0.15 × 9.8 × 3.2 = 4.704 J; Ek = Ep so v = √(2 × 4.704 ÷ 0.15) = 7.92 m/s (7.9 m/s)
(b) Some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the ball and surroundings by work done against air resistance, so less is in the kinetic store.
ms: (a) Ep = mgh = 4.704 J (1 mark)
(a) Sets Ek = Ep and rearranges: v² = 2Ep/m or v = √(2gh) (1 mark)
(a) v = 7.9 m/s (allow 7.92 m/s) (1 mark)
(b) Work done against air resistance / friction transfers energy to thermal stores of surroundings (dissipated), so less energy in kinetic store (1 mark)
questions.tip: The mass cancels: v = √(2gh). Show the energy equation step though, it carries a method mark.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Describe the changes in energy stores from the moment it leaves the hand to when it reaches its highest point. Ignore air resistance.
questions.answer: Energy in the kinetic store decreases and energy in the gravitational potential store increases by the same amount; at the highest point the kinetic store is zero.
ms: Kinetic energy store decreases (1 mark)
Gravitational potential energy store increases (by the same amount) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the stores properly: 'kinetic energy store', 'gravitational potential energy store'. 'Movement energy' gets nothing.

questions.q: A cyclist and bicycle have a total mass of 80 kg and a kinetic energy of 4.0 kJ. Calculate the speed of the cyclist.
ms: Converts 4.0 kJ = 4000 J (1 mark)
Rearranges: v² = 2Ek/m (1 mark)
v = 10 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rearranging Ek = ½mv² is a common grade 8 discriminator: multiply by 2, divide by m, then square root.

questions.q: An object's mass is halved and its speed is doubled. What happens to its kinetic energy?
options: It increases by a factor of 4
ms: Ek = ½mv²: halving m gives ×½, doubling v gives ×4, so overall ×2.
questions.tip: Speed is squared, mass isn't. Deal with each factor separately.

questions.q: What is meant by a closed system? State what happens to the total energy in a closed system.
questions.answer: A system where no energy enters or leaves (no net change in energy); the total energy stays constant, it is only transferred between stores.
ms: No energy transferred in or out of the system (1 mark)
Total energy remains constant / is conserved (1 mark). Do not accept 'energy is used up'.
questions.tip: Energy is never 'used up' or 'lost', it is transferred or dissipated.

questions.q:
A toy launcher fires a 0.50 kg ball vertically upwards at 12 m/s. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg.
Calculate the maximum height the ball could reach. Give your answer to 2 significant figures and state one assumption you made.
questions.answer: Ek = 0.5 × 0.50 × 12² = 36 J; h = Ep ÷ (mg) = 36 ÷ (0.50 × 9.8) = 7.35 m = 7.3 m (2 s.f.). Assumption: no air resistance / all kinetic energy is transferred to the gravitational potential store.
ms: Ek = 36 J (1 mark)
Rearranges Ep = mgh: h = Ep/(mg) (1 mark)
h = 7.3 m to 2 s.f. (1 mark). 7.35 m or 7.346 m without rounding does not get this mark.
Assumption: no energy dissipated / no air resistance (1 mark)
questions.tip: Read the sig fig instruction: 7.346... m to 2 s.f. is 7.3 m. Keep full values in your calculator until the last step.

questions.q: What is the specific heat capacity of a substance?
options: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of the substance
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C
The energy needed to raise the temperature of the substance by 1 °C
The total kinetic energy of the particles in 1 kg of the substance
ms: SHC is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 °C. Option A is specific latent heat.
questions.tip: Both '1 kg' and '1 °C' are needed for the mark.

questions.q: 2.0 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 65 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the water.
ms: Temperature change Δθ = 45 °C (1 mark)
Substitution: 2.0 × 4200 × 45 (1 mark)
378 000 J (allow 3.78 × 10⁵ J or 378 kJ) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the temperature CHANGE, not the final temperature.

questions.q: A heater transfers 63 kJ of energy to 0.75 kg of water at 18 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the final temperature of the water.
ms: Converts 63 kJ = 63 000 J (1 mark)
Rearranges: Δθ = ΔE/(mc) (1 mark)
Δθ = 20 °C (1 mark)
Final temperature 38 °C (1 mark)
questions.tip: The equation gives a change. If the question asks for final temperature, add it to the start temperature.

questions.q:
In the specific heat capacity required practical, a student heats a 1.0 kg aluminium block with a 50 W heater for 10 minutes. The temperature rises by 30 °C.
(a) Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium from these results. (3 marks)
(b) The accepted value is 900 J/kg °C. Explain why the student's value is higher. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
(a) E = Pt = 50 × 600 = 30 000 J; c = E ÷ (mΔθ) = 30 000 ÷ (1.0 × 30) = 1000 J/kg °C
(b) Some energy from the heater is transferred to the surroundings rather than the block, so the measured temperature rise is smaller than it should be (the energy used in the calculation is more than the energy that actually heated the block).
ms: (a) E = Pt = 30 000 J, with t = 600 s (1 mark)
(a) Rearranges c = ΔE/(mΔθ) (1 mark)
(a) 1000 J/kg °C (1 mark)
(b) Energy lost/dissipated to surroundings (not all heats block), so temperature rise is lower than expected (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two equations chained: E = Pt then ΔE = mcΔθ. Convert minutes to seconds.

questions.q: Describe a method to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block using an electric immersion heater. Include how you would use your measurements to calculate the specific heat capacity.
questions.answer: Measure mass of block on balance; insert heater and thermometer (with oil/water in hole); wrap in insulation; connect heater to power supply with joulemeter (or ammeter and voltmeter); record start temperature; switch on and time for 10 minutes; record energy (or V, I, t so E = VIt) and temperature every minute; plot temperature against energy, gradient = 1/(mc); or c = E/(mΔθ).
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A clear, logically ordered method that would produce valid results, including how energy is measured, how Δθ is found and how c is calculated (equation or graph), with a step to reduce energy losses.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): A method with most key steps (mass, energy measurement, temperature change) but some steps missing or out of order; may mention c = E/mΔθ without full detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements about some relevant steps, e.g. heat the block and measure the temperature.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: measure mass with balance; place heater and thermometer in holes; drop of water/oil in thermometer hole for good thermal contact; insulate block; joulemeter reading, or ammeter + voltmeter + stopwatch with E = VIt; record initial temperature; heat for fixed time (e.g. 10 min); record temperature at regular intervals; calculate Δθ; c = ΔE/(mΔθ); plot θ against E, gradient = 1/(mc); safety: hot block, don't touch heater.
questions.tip: Say HOW energy is measured (joulemeter or E = VIt). 'Measure the energy' on its own is weak.

questions.q: 4.62 kJ of energy raises the temperature of a 0.50 kg metal block by 24 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal?
ms: c = ΔE/(mΔθ) = 4620 ÷ (0.50 × 24) = 385 J/kg °C. 0.385 forgets to convert kJ to J.
questions.tip: Convert kJ to J before you divide.

questions.q: Give two ways to improve the accuracy of the specific heat capacity practical.
questions.answer: Insulate the block (reduce energy loss to surroundings); put a little water/oil in the thermometer hole for better thermal contact (also: record the highest temperature reached after switching off).
ms: Insulate the block / lid on top (1 mark)
Water or oil in the thermometer hole for good thermal contact / record maximum temperature after heater is switched off / use a digital thermometer with higher resolution (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Repeat it' improves reliability (repeatability), not accuracy. It won't get the mark here.

questions.q: Which of these is equal to 1 watt?
ms: Power is the rate of energy transfer: 1 W = 1 J/s. 1 C/s is 1 ampere.
questions.tip: P = E/t, so power units are J/s.

questions.q: A motor is supplied with 2.4 kJ of energy. 600 J is wasted. What is the efficiency of the motor?
ms: Useful = 2400 − 600 = 1800 J; efficiency = 1800 ÷ 2400 = 0.75. 0.25 uses the wasted energy.
questions.tip: Efficiency uses USEFUL output, never wasted energy. Efficiency can't be above 1 (100%).

questions.q: A crane lifts a 600 kg load through a height of 15 m in 25 s. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the useful power output of the crane.
ms: Ep = mgh = 88 200 J (1 mark)
3528 W (allow 3500 W or 3.53 kW) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Work done lifting = gain in gravitational potential energy. Then divide by time.

questions.q: A lift motor has an input power of 2.0 kW and an efficiency of 0.60. It raises a 300 kg load through 12 m. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the time taken.
ms: Useful power output = 0.60 × 2000 = 1200 W (1 mark)
Ep = mgh = 35 280 J (1 mark)
Rearranges P = E/t to t = E/P (1 mark)
t = 29.4 s (allow 29 s) (1 mark). Using 2000 W gives 17.6 s: max 2 marks.
questions.tip: Multi-step: find useful power with the efficiency first. Using input power is the classic error.

questions.q: Give two ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers in a machine or a house.
questions.answer: Lubricate moving parts to reduce friction; use thermal insulation (e.g. loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, double glazing).
ms: Lubrication to reduce friction (1 mark)
Thermal insulation / thicker walls / materials with low thermal conductivity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link each method to what it reduces (friction or heating of surroundings).

questions.q: A student wants to compare how well different materials insulate a beaker of hot water. Describe a method the student could use. Include the variables that should be controlled.
questions.answer: Place a small beaker inside a larger beaker, surround with the insulating material, pour in a fixed volume of hot water, put on a lid, record temperature with a thermometer every 3 minutes for 15-20 minutes; repeat for each material with the same starting temperature and volume; compare temperature drop (or cooling rate); control: volume of water, starting temperature, thickness/mass of material, time, room temperature, size of beaker.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, logically sequenced method allowing valid comparison, clearly stating how temperature change is measured over time and at least two control variables, with a clear way to compare results.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Method with key steps (hot water, insulation, temperature measured over time) and at least one control variable; some detail missing.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic relevant points, e.g. wrap beaker in material and measure temperature.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: beaker inside larger beaker; insulating material packed between; same volume of hot water (e.g. measuring cylinder 80 cm³) from kettle; lid; thermometer; start stopwatch; record temperature every 3 min for e.g. 15 min; repeat for different materials and a control with no insulation; compare temperature drop over time / plot cooling curves; smaller drop = better insulator; controls: volume, initial temperature, thickness of material, same beakers, room temperature; safety: hot water.
questions.tip: Not a Trilogy required practical (it is separate Physics only), but it tests thermal insulation and method skills. Name control variables specifically: 'same volume of water' not 'keep it fair'.

questions.q: Explain how the thickness and thermal conductivity of a house's walls affect its rate of cooling.
questions.answer: Higher thermal conductivity means a higher rate of energy transfer by conduction through the wall; thicker walls mean a lower rate of energy transfer; so thick walls of low thermal conductivity reduce the rate of cooling.
ms: Higher thermal conductivity → higher rate of energy transfer (by conduction) (1 mark)
Thicker walls → lower rate of energy transfer (1 mark)
So the house cools more slowly with thick, low-conductivity walls (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the phrase 'rate of energy transfer'. 'Keeps the heat in' is too vague.

questions.q: An electric motor has an efficiency of 0.85. Its useful power output is 340 W. What is its total power input?
ms: Input = useful output ÷ efficiency = 340 ÷ 0.85 = 400 W. 289 W multiplies instead of dividing.
questions.tip: Input power must be bigger than output power: sense-check your answer.

questions.q: A 1.5 kW motor runs for 90 s. Calculate the energy transferred by the motor in kJ.
ms: E = Pt / substitution 1500 × 90 (1 mark)
Converts to 135 kJ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Unit conversion marks are easy to lose. Check what unit the question asks for.

questions.q: Which energy resource is renewable?
ms: Geothermal energy can be replenished as it is used. Coal, gas and nuclear fuel will run out.
questions.tip: Nuclear is NOT renewable even though it doesn't release CO₂ when running.

questions.q: Which energy resource is reliable, releases no carbon dioxide when generating electricity, but produces radioactive waste?
ms: Nuclear power stations are reliable and emit no CO₂ when running, but produce long-lived radioactive waste.
questions.tip: Learn one advantage and one disadvantage for every resource.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a renewable and a non-renewable energy resource.
questions.answer: A renewable resource is replenished as it is used (won't run out); a non-renewable resource will run out because it is used faster than it can be replaced.
ms: Renewable: replenished as it is used / will not run out (1 mark)
Non-renewable: will run out / cannot be replaced (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Can be reused' is wrong. Renewable means it is replenished, not recycled.

questions.q: Give three main uses of energy resources and name one resource commonly used for each.
questions.answer: Transport (petrol/diesel); electricity generation (gas, wind, nuclear etc.); heating (natural gas).
ms: Transport with suitable fuel, e.g. petrol, diesel, biofuel (1 mark)
Electricity generation with suitable resource (1 mark)
Heating with suitable resource, e.g. gas, electricity, wood (1 mark)
questions.tip: The three uses on the spec are transport, electricity generation and heating.

questions.q: A town is choosing between a wind farm and a gas-fired power station. Evaluate the two options.
questions.answer: Wind: renewable, no CO₂ released when running, cheap to run, but unreliable (no wind, no output), visual/noise impact, needs a lot of land. Gas: reliable and can be switched on quickly to meet demand, but non-renewable and releases CO₂ (global warming). Judgement: e.g. wind farm better long term with gas as backup.
ms: Advantage of wind, e.g. renewable / no CO₂ when running (1 mark)
Disadvantage of wind, e.g. unreliable / visual pollution (1 mark)
Advantage and disadvantage of gas, e.g. reliable, quick start-up but releases CO₂ / non-renewable (1 mark)
Reasoned conclusion consistent with points made (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Evaluate' needs a conclusion. Without one you cap at 3 out of 4.

questions.q:
Data for a country's electricity generation:
Resource | Year 2010 | Year 2025
Coal | 28% | 1%
Gas | 46% | 32%
Nuclear | 16% | 13%
Wind | 3% | 30%
Solar | 0% | 5%
Other | 7% | 19%
Describe the trends and explain the possible reasons for them, including any problems the country may face.
questions.answer: Coal has almost been eliminated and gas reduced, while wind and solar have grown greatly. Reasons: concern about CO₂ emissions and climate change, government targets, falling cost of renewables, fossil fuels running out. Problems: wind and solar are unreliable so backup (gas) still needed; cost of building new capacity; public opposition (visual impact); nuclear decommissioning.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Uses data accurately to describe at least two trends AND gives detailed explanations of reasons AND identifies problems such as reliability, with logical links.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Describes trends with some use of data and gives some reasons or problems.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. coal went down and wind went up.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: coal down from 28% to 1%; gas down 46% to 32%; wind up tenfold 3% to 30%; solar 0% to 5%; total fossil fuels from 74% to 33%; reasons: carbon dioxide causes global warming, acid rain from coal (sulfur dioxide), political pressure/legal targets, cheaper renewable technology, fossil fuels non-renewable; problems: renewables weather dependent so unreliable, need reliable backup like gas, storage needed, high setup costs, visual pollution, ability to meet peak demand.
questions.tip: Quote the numbers. 'Wind increased from 3% to 30%' scores; 'wind went up a lot' is weaker.

questions.q: Suggest two reasons why many countries still use fossil fuels even though they release carbon dioxide.
questions.answer: Fossil fuels are reliable and can meet demand at any time; existing power stations and infrastructure already exist / relatively cheap to extract; renewable alternatives can be expensive to set up.
ms: Reliable / can meet sudden demand (1 mark)
Cheap / existing infrastructure / renewables expensive or unreliable (1 mark)
questions.tip: Think reliability, cost, and politics.

questions.q: A current of 0.50 A flows for 2.0 minutes. How much charge flows?
ms: Q = It = 0.50 × 120 s = 60 C. 1.0 C uses minutes instead of seconds.
questions.tip: Time in seconds, always.

questions.q: A resistor has a potential difference of 6.0 V across it and a current of 250 mA through it. What is its resistance?
ms: R = V/I = 6.0 ÷ 0.250 = 24 Ω. 0.024 Ω comes from not converting mA to A.
questions.tip: mA to A: divide by 1000.

questions.q: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 4.0 Ω resistor and an 8.0 Ω resistor. Calculate the current in the circuit and the potential difference across the 8.0 Ω resistor.
ms: Total resistance = 4.0 + 8.0 = 12 Ω (1 mark)
I = V/R = 1.0 A (1 mark)
V = 8.0 V (1 mark)
questions.tip: In series, resistances add and the current is the same everywhere.

questions.q:
A 6.0 V supply is connected to a 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor in parallel.
(a) Calculate the total current from the supply. (3 marks)
(b) Explain why the total resistance is less than 3.0 Ω. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
(a) I₁ = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 A; I₂ = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A; total = 3.0 A
(b) Adding a resistor in parallel gives the charge another path, so the total current increases for the same pd (total R = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 Ω).
ms: (a) pd across each branch = 6.0 V (1 mark)
(a) Branch currents 2.0 A and 1.0 A (1 mark)
(a) Total current 3.0 A (1 mark)
(b) Extra path for current / total current increases for same pd so total resistance decreases (1 mark)
questions.tip: In parallel, each branch gets the full supply pd. Branch currents add to give the total.

questions.q: A second resistor is connected in parallel with a resistor in a circuit. What happens to the total resistance of the circuit?
ms: Adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance because there are more paths for current.
questions.tip: Series: R goes up. Parallel: R goes down (less than the smallest resistor).

questions.q: 360 C of charge flows through a lamp and 4.32 kJ of energy is transferred. What is the potential difference across the lamp?
ms: V = E/Q = 4320 ÷ 360 = 12 V. 0.012 V forgets to convert kJ.
questions.tip: E = QV: pd is energy transferred per coulomb.

questions.q:
(a) What is electric current? (1 mark)
(b) State two things needed for a current to flow in a circuit. (1 mark)
questions.answer: (a) Rate of flow of electrical charge. (b) A closed circuit and a source of potential difference.
ms: (a) Rate of flow of (electrical) charge (1 mark)
(b) Closed (complete) circuit AND source of potential difference, e.g. cell (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Flow of electrons' alone isn't enough, you need 'rate of flow of charge'.

questions.q: A 9.0 V battery is connected across a 2.2 kΩ resistor. Calculate the current in milliamps. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
ms: Converts 2.2 kΩ = 2200 Ω (1 mark)
4.09 mA (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two conversions: kΩ into Ω, then A into mA (×1000).

questions.q: In a series circuit with two lamps, the supply pd is 9.0 V. The pd across lamp A is 5.5 V. Calculate the pd across lamp B and state the rule you used.
questions.answer: 9.0 − 5.5 = 3.5 V. In series, the total pd of the supply is shared between the components.
ms: 3.5 V (1 mark)
Supply pd is shared / pds add up to supply pd in series (1 mark)
questions.tip: Series: pd shared, current same. Parallel: pd same, current shared.

questions.q: What happens to the resistance of a thermistor as its temperature increases?
ms: Thermistor (NTC): resistance decreases as temperature increases.
questions.tip: Thermistor: hot = low resistance. LDR: bright = low resistance.

questions.q: Which component has a very high resistance when current flows in the reverse direction?
ms: A diode only lets current flow in one direction; its reverse resistance is very high.
questions.tip: Learn the shape of each I-V graph.

questions.q: Describe and explain the shape of the current-potential difference graph for a filament lamp.
questions.answer: The graph is an S-shaped curve through the origin (symmetrical for negative values); the gradient decreases as pd increases, so resistance increases; this is because the filament gets hotter, so ions vibrate more and electrons collide more.
ms: Curve through origin, gradient decreasing / gets flatter at higher pd (1 mark)
Resistance increases as current/pd increases (1 mark)
Because temperature of filament increases (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link shape → resistance → temperature. That chain is the 3 marks.

questions.q:
In the resistance required practical, a student measures the resistance of different lengths of wire.
Length (cm) | Resistance (Ω)
20 | 1.6
40 | 3.2
60 | 4.9
80 | 6.4
100 | 8.0
(a) Identify the anomalous result. (1 mark)
(b) Describe the relationship. (1 mark)
(c) Predict the resistance of a 70 cm length. (1 mark)
questions.answer: (a) 60 cm (4.9 Ω; should be 4.8 Ω) (b) Resistance is directly proportional to length (c) 5.6 Ω
ms: (a) 60 cm / 4.9 Ω (1 mark)
(b) Directly proportional (allow 'as length doubles, resistance doubles'); 'positive correlation' alone is insufficient (1 mark)
(c) 5.6 Ω (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Directly proportional' needs a straight line through the origin. Check by doubling.

questions.q: Describe a method to investigate the current-potential difference characteristic of a filament lamp. You should include a description of the circuit.
questions.answer: Lamp in series with ammeter and variable resistor (or variable supply); voltmeter in parallel with lamp; vary pd using variable resistor; record current and pd for range of values; reverse supply connections and repeat for negative values; plot I against V.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Full, correct circuit description and a logical method covering varying pd, measuring both I and V, reversing connections for negative values and plotting the graph.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Correct circuit with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel, and a method of changing pd and recording readings; may miss reversing or graph.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Some relevant points, e.g. use an ammeter and voltmeter.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: circuit: supply, variable resistor, ammeter in series with lamp, voltmeter in parallel across lamp; adjust variable resistor to change pd; record ammeter and voltmeter readings for at least 5 values; reverse connections to get negative values; repeat and calculate mean; plot graph of current (y) against potential difference (x); curve shows resistance increases with temperature.
questions.tip: Voltmeter in PARALLEL, ammeter in SERIES. Getting that wrong caps the answer.

questions.q: In the resistance of a wire practical, the student uses a low current and switches off between readings. Explain why.
questions.answer: A large current would heat the wire; an increase in temperature increases resistance, so the results would not be valid (resistance would change for a reason other than length).
ms: Current heats the wire / temperature increases (1 mark)
Resistance increases with temperature, so it would affect results / temperature must be controlled (1 mark)
questions.tip: Temperature is a control variable in this practical.

questions.q: A filament lamp draws 1.0 A at 3.0 V and 2.0 A at 12 V. Which statement is correct?
options: Its resistance is 6.0 Ω at 12 V, higher than at 3.0 V
Its resistance is 3.0 Ω at 12 V
Its resistance is 0.33 Ω at 3.0 V
ms: R = V/I: 3.0/1.0 = 3.0 Ω; 12/2.0 = 6.0 Ω. Resistance increased, so it is not ohmic.
questions.tip: Calculate R at each point. Don't read resistance as the gradient.

questions.q: Give one use of a thermistor and one use of a light-dependent resistor (LDR).
questions.answer: Thermistor: thermostat / fire alarm / temperature sensor in a car engine. LDR: automatic street lights / light sensor in a security light.
ms: Valid thermistor use (1 mark)
Valid LDR use (1 mark)
questions.tip: Both are input sensors in circuits; match each to what it senses.

questions.q: A resistor has a current of 0.15 A when the pd across it is 1.8 V. What is its resistance?
questions.tip: V = IR. Triangle it if you need to, but write the rearranged equation.

questions.q: What is the potential difference and frequency of the UK mains supply?
ms: UK mains is alternating current at 230 V and 50 Hz.
questions.tip: Learn the two numbers: 230 V and 50 Hz.

questions.q: What colour is the insulation on the earth wire in a three-core cable?
ms: Live is brown, neutral is blue, earth is green and yellow.
questions.tip: Live brown, neutral blue, earth green/yellow.

questions.q: A 2.2 kW kettle is switched on for 3.0 minutes. How much energy is transferred?
ms: E = Pt = 2200 W × 180 s = 396 000 J. 6.6 J uses kW and minutes.
questions.tip: kW → W (×1000) and min → s (×60).

questions.q: A current of 3.0 A flows through a 40 Ω heating element for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
ms: P = I²R = 360 W (1 mark)
t = 300 s (1 mark)
questions.tip: P = I²R: square the current only.

questions.q: A 1.5 kW hair dryer is connected to the 230 V mains. Calculate the current. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
ms: Converts 1.5 kW to 1500 W (1 mark)
I = P/V = 6.52 A (1 mark)
6.5 A to 2 s.f. (1 mark)
questions.tip: You must recall 230 V if the question just says 'mains'.

questions.q: Explain why the National Grid uses step-up and step-down transformers.
questions.answer: Step-up transformers increase the pd for transmission, which reduces the current; lower current means less heating of the cables (P = I²R), so less energy is wasted and the system is more efficient. Step-down transformers reduce the pd to a safe level (230 V) for homes.
ms: Step-up transformers increase pd / decrease current (1 mark)
Lower current reduces heating/energy loss in cables (1 mark)
So transmission is more efficient (1 mark)
Step-down transformers decrease pd to safer level for consumers (1 mark)
questions.tip: The key link: high pd → low current → less heating. Don't say 'high voltage travels faster'.

questions.q: Explain why a person can get an electric shock from touching the live wire of a lamp, even when the lamp is switched off.
questions.answer: The live wire is still connected to the supply so it is at a high potential (230 V), even if the lamp is off; the person's body is at 0 V (earth potential); so there is a large potential difference across the body and a current flows through it.
ms: Live wire is at 230 V / high potential even when switched off (1 mark)
Body at 0 V / earth potential (1 mark)
Large potential difference causes current to flow through body (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'potential difference' between the live wire and the body, then 'current flows'.

questions.q: Describe the difference between direct current (dc) and alternating current (ac).
questions.answer: Dc flows in one direction only; ac repeatedly changes direction.
ms: Dc: one direction only (1 mark)
Ac: continually/repeatedly changes direction (1 mark)
questions.tip: Batteries give dc; mains gives ac.

questions.q: The current in a transmission cable is reduced from 400 A to 100 A. The cable's resistance stays the same. By what factor does the power wasted in the cable change?
ms: P = I²R. Current × 1/4, so power × (1/4)² = 1/16.
questions.tip: Square the factor because P depends on I².

questions.q: A block has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. What is its density?
questions.tip: Check the units match the numbers you divided.

questions.q: What is the internal energy of a substance?
options: The total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles
The energy needed to melt it
The total kinetic energy of its particles
ms: Internal energy = total kinetic energy + potential energy of all the particles in the system.
questions.tip: Kinetic AND potential. Missing either loses the mark.

questions.q: What is specific latent heat?
options: Energy to change the state of 1 kg of a substance with no change in temperature
Energy to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 °C
Energy released when 1 kg cools by 1 °C
Energy needed to boil any amount of water
ms: Specific latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg with no temperature change.
questions.tip: Latent heat = state change; SHC = temperature change.

questions.q: Calculate the energy needed to melt 250 g of ice at 0 °C. Give your answer in kJ. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 kJ/kg.
ms: m = 0.250 kg (1 mark)
83.5 kJ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Fusion = melting/freezing; vaporisation = boiling/condensing.

questions.q: A solid is heated steadily until it becomes a gas. The temperature-time graph rises, then is flat, rises, is flat again, then rises. Explain why the graph has flat sections.
questions.answer: The flat sections are where the substance is changing state (melting then boiling). Energy is still being supplied but it is used to break bonds/overcome forces between particles, increasing the potential energy store of the particles (internal energy increases), not their kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant.
ms: Flat sections = changing state (melting and boiling) (1 mark)
Energy used to break bonds / overcome forces of attraction between particles (1 mark)
Potential energy of particles increases / internal energy increases (1 mark)
Kinetic energy of particles does not increase so temperature constant (1 mark)
questions.tip: Temperature relates to particle kinetic energy. During a state change, it's potential energy that goes up.

questions.q:
A kettle contains 0.40 kg of water at 20 °C. It heats the water to 100 °C and then boils away 0.10 kg of the water.
Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg.
(a) Calculate the total energy transferred to the water. (4 marks)
(b) The kettle has a power of 2.0 kW. Calculate the minimum time needed. (1 mark)
ms: (a) E = mL = 226 000 J (1 mark)
(a) Total 360 400 J (allow 3.6 × 10⁵ J) (1 mark)
(b) t = E/P = 180 s (allow ecf from (a)) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two stages: mcΔθ for heating, mL for boiling. Use the boiled mass, not the total mass, for mL.

questions.q: Describe methods to find the density of (i) a regular-shaped block and (ii) an irregular-shaped stone.
questions.answer: (i) Measure mass on top-pan balance; measure length, width, height with ruler; V = l × w × h; ρ = m/V. (ii) Measure mass; fill displacement (eureka) can to spout, place stone in, collect displaced water in measuring cylinder; volume of water = volume of stone; ρ = m/V. (Or measuring cylinder: volume rise.)
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear, logically sequenced methods for both objects, including mass measurement, both volume methods (dimensions and displacement), and calculation of density.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Methods for both objects with some detail missing, or one method described fully.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple relevant points, e.g. measure mass and volume, use ρ = m/V.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: balance for mass (zeroed); ruler/vernier callipers for dimensions; V = length × width × height; eureka can filled to spout; lower stone gently on thread; collect displaced water in measuring cylinder; read at bottom of meniscus at eye level; alternatively measure rise in water level in a measuring cylinder; ρ = m/V; repeat and average; units g/cm³ or kg/m³.
questions.tip: Say what equipment measures each quantity. 'Measure the volume' with no method gets little.

questions.q: A sealed container of gas is heated. The volume stays constant. Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure of the gas increases.
questions.answer: Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the particles so they move faster; they collide with the container walls more often and with more force; so the force per unit area (pressure) increases.
ms: Particles gain kinetic energy / move faster (1 mark)
Collide with walls more frequently (1 mark)
Greater force per collision / greater force on walls, so pressure increases (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'collisions with the walls of the container'. Collisions with each other don't cause pressure.

questions.q: 18 kJ of energy melts 54 g of a solid at its melting point. What is the specific latent heat of fusion of the solid?
ms: L = E/m = 18 000 ÷ 0.054 = 3.33 × 10⁵ J/kg. 333 J/kg comes from using 54 instead of 0.054 kg.
questions.tip: Convert g to kg AND kJ to J. Getting one right but not the other is the trap.

questions.q: When ice melts, the mass of the water is the same as the mass of the ice. Explain why.
questions.answer: Changing state is a physical change; the number of particles stays the same (no particles are added or removed), so mass is conserved.
ms: Physical change / material recovers original properties if reversed (1 mark)
Same number of particles so mass is conserved (1 mark)
questions.tip: Density changes on melting because particle spacing changes, but mass doesn't.

questions.q: A stone of mass 84 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 40.0 cm³ to 70.0 cm³. Calculate the density of the stone in kg/m³.
ms: Volume = 30.0 cm³ (1 mark)
ρ = m/V = 2.8 g/cm³ (1 mark)
2800 kg/m³ (1 mark)
questions.tip: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Multiply by 1000.

questions.q: What is the approximate radius of an atom?
ms: Atoms have a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. 10⁻¹⁴ m is the nucleus.
questions.tip: The nucleus is about 1/10 000 the radius of the atom.

questions.q: What are isotopes?
options: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of protons
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Atoms that have gained or lost electrons
Atoms with the same mass number but different elements
ms: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons.
questions.tip: Losing electrons makes an ion, not an isotope.

questions.q: In the alpha particle scattering experiment, which observation showed that the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a small nucleus?
options: Most alpha particles passed straight through
A few alpha particles were deflected through large angles
ms: A few large deflections (some bounced back) showed a small, dense, positive nucleus. Most passing straight through showed the atom is mostly empty space.
questions.tip: Match each observation to its conclusion: they are different.

questions.q: A sodium atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the atom.
questions.answer: 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons
ms: 11 protons (1 mark)
12 neutrons (1 mark)
11 electrons (1 mark)
questions.tip: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

questions.q: Describe how the model of the atom has changed over time, and explain why each change was made.
questions.answer: Atoms first thought to be tiny indivisible spheres. Electron discovered → plum pudding model (ball of positive charge with electrons embedded). Alpha scattering experiment: most went through, some deflected → nuclear model (positive nucleus, mass concentrated, mostly empty space). Bohr: electrons orbit at specific distances, agreed with experimental observations. Later experiments showed nucleus contains protons (smaller particles each with same positive charge). Chadwick (about 20 years later) discovered the neutron.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Describes at least three models in correct order with clear explanations linking new evidence to each change, including the alpha scattering results.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Describes at least two models with some explanation of why the model changed.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple description of one or two models, e.g. plum pudding model had electrons in positive charge.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: tiny spheres that couldn't be divided; discovery of electron led to plum pudding model; alpha scattering (Rutherford, Geiger, Marsden): most passed straight through (mostly empty space), some deflected (positive nucleus), few bounced back (mass concentrated); nuclear model replaced plum pudding; Bohr: electrons in fixed energy levels/shells, theoretical calculations agreed with experiment; protons identified as particles of positive charge in the nucleus; Chadwick's experiments showed neutrons exist; new evidence leads to models changing.
questions.tip: Always link the change to the evidence: 'because some alpha particles were deflected...'

questions.q: Describe what happens to an electron in an atom when the atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation, and when it emits electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: Absorbing: the electron moves to a higher energy level (further from the nucleus). Emitting: the electron moves to a lower energy level (closer to the nucleus).
ms: Absorbs → electron moves to a higher energy level / further from nucleus (1 mark)
Emits → electron drops to a lower energy level / closer to nucleus (1 mark)
questions.tip: If an outer electron is removed completely, the atom becomes a positive ion.

questions.q: Give three differences between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model of the atom.
questions.answer: Nuclear model has a nucleus, plum pudding does not; in the nuclear model positive charge is concentrated in the nucleus, in plum pudding it is spread throughout; in the nuclear model mass is concentrated in the nucleus; nuclear model is mostly empty space; electrons orbit the nucleus rather than being embedded.
ms: Nucleus present vs no nucleus / positive charge concentrated vs spread out (1 mark)
Mass concentrated in centre vs spread throughout (1 mark)
Mostly empty space / electrons in orbits (shells) vs embedded in positive charge (1 mark)
questions.tip: Write each difference as a comparison: 'in the nuclear model... whereas in the plum pudding model...'.

questions.q: An atom has a radius of 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Its nucleus has a radius about 1/10 000 of this. What is the radius of the nucleus?
questions.tip: Dividing by 10⁴ means subtract 4 from the power.

questions.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most ionising?
ms: Alpha particles are the most strongly ionising (and least penetrating).
questions.tip: Ionising and penetrating are opposites: alpha is most ionising, least penetrating.

questions.q: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) decays by alpha emission. Which nucleus is produced?
ms: Alpha particle is ⁴₂He: mass number falls by 4 (238 → 234), atomic number falls by 2 (92 → 90).
questions.tip: Alpha: −4 mass, −2 atomic. Beta: 0 mass, +1 atomic.

questions.q: What happens to the nucleus when it emits a beta particle?
options: Atomic number increases by 1, mass number unchanged
ms: A neutron turns into a proton and an electron is emitted, so atomic number +1, mass number unchanged.
questions.tip: The beta particle is a high-speed electron from the nucleus.

questions.q: A sample has an activity of 1200 Bq. Its half-life is 8 days. What is its activity after 24 days?
ms: 24 days = 3 half-lives: 1200 → 600 → 300 → 150 Bq. 400 Bq divides by 3.
questions.tip: Count half-lives, then halve that many times.

questions.q: (HT) A radioactive source has an initial activity of 640 Bq and a half-life of 5 hours. Calculate the net decline in activity after 15 hours, expressed as a ratio of the initial activity.
questions.answer: 15 hours = 3 half-lives; activity = 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 Bq; net decline = 640 − 80 = 560 Bq; ratio 560 : 640 = 7 : 8 (7/8 or 0.875)
ms: 3 half-lives (1 mark)
Final activity 80 Bq and decline 560 Bq (1 mark)
questions.tip: Net decline is how much it has DROPPED by, not what is left.

questions.q:
A count rate is measured from a radioactive source (background corrected):
Time (min) | Count rate (counts/min)
0 | 800
2 | 566
4 | 400
6 | 283
8 | 200
(a) Determine the half-life. (1 mark)
(b) Predict the count rate after 12 minutes. Show your reasoning. (2 marks)
questions.answer: (a) 4 minutes (800 → 400). (b) 12 min = 3 half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 counts/min.
ms: (a) 4 minutes (1 mark)
(b) 3 half-lives / continues halving from 200 at 8 min (1 mark)
(b) 100 counts/min (1 mark)
questions.tip: Find the time for any value to halve, e.g. 400 → 200 also takes 4 minutes.

questions.q: Give two definitions of half-life.
questions.answer: The time taken for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve; the time taken for the count rate (or activity) from a sample to fall to half its initial level.
ms: Time for number of unstable nuclei (in a sample) to halve (1 mark)
Time for count rate/activity to fall to half (1 mark). Do not accept 'time for the sample to halve' or 'half the time it takes to decay'.
questions.tip: Say 'number of nuclei' or 'activity'. 'Half the atoms disappear' is wrong.

questions.q: Explain the difference between radioactive contamination and irradiation, and explain why an alpha source is more dangerous inside the body than outside it.
questions.answer: Contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or in other materials; irradiation is exposing an object to nuclear radiation (the object doesn't become radioactive). Outside the body alpha is stopped by skin/a few cm of air; inside the body it is absorbed by nearby cells and, being highly ionising, causes a lot of damage.
ms: Contamination: radioactive atoms/material get onto or into an object (1 mark)
Irradiation: object exposed to radiation, does not become radioactive (1 mark)
Outside: alpha cannot penetrate skin / stopped by air (1 mark)
Inside: highly ionising so damages cells / DNA nearby (1 mark)
questions.tip: Irradiated objects do NOT become radioactive. Contaminated ones carry the source with them.

questions.q: Carbon-14 (atomic number 6) decays by beta emission to form nitrogen. Write the nuclear equation for this decay, stating the mass and atomic numbers of each particle.
questions.answer: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e
ms: Carbon-14: mass 14, atomic number 6 on left (1 mark)
Nitrogen: mass 14, atomic number 7 (1 mark)
Beta particle written as mass 0, charge/atomic number −1 (electron) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance on both sides.

questions.q: Radioactive decay is random. Explain what this means and why it is still possible to state a half-life.
questions.answer: You cannot predict which nucleus will decay next or when it will decay; but with very large numbers of nuclei, the time for half of them to decay is predictable (statistical).
ms: Cannot predict which nucleus / when a particular nucleus will decay (1 mark)
Large number of nuclei, so the overall rate/half-life is predictable (1 mark)
questions.tip: Random doesn't mean unpredictable for a whole sample.

questions.q: Compare alpha, beta and gamma radiation. Use your comparison to explain which would be most suitable for monitoring the thickness of paper in a factory.
questions.answer: Alpha: helium nucleus (2p, 2n), charge +2, stopped by paper, range a few cm in air, highly ionising. Beta: high-speed electron, charge −1, stopped by a few mm of aluminium, range about 1 m in air, moderately ionising. Gamma: EM wave, no charge, reduced by thick lead/concrete, very long range, weakly ionising. Beta used for paper: partly absorbed by paper, so count rate changes when thickness changes. Alpha would be completely stopped; gamma would pass through regardless.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed comparison of nature, penetration and ionising power for all three, and a fully justified choice of beta, explaining why alpha and gamma are unsuitable.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Comparison of some properties for at least two types, with beta chosen and some justification.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements about penetration or ionisation of one or two types.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: alpha = 2 protons + 2 neutrons; beta = electron from nucleus (neutron → proton); gamma = electromagnetic radiation from nucleus; penetration: alpha stopped by paper/skin, beta by aluminium (few mm), gamma by thick lead/concrete; range in air: alpha ~5 cm, beta ~1 m, gamma very far; ionising power: alpha strongest, gamma weakest; for paper: beta, as some absorbed so count rate depends on thickness; alpha all absorbed; gamma unaffected by paper; long half-life source needed so count doesn't drop.
questions.tip: For thickness monitoring, explain why the OTHER two don't work too.

questions.q: What is emitted when a nucleus emits gamma radiation, and how does this affect the nucleus?
questions.answer: An electromagnetic wave (gamma ray) is emitted; the mass number and atomic number do not change (the nucleus loses energy).
ms: Electromagnetic radiation / wave (1 mark)
No change to mass number or atomic number (1 mark)
questions.tip: Gamma is often emitted after alpha or beta decay as the nucleus gets rid of excess energy.

questions.q: What unit is activity measured in?
ms: Activity is the rate at which unstable nuclei decay, in becquerel (Bq). 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
questions.tip: Count rate is what a Geiger-Muller tube detects; activity is in Bq.

questions.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
ms: Velocity has magnitude and direction. Speed, mass and energy only have magnitude.
questions.tip: Vector = size + direction (velocity, displacement, force, acceleration, momentum).

questions.q: A person has a mass of 65 kg. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. What is their weight?
questions.tip: Weight is a force in newtons; mass is in kg.

questions.q: (HT) A force of 12 N acts east and a force of 5 N acts north on the same object. What is the size of the resultant force?
ms: Perpendicular forces: √(12² + 5²) = 13 N. 17 N adds them as if in the same direction.
questions.tip: Forces at right angles: use Pythagoras or a scale drawing.

questions.q: A student pushes a box with a force of 250 N. The box moves 160 cm in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done.
ms: Converts 160 cm to 1.60 m (1 mark)
W = Fs substitution (1 mark)
400 J (allow 400 Nm) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Distance must be in metres for joules.

questions.q: (HT) A rope pulls a sledge with a force of 20 N at 30° above the horizontal. Using a scale drawing (or otherwise), determine the horizontal and vertical components of this force.
questions.answer: Horizontal ≈ 17 N (17.3 N); vertical = 10 N
ms: Correct method: scale drawing of 20 N at 30° resolved into perpendicular components, or trigonometry (1 mark)
Horizontal component 17 N (allow 16.8 to 17.8 N from scale drawing) (1 mark)
Vertical component 10 N (allow 9.5 to 10.5 N) (1 mark)
questions.tip: State your scale (e.g. 1 cm = 2 N) on scale drawings. Measure carefully: tolerance is small.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a contact force and a non-contact force. Give one example of each.
questions.answer: Contact forces act when objects are physically touching, e.g. friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force. Non-contact forces act when objects are separated, e.g. gravity, magnetic force, electrostatic force.
ms: Contact: objects touching + example (1 mark)
Non-contact: objects physically separated + example (1 mark)
questions.tip: Air resistance is a contact force: the air particles touch the object.

questions.q: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop over a distance of 40 m. Calculate the average braking force.
questions.answer: Ek = 0.5 × 1200 × 20² = 240 000 J; work done by brakes = Ek; F = W/s = 240 000 ÷ 40 = 6000 N
ms: Ek = 240 000 J (1 mark)
Work done = Ek, F = W/s (1 mark)
6000 N (1 mark)
questions.tip: Work done by the brakes equals the kinetic energy removed. The energy goes to the thermal store of the brakes.

questions.q: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg on Earth. On the Moon, gravitational field strength is 1.6 N/kg. What is the astronaut's mass on the Moon?
ms: Mass doesn't change with location: still 70 kg. Their weight on the Moon would be 112 N.
questions.tip: Mass is the amount of matter; weight depends on g.

questions.q: State what is meant by the weight of an object and where weight can be considered to act.
questions.answer: Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity; it acts at the object's centre of mass.
ms: Force due to gravity (on the object) (1 mark)
Acts at the centre of mass (1 mark)
questions.tip: Weight is proportional to mass (W ∝ m), measured with a newtonmeter.

questions.q: Which statement describes the behaviour of a spring obeying Hooke's law?
options: Extension is inversely proportional to the force applied
Extension is directly proportional to the force applied
Length is directly proportional to the force applied
Extension is constant whatever the force
ms: Up to the limit of proportionality, extension ∝ force (F = ke).
questions.tip: Extension = new length − original length. Not the total length.

questions.q: A spring has a spring constant of 40 N/m. A force of 6.0 N is applied. What is the extension?
questions.tip: Rearrange F = ke to e = F/k.

questions.q: A spring with a spring constant of 40 N/m is stretched by 5.0 cm. It does not go past its limit of proportionality. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.
ms: e = 0.050 m (1 mark)
Substitution into ½ke² (1 mark)
0.050 J (allow 0.05 J) (1 mark). Using 5.0 cm gives 500 J: max 1 mark.
questions.tip: Square the extension in metres. 5 cm → 0.05 m before squaring.

questions.q:
A spring has an original length of 12.0 cm. When a 4.0 N weight is hung from it, its length becomes 17.0 cm.
(a) Calculate the spring constant. (3 marks)
(b) Calculate the elastic potential energy stored. (1 mark)
ms: (a) Extension = 17.0 − 12.0 = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m (1 mark)
(a) k = F/e (1 mark)
(a) 80 N/m (1 mark)
(b) 0.10 J (allow ecf) (1 mark). Also accept work done = ½ × F × e = 0.10 J.
questions.tip: Using 17.0 cm (total length) instead of extension is the top error on this topic.

questions.q: Describe a method to investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring.
questions.answer: Clamp a spring to a stand, hang a ruler beside it (vertical, zero at top of spring or use a pointer); measure original length; add 1 N masses one at a time, measure new length each time; extension = length − original length; repeat; plot force against extension; straight line through origin shows proportionality, gradient = k.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Logical and detailed method including measuring original length, calculating extension for a range of forces, ways to improve accuracy and how results are analysed.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Method covers adding masses and measuring length/extension, with some detail missing.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic relevant steps, e.g. hang masses on spring and measure it.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: clamp stand with boss and clamp, G-clamp to bench for stability; spring hung with ruler alongside; pointer on spring for accuracy; read at eye level (avoid parallax); measure original length; add masses in equal steps (e.g. 100 g = 0.98 N); record length; calculate extension; don't exceed elastic limit; remove masses to check spring returns to original length; plot force (y) vs extension (x); gradient = spring constant; safety: goggles, keep feet away from falling masses.
questions.tip: Mention a pointer and reading at eye level for accuracy. Extension, not length, goes on the graph.

questions.q: Explain the difference between elastic deformation and inelastic deformation.
questions.answer: Elastic deformation: the object returns to its original shape and length when the force is removed. Inelastic: the object does not return to its original shape (permanently deformed).
ms: Elastic: returns to original shape/length when forces removed (1 mark)
Inelastic: does not return to original shape / permanently stretched (1 mark)
questions.tip: Going past the limit of proportionality (elastic limit) can cause inelastic deformation.

questions.q: A student records: 2 N → 4 cm, 4 N → 8 cm, 6 N → 12 cm, 8 N → 17 cm, 10 N → 25 cm extension. What is the spring constant in the linear region?
ms: k = F/e = 2 ÷ 0.04 = 50 N/m (linear up to 6 N). 0.5 comes from using cm (that would be N/cm).
questions.tip: Use values from the proportional part only, and convert cm to m.

questions.q: Explain why more than one force must act on an object to stretch, bend or compress it.
questions.answer: If only one force acted, there would be a resultant force and the object would accelerate/move instead of changing shape; forces in opposite directions are needed.
ms: One force would make the object move/accelerate (resultant force) (1 mark)
Two (or more) forces in opposite directions needed to change shape (1 mark)
questions.tip: Example: stretching a spring needs the clamp pulling up and the weight pulling down.

questions.q: What is a typical walking speed for a person?
ms: Typical speeds: walking ~1.5 m/s, running ~3 m/s, cycling ~6 m/s.
questions.tip: Learn typical speeds; they come up in estimate questions.

questions.q: A car travels at 72 km/h. What is this in m/s?
A cyclist accelerates from 4.0 m/s to 16 m/s in 3.0 s. What is the acceleration?
ms: a = Δv/t = (16 − 4.0) ÷ 3.0 = 4.0 m/s². 5.3 uses the final speed only.
questions.tip: Δv means change in velocity: final minus initial.

questions.q: A cyclist travels 2.4 km in 8.0 minutes. Calculate the average speed in m/s.
ms: Converts 2.4 km = 2400 m (1 mark)
Converts 8.0 min = 480 s (1 mark)
5.0 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two conversions here. Do them before substituting.

questions.q:
A train travelling at 54 km/h accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m/s² over a distance of 40 m. Calculate its final velocity. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
Use: (final velocity)² − (initial velocity)² = 2 × acceleration × distance
ms: v² = u² + 2as rearrangement (1 mark)
v² = 425 (1 mark)
v = 20.6 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Square root at the end. Forgetting it (425 m/s) is common.

questions.q:
A car of mass 1500 kg travelling at 18 m/s brakes uniformly and stops in 27 m.
(a) Calculate the deceleration. (3 marks)
(b) Calculate the braking force. (1 mark)
Use: v² − u² = 2as
ms: (a) Substitution 0² − 18² = 2 × a × 27 (1 mark)
(a) Rearranges a = (v² − u²)/(2s) (1 mark)
(a) 6.0 m/s² (allow −6.0 m/s²) (1 mark)
(b) 9000 N (ecf from (a)) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Final velocity is 0 when something 'stops'. A negative acceleration is a deceleration.

questions.q: (HT) A velocity-time graph for a car shows: uniform acceleration from rest to 12 m/s in 6.0 s, then constant velocity of 12 m/s for 10 s, then uniform deceleration to rest in 4.0 s. Calculate the total distance travelled.
questions.answer: Area under graph: ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m; 10 × 12 = 120 m; ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m; total = 180 m
ms: Uses area under graph (1 mark)
At least two correct areas: 36 m, 120 m, 24 m (1 mark)
Total 180 m (1 mark)
questions.tip: Distance = area under a velocity-time graph. Gradient = acceleration.

questions.q: A skydiver jumps from a plane. After some time she opens her parachute. Describe and explain the motion of the skydiver from leaving the plane until just before landing.
questions.answer: Initially only weight acts, so she accelerates downwards (about 9.8 m/s²). As speed increases, air resistance increases, so resultant force decreases and acceleration decreases. Eventually air resistance = weight, resultant force zero, terminal velocity. Parachute opens: area increases, air resistance increases greatly, now greater than weight, resultant force upwards, so she decelerates. As speed falls, air resistance decreases until it equals weight again: new lower terminal velocity.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Full, ordered explanation of both phases, linking forces (weight, air resistance, resultant force) to acceleration and velocity, including two terminal velocities with the second lower.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Describes motion with some correct force explanations, e.g. reaches terminal velocity when forces balanced, slows down when parachute opens.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple descriptions, e.g. she speeds up then falls at a steady speed.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: weight constant; at start air resistance zero so acceleration 9.8 m/s²; speed increases → air resistance increases; resultant force decreases → acceleration decreases; air resistance = weight → resultant zero → constant (terminal) velocity; parachute increases surface area → air resistance > weight → resultant force upwards → decelerates; air resistance decreases as she slows; balanced again → lower terminal velocity, safe for landing.
questions.tip: The skydiver does NOT go up when the parachute opens. She slows down while still falling.

questions.q: (HT) Describe how the speed of an accelerating object can be found at a particular time from a distance-time graph.
questions.answer: Draw a tangent to the curve at that time; calculate the gradient of the tangent (change in distance ÷ change in time) which equals the speed.
ms: Draw a tangent to the curve at that point (1 mark)
Gradient of tangent = speed (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use a large triangle on the tangent to reduce error.

questions.q: A car travels around a roundabout at a constant speed. Which statement is correct?
options: It is accelerating because its direction is changing
There is no resultant force on it
ms: Velocity is a vector: changing direction changes velocity, so it is accelerating and there must be a resultant force.
questions.tip: Constant speed ≠ constant velocity in circular motion.

questions.q: An athlete runs exactly once around a 400 m track, finishing where she started. What are her distance and displacement?
ms: Distance is total path length (400 m); displacement is straight-line distance from start in a direction (0 m).
questions.tip: Displacement is a vector, distance is a scalar.

questions.q: State what the gradient of (a) a distance-time graph and (b) a velocity-time graph represents.
questions.answer: (a) Speed (b) Acceleration
ms: (a) Speed (1 mark)
(b) Acceleration (1 mark)
questions.tip: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph = stationary; on a velocity-time graph = constant velocity.

questions.q: What resultant force is needed to accelerate a 1500 kg car at 2.0 m/s²?
questions.tip: F = ma uses the RESULTANT force.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. The Earth pulls down on the book with a force of 5 N. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with this force?
options: The table pushes up on the book with 5 N
Air pressure pushes down on the book
The book pulls up on the Earth with 5 N
The book pushes down on the table with 5 N
ms: Third law pairs are the same type of force acting on DIFFERENT objects: Earth pulls book (gravity), book pulls Earth (gravity). The table's push is a different type of force on the same object.
questions.tip: Third-law pairs: same type, equal size, opposite direction, different objects.

questions.q: An object has a resultant force of zero acting on it. Which statement is correct?
options: It is stationary or moving at constant velocity
ms: Newton's first law: zero resultant force means velocity doesn't change (stationary or constant velocity).
questions.tip: Zero resultant force doesn't mean no motion.

questions.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and total resistive forces of 900 N. Calculate its acceleration.
ms: Resultant force = 1500 N (1 mark)
a = F/m (1 mark)
1.25 m/s² (allow 1.3) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Find the resultant force first. Using 2400 N gives 2.0 m/s²: wrong.

questions.q: A resultant force of 0.48 N gives a trolley an acceleration of 0.60 m/s². Calculate the mass of the trolley in grams.
ms: Rearranges to m = F/a (1 mark)
0.80 kg (1 mark)
800 g (1 mark)
questions.tip: The equation gives kg. Convert to grams if asked (× 1000).

questions.q: Describe a method to investigate how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the resultant force acting on it.
questions.answer: Trolley on a bench, string over a pulley to a mass hanger; light gates (or ticker tape / stopwatch with marked distances) to measure acceleration; force = weight of hanging masses (W = mg); start with masses on the trolley, transfer one at a time to hanger so total mass constant; release, record acceleration; repeat 3 times for each force; plot acceleration against force; straight line through origin shows a ∝ F.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A logically ordered method that produces valid results: describes how force is varied, how acceleration is measured, how mass is kept constant and how results are analysed.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Describes changing the force and measuring acceleration or time, with some detail missing (e.g. mass not kept constant).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple relevant statements, e.g. add masses and time the trolley.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: trolley, bench pulley, string, mass hanger, slotted masses; clamp pulley to edge; light gate and interrupt card connected to data logger (or two light gates / stopwatch and marked distances, a = Δv/t); force = weight of hanging masses (mg); keep total mass of system constant by moving masses from trolley to hanger; compensate for friction with a slight slope; repeat and mean; plot a vs F; expect directly proportional; safety: catch box under masses, stop trolley at end.
questions.tip: Keeping total mass constant (moving masses from trolley to hanger) is the detail that lifts answers to Level 3.

questions.q: (HT) What is meant by inertia, and how is inertial mass defined?
questions.answer: Inertia is the tendency of an object to stay at rest or continue moving at the same velocity (resist changes in motion). Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object, defined as force ÷ acceleration (m = F/a).
