ms: Inertia: tendency to remain at rest or in uniform motion (1 mark)
Inertial mass = force/acceleration / measure of how hard it is to change velocity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Inertia is linked to Newton's first law; inertial mass to the second.

questions.q:
In the acceleration practical, the total mass is kept constant. Results:
Force (N) | Acceleration (m/s²)
0.20 | 0.40
0.40 | 0.81
0.60 | 1.19
0.80 | 1.62
(a) State the conclusion. (1 mark)
(b) Use the results to determine the total mass being accelerated. (2 marks)
questions.answer: (a) Acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force. (b) m = F/a ≈ 0.20 ÷ 0.40 = 0.50 kg (gradient of F against a)
ms: (a) Acceleration directly proportional to force (1 mark)
(b) m = F/a or uses gradient (1 mark)
(b) 0.50 kg (allow 0.49 to 0.51 kg) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use a pair from the table, or the gradient of a graph. Both are fine.

questions.q: What is stopping distance?
ms: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
questions.tip: Thinking distance: during reaction time. Braking: after brakes applied.

questions.q: Which factor increases the thinking distance of a driver?
ms: Tiredness increases reaction time so thinking distance increases. The others affect braking distance.
questions.tip: Thinking distance factors are about the DRIVER (speed, tiredness, drugs, alcohol, distractions).

questions.q: What is a typical range of human reaction times?
ms: Reaction times typically vary from 0.2 s to 0.9 s between people.
questions.tip: Learn the range: 0.2 to 0.9 s.

questions.q: A car travels at 25 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.70 s. The braking distance is 48 m. Calculate the stopping distance.
questions.answer: Thinking distance = 25 × 0.70 = 17.5 m; stopping distance = 17.5 + 48 = 65.5 m
ms: s = vt for thinking distance (1 mark)
17.5 m (1 mark)
65.5 m (1 mark)
questions.tip: During the reaction time the car still moves at full speed.

questions.q: Explain why doubling the speed of a car more than doubles its stopping distance.
questions.answer: Thinking distance is directly proportional to speed (s = vt), so it doubles. Braking distance depends on kinetic energy (½mv²), which increases by 4 times; the work done by the brakes (F × d) must equal the kinetic energy, so with the same braking force the braking distance increases 4 times. So stopping distance more than doubles.
ms: Thinking distance doubles / ∝ speed (1 mark)
Kinetic energy ∝ v², so increases 4 times (1 mark)
Work done by brakes = KE, so braking distance ×4 (with same braking force) (1 mark)
Total therefore more than doubles (1 mark)
questions.tip: Connect braking distance to kinetic energy and work done. That's the higher-level link.

questions.q:
(HT) A car of mass 1000 kg travelling at 30 m/s makes an emergency stop in 3.0 s.
(a) Estimate the braking force. (2 marks)
(b) Explain two dangers of very large decelerations. (2 marks)
questions.answer:
(a) a = 30 ÷ 3.0 = 10 m/s²; F = ma = 1000 × 10 = 10 000 N
(b) Brakes may overheat (large energy transfer to thermal store); tyres may skid / lose control; passengers experience large forces and may be injured.
ms: (a) a = 10 m/s² (1 mark)
(b) Brakes overheat (1 mark)
(b) Skidding / loss of control / injury from large forces (1 mark)
questions.tip: Large deceleration = large force, which links to injuries and overheating brakes.

questions.q: Describe how to measure a person's reaction time using a ruler, and how you could make the investigation produce valid results.
questions.answer: Person A holds a metre ruler vertically with zero between person B's open finger and thumb; A drops the ruler without warning; B catches it; read distance at top of thumb; convert to time using a conversion table; repeat many times and calculate mean; control: same hand, same starting position, same person dropping, no warning, sitting at a table with arm resting; test one variable (e.g. caffeine) while keeping others the same.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear, ordered method including how distance is measured and converted to reaction time, repeats/means and at least two control variables explained.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Method for the ruler drop with some detail of measurement and at least one control variable.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. drop a ruler and catch it.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: ruler held vertically, zero mark level with catcher's thumb; dropper releases without warning; catcher grips as fast as possible; record distance fallen; longer distance = longer reaction time; convert distance to time via table; repeat 5+ times and average; ignore anomalies; controls: same hand (dominant), same ruler, rest arm on table edge, same gap between finger and thumb, no distractions; to test a factor (e.g. distraction), change only that.
questions.tip: The ruler falls further if reaction time is longer. Say how distance becomes time.

questions.q: Explain how an icy road affects the braking distance of a car.
questions.answer: There is less friction between the tyres and the road, so the braking force is smaller (or the car skids), so the braking distance increases.
ms: Less friction / grip between tyres and road (1 mark)
Braking distance increases (1 mark)
questions.tip: Road and car condition affect braking distance; the driver affects thinking distance.

questions.q: (HT) A 0.40 kg ball moves at 15 m/s. What is its momentum?
ms: p = mv = 0.40 × 15 = 6.0 kg m/s. 45 is the kinetic energy-style mistake (½mv²).
questions.tip: p = mv: no ½, no squaring.

questions.q: (HT) What is the unit of momentum?
ms: Momentum = mass × velocity, so kg × m/s = kg m/s.
questions.tip: kg m/s² is the newton (force).

questions.q: (HT) A lorry of mass 9000 kg travels at 54 km/h. Calculate its momentum.
ms: Converts 54 km/h = 15 m/s (1 mark)
p = mv substitution (1 mark)
135 000 kg m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Check speed units first.

questions.q:
(HT) Trolley A (mass 2.0 kg) moves at 3.0 m/s and collides with stationary trolley B (mass 1.0 kg). They stick together.
(a) Calculate their velocity after the collision. (3 marks)
(b) Show that kinetic energy is not conserved in this collision. (2 marks)
questions.answer:
(a) Momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m/s; after: 3.0 × v = 6.0; v = 2.0 m/s
(b) Ek before = ½ × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J; Ek after = ½ × 3.0 × 2.0² = 6.0 J; 3.0 J transferred (e.g. to thermal and sound), so kinetic energy decreased.
ms: (a) Momentum before = 6.0 kg m/s (1 mark)
(a) Total momentum before = after, combined mass 3.0 kg (1 mark)
(a) 2.0 m/s (1 mark)
(b) Ek before 9.0 J (1 mark)
(b) Ek after 6.0 J so not conserved (1 mark)
questions.tip: Momentum is always conserved in a closed system; kinetic energy usually isn't.

questions.q: (HT) A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Both are initially at rest. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle.
questions.answer: Total momentum before = 0; bullet momentum = 0.020 × 400 = 8.0 kg m/s; rifle: 4.0 × v = −8.0; v = 2.0 m/s in the opposite direction to the bullet
ms: Momentum before = 0 / bullet momentum 8.0 kg m/s (1 mark)
2.0 m/s in opposite direction (allow −2.0 m/s) (1 mark)
questions.tip: In an 'explosion' from rest, total momentum after is zero, so the momenta are equal and opposite.

questions.q: (HT) Two ice skaters, at rest, push apart. The 60 kg skater moves off at 2.0 m/s. The other skater has a mass of 40 kg. What is the velocity of the 40 kg skater?
ms: Total momentum = 0, so 40v = 60 × 2.0 = 120; v = 3.0 m/s, opposite direction.
questions.tip: Equal and opposite momentum: the lighter one moves faster.

questions.q: (HT) State the principle of conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event (collision or explosion) is equal to the total momentum after the event.
ms: Total momentum before = total momentum after (1 mark)
In a closed system / no external forces (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Closed system' is the condition. Without it you may lose a mark.

questions.q: (HT) Compare the momentum of a 1200 kg car moving at 20 m/s with a 16 000 kg lorry moving at 1.5 m/s.
questions.answer: Car: 1200 × 20 = 24 000 kg m/s; lorry: 16 000 × 1.5 = 24 000 kg m/s; they have equal momentum.
ms: Both momenta calculated: 24 000 kg m/s (1 mark)
Conclusion: equal momentum (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always compare with numbers, not just words.

questions.q: Which type of wave is sound?
ms: Sound waves are longitudinal: oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
questions.tip: Transverse: water ripples and all EM waves. Longitudinal: sound.

questions.q: What is the amplitude of a wave?
options: The number of waves passing a point each second
The distance from crest to trough
The distance from one crest to the next
The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position
ms: Amplitude is maximum displacement from the rest position. Crest-to-trough is TWICE the amplitude.
questions.tip: Don't measure amplitude from trough to crest.

questions.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. What is its speed?
questions.tip: v = fλ is on the spec's recall list. The full equation sheet is given in 2027 exams, but knowing it by heart saves time.

questions.q: A radio station broadcasts at 98.4 MHz. Speed of EM waves = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the wavelength?
questions.tip: M = 10⁶, k = 10³. Convert before dividing.

questions.q: A student counts 12 water waves passing a point in 30 s. The wavelength is 4.0 cm. Calculate the wave speed in m/s.
ms: f = 0.40 Hz (1 mark)
λ = 0.040 m (1 mark)
v = 0.016 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Frequency = number of waves per second.

questions.q: Describe how to measure the speed of water waves in a ripple tank.
questions.answer: Set up ripple tank with lamp above so wave pattern shows on paper/screen below; set vibrator to produce waves; measure wavelength by measuring across several waves (e.g. 10) on screen with ruler and dividing; measure frequency by counting waves passing a point in 10 s (or use signal generator setting); calculate v = fλ. Alternative: time a wave travelling a known distance and v = d/t.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear method that measures both frequency and wavelength (or distance and time) with techniques to improve accuracy, and calculates wave speed.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Method describing how to measure one of frequency or wavelength in detail, with v = fλ.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements about the apparatus or the equation.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: ripple tank with shallow water; motor/vibrating bar; lamp above, white card below to see shadows of waves; low frequency so waves can be counted; ruler on screen: measure length of e.g. 10 wavelengths and divide by 10; count waves passing a point in 10 s, f = count ÷ 10; or photograph the pattern with a ruler for scale; v = fλ; or measure time for one wave to travel length of tank, v = s/t; repeat and average; strobe can freeze pattern.
questions.tip: Measuring several wavelengths and dividing reduces uncertainty: say so.

questions.q: A cork floats on a pond. Water waves pass it. Describe what the cork does and what this shows about waves.
questions.answer: The cork bobs up and down but does not move along with the wave; this shows the wave transfers energy, not the water itself.
ms: Cork moves up and down (does not travel with the wave) (1 mark)
Waves transfer energy (and information) but not matter/water (1 mark)
questions.tip: Similar evidence for sound: air particles vibrate, they don't travel to your ear.

questions.q: Describe the differences between transverse and longitudinal waves. Give one example of each.
questions.answer: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer, e.g. water ripples, light. Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to direction of energy transfer, with compressions and rarefactions, e.g. sound.
ms: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer (1 mark)
Longitudinal: oscillations parallel, with compressions and rarefactions (1 mark)
One correct example of each (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'direction of energy transfer', not just 'direction of the wave'.

questions.q: Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water. A sound wave in water has a wavelength of 2.5 cm. Calculate its frequency in kHz.
ms: λ = 0.025 m (1 mark)
f = v/λ = 60 000 Hz (1 mark)
60 kHz (1 mark)
questions.tip: Hz ÷ 1000 = kHz.

questions.q:
A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate its period.
Use: period = 1 ÷ frequency
ms: T = 1/f substitution (1 mark)
questions.tip: Period is time for one complete wave, in seconds.

questions.q: Which electromagnetic wave has the highest frequency?
ms: Order of increasing frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma.
questions.tip: Highest frequency = shortest wavelength = gamma.

questions.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used for satellite communications?
ms: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere and are used for satellite communications and cooking.
questions.tip: Learn one use per wave and why it's suitable.

questions.q: What do all electromagnetic waves have in common?
ms: All EM waves travel at the same speed (3 × 10⁸ m/s) through a vacuum or air. They are all transverse.
questions.tip: Only UV, X-rays and gamma are ionising.

questions.q: Which type of radiation can cause the skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer?
ms: Ultraviolet causes premature skin ageing and increases skin cancer risk. X-rays and gamma cause mutation of genes and cancer.
questions.tip: UV: skin. X-rays and gamma: gene mutation and cancer.

questions.q: (HT) Light travels from air into glass at an angle to the normal. Use the idea of wavefronts to explain why it changes direction.
questions.answer: Light slows down when it enters glass; one side/end of the wavefront enters the glass first and slows down first while the rest of the wavefront is still in air moving faster; this causes the wavefront to change direction (bend towards the normal); the wavelength decreases (frequency stays the same).
ms: Light slows down in glass (1 mark)
One part of the wavefront enters glass first and slows first (1 mark)
So the wavefront changes direction / bends towards the normal (1 mark)
Wavelength decreases (frequency unchanged) (1 mark)
questions.tip: The bending happens because different parts of the wavefront change speed at different times.

questions.q: Explain why X-rays can be used to produce images of bones.
questions.answer: X-rays are absorbed by bone (dense material) but transmitted through soft tissue, so bones appear as shadows / white areas on the detector.
ms: Absorbed by bone (1 mark)
Transmitted/pass through soft tissue (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'absorbed' and 'transmitted'.

questions.q: (HT) Describe how radio waves are produced and what happens when they are absorbed by a receiver aerial.
questions.answer: Radio waves are produced by oscillations (alternating current) in electrical circuits; when absorbed by a conductor (aerial) they may create an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave itself.
ms: Produced by oscillations of electrons / alternating current in electrical circuits (1 mark)
Absorbed waves induce an alternating current in the receiver (1 mark)
Same frequency as the radio wave (1 mark)
questions.tip: The key phrase: 'alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave'.

questions.q: Describe how to investigate how the type of surface affects the amount of infrared radiation emitted, using a Leslie cube. State the expected results.
questions.answer: Fill a Leslie cube (faces: matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny silver) with hot water from a kettle; place on heatproof mat; use an infrared detector/thermometer at the same distance from each face; record readings for each face; repeat; matt black emits most, shiny silver least.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed logical method including how readings are taken from each surface, how fair test is ensured (same distance, same water temperature), and correct expected results.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Method with key steps and some control variables or the correct result.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. use a Leslie cube and measure each side.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: Leslie cube with different surfaces; fill with near-boiling water; put lid on; infrared detector or thermometer with blackened bulb; same distance from each face (use a ruler); measure each face quickly so water temperature doesn't drop much; repeat and average; results: matt black best emitter, shiny silver/white worst; dark, matt surfaces are good emitters and absorbers; safety: hot water, cube on heatproof mat.
questions.tip: Distance from each face is the key control variable. Also give the result: matt black emits most.

questions.q:
A CT scan gives a radiation dose of 8.0 mSv. A chest X-ray gives a dose of 0.020 mSv.
(a) Calculate how many chest X-rays give the same dose as one CT scan. (1 mark)
(b) What does radiation dose measure, and what is its unit? (2 marks)
questions.answer: (a) 8.0 ÷ 0.020 = 400 (b) Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm from exposure of the body to radiation, measured in sieverts (Sv); 1000 mSv = 1 Sv.
ms: (b) Measure of risk of harm (to the body) from radiation (1 mark)
(b) Sievert, Sv (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dose (Sv) measures risk of harm. Activity (Bq) measures decays per second. Don't mix them.

questions.q: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block at an angle to the normal. Describe what happens to the direction and speed of the light.
questions.answer: The light slows down and bends towards the normal (angle of refraction smaller than angle of incidence).
ms: Slows down (1 mark)
Bends towards the normal (1 mark)
questions.tip: Along the normal (at 0°), light doesn't bend but does still slow down.

questions.q: Two north poles of magnets are brought close together. What happens?
ms: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
questions.tip: Learn the field direction: north to south outside the magnet.

questions.q: What force is always produced between an induced magnet and a permanent magnet?
ms: Induced magnetism always causes attraction. Induced magnets lose most/all magnetism when removed from the field.
questions.tip: Repulsion is the only test that proves something is a permanent magnet.

questions.q: Describe the magnetic field around a long straight wire carrying a current.
options: Concentric circles around the wire, weaker further away
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Concentric circles, the same strength at all distances
ms: The field is concentric circles around the wire; strength decreases with distance and increases with current.
questions.tip: Field strength depends on current and distance from the wire.

questions.q:
(HT) A wire of length 5.0 cm carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. What force acts on the wire?
Use F = BIl
questions.tip: Length in metres. Unit of B is the tesla (T).

questions.q:
(HT) A wire of length 8.0 cm carries a current of 1.2 A at right angles to a magnetic field. A force of 0.048 N acts on it. Calculate the magnetic flux density.
Use F = BIl
ms: l = 0.080 m (1 mark)
Rearranges B = F/(Il) (1 mark)
0.50 T (1 mark)
questions.tip: Units of B: tesla, T.

questions.q: (HT) A horizontal wire carries a current from west to east. The magnetic field points north (horizontally). Use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on the wire.
questions.answer: Vertically upwards.
ms: Correct use of rule: First finger = field (north), seCond finger = current (east), thuMb = motion/force (1 mark)
Force vertically upwards (1 mark)
questions.tip: First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion. Use your LEFT hand.

questions.q: (HT) Explain how a simple dc electric motor works, and describe how the speed of rotation could be increased.
questions.answer: A coil of wire carrying current is placed in a magnetic field; current in the coil produces a magnetic field which interacts with the permanent magnet's field (motor effect); one side of the coil has a force up and the other down (opposite directions because current flows opposite ways, Fleming's left-hand rule), producing a turning effect so the coil rotates; split-ring commutator reverses current every half turn so the coil keeps turning in the same direction; brushes make contact. Increase speed: increase current/pd, stronger magnet, more turns on coil.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed explanation of the motor effect producing opposite forces on each side of the coil leading to rotation, role of the commutator, and at least two ways to increase speed.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Explains that current in the field causes forces and rotation, with at least one way to increase speed; commutator may be missing or incomplete.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. current and magnets make it turn; use a bigger battery.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: coil in magnetic field between poles; current in wire → force (motor effect); F = BIl; forces on the two sides in opposite directions; creates rotation; Fleming's left-hand rule gives direction; split-ring commutator reverses current direction every half turn to keep rotation in one direction; brushes; increase speed by increasing current, increasing magnetic flux density, more turns on the coil, (iron core).
questions.tip: Don't forget the commutator: without it the coil would just rock back and forth.

questions.q: Describe how to use a plotting compass to show the magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet.
questions.answer: Place the magnet on paper; put the compass near one pole; mark the direction the needle points with a dot; move the compass so its tail is at the dot and mark again; repeat to the other pole; join dots to form a field line with an arrow from N to S; repeat from different starting points.
ms: Place compass near magnet and mark direction of needle (dots) (1 mark)
Move compass along, repeat, join dots into a line (1 mark)
Repeat from different start points / arrows from north to south (1 mark)
questions.tip: Field lines go from north to south and never cross.

questions.q: Describe the magnetic field of a solenoid and give two ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
questions.answer: Inside the solenoid the field is strong and uniform (parallel lines); outside it is like a bar magnet's field. Stronger: add an iron core, increase the current, increase the number of turns (coils per unit length).
ms: Inside: strong and uniform field (1 mark)
Outside: similar to a bar magnet (1 mark)
Two of: iron core / more current / more turns (1 mark each, max 2 for ways)
questions.tip: An iron core becomes an induced magnet, adding to the field.

questions.q: Explain what a magnetic compass shows about the Earth.
questions.answer: A compass contains a small bar magnet that points north; this shows the Earth has a magnetic field (its core is magnetic).
ms: Compass needle is a small (bar) magnet (1 mark)
It aligns with Earth's magnetic field, which is evidence the Earth has a magnetic field / magnetic core (1 mark)
questions.tip: The compass's north pole points to Earth's geographic north.

questions.q: (HT) State two factors that affect the size of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.
questions.answer: Magnetic flux density, current in the wire, length of wire in the field (and the wire must be at an angle to the field, maximum at right angles).
ms: Any one: magnetic flux density / current / length of wire (1 mark)
Any second correct factor (1 mark)
questions.tip: If the wire is parallel to the field there is no force.

questions.q: Which sub-cellular structure is the site of aerobic respiration?
ms: Aerobic respiration takes place in the mitochondria.
questions.tip: Do not write that mitochondria 'make energy'. Energy is released, never made.

questions.q: A red blood cell is 8 µm in diameter. An image of it in a textbook is 24 mm wide. What is the magnification of the image?
ms: Convert to the same units: 24 mm = 24 000 µm. Magnification = 24 000 ÷ 8 = × 3000.
questions.tip: Always convert image and real size to the same unit before dividing.

questions.q: A virus particle is 120 nm across. What is this in metres, in standard form?
questions.tip: Count the shift: moving the decimal two places left adds 2 to the power (10^-9 becomes 10^-7).

questions.q: Give the function of the cell wall and the permanent vacuole in a plant cell.
questions.answer: Cell wall: made of cellulose, strengthens/supports the cell. Permanent vacuole: contains cell sap, keeps the cell rigid/turgid.
ms: Cell wall strengthens or supports the cell (allow made of cellulose) (1 mark)
Permanent vacuole contains cell sap / keeps the cell firm or turgid (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not say the cell wall 'controls what enters'. That is the cell membrane.

questions.q: Name the part of a light microscope you would use to focus on a cell at high power, and explain why you should not use the other focusing knob.
questions.answer: Fine focus knob. The coarse focus moves the stage a large distance so the objective lens could hit and break the slide.
ms: Fine focusing knob (1 mark)
Coarse focus moves the lens/stage too far, so it may crack the slide or damage the lens (allow image goes out of focus too quickly) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Start on the lowest power objective with coarse focus, then switch to high power and use fine focus only.

questions.q: A student draws a cheek cell seen through a microscope. Give three rules she should follow to produce a good scientific drawing.
questions.answer: Use a sharp pencil, draw clear continuous lines with no shading, label with straight ruled lines (plus title and magnification), draw in proportion.
ms: Sharp pencil / clear unbroken lines (1 mark)
No shading or colouring (1 mark)
Any one: label lines drawn with a ruler and not crossing / include a title and magnification or scale / structures drawn in proportion / drawing takes up at least half the space (1 mark)
questions.tip: Biology drawings are line drawings. Shading always loses a mark.

questions.q: Compare the structure of a prokaryotic cell with a eukaryotic animal cell.
questions.answer: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes. Prokaryotes have no nucleus: DNA is a single loop free in the cytoplasm plus plasmids. Prokaryotes have a cell wall (not cellulose) and are much smaller. Eukaryotic animal cells have a nucleus and mitochondria.
ms: Similarity: both have cell membrane / cytoplasm / ribosomes (1 mark)
Prokaryote has no nucleus; eukaryote's DNA is enclosed in a nucleus (1 mark)
Prokaryote DNA is a single loop and it may have plasmids (1 mark)
Any one: prokaryote has a cell wall but animal cell does not / prokaryote is smaller (about 1 to 10 µm vs 10 to 100 µm) / prokaryote has no mitochondria (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Compare' needs similarities AND differences. Use comparative words like 'whereas'.

questions.q: A student sees 12 onion cells across the diameter of the field of view. The diameter of the field of view is 3 mm. Estimate the length of one cell in micrometres.
ms: = 250 µm (1 mark)
questions.tip: Divide the field of view by the number of cells, then convert mm to µm (× 1000).

questions.q: A scientist measures an image of a chloroplast on an electron micrograph. The image is 40 mm long and the magnification is × 8000. Calculate the real length of the chloroplast in micrometres. Then explain why this structure would not be visible in this much detail with a light microscope.
questions.answer: Real size = 40 ÷ 8000 = 0.005 mm = 5 µm. An electron microscope has a much higher resolution, so it can distinguish internal detail (e.g. membranes) that a light microscope cannot.
ms: real size = image ÷ magnification = 40 ÷ 8000 = 0.005 mm (1 mark)
= 5 µm (1 mark)
Electron microscope has higher resolving power / resolution, so can show smaller structures or internal detail (1 mark). Do not accept 'higher magnification' alone.
questions.tip: Resolution is the key word. Magnification alone does not give more detail.

questions.q: Muscle cells contain many more mitochondria than skin cells. A nerve cell can be up to 1 m long with many branched endings. Explain how each of these features helps the cell carry out its function.
questions.answer: Muscle cells contract, which needs a lot of energy; more mitochondria means more aerobic respiration to release energy. Nerve cells carry electrical impulses around the body; being long carries impulses over long distances, branched endings (dendrites) connect with many other cells.
ms: Muscle cells need lots of energy to contract (1 mark)
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing more energy (1 mark)
Long axon carries impulses over long distances (quickly) (1 mark)
Branched endings connect to / receive impulses from many other cells (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always link the feature to the function with 'so that' or 'which means'.

questions.q: Which statement describes diffusion?
options: The net movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration
The net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
The movement of water from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of particles against a concentration gradient using energy
ms: Diffusion is the spreading out of particles, giving net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
questions.tip: Say 'net movement'. Particles move both ways but more move down the gradient.

questions.q: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 4 µm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.tip: Surface area of a cube = 6 × side²; volume = side³. Divide SA by volume, not the other way round.

questions.q: Red blood cells were placed in a salt solution more concentrated than their cytoplasm. What would be observed?
options: The cells shrink because water leaves by osmosis
No change because the cell wall stops them shrinking
The cells burst because water enters by osmosis
The cells shrink because salt leaves by active transport
ms: Water moves from the dilute cytoplasm into the more concentrated solution by osmosis, so the cells shrink. Animal cells have no cell wall.
questions.tip: Osmosis is about water molecules moving, never the solute.

questions.q: Give two factors that affect the rate of diffusion.
questions.answer: Difference in concentration (concentration gradient), temperature, surface area of the membrane.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): concentration gradient / temperature / surface area of membrane. Allow distance or thickness of membrane.
questions.tip: Write 'concentration gradient', not just 'concentration'.

questions.q: Give one substance that moves by diffusion from the blood into body cells.
questions.answer: Oxygen (or glucose).
ms: Oxygen / glucose (allow amino acids) (1 mark). Do not accept carbon dioxide or urea, which move out of cells.
questions.tip: Watch the direction. Carbon dioxide and urea diffuse out of cells.

questions.q: Fish gills are an exchange surface. Each gill has many thin filaments with a good blood supply, and water flows over them continuously. Explain how these features increase the rate of oxygen uptake.
questions.answer: Many filaments give a large surface area. Thin filaments give a short diffusion distance. Good blood supply and constant water flow maintain a steep concentration gradient.
ms: Many filaments give a large surface area (1 mark)
Thin walls/filaments give a short diffusion distance (1 mark)
Blood carries oxygen away and fresh water brings more oxygen, maintaining a steep concentration gradient (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name all three: large surface area, thin/short distance, steep concentration gradient.

questions.q: Plants absorb mineral ions from the soil by active transport. Explain why active transport is needed, and why root hair cells contain many mitochondria.
questions.answer: The concentration of mineral ions in the soil is lower than in the root hair cell, so ions must be moved against the concentration gradient. This needs energy from respiration, released in mitochondria.
ms: Ions moved from low (soil) to high (cell) concentration / against the concentration gradient (1 mark)
Needs energy from respiration, which happens in mitochondria (1 mark)
questions.tip: Active transport always needs two ideas: against the gradient AND energy from respiration.

questions.q: Cells A and B are cubes. Cell A has sides of 1 µm; cell B has sides of 3 µm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each and explain which cell would get oxygen to its centre more efficiently by diffusion.
questions.answer: A: SA 6, V 1, ratio 6 : 1. B: SA 54, V 27, ratio 2 : 1. Cell A has the larger SA:V ratio and a shorter distance to the centre, so diffusion meets its needs more efficiently.
ms: Cell A ratio 6 : 1 (1 mark)
Cell B: 54 ÷ 27 = 2 : 1 (1 mark)
Cell A, because larger SA:V ratio / shorter diffusion distance to the centre (1 mark)
questions.tip: As size increases, SA:V ratio decreases. That is why large organisms need exchange surfaces.

questions.q:
A student cut potato cylinders and put them in sucrose solutions for 30 minutes. Results (% change in mass): 0.0 mol/dm³ | +18 ; 0.2 mol/dm³ | +7 ; 0.4 mol/dm³ | -4 ; 0.6 mol/dm³ | -12 ; 0.8 mol/dm³ | -19.
(a) Estimate the concentration of the potato cell sap. (b) Explain why the student calculated percentage change instead of using change in mass.
questions.answer: (a) About 0.33 mol/dm³ (where line crosses 0, between 0.2 and 0.4). (b) The cylinders had different starting masses, so percentage change allows a fair comparison.
ms: (a) Answer in the range 0.30 to 0.36 mol/dm³ (2 marks). Allow 1 mark for 'between 0.2 and 0.4 mol/dm³' or showing interpolation where change is 0.
(b) Cylinders had different starting masses (1 mark)
so percentage change allows results to be compared fairly (1 mark)
questions.tip: The point of no change in mass is where the solution concentration equals the cell sap concentration.

questions.q: In an osmosis practical, a student rinsed freshly cut potato cylinders in water and weighed them without blotting. After 30 minutes in the sucrose solutions she blotted each cylinder dry before reweighing. Explain the effect of this on her calculated percentage changes in mass, and state the type of error.
questions.answer: The starting masses include surface water so are too high. The final masses do not, so every percentage change is too low (gains look smaller, losses look larger). This is a systematic error: it shifts all results in the same direction, reducing accuracy.
ms: Initial mass includes surface water, so initial mass is too high (1 mark)
So calculated percentage change is too low / gains appear smaller and losses larger (1 mark)
Systematic error (allow: affects all results in the same way, so accuracy not precision is affected) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say which way the error pushes the result. 'It makes it inaccurate' alone scores little.

questions.q: What is the name of the type of cell division that produces two genetically identical cells?
ms: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
questions.tip: Mitosis = identical (both have a 't'). Meiosis = gametes, varied.

questions.q: What is a stem cell?
options: A cell with half the normal number of chromosomes
An undifferentiated cell that can divide and become many types of cell
A specialised cell that carries out one function
A cell found only in plant stems
ms: Stem cells are undifferentiated and can give rise to many types of specialised cell.
questions.tip: Key word: undifferentiated.

questions.q: A cell grown in a laboratory culture divides by mitosis every 20 hours. One cell is placed in the culture. Assuming every cell survives and keeps dividing at this rate, how many cells are there after 120 hours?
ms: 120 hours ÷ 20 hours = 6 rounds of mitosis. Each round doubles the number of cells, so 2^6 = 64.
questions.tip: Count the number of divisions first, then use 2 to the power of that number. Do not just divide 120 by 20 and stop.

questions.q: During the cell cycle, a cell grows before it divides. Give two things that happen in this stage.
questions.answer: The DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome; the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria increases.
ms: DNA replicates / chromosomes are copied (1 mark)
Number of sub-cellular structures (e.g. mitochondria, ribosomes) increases / cell grows (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say DNA 'replicates'. Examiners accept 'copies' but not 'divides'.

questions.q: A scientist counted cells in each stage of the cell cycle in a root tip. Of 400 cells, 352 were in the growth/DNA replication stage, 40 were in mitosis and 8 were in cytokinesis. The whole cycle takes 16 hours. Calculate how long cells spend in mitosis. Give your answer in hours.
ms: Fraction in mitosis = 40 ÷ 400 = 0.1 (1 mark)
= 1.6 hours (1 mark)
questions.tip: The fraction of cells in a stage equals the fraction of time spent in that stage.

questions.q: Explain why meristem tissue is used to clone rare plant species to stop them becoming extinct.
questions.answer: Meristem cells are stem cells that can differentiate into any plant cell type, so whole new plants can be grown quickly and cheaply, and the clones are genetically identical to the parent.
ms: Meristem cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell / grow into a whole plant (1 mark)
Large numbers of identical plants can be produced quickly/cheaply (1 mark)
questions.tip: Plant stem cells are only in meristems (root tips and shoot tips).

questions.q: Describe how therapeutic cloning could be used to produce stem cells to treat a patient, and explain why the patient's body would not reject them.
questions.answer: An embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient (nucleus from patient's body cell). Stem cells are taken from the embryo and grown into the needed cell type. The cells have the same genes/antigens as the patient so the immune system does not attack them.
ms: Embryo is produced using the patient's own genetic material / nucleus from the patient's cell (1 mark)
Stem cells are removed from the embryo (1 mark)
and are made to differentiate into the required cell type, then transplanted (1 mark)
Cells are genetically identical to the patient, so not rejected by the immune system (1 mark)
questions.tip: The point of therapeutic cloning is matching genes so there is no rejection.

questions.q: Scientists want to use stem cells to treat type 1 diabetes. Suggest how stem cells could be used, and explain one risk of this treatment.
questions.answer: Stem cells could be made to differentiate into insulin-producing pancreas cells and transplanted. Risk: the stem cells may be contaminated with a virus, which could pass on infection (or cells may divide uncontrollably forming a tumour).
ms: Stem cells made to differentiate into cells that produce insulin (1 mark)
Transplanted into the patient's pancreas/body (1 mark)
Risk: transfer of viral infection from contaminated stem cells (allow rejection if not from patient, or uncontrolled division/cancer) (1 mark)
questions.tip: The specification names viral infection as the risk of using stem cells. Learn it.

questions.q: A patient has a damaged spinal cord. Doctors could use embryonic stem cells, or adult stem cells from the patient's own bone marrow. Evaluate these two options.
questions.answer: Embryonic: can become any cell type including nerve cells, plentiful from spare IVF embryos, but ethical/religious objections (embryo destroyed) and risk of rejection unless from therapeutic cloning, risk of viral contamination. Bone marrow: no rejection if own cells, fewer ethical issues, but can only form some cell types (mainly blood cells), so may not produce nerve cells. Conclusion: embryonic more likely to work for nerve damage but raises more ethical issues.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed advantages and disadvantages of both types, linked to nerve repair and rejection/ethics, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Some advantages and disadvantages of both, or detailed points about one type. Conclusion may be missing.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple points, e.g. embryonic stem cells are unethical, bone marrow cells come from the patient.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: Evaluate means you must give a judgement at the end, backed by reasons.

questions.q: What are the products of protein digestion?
ms: Proteases break proteins down into amino acids.
questions.tip: Lipids give fatty acids AND glycerol. Carbohydrates give simple sugars.

questions.q: Which colour does Benedict's reagent turn when heated with a solution containing a large amount of glucose?
ms: Benedict's goes from blue through green and yellow to brick red as reducing sugar concentration increases.
questions.tip: Benedict's must be heated in a water bath (about 80 °C) for the colour to change.

questions.q: Which statement correctly explains why pepsin works in the stomach but not in the small intestine?
options: There is no protein in the small intestine
Bile breaks down pepsin into amino acids
The higher temperature in the small intestine denatures pepsin
The alkaline pH in the small intestine changes the shape of pepsin's active site
ms: Pepsin (a stomach protease) has an acidic optimum pH. The small intestine is slightly alkaline, which changes the active site shape so the substrate no longer fits.
questions.tip: Body temperature is the same throughout the gut. pH is the variable here.

questions.q: Describe the function of the small intestine and the stomach in digestion.
questions.answer: Stomach: churns food, produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens, and protease enzymes begin protein digestion. Small intestine: enzymes complete digestion and soluble products are absorbed into the blood.
ms: Stomach: any one of produces protease / acid kills bacteria / churns food (1 mark)
Small intestine: digestion completed and/or absorption of soluble food molecules into blood (1 mark)
questions.tip: Absorption happens mainly in the small intestine, not the stomach.

questions.q: Give the reagent used to test for lipids and state the positive result.
questions.answer: Ethanol (shake with sample then add water). A cloudy white emulsion forms. (Allow Sudan III: red layer.)
ms: Ethanol (allow Sudan III stain) (1 mark)
Cloudy white emulsion / milky layer (allow red top layer for Sudan III) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not mix up results: biuret purple, iodine blue-black, Benedict's brick red, ethanol cloudy.

questions.q: Name the three organs that produce amylase.
questions.answer: Salivary glands, pancreas, small intestine.
ms: Salivary glands (1 mark)
Pancreas (1 mark)
Small intestine (1 mark)
questions.tip: The liver makes bile, not enzymes. Do not include it.

questions.q: In an amylase experiment at pH 7, starch was fully broken down in 90 seconds. At pH 5 it took 180 seconds. Calculate the rate of reaction at each pH using rate = 1000 ÷ time, and state what the results show.
questions.answer: pH 7: 1000 ÷ 90 = 11.1 s⁻¹. pH 5: 1000 ÷ 180 = 5.6 s⁻¹. Rate is about twice as fast at pH 7, so pH 7 is closer to the optimum.
ms: Rate at pH 7 is double the rate at pH 5 / pH 7 nearer optimum pH (1 mark)
questions.tip: Shorter time = faster rate. The rate is inversely proportional to time.

questions.q: A student tested a food sample. Biuret reagent turned purple; iodine stayed orange-brown; Benedict's stayed blue after heating. Identify what the food contains, and describe one safety precaution for the Benedict's test.
questions.answer: Contains protein, no starch, no reducing sugar. Safety: heat in a water bath (not a direct flame) / wear eye protection.
ms: Protein present (1 mark)
No starch and no reducing sugar (both needed) (1 mark)
Use a water bath rather than a Bunsen flame / wear goggles (1 mark)
questions.tip: A negative result is still a result. Say what is absent as well as present.

questions.q: A student investigates the effect of pH on amylase. Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables. Explain why one control variable must be kept the same.
questions.answer: IV: pH (buffer solution). DV: time taken for starch to be broken down (iodine no longer turns blue-black). Controls: temperature (water bath), volume/concentration of starch and amylase. Temperature must be controlled because it also affects the rate of enzyme activity.
ms: Independent: pH (1 mark)
Dependent: time until iodine stays orange / starch is broken down (1 mark)
Two control variables, e.g. temperature, volume or concentration of amylase, volume or concentration of starch (1 mark)
Explanation: e.g. temperature affects rate of enzyme reaction, so changing it would mean the results were not only due to pH (a fair/valid test) (1 mark)
questions.tip: The dependent variable is what you measure. Here it is time, not 'colour'.

questions.q: A meal of bread contains starch. Describe what happens to the starch from when it enters the mouth until the products are used in body cells.
questions.answer: Amylase in saliva starts to digest starch to maltose/sugars in the mouth. Acid in stomach stops amylase. In the small intestine amylase from the pancreas continues digestion; sugars to glucose. Glucose is absorbed through villi into blood by diffusion and active transport. Carried in blood plasma to cells. Used in respiration in mitochondria to release energy, or stored as glycogen in the liver/muscles.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear sequence: digestion by amylase in mouth and small intestine, products named, absorption by villi into blood, transport in plasma, use in respiration or storage as glycogen.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Some correct stages, e.g. amylase breaks starch into sugars, absorbed in the small intestine, used for respiration. Some gaps in sequence.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. starch is broken down by enzymes, sugar goes into the blood.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: Name the enzyme, the site and the product at each stage.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood to the body?
ms: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta to the body.
questions.tip: Left = body (has a thicker muscle wall). Right = lungs.

questions.q: What is the function of plasma?
options: To form clots at a wound
To carry dissolved substances such as glucose, carbon dioxide and urea
To carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin
ms: Plasma is the liquid that transports dissolved substances, hormones, cells and platelets.
questions.tip: Oxygen is carried by red blood cells, not plasma.

questions.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle?
options: It must pump blood at higher pressure all around the body
It holds a larger volume of blood
It receives blood from the lungs at high pressure
ms: The left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body, so it needs to generate higher pressure.
questions.tip: Both ventricles pump the same volume. The difference is pressure.

questions.q: Name the blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs, and the vessel that carries blood to the heart muscle itself.
questions.answer: Pulmonary artery; coronary arteries.
ms: Pulmonary artery (1 mark)
Coronary artery (1 mark)
questions.tip: The pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood.

questions.q: A blood sample contains 5 000 000 red blood cells per mm³. Write this in standard form. A person with anaemia has 3.6 × 10^6 red cells per mm³. Calculate the percentage decrease compared with the normal sample.
questions.tip: Percentage decrease: divide the change by the ORIGINAL value.

questions.q: Explain why veins have valves but arteries do not.
questions.answer: Blood in veins is at low pressure, so valves prevent blood flowing backwards. Arteries have high pressure from the heart, keeping blood flowing forwards.
ms: Blood in veins is at low pressure (1 mark)
Valves prevent backflow (1 mark)
questions.tip: Valves stop backflow. Do not say they 'pump' blood.

questions.q: Describe the path of air from the mouth to the blood, and explain how alveoli are adapted for gas exchange.
questions.answer: Air passes down the trachea, into the bronchi, then bronchioles, then alveoli. Oxygen diffuses into capillaries. Alveoli: very large surface area (many alveoli), walls one cell thick (short diffusion distance), moist, rich capillary network maintains concentration gradient.
ms: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli in correct order (1 mark)
Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood capillaries (1 mark)
Large surface area / thin walls one cell thick (1 mark)
Good blood supply maintains a steep concentration gradient (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not write 'thin cell walls'. Animal cells have no cell walls. Write 'thin walls'.

questions.q: Describe the structure of the heart's blood supply and explain why a blockage in a coronary artery causes a heart attack.
questions.answer: Coronary arteries branch over the surface of the heart, supplying the heart muscle with oxygenated blood. A blockage stops oxygen and glucose reaching part of the heart muscle, so it cannot respire aerobically; the muscle cells stop contracting/die.
ms: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with (oxygenated) blood (1 mark)
Blockage stops oxygen (and glucose) reaching heart muscle (1 mark)
No (aerobic) respiration so muscle cannot contract / dies (1 mark)
questions.tip: The heart muscle needs its own blood supply. The blood inside the chambers does not supply it.

questions.q: A person has an irregular heartbeat. Explain how an artificial pacemaker helps, and why an irregular heartbeat can cause tiredness.
questions.answer: The natural pacemaker in the right atrium controls heart rate; an artificial pacemaker is an electrical device that corrects the irregular rhythm. With an irregular beat, less oxygenated blood reaches muscles, so less aerobic respiration, less energy released, causing tiredness.
ms: Artificial pacemaker is an electrical device that corrects/regulates the heart rhythm (1 mark)
Irregular beat means less blood/oxygen is pumped to the body's cells (1 mark)
Less aerobic respiration, so less energy released (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link through the chain: blood → oxygen → respiration → energy.

questions.q: Heart transplants can replace a failing heart. Artificial hearts are sometimes used while a patient waits. Give one advantage and two disadvantages of artificial hearts compared with donor transplants.
questions.answer: Advantage: no need to wait for a donor / not rejected by the immune system. Disadvantages: risk of blood clots so patient needs anticoagulant drugs, risk of infection, usually only temporary/battery must be carried, may wear out.
ms: Advantage: not rejected by immune system / no waiting for a donor (1 mark)
Disadvantage 1: blood clots / need for drugs to thin blood (1 mark)
Disadvantage 2: infection risk / mechanical failure / temporary only / limits movement (1 mark)
questions.tip: Make the comparison clear: 'unlike a donor heart...'

questions.q: During exercise, a student's heart rate rose from 72 to 156 beats per minute. Calculate the percentage increase. Then explain how changes in the heart and breathing supply muscles with what they need during exercise.
questions.answer: (156 - 72) ÷ 72 × 100 = 117% (3 s.f.). Heart rate increases so more blood is pumped per minute, delivering more oxygen and glucose to muscles and removing more carbon dioxide. Breathing rate and depth increase, so more oxygen diffuses into blood in the alveoli and more carbon dioxide is removed. This allows more aerobic respiration in muscle mitochondria, releasing more energy for contraction.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Correct calculation (117%) AND a detailed explanation linking heart rate and breathing changes to delivery of oxygen/glucose and removal of CO₂, and to increased aerobic respiration releasing energy for contraction.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Correct calculation with some explanation, or a detailed explanation with a calculation error.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Calculation attempted, or simple statements such as more oxygen is needed by muscles.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: In 6-markers that include a calculation, show the working clearly. Method marks still count if the final answer slips.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-communicable disease?
ms: Non-communicable diseases cannot be passed from person to person. Coronary heart disease is caused by fatty deposits in the coronary arteries.
questions.tip: Communicable = caused by a pathogen and can spread.

questions.q: In a town of 65 000 people, 260 people were diagnosed with lung cancer in one year. What is the rate per 100 000 people?
questions.tip: Divide by the population first, then multiply up to the 'per 100 000'.

questions.q: Give two risk factors for cardiovascular disease that a person could change through their lifestyle.
questions.answer: Smoking, diet (high in saturated fat), lack of exercise, obesity.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): smoking / diet high in fat or salt / lack of exercise / obesity. Do not accept genes or age (cannot be changed).
questions.tip: The question says 'could change', so genetic factors and age are wrong.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by a 'risk factor' for a disease.
questions.answer: Something (a factor in lifestyle or environment, or a substance in the body) that is linked to an increased chance/rate of developing that disease.
ms: Aspect of lifestyle / substance in body or environment (1 mark)
linked to an increased rate/likelihood of the disease (1 mark). Do not accept 'causes' the disease.
questions.tip: A risk factor increases the chance. It does not always cause the disease.

questions.q: Ionising radiation is a risk factor for cancer. Explain how cancer develops from a normal body cell.
questions.answer: Radiation causes a change (mutation) in the DNA/genes that control cell division. The cell divides uncontrollably by mitosis, forming a mass of cells called a tumour.
ms: Change/mutation in genes or DNA (1 mark)
Uncontrolled cell division / uncontrolled mitosis (1 mark)
Forms a tumour (1 mark)
questions.tip: Cancer is uncontrolled division. Do not say cells 'multiply'. Say 'divide by mitosis'.

questions.q:
Data from a study: Units of alcohol per week | Relative risk of liver disease
0 | 1.0
14 | 1.4
28 | 2.6
42 | 4.9
(a) Describe the relationship shown. (b) A newspaper says 'drinking alcohol causes liver disease'. Explain why this study alone does not prove this.
questions.answer: (a) As alcohol intake increases, risk of liver disease increases; the increase gets steeper at higher intakes (risk almost doubles from 28 to 42 units). (b) It shows a correlation only; other factors (e.g. obesity, diet, hepatitis infection) could also cause liver disease; a causal mechanism is needed.
ms: (a) Positive correlation: more alcohol, higher risk (1 mark)
(a) Use of data, e.g. risk increases faster at higher intakes / risk is 4.9 times higher at 42 units (1 mark)
(b) Correlation does not prove causation (1 mark)
(b) Other factors may be involved, e.g. diet, obesity, infection / need a mechanism (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always quote data with units when the question gives you a table.

questions.q: Explain how smoking increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.
questions.answer: Chemicals in smoke damage the lining of arteries; fatty deposits build up, narrowing coronary arteries (nicotine also raises heart rate/blood pressure; carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried).
ms: Damages the lining of the blood vessels / increases blood pressure (allow carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried) (1 mark)
Leads to build-up of fatty material narrowing the (coronary) arteries (1 mark)
questions.tip: Lung cancer is about tar. Cardiovascular disease is about arteries.

questions.q: In one country, 3.3 × 10^11 pounds is spent each year on treating non-communicable diseases. Total health spending is 3.7 × 10^13 pounds. Calculate the percentage of health spending used for non-communicable diseases. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.tip: Do the standard form division on your calculator in one go to avoid power errors.

questions.q: Explain why a malignant tumour can lead to secondary tumours in other parts of the body.
questions.answer: Malignant tumour cells invade neighbouring tissues; they can break off and spread to other parts of the body in the blood, forming secondary tumours.
ms: Cells invade neighbouring tissues / break away (1 mark)
Carried in the blood to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumours (1 mark)
questions.tip: Benign tumours are contained in one area, usually within a membrane.

questions.q: Type 2 diabetes cases are rising globally. Suggest and explain two economic costs of this increase for a country.
questions.answer: Cost of treatment/healthcare (medicines, monitoring, hospital care, NHS spending). Loss of working days/productivity as people are ill, reducing tax income. Funding research.
ms: Healthcare/treatment costs for the health service (1 mark)
Lost working days / reduced productivity or income (1 mark)
One point explained, e.g. costs rise because the disease is long-term and needs lifelong management (1 mark)
questions.tip: Separate economic costs (money) from human costs (illness, death). The question asks only for economic.

questions.q: Explain why non-communicable diseases are often caused by interactions of several risk factors. Use obesity and type 2 diabetes as an example.
questions.answer: Many diseases have more than one risk factor, e.g. a person who eats a high-sugar diet and does little exercise is more likely to be obese. Obesity is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, so the factors combine. Genetic factors also affect the chance. Risk factors can increase each other's effect, so it is hard to identify one single cause.
ms: Many diseases are caused by the interaction of several factors (1 mark)
Example: poor diet/lack of exercise leads to obesity (1 mark)
Obesity is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes (1 mark)
Genetics/other factors also contribute, so a single cause is hard to identify (1 mark)
questions.tip: Show the chain: one factor leads to another, which increases the risk.

questions.q: What is the main function of xylem tissue?
options: Transporting water and mineral ions from the roots
Transporting dissolved sugars to growing tissues
ms: Xylem carries water and mineral ions upwards from the roots to the stem and leaves.
questions.tip: Xylem = water up. Phloem = food (sugars) both directions.

questions.q: Through which openings is most water vapour lost from a leaf?
ms: Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata, mainly on the lower surface of the leaf.
questions.tip: Guard cells control the size of the stomata. They are not the openings themselves.

questions.q: A potometer bubble moves 45 mm in 10 minutes. The capillary tube has a radius of 0.5 mm. Using volume = πr² × length, what is the rate of water uptake?
ms: Volume = π × 0.5² × 45 = 35.3 mm³. 35.3 ÷ 10 = 3.5 mm³ per minute.
questions.tip: Use the radius, not the diameter, and remember to divide by time.

questions.q: Name the process by which sugars are moved through a plant, and the tissue it happens in.
questions.answer: Translocation; phloem.
ms: Translocation (1 mark)
Phloem (1 mark)
questions.tip: Spelling matters for key terms. Learn 'translocation' exactly.

questions.q: Give two organs of a plant that work together to transport substances.
questions.answer: Roots, stem, leaves.
ms: Any two of roots / stem / leaves (1 mark each). Do not accept xylem or phloem (these are tissues).
questions.tip: Know the difference: xylem and phloem are tissues; roots, stems and leaves are organs.

questions.q: Explain why water loss from a plant increases on a hot, dry, windy day.
questions.answer: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy so they evaporate and diffuse faster. Low humidity and wind keep the concentration of water vapour outside the leaf low, so the concentration gradient stays steep.
ms: Higher temperature increases rate of evaporation/diffusion (particles have more energy) (1 mark)
Dry air: lower humidity outside leaf so steeper concentration gradient (1 mark)
Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, maintaining the gradient (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'concentration gradient of water vapour'. 'Wind blows the water away' alone will not score.

questions.q: A student set up a potometer. Give three precautions she should take when setting it up so that the results are valid.
questions.answer: Cut the shoot underwater (and at an angle), assemble the apparatus underwater so no air enters, seal joints with petroleum jelly so it is airtight/watertight, dry the leaves, allow time to acclimatise before readings.
ms: Any three (1 mark each): cut stem underwater / set up apparatus underwater / no air bubbles except the one being measured / seal joints with petroleum jelly / dry leaves before starting / allow time to equilibrate / same shoot for each condition
questions.tip: Air in the xylem stops water uptake. That is why it is cut underwater.

questions.q: Phloem tissue has sieve tube elements with pores in the end walls and few sub-cellular structures. Xylem is made of dead cells with walls strengthened by lignin. Explain how each structure is adapted to its function.
questions.answer: Phloem: pores in end walls (sieve plates) let cell sap move from one cell to the next; few organelles so the sap flows more easily. Xylem: dead cells form hollow continuous tubes so water flows freely; lignin strengthens the walls to withstand pressure and supports the plant.
ms: Phloem: pores allow cell sap/sugar solution to move between cells (1 mark)
Phloem: little/no cytoplasm or organelles so flow is not obstructed (1 mark)
Xylem: hollow tube with no end walls allows continuous flow of water (1 mark)
Xylem: lignin strengthens walls / supports plant / stops collapse (1 mark)
questions.tip: Pair each feature with a 'so that' about its function.

questions.q: Leaves of plants that live in dry deserts often have fewer stomata, and the stomata are found in pits. Suggest how these features help the plant survive.
questions.answer: Fewer stomata means fewer openings for water vapour to diffuse out, so less transpiration. Stomata in pits trap humid air, reducing the concentration gradient of water vapour, so water loss is slower. The plant conserves water in a dry environment.
ms: Fewer stomata reduces water loss by transpiration (1 mark)
Pits trap moist/humid air near stomata (1 mark)
so the concentration gradient of water vapour is reduced (1 mark)
questions.tip: Unfamiliar context: apply the transpiration factors you already know.

questions.q: Which type of pathogen causes measles?
ms: Measles is a viral disease spread by inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs.
questions.tip: Measles, HIV and TMV are viruses. Salmonella and gonorrhoea are bacteria.

questions.q: Which feature of the body is a non-specific defence?
ms: Stomach acid kills pathogens and works against all pathogens, so it is non-specific.
questions.tip: Antibodies are specific to one antigen. Skin, nose, trachea and stomach are non-specific.

questions.q: How does Salmonella cause the symptoms of food poisoning?
options: The virus lives and reproduces inside cells
The protist damages red blood cells
The fungus produces spores that block the gut
ms: Salmonella bacteria secrete toxins that cause fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea.
questions.tip: Bacteria make you ill with toxins; viruses damage cells as they reproduce inside them.

questions.q: Give two ways the spread of gonorrhoea can be reduced.
questions.answer: Use of a barrier method of contraception such as a condom; treatment of infected people with antibiotics (and tracing sexual partners).
ms: Condoms / barrier contraception (1 mark)
Antibiotic treatment of infected people (allow contact tracing, testing) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Gonorrhoea is now often resistant to penicillin, so other antibiotics are used.

questions.q: Describe how malaria is spread and give two ways its spread can be controlled.
questions.answer: Malaria is caused by a protist; it is spread by mosquitoes (vectors) when they bite. Control: stop mosquitoes breeding (drain standing water, insecticides), use mosquito nets.
ms: Spread by mosquitoes (vectors) when they feed on blood (1 mark)
Any two control methods (1 mark each): mosquito nets / insecticide / remove standing water to stop breeding / anti-malarial drugs
questions.tip: Malaria is a protist, not a bacterium or virus.

questions.q: A gardener notices purple-black spots on the leaves of her roses, which then turn yellow and drop early. Name the disease, and explain why it reduces the growth of the plant and how it can be treated.
questions.answer: Rose black spot (a fungal disease). Fewer leaves / less chlorophyll means less photosynthesis, so less glucose for growth. Treat with fungicides and remove and destroy affected leaves.
ms: Rose black spot (1 mark)
Reduced photosynthesis because leaves are lost / yellow (1 mark)
So less glucose made for growth/respiration (1 mark)
Fungicides and/or remove and destroy infected leaves (1 mark)
questions.tip: The link to reduced photosynthesis is the mark most students miss.

questions.q: Explain how tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) spreads between plants and how growers reduce its spread.
questions.answer: Spread by contact between plants (and on hands/tools of workers). Growers remove and destroy infected plants / wash hands and tools / grow resistant varieties.
ms: Spread by direct contact (allow on hands/tools) (1 mark)
Remove and destroy infected plants / hygiene / resistant varieties (1 mark)
questions.tip: TMV is a virus, so fungicides and antibiotics do not work.

questions.q: Explain why a person who has had chickenpox as a child usually does not get it again.
questions.answer: The first infection caused lymphocytes to make specific antibodies and memory cells were produced. On re-infection, memory cells cause a faster production of more antibodies, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop.
ms: White blood cells (lymphocytes) produce antibodies specific to the antigen (1 mark)
Memory cells remain in the blood (1 mark)
On re-infection antibodies are made more rapidly and in larger amounts, destroying pathogen before symptoms (1 mark)
questions.tip: Antibodies are specific to antigens on the pathogen. Use both words.

questions.q: In a clinical trial of a new drug, 200 patients received the drug and 200 received a placebo. After 6 months, 124 patients in the drug group and 30 in the placebo group had improved. Calculate the percentage that improved in each group, and explain why a placebo group was used.
questions.answer: Drug: 124 ÷ 200 × 100 = 62%. Placebo: 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%. The placebo group acts as a control to show whether the effect is due to the drug and not to the patients' expectations (placebo effect).
ms: Drug group: 62% (1 mark)
Placebo group: 15% (1 mark)
Placebo acts as a control / comparison (1 mark)
to show the improvement is due to the drug and not a psychological effect (1 mark)
questions.tip: Some people improve on a placebo. That is why you compare against it.

questions.q: Antibiotics have greatly reduced deaths from bacterial diseases. Explain why it is now difficult to develop new antibiotics fast enough.
questions.answer: Bacteria mutate and resistant strains spread by natural selection faster than new drugs can be developed; developing and testing a new drug takes many years and is expensive.
ms: Resistant strains of bacteria emerge/spread (due to mutation and overuse of antibiotics) (1 mark)
Drug development and testing takes many years / is expensive (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two sides: bacteria evolve fast, drug development is slow.

questions.q: Which gas is a product of photosynthesis?
ms: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
questions.tip: Reactants: CO₂ and water. Products: glucose and oxygen.

questions.q: A plant is kept at a low light intensity but a high CO₂ concentration. Which is most likely the limiting factor?
ms: The factor in shortest supply limits the rate. Here light is low, so light intensity limits the rate.
questions.tip: Increasing a non-limiting factor will not increase the rate.

questions.q: A lamp is 10 cm from pondweed. It is moved to 15 cm. Using light intensity ∝ 1/d², by what percentage does the light intensity fall?
ms: New intensity = (10/15)² = 0.444 of the original, so it falls by 1 - 0.444 = 0.556, about 56%.
questions.tip: The new intensity is 44% of the original. The question asks for the fall, not the new value.

questions.q: Give two ways a plant uses the glucose it makes in photosynthesis, apart from respiration.
questions.answer: Converted to starch for storage; cellulose for cell walls; combined with nitrate ions to make amino acids/proteins; converted to fats or oils for storage.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): starch for storage / cellulose for cell walls / amino acids or proteins (with nitrate ions) / fats or oils for storage
questions.tip: For amino acids, say glucose is combined with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil.

questions.q: Name the green pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Chlorophyll.
ms: Chlorophyll (1 mark). Do not accept chloroplast.
questions.tip: Chloroplast is the structure; chlorophyll is the pigment inside it.

questions.q: In the pondweed practical, the student counted bubbles per minute at different lamp distances. Give two control variables and explain why the student should leave the pondweed for a few minutes at each new distance before counting.
questions.answer: Control variables: temperature (use a beaker of water as a heat filter or LED lamp), CO₂ concentration (same amount of sodium hydrogencarbonate), same piece of pondweed, same type of lamp. Leave so the rate of photosynthesis can adjust to the new light intensity before measuring.
ms: Control variable 1, e.g. temperature (1 mark)
Control variable 2, e.g. CO₂ concentration / same pondweed / same lamp (1 mark)
To let the plant acclimatise / rate stabilise at the new light intensity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Lamps give off heat. Controlling temperature is the classic control variable here.

questions.q: Explain why photosynthesis is described as an endothermic reaction.
questions.answer: Energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light. The energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and used to make glucose, which stores energy.
ms: Energy transferred from surroundings to the chloroplasts (1 mark)
by light (1 mark)
Energy absorbed/taken in, so endothermic (energy stored in glucose) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Endothermic = energy taken in. Light is the energy source.

questions.q: Explain why sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to the water in a pondweed photosynthesis investigation.
questions.answer: It releases carbon dioxide into the water, so CO₂ is not a limiting factor and only light intensity affects the rate.
ms: Provides carbon dioxide (1 mark)
so CO₂ does not limit the rate / so light is the only variable affecting the rate (1 mark)
questions.tip: This is a control: you want only the independent variable to change the rate.

questions.q: A farmer adds paraffin heaters to her greenhouse. These increase the temperature and CO₂ concentration. Yield rose from 12 000 kg to 15 600 kg per season. Calculate the percentage increase in yield, and explain why the farmer must consider costs before adding even more heaters.
questions.answer: (15 600 - 12 000) ÷ 12 000 × 100 = 30%. Beyond a point another factor (e.g. light) becomes limiting, so more heaters increase cost without increasing yield; the farmer must balance extra income against extra cost to make a profit.
ms: Another factor (light / temperature too high) becomes limiting, so yield stops increasing (1 mark)
Extra cost may be more than the extra income from the yield, reducing profit (1 mark)
questions.tip: Greenhouse economics: rate must increase enough to pay for the extra input.

questions.q:
Data for the rate of photosynthesis at two CO₂ concentrations:
Light intensity (arbitrary units) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Rate at 0.04% CO₂ | 10 | 18 | 22 | 22 | 22
Rate at 0.10% CO₂ | 10 | 19 | 28 | 35 | 35
Explain what limits the rate at light intensity 1, and at light intensity 4 for 0.04% CO₂.
questions.answer: At intensity 1 both CO₂ levels give the same rate, so light intensity is limiting. At intensity 4 with 0.04% CO₂, rate has levelled off at 22 but is higher (35) at 0.10% CO₂, so CO₂ concentration is limiting.
ms: At light intensity 1, light is the limiting factor (1 mark)
because raising CO₂ does not increase the rate (both 10) (1 mark)
At intensity 4 at 0.04% CO₂, CO₂ concentration is limiting, as rate is higher (35) with more CO₂ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use data from the table to justify each limiting factor.

questions.q: Where does anaerobic respiration take place in a muscle cell?
ms: Anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm. Aerobic respiration is completed in the mitochondria.
questions.tip: Mitochondria are only needed for aerobic respiration.

questions.q: What is the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast?
ms: Anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells is fermentation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
questions.tip: Muscles make lactic acid only. Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which is NOT an example of a metabolic reaction?
options: Amino acids being joined to form proteins
Diffusion of oxygen into a cell
Excess proteins being broken down to form urea
ms: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions in a cell or body. Diffusion is a physical process, not a chemical reaction.
questions.tip: Metabolic reactions are chemical reactions controlled by enzymes.

questions.q: Give two ways that animals use the energy released by respiration.
questions.answer: Muscle contraction (movement); keeping warm (body temperature); building larger molecules from smaller ones (e.g. proteins); active transport.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): muscle contraction / keeping warm / building larger molecules / active transport. Do not accept 'to make energy'.
questions.tip: Respiration releases energy. Never write that it 'produces' or 'makes' energy.

questions.q: A student investigated the effect of temperature on yeast respiration by counting bubbles of CO₂ in one minute. Results: 20 °C | 12 bubbles ; 30 °C | 26 bubbles ; 40 °C | 41 bubbles ; 60 °C | 2 bubbles. Explain the results.
questions.answer: From 20 to 40 °C the rate increases because enzymes and substrate have more kinetic energy, so more collisions and enzyme-substrate complexes form. At 60 °C the rate falls because enzymes in yeast are denatured: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.
ms: Rate increases from 20 to 40 °C because more kinetic energy / more collisions (1 mark)
At 60 °C enzymes are denatured (1 mark)
Active site changes shape so substrate no longer fits (1 mark)
questions.tip: Respiration is controlled by enzymes, so explain using enzyme ideas.

questions.q: Suggest one improvement to the yeast bubble-counting method and explain why it would make the results more accurate.
questions.answer: Collect the gas in an upturned measuring cylinder or gas syringe to measure the volume, because bubbles can be different sizes and are easy to miscount.
ms: Measure the volume of gas with a gas syringe / measuring cylinder (1 mark)
because bubbles vary in size (1 mark)
and counting fast bubbles leads to errors, so volume gives a more accurate measure (1 mark)
questions.tip: Bubble counting is a classic weakness. Volume of gas is the classic improvement.

questions.q: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells.
questions.answer: Both use glucose and release energy, both controlled by enzymes. Aerobic needs oxygen, anaerobic does not. Aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic produces lactic acid. Aerobic releases much more energy per glucose because glucose is fully oxidised; anaerobic oxidation is incomplete.
ms: Similarity: both break down glucose / both release energy (1 mark)
Aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not (1 mark)
Products: CO₂ and water vs lactic acid (1 mark)
Aerobic releases more energy because of complete oxidation of glucose (1 mark)
questions.tip: For the energy difference, use the phrase 'incomplete oxidation of glucose'.

questions.q: A sprinter has a high concentration of lactic acid in her muscles after a race. Explain how the lactic acid is removed from her body after the race.
questions.answer: Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver. In the liver, lactic acid is converted back into glucose. This needs oxygen, which is why breathing stays fast after exercise (repaying the oxygen debt).
ms: Lactic acid is carried in the blood to the liver (1 mark)
It is converted back into glucose (1 mark)
which requires oxygen (the oxygen debt) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Higher tier key point: liver converts lactic acid back to glucose.

questions.q:
Scientists measured the oxygen consumption of an athlete. At rest: 0.3 dm³ per minute. During running: 3.0 dm³ per minute. For 5 minutes after stopping: 1.2 dm³ per minute on average.
Calculate how many times greater oxygen consumption was during running than at rest. Then explain the changes in oxygen consumption during and after the run.
questions.answer: 3.0 ÷ 0.3 = 10 times. During running muscles contract more so need more energy; more aerobic respiration needs more oxygen, so heart and breathing rates increase. Some anaerobic respiration occurs as oxygen supply is not enough, producing lactic acid and an oxygen debt. After stopping, consumption stays above resting (1.2 vs 0.3) because extra oxygen is needed to react with/remove lactic acid in the liver (converted back to glucose).
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Correct calculation (10 times) plus a full explanation of increased aerobic respiration during exercise, anaerobic respiration producing lactic acid, oxygen debt and its repayment in the liver after exercise.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Correct calculation and an explanation of either the increase during exercise or the raised consumption after exercise.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Calculation attempted, or simple statements, e.g. muscles need more oxygen when running.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: Use the data in your answer. Quote the 1.2 vs 0.3 dm³ per minute after exercise.

questions.q: What is the function of a sensory neurone?
options: To pass impulses across a synapse
To carry impulses from the CNS to effectors
To carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system
ms: Sensory neurones carry electrical impulses from receptors to the CNS (brain or spinal cord).
questions.tip: Receptors detect stimuli. Neurones carry impulses.

questions.q: In the ruler drop test, why should the person use the same hand in every trial?
options: It makes the ruler fall faster
It is a control variable, so the results are valid
ms: Using the same (dominant) hand keeps a control variable constant so only the independent variable affects reaction time.
questions.tip: Variables that are kept the same are control variables.

questions.q: Name the two parts of the central nervous system.
questions.answer: Brain and spinal cord.
ms: Brain (1 mark)
Spinal cord (1 mark)
