questions.tip: Nerves are not part of the CNS.

questions.q: Give two conditions inside the body that are controlled by homeostasis.
questions.answer: Blood glucose concentration, body temperature, water levels.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): blood glucose concentration / body temperature / water levels
questions.tip: Say 'blood glucose concentration', not just 'sugar'.

questions.q: Name the receptor, coordinator and effector when a person hears a phone ring and picks it up.
questions.answer: Receptor: ear (sound receptors). Coordinator: brain/CNS. Effector: muscles in the arm/hand.
ms: Receptor: (cells in the) ear (1 mark)
Coordinator: brain / CNS (1 mark)
Effector: (arm) muscles (1 mark)
questions.tip: Effectors are muscles or glands. Do not write 'hand' alone; say 'muscles in the hand/arm'.

questions.q: Explain how information passes from a relay neurone to a motor neurone across a synapse.
questions.answer: An electrical impulse arrives at the end of the relay neurone, causing a chemical (neurotransmitter) to be released. The chemical diffuses across the gap (synapse). It binds to receptors on the motor neurone, starting a new electrical impulse.
ms: Impulse triggers release of a chemical (neurotransmitter) (1 mark)
Chemical diffuses across the gap (1 mark)
Chemical stimulates a new electrical impulse in the next neurone (1 mark)
questions.tip: The impulse is electrical in neurones but chemical across the synapse.

questions.q:
Ruler drop results for a student. Distance caught (cm): 18, 20, 22, 19, 21.
(a) Calculate the mean distance. (b) Using t = √(2d ÷ 9.8), with d in metres, calculate the mean reaction time to 2 significant figures.
ms: (b) convert 20 cm = 0.20 m (1 mark)
questions.tip: Convert cm to m before using the equation.

questions.q: Explain why reflex actions are important to animals.
questions.answer: They are automatic and rapid, so they protect the body from harm (e.g. pulling away from heat) without the delay of conscious thought.
ms: Automatic / do not involve the conscious brain (1 mark)
Rapid, so reduces damage / protects the body (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two key words: automatic and rapid.

questions.q: A student wants to find out whether people who play computer games have faster reaction times. Suggest a suitable hypothesis and give two variables she should control.
questions.answer: Hypothesis: people who play computer games regularly have shorter reaction times than people who do not. Controls: same hand (dominant), same ruler and drop method, same time of day/no caffeine, similar age.
ms: Testable hypothesis linking gaming to faster/shorter reaction time (1 mark)
Control variable 1, e.g. dominant hand / same ruler (1 mark)
Control variable 2, e.g. age / caffeine intake / tiredness / same person dropping (1 mark)
questions.tip: A hypothesis is a testable prediction that states a relationship.

questions.q: A student says the ruler drop test is not a reliable way to compare two people's reaction times. Suggest two ways to improve the investigation and explain why each would improve it.
questions.answer: Repeat each test many times and calculate a mean, to reduce the effect of random errors. Have the same person drop the ruler from the same height with no warning (or use a computer test), so the catcher cannot predict the drop. Same hand, same starting position.
ms: Repeat and calculate a mean (1 mark) to reduce the effect of random error / anomalies (1 mark)
Any one further improvement with reason: same dropper/no warning so cannot anticipate / same hand / ruler start at zero / use a computer timer for more precise measurement (1 mark)
questions.tip: Repeats improve repeatability. A mean reduces the effect of random error.

questions.q: A person treads on a drawing pin and immediately lifts their foot before feeling pain. Explain how this response happens and why it is important. Refer to the structures involved.
questions.answer: Pain receptors in the foot detect the stimulus. An electrical impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord. At a synapse, a chemical diffuses to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, then across another synapse to a motor neurone. The impulse travels to the effector (leg muscles), which contract, lifting the foot. This is a reflex: automatic and rapid, does not involve the conscious part of the brain, so it reduces damage. The brain later receives impulses so pain is felt afterwards.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Full reflex arc in order (receptor, sensory, relay in spinal cord, motor, effector muscle), synapses with chemical transmission, and explanation that the response is fast/automatic so avoids injury and does not involve the conscious brain.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Most of the reflex arc in order with a reason it is important; synapses may be missing.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. nerves send a message to muscles which move the foot.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: Name all three neurones in order and say the relay neurone is in the spinal cord.

questions.q: Which organ monitors and controls blood glucose concentration?
ms: The pancreas detects blood glucose concentration and releases insulin (or glucagon).
questions.tip: The liver stores glycogen, but the pancreas is the gland that controls the response.

questions.q: How is type 1 diabetes usually treated?
ms: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas produces too little insulin, so insulin is injected.
questions.tip: Type 2 is first treated with diet and exercise.

questions.q: Glucagon is released when blood glucose falls. What does glucagon cause?
options: Glucose to be converted into glycogen
Cells to take up more glucose
Glycogen in the liver to be converted into glucose
ms: Glucagon makes the liver convert glycogen back into glucose, which is released into the blood.
questions.tip: Spelling counts: glycogen (stored), glucagon (hormone), glucose (sugar).

questions.q: Name the gland that produces adrenaline and give one effect adrenaline has on the body.
questions.answer: Adrenal gland. Increases heart rate (boosts delivery of oxygen and glucose to brain and muscles).
ms: Adrenal gland (1 mark)
Increases heart rate / increases oxygen and glucose delivery to muscles and brain (1 mark)
questions.tip: Adrenaline prepares the body for 'fight or flight'.

questions.q: A person with type 2 diabetes has a blood glucose concentration that stays high after a meal. Explain why, and give two ways it can be treated.
questions.answer: In type 2 diabetes body cells no longer respond to insulin, so less glucose moves from the blood into cells. Treatment: carbohydrate-controlled diet and an exercise regime (allow medication).
ms: Body cells do not respond to insulin (are resistant) (1 mark)
Carbohydrate-controlled diet (1 mark)
Exercise regime (allow drugs) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Type 2: insulin is still made but cells do not respond. Type 1: pancreas makes too little.

questions.q:
A person's blood glucose was measured after a glucose drink.
Time (minutes) | 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120
Blood glucose (mg/dm³) | 900 | 1500 | 1200 | 950 | 900
Calculate the rate of fall in blood glucose between 30 and 90 minutes, and explain why it falls.
questions.answer: (1500 - 950) ÷ 60 = 9.2 mg/dm³ per minute. Pancreas releases insulin, which causes glucose to move from the blood into cells; in liver and muscle it is converted into glycogen for storage.
ms: = 9.2 mg/dm³ per minute (allow 9.17) (1 mark)
Insulin released, causing glucose to move into cells / be stored as glycogen (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rate = change ÷ time. Include the units 'per minute'.

questions.q: Describe how the pituitary gland is involved in controlling other glands.
questions.answer: The pituitary is in the brain and secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions. These hormones act on other glands to stimulate them to release their own hormones (e.g. FSH and LH from the pituitary act on the ovaries; FSH stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen).
ms: Secretes (several) hormones into the blood in response to body conditions (1 mark)

These hormones act on other glands, stimulating them to release their own hormones, with an example, e.g. FSH stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen / a pituitary hormone stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine (1 mark)
questions.tip: That is why the pituitary is called the 'master gland'.

questions.q: Thyroxine is released by the thyroid gland and stimulates the basal metabolic rate. The pituitary gland releases a hormone that stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. High levels of thyroxine in the blood inhibit the release of this pituitary hormone. Explain how negative feedback keeps the level of thyroxine in the blood within normal limits.
questions.answer: If the thyroxine level falls, the pituitary releases more of its stimulating hormone, so the thyroid releases more thyroxine and the level rises. If the thyroxine level rises too high, the release of the pituitary hormone is inhibited, so the thyroid releases less thyroxine and the level falls. A change in the level triggers a response that reverses the change, keeping the level close to normal.
ms: Low thyroxine: pituitary releases more of the (stimulating) hormone (1 mark)
so the thyroid releases more thyroxine and the level rises (1 mark)
High thyroxine inhibits release of the pituitary hormone, so less thyroxine is released (1 mark)
The change is reversed so the level returns to normal (1 mark). Allow the pituitary hormone named as TSH, but the name is not required.
questions.tip: Negative feedback always reverses the change. Say what happens if the level is too high AND too low.

questions.q: Compare the way the nervous system and the endocrine system bring about responses.
questions.answer: Nervous: electrical impulses along neurones; very fast; short-lasting; acts on a precise area. Endocrine: hormones (chemicals) carried in the blood; slower; longer-lasting; can act on target organs anywhere in the body.
ms: Electrical impulses vs chemical hormones (1 mark)
Neurones vs carried in the blood (1 mark)
Nervous is faster and shorter-acting; hormones slower and longer-lasting (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use comparative words: 'faster', 'whereas', 'longer-lasting'.

questions.q: Suggest why people with type 1 diabetes must monitor their blood glucose more carefully when they exercise.
questions.answer: Exercise increases respiration in muscles, using more glucose, so blood glucose can fall too low (hypoglycaemia) if they have injected their usual dose of insulin.
ms: Muscles respire more so use more glucose from the blood (1 mark)
Blood glucose may fall too low with the usual insulin dose, so dose/food intake must be adjusted (1 mark)
questions.tip: Unfamiliar context: link exercise to respiration, then to glucose use.

questions.q: Which hormone is the main male reproductive hormone, produced by the testes?
ms: Testosterone stimulates sperm production and is made in the testes.
questions.tip: FSH is made in the pituitary in both sexes.

questions.q: Roughly how often is an egg released in a typical menstrual cycle?
ms: Ovulation happens about once every 28 days, around day 14 of the cycle.
questions.tip: Ovulation happens AT day 14, but the cycle repeats every 28 days.

questions.q: Which hormone maintains the lining of the uterus in the second half of the menstrual cycle?
ms: Progesterone maintains the uterus lining. When its level falls, menstruation begins.
questions.tip: Oestrogen builds the lining. Progesterone maintains it.

questions.q: Give two non-hormonal methods of contraception.
questions.answer: Condoms/diaphragms (barrier), spermicidal agents, abstinence around ovulation, surgical sterilisation.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): condom / diaphragm / spermicide / abstaining around ovulation / sterilisation. Allow copper IUD.
questions.tip: Hormonal implants and the pill are not acceptable answers here.

questions.q: Explain how barrier methods of contraception and spermicides each prevent pregnancy.
questions.answer: Barrier methods (condoms, diaphragms) stop sperm reaching an egg. Spermicidal agents kill or disable sperm. Both prevent fertilisation.
ms: Barrier methods prevent sperm reaching the egg (1 mark)
Spermicides kill or disable sperm (1 mark)
So fertilisation cannot happen (1 mark)
questions.tip: Contraception works by preventing fertilisation or implantation. Say which.

questions.q: Describe the role of oestrogen in the menstrual cycle.
questions.answer: Oestrogen is produced in the ovaries. It causes the lining of the uterus to thicken/build up. (Higher) It inhibits FSH production and stimulates LH release.
ms: Made by the ovaries (1 mark)
Causes the uterus lining to thicken (1 mark)
Inhibits FSH / stimulates LH release (1 mark)
questions.tip: Oestrogen has two Higher tier effects: inhibits FSH, stimulates LH.

questions.q: Explain how a contraceptive injection or implant containing progesterone prevents pregnancy.
questions.answer: Progesterone inhibits the maturation and release of eggs, so no egg is available for fertilisation; it lasts for months or years.
ms: Inhibits maturation and/or release of eggs (1 mark)
so fertilisation cannot occur (allow long-lasting / lasts months or years) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Progesterone-only methods stop eggs maturing and being released.

questions.q:
Data from an IVF clinic: Age of woman | Success rate (% of cycles leading to a birth)
Under 35 | 32
35-37 | 25
38-39 | 19
40-42 | 11
43-44 | 5
(a) Describe the trend. (b) Calculate the percentage decrease in success rate from 'under 35' to '40-42'. (c) Give one emotional and one physical stress of IVF.
questions.answer: (a) Success rate decreases as age increases. (b) (32 - 11) ÷ 32 × 100 = 66% (65.6%). (c) Emotional: low success rate so repeated failures are distressing. Physical: risk of multiple births / side effects of fertility drugs.
ms: (a) As age increases, success rate falls (1 mark)
(c) Emotional stress, e.g. disappointment when treatment fails (1 mark)
(c) Physical stress, e.g. multiple births risk, side effects of drugs, egg collection procedure (1 mark)
questions.tip: Percentage decrease uses the starting value (32) as the denominator.

questions.q: A woman is not ovulating because her FSH levels are too low. Explain how a fertility drug could help her become pregnant.
questions.answer: A drug containing FSH and LH is given. FSH stimulates eggs to mature in the ovary. LH stimulates the release of the egg (ovulation), so it can be fertilised.
ms: Drug contains FSH and LH (1 mark)
FSH causes eggs/follicles to mature (1 mark)
LH stimulates ovulation (1 mark)
questions.tip: Fertility drugs use FSH and LH. The pill uses oestrogen and progesterone.

questions.q: A couple are choosing between a contraceptive implant and condoms. Evaluate the two methods.
questions.answer: Implant: releases progesterone for several years, very effective, no need to remember daily, but does not protect against STIs, may have side effects, needs a medical procedure. Condoms: protect against STIs, no hormones/side effects, cheap and easy to get, but less effective if used incorrectly and must be used each time. Judgement: e.g. implant is better for long-term reliable contraception, condoms if STI protection is needed.
ms: Implant advantage: long-lasting / highly effective (1 mark)
Implant disadvantage: no STI protection / side effects (1 mark)
Condom advantage: protects against STIs / no hormones (1 mark)
Justified conclusion (1 mark)
questions.tip: Evaluate needs pros and cons of both plus a conclusion.

questions.q: What is a mutation?
options: A difference caused by the environment
A change in a DNA base sequence
ms: Mutations are changes in DNA. They happen continuously and most have no effect on the phenotype.
questions.tip: Mutation is a change in DNA. Variation is the differences between individuals.

questions.q: What is the probability that two parents, both with genotype Tt, will have a child with genotype TT?
ms: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. One out of four is TT = 25%.
questions.tip: Distinguish TT (homozygous dominant, 1/4) from 'shows the dominant phenotype' (3/4).

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of asexual reproduction?
options: It involves only one parent and produces clones
It involves the fusion of gametes
ms: Asexual reproduction uses mitosis, needs one parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones).
questions.tip: No gametes, no mixing of genetic information.

questions.q: A couple already have one child with cystic fibrosis. Neither parent has the disorder. What is the probability that their next child will have cystic fibrosis?
ms: Both parents must be carriers (Ff). Each pregnancy is independent, so the chance of ff is still 1/4.
questions.tip: Each fertilisation is independent. Previous children do not change the probability.

questions.q: State the difference between genotype and phenotype.
questions.answer: Genotype is the alleles an organism has (e.g. Bb). Phenotype is the characteristic that is expressed (e.g. brown eyes).
ms: Genotype: the combination of alleles (1 mark)
Phenotype: the characteristic shown/expressed (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give an example of each to make it clear you know the difference.

questions.q: Name the sex chromosomes found in human males and females.
questions.answer: Males XY, females XX.
ms: Males: XY (1 mark)
Females: XX (1 mark)
questions.tip: Sex chromosomes are one of the 23 pairs.

questions.q: Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele, D. A man with genotype DD has children with a woman who does not have polydactyly. Use a genetic diagram to find the probability that a child will have polydactyly.
questions.answer: Woman is dd. DD × dd: all offspring Dd. Probability = 100% (1).
ms: Woman's genotype is dd (1 mark)
Correct genetic diagram / gametes D and d giving all Dd (1 mark)
Probability = 1 / 100% (1 mark)
questions.tip: One copy of a dominant allele is enough to show the characteristic.

questions.q: Explain why meiosis is important for sexual reproduction.
questions.answer: It halves the number of chromosomes to make gametes (23 in humans), so when gametes fuse at fertilisation the normal number (46) is restored. It also produces genetic variation as all gametes are genetically different.
ms: Gametes have half the number of chromosomes so the full number is restored at fertilisation (1 mark)
Produces genetically different gametes / variation (1 mark)
questions.tip: Meiosis halves; fertilisation restores.

questions.q: Most phenotypic features are the result of multiple genes rather than one gene. Explain what this means for predicting a child's height.
questions.answer: Height is controlled by many genes (and the environment, e.g. diet), so it cannot be predicted from a simple Punnett square of one gene; there is a continuous range of heights.
ms: Many genes interact to control height (1 mark)
So it cannot be predicted with a single-gene genetic cross / environment also affects it (1 mark)
questions.tip: Single-gene inheritance only applies to a few characteristics, e.g. cystic fibrosis.

questions.q: Two rabbits with normal fur both have genotype Ww. W is the dominant allele for normal fur; w gives white fur. They have 48 offspring. (a) Predict the number of white offspring. (b) The actual number was 9. Suggest why this differs from the prediction.
questions.answer: (a) Ww × Ww gives 1 WW : 2 Ww : 1 ww, so 1/4 white. 48 × 1/4 = 12. (b) Fertilisation is random; ratios are probabilities and actual numbers vary, especially in small samples.
ms: (a) Correct genetic diagram / Punnett square (1 mark)
(a) Probability of ww = 1/4 (1 mark)
(b) Fertilisation is random / ratios are only probabilities / small sample size (1 mark)
questions.tip: Ratios predict probability. Real numbers rarely match exactly.

questions.q: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. A person with genotype Ff does not have the disorder. Explain why.
questions.answer: The dominant allele F is expressed; one copy of the dominant allele is enough to produce the normal (functional) characteristic. The recessive allele f is only expressed when two copies are present (ff). The person is a carrier.
ms: F is dominant, so it is expressed when present (1 mark)
Recessive allele only expressed if two copies / homozygous recessive (1 mark)
The person is a carrier who can pass on the allele (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'carrier' for heterozygous people with a recessive disorder allele.

questions.q: Scientists have sequenced the whole human genome. Explain why this is important for medicine, and discuss the ethical issues of screening embryos for genetic disorders.
questions.answer: Genome knowledge helps search for genes linked to diseases, helps understand and treat inherited disorders (e.g. cystic fibrosis), and tracing human migration patterns. Embryo screening: in IVF, a cell can be tested before implantation; benefits include reducing suffering and lifelong treatment costs. Issues: expensive, embryos with the allele are destroyed (some think this is wrong), could lead to 'designer babies', implies people with disorders are less valued, false results possible.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear explanation of how the genome helps medicine (finding disease genes, treating inherited disorders) and a balanced discussion of several ethical, economic and social issues of embryo screening, with arguments for and against.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Some uses of genome research and some issues of screening, but limited balance or detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. it can find diseases, some people think it is wrong.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: Ethical answers need both sides. Use words like 'however' and 'on the other hand'.

questions.q: Who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
ms: Darwin proposed natural selection after observations made on a round-the-world expedition.
questions.tip: Darwin = natural selection. Linnaeus = classification system and binomial names.

questions.q: Carl Woese proposed the three-domain system. Which are the three domains?
ms: The three domains are Archaea (primitive bacteria often in extreme environments), Bacteria (true bacteria) and Eukaryota.
questions.tip: Archaea are prokaryotes but are a separate domain from bacteria.

questions.q: Two populations of the same species are separated by a mountain range for many thousands of years. Eventually they cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring. What has happened?
ms: When populations change so much that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, they have formed two new species.
questions.tip: Definition of species: can interbreed to produce FERTILE offspring.

questions.q: Give two ways fossils can be formed.
questions.answer: From parts of organisms that have not decayed (conditions lack oxygen, moisture or are too cold); when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay; as preserved traces such as footprints, burrows and root pathways.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): parts that have not decayed because of lack of oxygen/moisture/temperature / replacement of parts by minerals / preserved traces e.g. footprints or burrows
questions.tip: Mention WHY decay did not happen: no oxygen, no moisture, too cold.

questions.q: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection is now widely accepted. Describe two types of evidence that support the theory, and explain how later discoveries about inheritance support it.
questions.answer: Fossils show how organisms have changed over millions of years. Antibiotic resistance in bacteria shows natural selection happening quickly: resistant strains survive and reproduce. It is now known that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes, which explains how favourable variations are inherited.
ms: Fossils show that organisms have changed gradually over time (1 mark)
Development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria (resistant bacteria survive and reproduce) (1 mark)
Characteristics are now known to be passed on to offspring in genes, explaining how variations are inherited (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the evidence the specification uses: fossils and antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

questions.q: Describe how scientists could produce a crop plant that is resistant to a herbicide using genetic engineering.
questions.answer: The gene for herbicide resistance is identified and cut out using enzymes. It is inserted into a vector (e.g. bacterial plasmid or virus). The vector inserts the gene into the plant cells at an early stage of development. The plant cells are grown into plants with the desired characteristic.
ms: Gene is cut out of the DNA of an organism using enzymes (1 mark)
Inserted into a vector such as a plasmid or virus (1 mark)
Vector used to insert gene into plant cells (1 mark)
at an early stage of development, so the plant develops with the characteristic (1 mark)
questions.tip: Higher tier: use the words 'enzymes', 'vector' and 'early stage of development'.

questions.q: Explain why an evolutionary tree can be used to show how organisms are related.
questions.answer: It shows common ancestors; organisms that share a more recent common ancestor are more closely related. It uses current classification data and, for extinct organisms, fossil data.
ms: Shows common ancestors / branching points (1 mark)
More recent common ancestor means more closely related (allow uses fossil/DNA data) (1 mark)
questions.tip: The closer the branch point, the more closely related.

questions.q: Describe how scientists classify organisms using the Linnaean system.
questions.answer: Organisms are grouped by their structure and characteristics into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Each is given a binomial name made of genus and species.
ms: Groups in order: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species (1 mark)
Binomial name made of genus and species (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mnemonic: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

questions.q: Data: in a hospital, the percentage of Staphylococcus infections resistant to an antibiotic rose from 2% in 1995 to 24% in 2015. (a) Calculate the percentage point increase per year. (b) Suggest two ways hospitals can reduce the spread of resistant strains.
questions.answer: (a) (24 - 2) ÷ 20 = 1.1 percentage points per year. (b) Doctors should not prescribe antibiotics for viral or non-serious infections; patients should complete the course; strict hygiene/hand washing; isolate infected patients.
ms: (a) 22 ÷ 20 = 1.1 per year (1 mark)
(b) Any two (1 mark each): do not prescribe for non-serious or viral infections / complete the course / hand washing or hygiene / isolate patients / restrict agricultural use
questions.tip: Find the time span carefully: 1995 to 2015 is 20 years.

questions.q: Peppered moths were mostly pale before industrial pollution blackened tree trunks with soot. After the Industrial Revolution, most moths were dark. Explain this change using natural selection.
questions.answer: Variation existed: some moths had a mutation giving dark colour. On soot-blackened trees, dark moths were better camouflaged, so fewer were eaten by birds. Dark moths survived and reproduced, passing on the allele for dark colour. Over many generations, the proportion of dark moths increased.
ms: Variation in colour caused by mutation / alleles (1 mark)
Dark moths camouflaged so less likely to be eaten; more survive and breed (1 mark)
Pass on the allele for dark colour; proportion increases over generations (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not say moths 'changed colour to match'. Individuals do not adapt in natural selection.

questions.q: Many farmers grow GM crops that produce a toxin that kills insect pests. Evaluate the use of these crops.
questions.answer: Advantages: higher yields, less insecticide spraying (cheaper, less harm to other insects). Disadvantages: effect on wild flowers and insects not fully known, concern the genes may spread to wild plants, possible effect on human health not fully explored. Judgement given.
ms: One advantage, e.g. increased yield / less insecticide needed (1 mark)
One disadvantage, e.g. may harm other insect populations / genes may transfer to wild plants / long-term health effects unknown (1 mark)
Justified conclusion (1 mark)
questions.tip: Evaluate: give both sides and finish with a reasoned judgement.

questions.q: Which of these is a biotic factor?
ms: Biotic factors are living factors: availability of food, new predators, new pathogens, competition.
questions.tip: Abiotic = non-living (light, temperature, water, pH, CO₂, wind, mineral content).

questions.q: What is the original source of energy for most food chains?
ms: Producers use light energy for photosynthesis. Producers then pass on energy as biomass.
questions.tip: The producer is the first organism, but the Sun is the source of energy.

questions.q: A student places 8 quadrats, each 0.5 m², in a field of 1500 m². She counts a total of 28 dandelions. What is the estimated population?
ms: Total area sampled = 8 × 0.5 = 4 m². Mean density = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 per m². 7 × 1500 = 10 500.
questions.tip: Work out the total area sampled first. Many students forget the quadrat is not 1 m².

questions.q: In a predator-prey graph, the number of hares falls sharply. What is the most likely effect on the lynx (predator) population, and when?
options: Lynx numbers do not change because they eat other food
Lynx numbers fall before the hares, causing the hare decline
Lynx numbers fall shortly afterwards because there is less food
Lynx numbers rise at the same time because there is more space
ms: With less prey, fewer predators survive and breed, so the predator population falls after a time lag.
questions.tip: Predator peaks and troughs lag behind prey peaks and troughs.

questions.q: Give two things plants compete with each other for.
questions.answer: Light, space, water, mineral ions from the soil.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): light / space / water / mineral ions. Do not accept 'food' or 'nutrients' alone.
questions.tip: Plants make their own food. 'Food' will not get the mark.

questions.q: Describe what is meant by interdependence.
questions.answer: Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. If one species is removed it can affect the whole community.
ms: Species depend on other species (for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal) (1 mark)
Removing one species affects others in the community (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give a specific example of dependence for full marks.

questions.q: Describe how decomposers help to recycle materials in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste. They respire, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, which plants use for photosynthesis. Mineral ions are returned to the soil for plants to absorb.
ms: Microorganisms break down dead material / waste (1 mark)
Respire, releasing CO₂ to the atmosphere (1 mark)
Return mineral ions to the soil (1 mark)
questions.tip: Decomposers release CO₂ by respiration. That is the link to the carbon cycle.

questions.q:
A student used a transect from a tree into an open field. Results:
Distance from tree (m) | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8
Light intensity (arbitrary units) | 12 | 25 | 48 | 70 | 72
Number of daisies per quadrat | 0 | 2 | 7 | 13 | 14
Describe how to carry out the transect, and use the data to explain the distribution of daisies.
questions.answer: Lay a tape measure from the tree into the field; place a quadrat at regular intervals (every 2 m); count daisies and measure light intensity with a light meter at each point. Daisies increase as light intensity increases, as more light allows more photosynthesis; near the tree it is shady, so few daisies grow.
ms: Tape measure laid out from the tree (1 mark)
Quadrats placed at regular intervals and daisies counted (1 mark)
Daisies increase as light intensity increases (using data) (1 mark)
More light gives more photosynthesis / shade from the tree limits growth (1 mark)
questions.tip: Random quadrats estimate population; transects show distribution along a gradient.

questions.q: Describe the processes in the carbon cycle that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and that return it.
questions.answer: Removed: photosynthesis by green plants and algae. Returned: respiration by plants, animals and decomposers; combustion of fuels.
ms: Removed by photosynthesis (1 mark)
Returned by respiration (of animals, plants and microorganisms) (1 mark)
Returned by combustion / burning of fossil fuels or wood (1 mark)
questions.tip: Photosynthesis is the only process that removes CO₂ from the air in the carbon cycle at GCSE.

questions.q: A pesticide accidentally kills most of the bacteria and fungi in the soil of a woodland. Suggest what would happen to the recycling of carbon and to the growth of the trees over the following years. Explain your answer.
questions.answer: Dead leaves and organisms would not be decayed, so carbon stays locked in dead material and less CO₂ is released by microbial respiration. Mineral ions would not be returned to the soil, so trees absorb fewer minerals and grow less.
ms: Dead material not decayed / builds up (1 mark)
Less CO₂ released by respiration of decomposers, so less carbon returned to the atmosphere (1 mark)
Mineral ions not returned to the soil, so tree growth is reduced (1 mark)
questions.tip: Decomposers return both carbon (as CO₂) and mineral ions.

questions.q: Polar bears have small ears, thick fur and a thick layer of fat. Some extremophile bacteria live in hot springs at 80 °C. Explain how the bear's features help it survive, and suggest why the bacteria can survive at a temperature that would kill most organisms.
questions.answer: Small ears give a small surface area to volume ratio so less heat is lost. Thick fur and fat insulate, reducing heat loss. The bacteria have enzymes that are not denatured at high temperatures (different shape/structure, higher optimum temperature).
ms: Small ears reduce surface area for heat loss (1 mark)
Fur and fat provide insulation, reducing heat loss (1 mark)
Bacteria's enzymes have a high optimum temperature (1 mark)
so they do not denature at 80 °C (1 mark)
questions.tip: For extremophiles, link to enzymes and denaturing, which you know from Paper 1.

questions.q: Which human activity reduces biodiversity by removing habitat?
ms: Building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste reduce the land available for other organisms.
questions.tip: Hedgerows, breeding programmes and recycling all help biodiversity.

questions.q: Which of these is a greenhouse gas that is also released by cattle and rice fields?
ms: Methane is produced by cattle and rice paddy fields and is a greenhouse gas.
questions.tip: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain, not global warming.

questions.q: Why is it important to protect peat bogs rather than use peat as compost?
options: Peat is needed by farmers for animal feed
Peat stores carbon, and when it decays or burns it releases CO₂
Peat contains fossils that prove evolution
Peat absorbs oxygen from the air
ms: Peat bogs store carbon. Draining or using peat lets microorganisms decay it aerobically, releasing CO₂ and contributing to global warming, and destroys the bog habitat.
questions.tip: Two marks often asked: release of CO₂ AND loss of habitat/biodiversity.

questions.q: Give two pollutants that can kill plants and animals in water.
questions.answer: Sewage, fertiliser, toxic chemicals.
ms: Any two (1 mark each): sewage / fertiliser / toxic chemicals. Allow named examples, e.g. pesticides, oil.
questions.tip: AQA lists sewage, fertiliser and toxic chemicals for water. Learn that list.

questions.q: A country cut down 3.1 × 10^6 hectares of rainforest in a year. Its total rainforest area was 6.6 × 10^7 hectares. Calculate the percentage of rainforest lost in that year, and give two consequences of large-scale deforestation.
questions.answer: 3.1 × 10^6 ÷ 6.6 × 10^7 × 100 = 4.7%. Consequences: more CO₂ released by burning/decay and less CO₂ absorbed by photosynthesis; loss of habitat and biodiversity.
ms: Increased atmospheric CO₂ (burning and less photosynthesis) (1 mark)
Reduced biodiversity / loss of habitats (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use your calculator's standard form button carefully. 4.7%, not 47%.

questions.q: Describe four programmes used to protect biodiversity.
questions.answer: Breeding programmes for endangered species; protection and regeneration of rare habitats; reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows where there is monoculture; reducing deforestation and CO₂ emissions by governments; recycling to reduce landfill.
ms: Any four (1 mark each): breeding programmes / protecting and regenerating rare habitats / field margins and hedgerows / reduce deforestation and carbon emissions / recycling instead of landfill
questions.tip: Each point should be a distinct programme. Do not repeat the same idea.

questions.q: Explain how acid rain is produced and why it reduces biodiversity.
questions.answer: Burning fossil fuels releases sulfur dioxide (and nitrogen oxides), which dissolve in rain water forming acid rain. Acid rain damages trees/plants and lowers the pH of lakes, killing organisms.
ms: Sulfur dioxide (or nitrogen oxides) from burning fuels dissolve in rain (1 mark)
Kills plants/trees or aquatic organisms by acidifying soil or water (1 mark)
questions.tip: Acid rain is air pollution. Do not confuse it with the greenhouse effect.

questions.q: A farmer replaces a hedgerow with a larger field to grow a single crop. Explain the effect this has on biodiversity, and suggest why reintroducing field margins could help.
questions.answer: Removing hedgerows removes habitats and food for many species (insects, birds), reducing biodiversity; monoculture has only one plant species. Field margins of wild flowers and grasses provide habitat and food so more species can live there, increasing biodiversity (and pollinators/pest predators that may help the crop).
ms: Habitat/food source for many species is lost (1 mark)
Monoculture means fewer species, so biodiversity falls (1 mark)
Field margins provide habitats/food for wild species, increasing biodiversity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Monoculture is the key word for growing one crop over a large area.

questions.q: Global average temperatures are rising. Explain how this could change the distribution of species, and why it threatens biodiversity.
questions.answer: Species may move to new areas as the climate there becomes suitable (e.g. towards the poles or uphill); species unable to move may die out in their current area. Changes in migration patterns; sea levels rise causing habitat loss; seasonal timing changes; this can lead to extinction and loss of biodiversity because species cannot adapt quickly enough.
ms: Species distribution shifts to cooler areas (towards the poles / higher altitude) (1 mark)
Changes in migration patterns (1 mark)
Loss of habitat, e.g. flooding from rising sea levels / melting ice (1 mark)
Species unable to adapt or move may become extinct, reducing biodiversity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link each change to a biological consequence for full marks.

questions.q: A government plans to protect biodiversity. Evaluate the following options: (1) captive breeding programmes, (2) protecting rainforest from deforestation, (3) encouraging recycling to reduce landfill.
questions.answer: Breeding programmes: save specific endangered species, but expensive, limited genetic variation, animals may not survive release. Protecting rainforest: protects huge numbers of species and stores carbon, but economic conflict with local farmers/biofuel industries, hard to enforce. Recycling: reduces land used for landfill and pollution, cheap per person, but smaller direct effect on biodiversity. Conclusion: protecting rainforest probably benefits the most species, though combining methods is best.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Benefits and drawbacks of all three options, using biological reasons (habitat, number of species, carbon storage, genetic variation) and economic/social conflicts, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Benefits and/or drawbacks of at least two options with some reasoning; conclusion may be weak.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements about one or two options, e.g. recycling stops landfill.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.tip: Every 'evaluate' needs a conclusion that compares options, not just a list.

questions.q: Which ion has the same electronic structure as an argon atom (2,8,8)?
ms: Chlorine is 2,8,7. Gaining one electron gives Cl⁻ = 2,8,8, the same as argon. Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and F⁻ are all 2,8 (like neon).
questions.tip: Work out the electrons in the ION, not the atom: add electrons for negative ions, subtract for positive ions.

questions.q: Gallium has two isotopes: 60.1% gallium-69 and 39.9% gallium-71. What is the relative atomic mass of gallium to 1 decimal place?
ms: Ar = (60.1 × 69 + 39.9 × 71) ÷ 100 = (4146.9 + 2832.9) ÷ 100 = 69.798 = 69.8. It is closer to 69 because gallium-69 is more abundant.
questions.tip: Sense-check: the answer must lie closer to the more abundant isotope. 70.0 is just the unweighted average.

questions.q: Why do chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 have the same chemical properties?
options: They have the same mass number
They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same relative atomic mass
They have the same number of electrons in the outer shell
ms: Chemical properties depend on the electrons, especially the outer shell. Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons and so the same electronic structure (2,8,7).
questions.tip: Isotopes differ ONLY in neutrons. Neutrons affect mass and physical properties, not chemical reactions.

questions.q: Which scientist provided the experimental evidence for neutrons in the nucleus?
ms: Chadwick showed the existence of neutrons about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted. Thomson discovered the electron, Rutherford (with Geiger and Marsden) the nucleus, Bohr the electron shells.
questions.tip: Learn the order: Thomson (plum pudding), Rutherford (nucleus), Bohr (shells), Chadwick (neutron).

questions.q: A sulfide ion is written as ³²S²⁻. The atomic number of sulfur is 16. Give the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion.
questions.answer: 16 protons, 16 neutrons, 18 electrons.
ms: 16 protons AND 16 neutrons (1 mark)
18 electrons (1 mark). Do not accept 14 electrons (2− means two electrons GAINED).
questions.tip: A 2− charge means two extra electrons. Students who subtract lose the mark.

questions.q:
Element X has the electronic structure 2,8,8,2.
(a) State the group and period of X.
(b) Is X a metal or a non-metal? Explain your answer.
(c) Give the formula of the compound formed between X and chlorine.
questions.answer: (a) Group 2, period 4. (b) Metal, because it has 2 outer electrons which it loses to form a positive ion. (c) XCl₂.
ms: (a) Group 2 AND period 4 (1 mark): group = number of outer electrons, period = number of shells
(b) Metal (1 mark)
(b) It loses (2 outer) electrons to form positive ions / X²⁺ (1 mark). Do not accept 'it has few electrons'.
(c) XCl₂ (1 mark). Allow CaCl₂ only if X is identified as calcium.
questions.tip: Group comes from the outer shell, period from the number of shells. Mixing these up is very common.

questions.q:
Astatine is below iodine in Group 7. Predict:
(a) the state of astatine at room temperature
(b) whether astatine would react with potassium iodide solution.
Explain each prediction.
questions.answer: (a) Solid, because melting/boiling points increase down Group 7 and iodine is already a solid. (b) No reaction, because astatine is less reactive than iodine, so it cannot displace iodine from potassium iodide.
ms: (a) Solid (1 mark)
(a) Melting point / boiling point increases down the group (and iodine is already a solid) (1 mark)
(b) No reaction / no displacement (1 mark)
(b) Astatine is less reactive than iodine (because reactivity decreases down Group 7: outer shell further from nucleus, so it is harder to GAIN an electron) (1 mark)
questions.tip: For Group 7 reactivity the key idea is GAINING an electron. Writing 'loses electrons less easily' is a Group 1 answer and scores zero.

questions.q:
Rubidium is in Group 1, below potassium.
(a) Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of rubidium with water.
(b) Predict one way in which the reaction would differ from the reaction of potassium with water.
questions.answer: (a) 2Rb(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2RbOH(aq) + H₂(g). (b) It would be more vigorous / faster, e.g. it may explode or the hydrogen ignites immediately.
ms: (a) Correct formulae RbOH and H₂ (1 mark)
(a) Correctly balanced with correct state symbols (1 mark)
(b) More vigorous / more violent / faster reaction / explodes (1 mark). Do not accept 'produces more hydrogen' (same amount per mole).
questions.tip: Group 1 hydroxides are MOH, not M(OH)₂. Hydrogen must be H₂, so the equation needs 2 of everything except H₂.

questions.q:
Chlorine gas is bubbled through sodium bromide solution. The solution turns orange.
(a) Write the ionic equation for this reaction.
(b) Identify the species that is oxidised. Explain your answer in terms of electrons.
questions.answer: (a) Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. (b) Bromide ions are oxidised because they lose electrons.
ms: (a) Correct species Cl₂, Br⁻, Cl⁻, Br₂ (1 mark)
(a) Correctly balanced (1 mark). Na⁺ must not appear (spectator ion).
(b) Bromide ions / Br⁻ oxidised because they LOSE electrons (1 mark). Do not accept 'bromine is oxidised' without specifying the ion.
questions.tip: OIL RIG. Name the ion precisely: 'bromide ions lose electrons'. Saying 'bromine' (the element) is a different species.

questions.q: Bohr and Chadwick both changed the model of the atom after Rutherford's nuclear model. Describe the contribution of each scientist and the evidence that supported it.
questions.answer: Bohr suggested electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (in shells/energy levels); his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations. Chadwick provided evidence for neutral particles (neutrons) in the nucleus.
ms: Bohr: electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances / in fixed shells / energy levels (1 mark)
Bohr's calculations agreed with experimental observations (1 mark)
Chadwick: experimental evidence for neutrons (uncharged particles) in the nucleus (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'specific distances' or 'energy levels'. Vague 'electrons go round' does not get the Bohr mark.

questions.q:
Before Mendeleev, early periodic tables placed elements strictly in order of atomic weight.
Explain why Mendeleev's periodic table was more successful than earlier tables, and how the discovery of protons and isotopes later explained the arrangement of the modern periodic table.
questions.answer: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties; later discoveries (e.g. germanium) matched. He swapped some elements (e.g. tellurium/iodine) so that elements with similar properties were in the same group. Early tables were incomplete and some elements were placed in wrong groups. The modern table orders by atomic number (protons). Isotopes explain why ordering by atomic weight did not always work: an element's relative atomic mass depends on its mix of isotopes, so some elements with more protons have lower Ar.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A detailed, coherent explanation covering both Mendeleev's methods and evidence AND the later explanation using atomic number and isotopes, with linked reasoning.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): A clear explanation of Mendeleev's success OR the role of protons/isotopes, with some linking; the other part may be brief.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. 'he left gaps', with little explanation.
Indicative content: early tables incomplete, some elements put in inappropriate groups when strict atomic weight order was used
Indicative content: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements; predicted their properties; elements later discovered (e.g. gallium, germanium) fitted the gaps with properties close to predictions
Indicative content: changed order of some pairs (Te/I) so elements with similar properties lined up in groups
Indicative content: modern table is in order of atomic number (proton number); isotopes mean Ar is not proportional to proton number, so atomic weight order was sometimes wrong
questions.tip: Top band needs the LINK: 'isotopes explain why some pairs had to be swapped'. Listing facts without that link caps you at Level 2.

questions.q: Explain why the mass number of an atom gives approximately the mass of the atom, even though electrons are not counted.
questions.answer: Mass number = protons + neutrons, which each have relative mass 1. Electrons have a very small mass, so almost all the mass is in the nucleus.
ms: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1 / mass number counts protons + neutrons (1 mark)
Electrons have very small (negligible) mass so almost all the mass is in the nucleus (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the phrase 'very small' for the electron's mass. Do not say electrons have 'no mass'.

questions.q: Iron forms Fe³⁺ ions and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of iron(III) sulfate?
ms: Charges must balance: 2 × (+3) = +6 and 3 × (−2) = −6. So Fe₂(SO₄)₃. Brackets are needed around a molecular ion when there is more than one.
questions.tip: Swap-and-drop the charges, then put brackets round SO₄. Fe₃(SO₄)₂ comes from swapping the wrong way.

questions.q: Substance X melts at 1710 °C, is insoluble in water and does not conduct electricity when solid or molten. What type of structure does X have?
ms: A very high melting point means a giant structure. No conduction even when molten rules out ionic (ions free when molten) and metallic (always conducts). So giant covalent (this is silicon dioxide).
questions.tip: Use the molten conductivity test: ionic conducts when molten, giant covalent (except graphite) does not.

questions.q: Graphite is soft but has a very high melting point. Which statement explains both properties?
options: There are weak forces between the layers, but many strong covalent bonds within the layers must be broken to melt it
Each carbon has one delocalised electron, which holds the layers together weakly
Graphite is a simple molecule with strong intermolecular forces
The layers are held by strong covalent bonds, but the atoms in each layer are held by weak forces
ms: Soft: weak intermolecular forces between layers let layers slide. High melting point: melting needs the many strong covalent bonds in each layer to be broken.
questions.tip: Keep the two forces separate: weak BETWEEN layers, strong covalent WITHIN layers.

questions.q: Which observation shows that a substance has a simple molecular structure?
options: It has a low boiling point and does not conduct electricity
It is hard and has a high melting point
ms: Simple molecular substances have weak intermolecular forces (low melting/boiling points) and no overall charge or free electrons, so they do not conduct.
questions.tip: Dissolving in water does not identify a structure: many ionic AND some molecular substances dissolve.

questions.q:
Magnesium oxide (Mg²⁺ O²⁻) melts at 2852 °C. Sodium chloride (Na⁺ Cl⁻) melts at 801 °C. Both have giant ionic lattices.
Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point.
questions.answer: Magnesium and oxide ions have higher charges (2+ and 2−) than sodium and chloride ions (1+ and 1−), so the electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions are stronger, so more energy is needed to overcome them.
ms: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have greater / double charges (than Na⁺ and Cl⁻) (1 mark)
Stronger electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions (1 mark)
More energy needed to overcome these forces / break the lattice (1 mark). Do not accept 'stronger covalent bonds' or 'intermolecular forces': max 1 mark if either is used.
questions.tip: Ionic answers must say 'electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions'. Any mention of molecules or intermolecular forces loses marks.

questions.q: Explain why copper is malleable and why it conducts electricity.
questions.answer: Copper is a giant structure of positive ions arranged in layers; the layers can slide over each other, so it is malleable. It has delocalised electrons that can move through the structure and carry charge.
ms: Layers of (positive) ions / atoms (1 mark)
Layers can slide over each other (1 mark)
Delocalised electrons move through the structure and carry (electrical) charge (1 mark). Do not accept 'free ions'.
questions.tip: 'Delocalised electrons that move through the whole structure' is the phrase examiners want. 'Free electrons' is accepted but 'ions move' is not.

questions.q:
The table shows data about four substances.
Substance | Melting point (°C) | Conducts when solid? | Conducts when molten?
A | 1083 | yes | yes
B | 770 | no | yes
C | −95 | no | no
D | 3550 | no | no
Identify the type of structure of each substance. Give a reason for each.
questions.answer: A giant metallic: high mp, conducts solid and molten. B giant ionic: conducts only when molten (ions free to move). C simple molecular: low mp, no conduction. D giant covalent: very high mp, no conduction.
ms: A: giant metallic, because it conducts when solid (delocalised electrons) (1 mark)
B: giant ionic, because it conducts only when molten (ions free to move) (1 mark)
C: simple molecular, because of very low melting point (weak intermolecular forces) and no conduction (1 mark)
D: giant covalent, because of very high melting point and no conduction (1 mark)
questions.tip: Each mark needs the structure AND the reason. A bare list of four names scores at most 2.

questions.q: Pentane (C₅H₁₂) has a higher boiling point than propane (C₃H₈). Explain why.
questions.answer: Pentane molecules are larger, so the intermolecular forces between them are stronger, so more energy is needed to overcome them.
ms: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces (1 mark)
More energy needed to overcome the intermolecular forces (1 mark). Any statement that covalent bonds break scores 0 for this mark.
questions.tip: Boiling a simple molecular substance never breaks covalent bonds. Write 'intermolecular forces' every time.

questions.q:
A student writes: 'When water boils, the covalent bonds between the hydrogen and oxygen atoms break.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
questions.answer: When water boils, only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome. The strong covalent bonds within each molecule do not break, so the molecules are still H₂O in the gas.
ms: Intermolecular forces / forces between molecules are overcome (1 mark)
Covalent bonds within the molecules do not break / are strong (1 mark)
The gas is still made of H₂O molecules / no new substance forms (1 mark)
questions.tip: Be precise: 'between molecules' versus 'within molecules'. This distinction is a grade 7/8 discriminator.

questions.q:
Ammonia, NH₃, is a gas at room temperature.
(a) Describe the bonding in an ammonia molecule.
(b) Explain why ammonia is a gas at room temperature.
questions.answer: (a) Nitrogen shares one pair of electrons with each of three hydrogen atoms: three single covalent bonds (N also has a lone pair). (b) It is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces, so little energy is needed to overcome them; its boiling point is below room temperature.
ms: (a) Three covalent bonds / three shared pairs of electrons between N and H (1 mark)
(b) Small molecules / simple molecular (1 mark)
(b) Weak intermolecular forces need little energy to overcome / boiling point below room temperature (1 mark)
questions.tip: A covalent bond is a SHARED PAIR of electrons. 'Sharing electrons' alone may be marked down.

questions.q: Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes. Give two properties of carbon nanotubes and a use linked to each.
questions.answer: High tensile strength, used to reinforce materials (e.g. tennis rackets). Good electrical (and thermal) conductivity, used in electronics.
ms: High tensile strength / high length to diameter ratio with linked use (reinforcing materials) (1 mark)
Conducts electricity / heat with linked use (electronics, nanotechnology) (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Strong' needs to be 'high tensile strength' for full credit in a precise answer.

questions.q: Compare the electrical conductivity of sodium chloride, graphite, diamond and copper. Explain your answers in terms of structure and bonding.
questions.answer: Sodium chloride: giant ionic lattice; does not conduct when solid because ions are fixed in place; conducts when molten or dissolved because ions are free to move and carry charge. Graphite: each carbon forms 3 covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that moves between layers, so it conducts. Diamond: each carbon forms 4 covalent bonds, no delocalised electrons or ions, does not conduct. Copper: metallic bonding with delocalised electrons that move through the structure carrying charge, conducts as solid and liquid.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): All four substances covered with correct conductivity AND an explanation based on mobile charged particles (ions or delocalised electrons) for each, including conditions for NaCl.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): At least three substances correctly described with some explanation in terms of ions or electrons.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Some correct statements about conductivity with little or no explanation.
Indicative content: NaCl solid: ions in fixed positions, cannot move; molten/aqueous: ions free to move and carry charge
Indicative content: graphite: 3 bonds per C, one delocalised electron per C atom, electrons move along layers
Indicative content: diamond: 4 covalent bonds per C, all outer electrons in bonds, no free charged particles
Indicative content: copper: delocalised electrons move through the structure. Do not accept 'electrons move' for NaCl.
questions.tip: Saying 'NaCl conducts because electrons move' is a classic error that drops you a level. Ionic = ions move.

questions.q: What is the relative charge of a proton?
ms: A proton has relative charge +1 and relative mass 1.
questions.tip: Do not confuse the proton (+1) with the electron (−1).

questions.q: State why an atom has no overall charge.
questions.answer: It has the same number of protons and electrons.
ms: Equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative) (1 mark). Do not accept 'protons and neutrons cancel'.
questions.tip: Neutrons are neutral and play no part in this. Name protons AND electrons.

questions.q:
Lithium reacts with chlorine to form lithium chloride.
(a) Name the type of compound formed.
(b) Give the colour of lithium chloride.
questions.answer: (a) Ionic compound (a salt / metal chloride). (b) White.
ms: (a) Ionic / salt (1 mark)
(b) White (solid) (1 mark). Allow colourless solution if dissolved.
questions.tip: Group 1 compounds are white solids that dissolve to form colourless solutions.

questions.q: Which type of bonding is found in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?
ms: Hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so they share a pair of electrons: a covalent bond.
questions.tip: Non-metal + non-metal = covalent. Intermolecular forces are BETWEEN molecules, not a bond within one.

questions.q: Give the state symbol used for a substance dissolved in water.
questions.answer: (aq)
ms: (aq) / aqueous (1 mark)
questions.tip: (l) is for pure liquids only, e.g. water itself or molten metal.

questions.q: Give two properties of ionic compounds.
questions.answer: High melting and boiling points; conduct electricity when molten or dissolved (not when solid).
ms: High melting point / boiling point (1 mark)
Conduct electricity when molten or in solution (1 mark). Do not accept 'conduct electricity' with no condition.
questions.tip: Always add the condition: 'when molten or dissolved'. Unqualified 'conducts' loses the mark.

questions.q: What is meant by a polymer? Give one example.
questions.answer: A very large molecule made of many small repeating units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds, e.g. poly(ethene).
ms: Very large / long-chain molecule made of many repeating units (1 mark)
Valid example, e.g. poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'very large molecules', not 'large compounds'.

questions.q:
What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂?
Ar: Mg = 24, N = 14, O = 16
ms: Mr = 24 + 2 × (14 + 3 × 16) = 24 + 2 × 62 = 148. 86 forgets the bracket multiplier; 100 doubles only the N.
questions.tip: Everything inside the bracket is multiplied by the subscript outside it.

questions.q:
How many oxygen atoms are in 0.1 mol of carbon dioxide molecules, CO₂?
(Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ per mole)
ms: 0.1 mol CO₂ contains 0.2 mol O atoms. 0.2 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²³. 6.02 × 10²² is molecules; 1.806 × 10²³ is ALL atoms.
questions.tip: Read whether the question asks for molecules, atoms of one element, or all atoms.

questions.q: What volume of a solution with a concentration of 15.0 g/dm³ contains 0.300 g of solute?
ms: Volume = mass ÷ concentration = 0.300 ÷ 15.0 = 0.0200 dm³ = 20.0 cm³. 4.50 comes from multiplying instead of dividing; 2.00 and 200 are conversion slips.
questions.tip: Volume comes out in dm³ first. Multiply by 1000 to get cm³.

questions.q:
Aluminium reacts with chlorine: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃
2.16 g of aluminium (Ar 27) is heated with 8.52 g of chlorine, Cl₂ (Mr 71). Which statement is correct?
options: Chlorine is in excess; 16.02 g AlCl₃ forms
Both react completely; 10.68 g AlCl₃ forms
Aluminium is in excess; 10.68 g AlCl₃ forms
Chlorine is in excess; 10.68 g AlCl₃ forms
ms: Moles Al = 2.16 ÷ 27 = 0.080. Moles Cl₂ = 8.52 ÷ 71 = 0.120. Ratio needed 2 : 3 = 0.080 : 0.120 exactly, so neither is in excess. Moles AlCl₃ = 0.080, mass = 0.080 × 133.5 = 10.68 g.
questions.tip: Always compare moles divided by the equation coefficients. Do not assume one reactant must be in excess.

questions.q:
Aluminium reacts with acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂
How many moles of hydrogen form when 0.30 mol of aluminium reacts with excess acid?
ms: Ratio Al : H₂ = 2 : 3. Moles H₂ = 0.30 × 3/2 = 0.45 mol. 0.20 uses the ratio upside down; 0.90 uses the HCl coefficient.
questions.tip: Write the two coefficients you need under the formulae, then scale. Ignore the species you are not asked about.

questions.q:
Calculate the number of moles in 9.8 g of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄.
Ar: H = 1, S = 32, O = 16
ms: Mr = 98 (1 mark)
Moles = 9.8 ÷ 98 = 0.10 (mol) (1 mark). Allow ECF from incorrect Mr.
questions.tip: Write Mr first and show the division: method marks are given even if the arithmetic slips.

questions.q:
A student dissolves 5.0 g of copper sulfate in water and makes the solution up to 200 cm³.
Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.
ms: Converts 200 cm³ to 0.200 dm³ (1 mark)
25 (g/dm³) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dividing by 200 instead of 0.200 gives 0.025: always convert cm³ to dm³ first.

questions.q:
Sodium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid:
Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
5.30 g of sodium carbonate (Mr 106) reacts with excess acid.
Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide (Mr 44) produced.
questions.answer: Moles Na₂CO₃ = 5.30 ÷ 106 = 0.0500; ratio 1:1 so 0.0500 mol CO₂; mass = 0.0500 × 44 = 2.20 g
ms: Moles of Na₂CO₃ = 5.30 ÷ 106 = 0.0500 (1 mark)
Uses 1 : 1 ratio, moles CO₂ = 0.0500 (1 mark)
Mass CO₂ = 2.20 g (1 mark). Correct answer with no working scores 3.
questions.tip: Three-step method: mass → moles, use the ratio, moles → mass. Label each step.

questions.q:
Ammonia is made by the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
Calculate the maximum mass of ammonia that can be made from 1.2 kg of hydrogen.
Ar: N = 14, H = 1. Give your answer in kg.
questions.answer: Moles H₂ = 1200 ÷ 2 = 600 mol; moles NH₃ = 600 × 2/3 = 400 mol; mass = 400 × 17 = 6800 g = 6.8 kg
ms: Converts 1.2 kg to 1200 g and finds moles H₂ = 600 (1 mark)
Uses ratio 3 : 2 to get 400 mol NH₃ (1 mark)
Mr NH₃ = 17 and mass = 6800 g (1 mark)
6.8 kg (1 mark). Allow ratio method using masses: 6 g H₂ → 34 g NH₃.
questions.tip: The mole ratio is 3 H₂ : 2 NH₃. Using 1 : 2 or 1 : 1 is the most common error.

questions.q:
Copper(II) oxide reacts with hydrogen: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O
A student heats 4.0 g of copper(II) oxide in a stream of hydrogen. She obtains 2.9 g of copper.
(a) Calculate the maximum mass of copper that could form. Ar: Cu = 63.5, O = 16. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
(b) Suggest two reasons why she obtained less copper than the maximum.
questions.answer: (a) Mr CuO = 79.5; moles = 4.0 ÷ 79.5 = 0.0503; mass Cu = 0.0503 × 63.5 = 3.2 g (3.19). (b) Not all the copper oxide was reduced (heated for too short a time); some copper reoxidised when hot copper met air; some solid lost when transferring/weighing.
ms: (a) Mr CuO = 79.5 and moles CuO = 4.0 ÷ 79.5 (= 0.0503) (1 mark)
(a) Mass Cu = 3.2 g (1 mark). Allow 3.19.

(b) Any one reason (1 mark): reaction incomplete / not all CuO reduced; hot copper reacted with oxygen in air when cooling (hydrogen flow stopped too soon); solid lost on transfer; copper oxide impure
(b) A second, different reason from the list (1 mark)
questions.tip: Reasons must be specific to THIS experiment. 'Human error' scores nothing.

questions.q:
A student needs 150 cm³ of sodium chloride solution with a concentration of 30 g/dm³.
(a) Calculate the mass of sodium chloride she must dissolve.
(b) She accidentally makes the solution up to 300 cm³ with the same mass of solid. State the new concentration and explain your answer.
questions.answer: (a) 30 × 0.150 = 4.5 g. (b) 15 g/dm³: the same mass is spread through twice the volume, so concentration halves.
ms: (a) Converts 150 cm³ to 0.150 dm³ (1 mark)
(a) 4.5 g (1 mark)
(b) 15 g/dm³ with reason: same mass of solute in double the volume (1 mark)
questions.tip: mass = concentration × volume in dm³. Keep the unit triangle in your head and convert cm³ first.

questions.q:
Calcium reacts with oxygen: 2Ca + O₂ → 2CaO
Calculate the mass of oxygen needed to react completely with 6.0 g of calcium.
Ar: Ca = 40, O = 16
ms: Moles Ca = 0.15 (1 mark)
Moles O₂ = 0.075 (ratio 2 : 1) (1 mark)
Mass O₂ = 2.4 g (Mr O₂ = 32) (1 mark). Using Mr 16 gives 1.2 g: max 2 marks.
questions.tip: Oxygen gas is O₂, Mr 32. Using 16 is a frequent lost mark.

questions.q:
2.8 g of iron reacts completely with 1.2 g of oxygen, O₂, to form 4.0 g of iron oxide, Fe₂O₃.
Use these masses to work out the balanced symbol equation. Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16
ms: Moles of all three: 0.050, 0.0375, 0.025 (1 mark)
Divides by smallest / converts to whole number ratio 4 : 3 : 2 (1 mark)
4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Divide by the SMALLEST value; if that gives 1.5 or 1.33, multiply all by 2 or 3 to get whole numbers.

questions.q:
A student has 50 cm³ of a solution with a concentration of 12 g/dm³. She adds water to make the total volume 250 cm³.
Calculate the new concentration in g/dm³.
questions.answer: Mass of solute = 12 × 0.050 = 0.60 g; new concentration = 0.60 ÷ 0.250 = 2.4 g/dm³
ms: Mass of solute = 0.60 g (1 mark)
2.4 g/dm³ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Adding water does not change the mass of solute, only the volume.

questions.q: A student calculates that a reaction should produce 0.44 g of carbon dioxide but measures a smaller mass loss. Explain why this can happen even though mass is conserved.
questions.answer: Some carbon dioxide dissolves in the solution instead of escaping; the reaction may not go to completion; the reactant may be impure; some gas may escape before the starting mass is recorded.
ms: Any one (1 mark): some CO₂ dissolves in the solution / stays in the flask; reaction does not go to completion; reactant is impure; gas escapes before the starting mass is recorded
A second, different reason from the list (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not say 'mass is destroyed'. Mass is conserved but it may not all be collected.

questions.q: Calculate the mass of 0.25 mol of sodium hydroxide, NaOH. Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1
ms: 10 g (1 mark)
questions.tip: mass = moles × Mr. Rearrange the triangle carefully.

questions.q: What is the name of the salt made when zinc oxide reacts with nitric acid?
ms: Nitric acid makes nitrates. Zinc oxide + nitric acid → zinc nitrate + water.
questions.tip: Nitric → nitrate, sulfuric → sulfate, hydrochloric → chloride. 'Nitride' is a different compound.

questions.q: Metal M displaces copper from copper sulfate solution but does not react with zinc sulfate solution. Where is M in the reactivity series?
ms: M is more reactive than copper (it displaces it) but less reactive than zinc (it cannot displace zinc). So M is between zinc and copper, e.g. iron.
questions.tip: A metal only displaces metals BELOW it in the reactivity series.

questions.q: In the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + Zn → 2Fe²⁺ + Zn²⁺, which statement is correct?
options: Zinc is reduced and Fe³⁺ is oxidised
Neither is oxidised or reduced because no oxygen is involved
Zinc is oxidised and Fe³⁺ is reduced
ms: Zinc loses two electrons (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻): oxidation. Each Fe³⁺ gains one electron (Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺): reduction.
questions.tip: Use electron transfer (OIL RIG), not oxygen. Reduction does not have to make a metal.

questions.q: The pH of a solution of hydrochloric acid is 2. The acid is diluted so that the hydrogen ion concentration is 1/10 of the original. What is the new pH?
ms: Each tenfold decrease in H⁺ concentration increases pH by 1. So pH 2 → pH 3.
questions.tip: Diluting an acid RAISES its pH. Remember: a factor of 10 = 1 pH unit.

questions.q: Give the general word equation for the reaction of an acid with a metal carbonate. Give one observation for this reaction.
questions.answer: acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide; fizzing / bubbles
ms: salt + water + carbon dioxide (all three) (1 mark)
Fizzing / effervescence / bubbles / carbonate disappears (1 mark). Do not accept 'gas is produced' (that is not an observation).
questions.tip: An observation is what you SEE. 'Carbon dioxide is given off' is a conclusion, not an observation.

questions.q:
Lithium oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.
(a) Write a balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
(b) Explain why lithium oxide is described as a base.
questions.answer: (a) Li₂O + 2HCl → 2LiCl + H₂O. (b) It reacts with (neutralises) an acid to form a salt and water.
ms: (a) Correct formulae Li₂O, LiCl, H₂O (1 mark)
(a) Balanced (1 mark)
(b) Neutralises acids / reacts with an acid to form a salt and water (1 mark)
questions.tip: A base is defined by what it DOES: neutralises acids. 'It is an alkali' is not enough, since many bases are insoluble.

questions.q: Explain why potassium cannot be extracted from potassium oxide by heating with carbon.
questions.answer: Potassium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove oxygen from (reduce) potassium oxide.
ms: Potassium is more reactive than carbon / above carbon in the reactivity series (1 mark)
So carbon cannot reduce the oxide / remove the oxygen (so electrolysis is used) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the word 'reduce'. Examiners want 'carbon can only reduce oxides of metals below it'.

questions.q:
Iron reacts with copper(II) sulfate solution.
(a) Write the two half equations for this reaction.
(b) Explain why this is a redox reaction.
questions.answer: (a) Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. (b) Iron atoms lose electrons (oxidation) and copper ions gain electrons (reduction) at the same time.
ms: (a) Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (1 mark)
(a) Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (1 mark)
(b) Oxidation and reduction happen together / both electron loss by Fe and electron gain by Cu²⁺ identified (1 mark)
questions.tip: In half equations, electrons go on the right for oxidation, on the left for reduction. Charges must balance.

questions.q:
Ethanoic acid is a weak acid. Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid.
Two solutions are made with the same concentration. Explain why the hydrochloric acid has a lower pH.
questions.answer: Hydrochloric acid is completely ionised in water, whereas ethanoic acid is only partially ionised. So at the same concentration, hydrochloric acid has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions, so a lower pH.
ms: Hydrochloric acid is fully / completely ionised (in aqueous solution) (1 mark)
Ethanoic acid is only partially ionised (1 mark)
So HCl has a greater concentration of H⁺ ions (so lower pH) (1 mark). Do not accept 'dissociated' alone without H⁺ link; do not accept 'stronger acid so lower pH' without explanation.
questions.tip: Use 'ionised', not 'dissolved'. Both acids dissolve completely; only one ionises completely.

questions.q: Describe how to prepare a pure, dry sample of zinc chloride crystals starting from zinc carbonate (an insoluble solid) and dilute hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: Warm a measured volume of dilute HCl in a beaker. Add zinc carbonate a spatula at a time, stirring, until fizzing stops and solid remains (excess). Filter to remove the excess zinc carbonate. Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to concentrate it until crystals begin to form. Leave to cool and crystallise. Filter/pat the crystals dry with filter paper or leave in a warm place.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A coherent, logically sequenced method that would produce pure, dry crystals, including adding excess, filtering, and crystallisation by partial evaporation then cooling, with reasons.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): A method with the main steps in a sensible order but some detail missing (e.g. how excess is judged, or drying).
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Some relevant steps but not in a workable order.
Indicative content: measure acid into beaker, warm gently
Indicative content: add zinc carbonate in small portions, stir, until no more fizzing and solid remains (excess ensures all acid used up)
Indicative content: filter to remove excess zinc carbonate

Indicative content: heat filtrate in evaporating basin until about half the water is gone / crystals form on a glass rod, then leave to cool; filter crystals and dry between filter paper. Do not accept 'heat until all the water evaporates' for top band.
questions.tip: Never boil to dryness for the top band: it can decompose the salt and gives a powder, not crystals.

questions.q: State the meaning of 'oxidation' and 'reduction' in terms of oxygen.
questions.answer: Oxidation is gain of oxygen; reduction is loss of oxygen.
ms: Oxidation = gain of oxygen (1 mark)
Reduction = loss of oxygen (1 mark)
questions.tip: At Higher you also need the electron definitions: oxidation is loss of electrons.

questions.q: Sodium hydroxide reacts with hydrochloric acid. Write the ionic equation for this reaction, including state symbols.
questions.answer: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
ms: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O (1 mark)
Correct state symbols (aq), (aq), (l) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Spectator ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻) do not appear in an ionic equation.

questions.q: A student adds dilute hydrochloric acid to magnesium, iron and copper. She uses the same mass of each metal. Explain why her method does not give a fair comparison of reactivity, and suggest an improvement.
questions.answer: Pieces of different metals may have different surface areas (e.g. ribbon vs filings), so use the same size/form of each metal (or same surface area), with the same volume and concentration of acid.
ms: Same mass does not mean same surface area / particle size (1 mark)
Use metal pieces of equal surface area / powders of same size, with same volume and concentration of acid and same temperature (1 mark)
questions.tip: Fair test answers must name the variable that is NOT controlled, not just say 'make it fair'.

questions.q: Name the ion that makes a solution alkaline.
questions.answer: Hydroxide ion, OH⁻
ms: OH⁻ / hydroxide (1 mark). Do not accept 'hydroxyl'.
questions.tip: H⁺ makes solutions acidic, OH⁻ makes them alkaline.

questions.q: Molten zinc chloride is electrolysed. Which half equation happens at the anode?
ms: Negative chloride ions are attracted to the positive anode, where they lose electrons (oxidation) to form chlorine gas. There is no water in a molten salt, so no OH⁻.
questions.tip: Molten = only the ions of the compound. Aqueous = also H⁺ and OH⁻ from water.

questions.q: Which aqueous solution, electrolysed with inert electrodes, gives oxygen at the anode and a metal at the cathode?
ms: Silver is less reactive than hydrogen so silver forms at the cathode. Nitrate is not a halide, so oxygen forms at the anode. Copper chloride gives chlorine at the anode; NaCl and KBr give hydrogen at the cathode.
questions.tip: Two rules: cathode gives the metal only if it is less reactive than hydrogen; anode gives the halogen if a halide is present, otherwise oxygen.

questions.q: In electrolysis, towards which electrode do positive ions move?
ms: Positive ions (cations) are attracted to the negative electrode, the cathode.
questions.tip: PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

questions.q: Molten potassium iodide is electrolysed. Name the product at each electrode.
questions.answer: Cathode: potassium. Anode: iodine.
ms: Cathode (negative): potassium (1 mark)
Anode (positive): iodine (1 mark). Do not accept 'iodide'.
questions.tip: The product is the element (iodine), not the ion (iodide).

questions.q:
Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
Name the products at each electrode and explain why sodium is not produced.
questions.answer: Cathode: hydrogen. Anode: oxygen. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions (from water) are discharged instead of Na⁺.
ms: Hydrogen at the cathode (1 mark)
Oxygen at the anode (1 mark)
Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so hydrogen ions are discharged (1 mark)
questions.tip: Sulfate is not a halide, so oxygen (not sulfur) forms at the anode.

questions.q: Write the half equation for the formation of oxygen at the anode during the electrolysis of an aqueous solution.
questions.answer: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
ms: Correct species OH⁻, O₂, H₂O (1 mark)
Balanced with 4e⁻ on the right (1 mark). Allow 4OH⁻ − 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O.
questions.tip: This is the hardest half equation on the spec: learn it exactly. Electrons are on the RIGHT (oxidation).

questions.q: Aluminium is extracted by the electrolysis of a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, using a very large current. Explain why aluminium is expensive to produce, using information about the process.
questions.answer: Large amounts of electricity are needed: to melt the mixture (high temperature, though cryolite lowers it) and to supply the very large current for electrolysis. Carbon anodes react with oxygen to form CO₂ and must be replaced regularly. Electricity is expensive.
ms: Large amounts of electrical energy needed to supply the very large current for electrolysis (1 mark)
Energy also needed to keep the aluminium oxide / cryolite mixture molten at a high temperature (1 mark)
Anodes burn away (react with oxygen to form CO₂) and need replacing (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link costs to specific steps of the process. 'It uses a lot of energy' alone scores 1.

questions.q: Describe how you would carry out an electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate solution using inert electrodes, and how you would identify the products at each electrode.
questions.answer: Pour copper sulfate solution into a beaker. Place two inert (graphite) electrodes in the solution, not touching. Connect to a low-voltage dc supply. Place an inverted test tube full of solution over the anode to collect gas. Switch on. Cathode: pink/brown solid (copper) coats the electrode.
