Anode: bubbles; collect gas and test with a glowing splint, which relights (oxygen). The blue colour fades as Cu²⁺ ions are removed.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A clear, workable method including apparatus and safety, AND correct identification of both products with the correct tests/observations.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): A workable method with at least one product correctly identified with a test or observation.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Some relevant apparatus or a product named, with no clear method.
Indicative content: graphite / inert electrodes in a beaker or petri dish of solution; electrodes not touching; dc supply at low voltage (e.g. 4-6 V)
Indicative content: collect gas at anode in a test tube filled with solution
Indicative content: cathode: pink-brown coating of copper; anode: bubbles of oxygen, glowing splint relights
Indicative content: solution gets paler blue; safety: eye protection, avoid skin contact, low voltage
questions.tip: The oxygen test is a GLOWING splint that RELIGHTS. A lit splint is the hydrogen test.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of molten lead bromide, which species is oxidised and which is reduced? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: Bromide ions are oxidised because they lose electrons (2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻). Lead ions are reduced because they gain electrons (Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb).
ms: Bromide ions oxidised, as they lose electrons (1 mark)
Lead ions reduced, as they gain electrons (1 mark)
questions.tip: Reduction always happens at the cathode, oxidation always at the anode.

questions.q: Sodium chloride solution (brine) is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the gas produced at the cathode.
questions.answer: Hydrogen
ms: Hydrogen / H₂ (1 mark). Do not accept sodium: sodium is more reactive than hydrogen.
questions.tip: In aqueous solutions, a metal more reactive than hydrogen is never produced at the cathode: hydrogen forms instead.

questions.q: Explain why electrolysis cannot happen when the electrolyte is solid.
questions.answer: In a solid ionic compound the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so they cannot move to the electrodes and carry charge.
ms: Ions are in fixed positions / cannot move (1 mark)
So cannot move to the electrodes / carry charge (1 mark). Do not accept 'electrons cannot move'.
questions.tip: Current in electrolytes is carried by ions, never by electrons.

questions.q: Which observation shows that a reaction is exothermic?
options: The temperature of the surroundings increases
The temperature of the surroundings decreases
ms: An exothermic reaction transfers energy TO the surroundings, so the surroundings get hotter.
questions.tip: Think about the surroundings (the solution and thermometer), not the reacting particles.

questions.q: On a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, which statement is true?
options: Products are at a higher energy than reactants
The activation energy is the difference between reactants and products
Products are at a lower energy than reactants
ms: Energy is released, so products end lower than reactants. Activation energy is from reactants to the peak.
questions.tip: The overall energy change is reactants to products; activation energy is reactants to the top of the hump.

questions.q:
Hydrogen burns: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H = 436, O=O = 498, O–H = 464
What is the energy change for the reaction as written?
ms: Bonds broken = 2 × 436 + 498 = 1370. Bonds made = 4 × 464 = 1856. Change = 1370 − 1856 = −486 kJ/mol.
questions.tip: Each H₂O has TWO O–H bonds, so 2H₂O = 4 O–H. Using 2 × 464 gives the wrong answer.

questions.q:
Ethene reacts with hydrogen: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆
Bond energies (kJ/mol): C=C = 614, C–C = 347, C–H = 413, H–H = 436
What is the energy change?
questions.tip: Count every bond in the displayed formula, or cancel bonds that appear on both sides carefully.

questions.q: Give two uses of endothermic reactions in everyday life.
questions.answer: Instant cold packs for sports injuries; sherbet sweets (citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate gives a cooling feeling).
ms: Any one (1 mark): sports injury / instant cold packs; sherbet sweets (citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate); photosynthesis in plants
A second, different use from the list (1 mark). Do not accept hand warmers or self-heating cans (exothermic).
questions.tip: Hand warmers and self-heating cans are EXOTHERMIC. Don't mix them up.

questions.q: Explain why a reaction with a low activation energy can happen quickly at room temperature.
questions.answer: Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react. If it is low, more particles have enough energy at room temperature, so more collisions are successful.
ms: Activation energy = minimum energy needed for particles to react when they collide (1 mark)
Low Ea means a greater proportion of particles / collisions have enough energy, so more successful collisions (per second) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always say 'minimum energy'. 'The energy needed to start a reaction' is accepted by some boards but 'minimum energy for particles to react' is safest.

questions.q:
Hydrazine burns in oxygen: N₂H₄ + O₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O
Bond energies (kJ/mol): N–N = 158, N–H = 391, O=O = 498, N≡N = 945, O–H = 464
Calculate the energy change for the reaction.
ms: Energy to break bonds = 2220 kJ (1 mark)
Energy released making bonds = 2801 kJ (1 mark)
−581 kJ/mol (sign required) (1 mark). Allow ECF.
questions.tip: The negative sign is part of the answer. A correct number with no sign often loses the last mark.

questions.q:
Methane reacts with chlorine: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. The energy change is −115 kJ/mol.
Bond energies (kJ/mol): C–H = 413, Cl–Cl = 243, H–Cl = 432. Calculate the bond energy of the C–Cl bond.
ms: Correct expression for bonds broken (1895, or 656 if cancelling) (1 mark)
Sets up broken − made = −115 with x for C–Cl (1 mark)
C–Cl = 339 kJ/mol (1 mark)
questions.tip: Write the equation broken − made = ΔH with x in it, then rearrange. Don't try to do it in your head.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of energy, why a reaction is endothermic.
questions.answer: More energy is needed to break the bonds in the reactants than is released when new bonds form in the products. So overall energy is taken in from the surroundings.
ms: Energy taken in / needed to break bonds (1 mark)
Energy released when bonds are made (1 mark)
Energy needed to break bonds is greater than energy released making bonds (1 mark)
questions.tip: The comparison is the key mark. 'Breaking bonds takes in energy' alone is only 1 mark.

questions.q: Describe a method to investigate how the temperature change of a neutralisation reaction varies with the volume of sodium hydroxide solution added to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: Measure 25 cm³ HCl with a measuring cylinder (or pipette) into a polystyrene cup inside a beaker. Record initial temperature. Add 5 cm³ NaOH, stir, record highest temperature. Repeat additions of 5 cm³ up to 40 cm³. Repeat the whole experiment and calculate means. Plot maximum temperature against volume; two lines of best fit cross at the volume needed for neutralisation.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A coherent, detailed method that would give valid results, including insulation, control of variables, measurement of temperature after each addition, and repeats/processing.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): A workable method with key steps, missing some detail about control variables or processing.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Some relevant steps, not in a coherent order.
Indicative content: polystyrene cup with lid, placed in a beaker for stability
Indicative content: measure 25 cm³ acid; record starting temperature with thermometer
Indicative content: add NaOH in 5 cm³ portions, stir, record highest temperature each time
Indicative content: same concentration of acid and alkali; repeat and calculate mean; plot graph of temperature against volume
questions.tip: Mention the polystyrene cup AND the lid: reducing energy transfer to the surroundings is a key validity point.

questions.q: Two students do the same neutralisation. Student A uses a polystyrene cup with a lid and records a rise of 6.8 °C. Student B uses an open metal can and records 4.1 °C. Explain why B's value is lower and which result is more valid.
questions.answer: More energy is transferred from B's solution to the surroundings through the metal and open top. A's result is more valid because insulation reduces this energy transfer.
ms: Metal is a good thermal conductor and the open top lets energy transfer to the surroundings, so less of the energy released raises the solution temperature (1 mark)
A's result is more valid because the insulated cup and lid reduce energy transfer to the surroundings (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'energy transferred to surroundings', not 'heat escaped'.

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'endothermic'?
questions.answer: A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings.
ms: Takes in energy from the surroundings (so temperature of surroundings decreases) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Include 'from the surroundings'.

questions.q: A reaction has an overall energy change of +50 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 120 kJ/mol. Calculate the activation energy for the reverse reaction.
questions.answer: Reverse Ea = 120 − 50 = 70 kJ/mol
ms: Recognises products are 50 kJ above reactants so reverse barrier = 120 − 50 (1 mark)
70 kJ/mol (1 mark)
questions.tip: Sketch the profile. Answers of 170 come from adding instead of subtracting.

questions.q: What is the unit of rate of reaction if gas volume is measured in cm³ and time in seconds?
ms: Mean rate = quantity of product ÷ time, so cm³/s.
questions.tip: Rate = amount ÷ time. The time unit goes underneath.

questions.q: A student halves the concentration of acid in a reaction with excess magnesium ribbon, keeping the volume the same. What happens?
options: Rate stays the same and final volume halves
Rate increases and final volume halves
Rate decreases and final volume of hydrogen halves
Rate decreases and final volume of hydrogen is the same
ms: Halving concentration means fewer particles per volume (fewer collisions per second) AND half the moles of acid. Acid is limiting (magnesium excess), so final volume also halves.
questions.tip: Check which reactant is limiting: the limiting reactant controls the final amount of product.

questions.q: On a graph of volume of gas against time, a tangent at 30 s passes through (10 s, 14 cm³) and (50 s, 54 cm³). What is the rate at 30 s?
questions.tip: Use two points ON THE TANGENT, far apart, not points on the curve.

questions.q: Why does increasing pressure increase the rate of a reaction between gases?
options: There are more particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions
ms: Higher pressure = same number of particles in a smaller volume, so more frequent collisions. Energy of particles is unchanged.
questions.tip: Pressure and concentration change collision FREQUENCY, not collision energy.

questions.q: The volume of hydrogen collected after 40 s was 96 cm³. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 40 s.
ms: 2.4 cm³/s (unit needed) (1 mark)
questions.tip: The unit is part of the answer mark here.

questions.q: Explain why a reaction slows down and then stops, in terms of particles.
questions.answer: As the reaction proceeds, reactants are used up, so the concentration of reactant particles decreases. So there are fewer collisions per second and the rate decreases. It stops when one reactant (the limiting reactant) has been used up.
ms: Reactant particles used up / concentration decreases (1 mark)
Fewer collisions per second / lower frequency of collisions (1 mark)
Stops when (limiting) reactant is used up (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'frequency of collisions' or 'collisions per second'. 'Fewer collisions' alone is often not credited.

questions.q: Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction. Use the term 'activation energy' in your answer.
questions.answer: Particles move faster so collide more frequently. Particles have more energy, so a greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy. So there are more successful collisions per second.
ms: Particles move faster / have more kinetic energy, so collide more frequently (1 mark)
A greater proportion of particles / collisions have energy ≥ activation energy (1 mark)
More successful collisions per second (1 mark)
questions.tip: The 'energy' effect is more important than the 'more collisions' effect. Mention both for full marks.

questions.q: Describe an investigation to find how the surface area of marble chips affects the rate of their reaction with hydrochloric acid, by measuring the loss in mass.
questions.answer: Place a conical flask with 50 cm³ of dilute HCl on a balance. Add 10 g of large marble chips, put a loose cotton wool plug in the neck, start the timer and record the mass every 30 s for 5 minutes. Repeat with the same mass of medium and small chips. Keep acid volume, concentration and temperature the same. Calculate mass lost and plot mass lost against time for each size. Steeper initial gradient = faster rate. Repeat and take means.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A coherent method that would give valid results, with clear independent, dependent and control variables, timed mass readings, and a way of processing the results to compare rates.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): A workable method with mass measured at intervals and some variables controlled.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Some relevant steps, e.g. 'use different chips and weigh', without a workable method.
Indicative content: flask of acid on a top-pan balance; cotton wool plug lets CO₂ out but stops acid spray
Indicative content: add chips, start timer, record mass at regular intervals (e.g. every 30 s)
Indicative content: same mass of chips each time; same volume, concentration and temperature of acid; only chip size changed
Indicative content: calculate mass lost; plot graph of mass lost against time; compare initial gradients; repeat for reliability
questions.tip: Explain the cotton wool plug: it lets carbon dioxide escape (so mass falls) but stops acid spray being lost.

questions.q: In the 'disappearing cross' experiment, the time at 20 °C was 80 s and at 40 °C was 20 s. By what factor did the rate increase? Show your working.
ms: Calculates 1/t for both (1 mark)
Factor of 4 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rate is proportional to 1/time. A shorter time means a higher rate.

questions.q:
The mass of a flask and contents was recorded as marble chips reacted with acid.
Time (s) | 0 | 60 | 120 | 180
Mass (g) | 86.40 | 85.88 | 85.62 | 85.50
Calculate the mean rate of reaction for the first 60 s and explain why the rate between 120 and 180 s is lower.
questions.answer: Mass lost = 0.52 g; mean rate = 0.52 ÷ 60 = 0.0087 g/s. Between 120 and 180 s mass lost = 0.12 g (0.0020 g/s) because the concentration of acid has fallen, so fewer collisions per second.
ms: Mean rate = 0.52 ÷ 60 (1 mark)
Later rate lower because concentration of acid decreases / reactants used up, so fewer collisions per second (1 mark)
questions.tip: Calculate mass LOST, not the mass at a given time.

questions.q: Explain why enzymes are described as biological catalysts.
questions.answer: They are proteins made by living organisms that speed up reactions without being used up.
ms: Made by living organisms / proteins (1 mark)
Increase rate of reaction without being used up (1 mark)
questions.tip: A catalyst is NOT used up; do not write 'it is not involved in the reaction'.

questions.q:
A student investigates the reaction of calcium carbonate with acid. Experiment A uses 5 g of large chips. Experiment B uses 5 g of powder. Acid is in excess in both.
Describe and explain how the graph of volume of CO₂ against time for B would differ from A.
questions.answer: B's curve is steeper at the start (higher initial rate) and levels off sooner, but reaches the same final volume. Powder has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so more frequent collisions. Same mass of carbonate (limiting) so same amount of CO₂.
ms: Steeper initial gradient / levels off sooner (1 mark)
Same final volume because same mass of CaCO₃ / acid in excess (1 mark)
Larger surface area to volume ratio so more frequent collisions (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always comment on BOTH the gradient and the final volume when describing rate graphs.

questions.q: Give the definition of a catalyst.
questions.answer: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up.
ms: Increases rate without being used up / chemically unchanged at end (1 mark)
questions.tip: Add 'provides a different pathway with lower activation energy' for the explanation questions.

questions.q: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g). Brown NO₂ forms colourless N₂O₄. The forward reaction is exothermic. The mixture is put in ice. What is observed?
ms: Lowering temperature favours the exothermic direction (forward), so more colourless N₂O₄ forms and the mixture becomes paler.
questions.tip: Decrease in temperature → equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction.

questions.q: CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g). What is the effect of increasing the pressure on the yield of hydrogen?
ms: There are 2 moles of gas on each side, so changing pressure does not shift the position of equilibrium. (The rate increases.)
questions.tip: Count gas molecules on each side before answering any pressure question.

questions.q: What is meant by a closed system?
options: A system where no substances can enter or leave
A system where no reactions happen
A system kept at constant temperature
ms: In a closed system, reactants and products cannot escape or be added, so equilibrium can be reached.
questions.tip: Equilibrium only happens in a closed system.

questions.q: CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g). Methanol is removed from the equilibrium mixture as it forms. What happens?
options: More methanol forms as equilibrium shifts right
Rate of forward reaction becomes zero
ms: Removing a product lowers its concentration. The system responds to counteract the change by making more product, so equilibrium shifts right.
questions.tip: Le Chatelier: the system opposes any change. Removing product → more product made.

questions.q: Hydrated cobalt chloride is pink; anhydrous cobalt chloride is blue. Describe what you would see when water is added to anhydrous cobalt chloride, and state one other thing you would observe.
questions.answer: It turns from blue to pink; the mixture gets warm (energy released).
ms: Blue to pink (1 mark)
Gets hot / temperature rises (exothermic) (1 mark)
questions.tip: If the forward reaction is endothermic, the reverse is exothermic by the same amount.

questions.q: State two features of a reaction at dynamic equilibrium.
questions.answer: The forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate; concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
ms: Rate of forward reaction = rate of reverse reaction (1 mark)
Concentrations / amounts of reactants and products remain constant (1 mark). Do not accept 'are equal'.
questions.tip: Concentrations are CONSTANT, not EQUAL. This mistake costs a mark every year.

questions.q:
Sulfur trioxide is made in the Contact process: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. A temperature of 450 °C and a pressure of 2 atm are used.
Explain why these conditions are a compromise.
questions.answer: Low temperature would favour the exothermic forward reaction (higher yield) but the rate would be too slow, so 450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate. High pressure favours the forward reaction (3 moles of gas → 2), but the yield is already high at low pressure, and high pressure is expensive, so 2 atm is used.
ms: Lower temperature gives higher yield because forward reaction is exothermic (1 mark)
But lower temperature gives a slower rate, so moderate temperature is a compromise (1 mark)
Higher pressure gives higher yield because fewer moles of gas on the right (3 → 2) (1 mark)
High pressure is expensive / dangerous / yield already high enough at low pressure (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always justify pressure using the number of moles of GAS on each side, with the numbers.

questions.q: Explain what happens to the yield of ammonia in the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), if the pressure is increased.
questions.answer: Yield increases. There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules (right), to reduce the pressure.
ms: Yield increases / equilibrium shifts right (1 mark)
4 moles of gas on left, 2 on right / fewer gas molecules on right (1 mark)
Equilibrium shifts to reduce / oppose the increase in pressure (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give the numbers of gas molecules. 'Fewer molecules on the right' without numbers can still score, but numbers are safer.

questions.q: A reversible reaction is endothermic in the forward direction. State what happens to the yield of product if the temperature is increased, and explain why.
questions.answer: Yield increases, because the equilibrium moves in the endothermic direction to oppose the temperature rise (absorbing energy).
ms: Yield of product increases (1 mark)
Equilibrium shifts in the endothermic (forward) direction to oppose / reduce the temperature increase (1 mark)
questions.tip: Increase temp → endothermic direction. Decrease temp → exothermic direction.

questions.q:
Hydrogen is made industrially by: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g). The forward reaction is endothermic.
Evaluate the effect of temperature, pressure and a catalyst on the yield and rate of hydrogen production, and suggest suitable conditions.
questions.answer: High temperature favours the endothermic forward reaction (higher yield) and increases rate, so high temperature is good for both (limited by energy cost and equipment). Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium left (2 moles gas → 4 moles), lowering yield, but increases rate; so low or moderate pressure is chosen. A catalyst increases rate of both forward and reverse reactions equally, so does not change yield but reaches equilibrium faster. Suitable: high temperature (e.g. 800 °C), low pressure, catalyst.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): All three factors evaluated for BOTH yield and rate with correct reasoning (endothermic, moles of gas), and a justified conclusion about conditions.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Two factors explained correctly for yield and/or rate, with some reasoning.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple correct statements about one or two factors.
Indicative content: forward reaction endothermic, so higher temperature shifts equilibrium right, increasing yield; higher temperature also increases rate
Indicative content: 2 moles of gas on left, 4 on right; higher pressure shifts equilibrium left, lowering yield; but higher pressure increases rate
Indicative content: catalyst increases rate of forward and reverse reactions equally; position of equilibrium / yield unchanged; equilibrium reached faster
Indicative content: conclusion: high temperature, low/moderate pressure, catalyst; energy costs of high temperature
questions.tip: 'Evaluate' needs a conclusion. Without suggested conditions you cannot reach Level 3.

questions.q: Give the symbol used to show a reversible reaction.
ms: ⇌ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not use ↔ or a single arrow.

questions.q: What is the formula of the alkane with 6 carbon atoms?
ms: Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: 2 × 6 + 2 = 14, so C₆H₁₄ (hexane).
questions.tip: Alkanes always fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. C₆H₁₂ has two hydrogens too few to be an alkane.

questions.q: Which fraction from crude oil has the highest viscosity?
ms: Bitumen has the longest chains, so the strongest intermolecular forces and highest viscosity.
questions.tip: Longer chains: higher boiling point, more viscous, less flammable.

questions.q: Hexadecane, C₁₆H₃₄, is cracked to form one molecule of octane, C₈H₁₈, and two molecules of an alkene only. What is the alkene?
ms: Remaining atoms: C₁₆H₃₄ − C₈H₁₈ = C₈H₁₆. Split between two identical molecules: C₄H₈ (butene).
questions.tip: Balance carbons first, then hydrogens, then divide by the number of molecules.

questions.q: Bromine water is added to propene. What colour change is seen?
ms: Alkenes decolourise bromine water: orange to colourless. Alkanes give no change.
questions.tip: Write 'decolourises' or 'orange to colourless'. Never write 'clear' (clear does not mean colourless).

questions.q: Give the names and formulae of the first two alkanes.
questions.answer: Methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆
ms: Methane CH₄ (1 mark)
Ethane C₂H₆ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mnemonic: Monkeys Eat Peanut Butter (methane, ethane, propane, butane).

questions.q: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈.
questions.answer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
ms: Correct products CO₂ and H₂O (1 mark)
Correctly balanced (1 mark)
questions.tip: Balance C, then H, then O last.

questions.q: Octane, C₈H₁₈, burns in a car engine. Write a balanced equation for its complete combustion, and suggest why some carbon monoxide is also produced in engines.
questions.answer: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. CO forms because there is not enough oxygen for complete combustion (incomplete combustion).
ms: Correct formulae (1 mark)
Balanced: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O (allow C₈H₁₈ + 12½O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O) (1 mark)
Limited supply of oxygen / incomplete combustion (1 mark)
questions.tip: Odd oxygen totals: double everything to avoid halves.

questions.q: Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil, and why the fractions have different properties.
questions.answer: Crude oil is heated until most of it evaporates. Vapour enters a column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Vapours rise and cool; each fraction condenses at the level where the temperature equals its boiling point. Fractions are mixtures of hydrocarbons with similar chain lengths. Longer chains have stronger intermolecular forces, so higher boiling points, higher viscosity and lower flammability; they condense lower down. Bitumen leaves at the bottom as a liquid; gases leave at the top.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A clear description of the process with temperature gradient and condensing at boiling points, linked to chain length and intermolecular forces to explain properties.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): A description of the process with some link to boiling point or chain length.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Basic statements, e.g. 'oil is heated and separated'.
Indicative content: heated / vaporised; temperature gradient (hot bottom, cool top)
Indicative content: vapours rise, condense when they reach their boiling point, collected at different levels
Indicative content: fraction = hydrocarbons with similar number of carbon atoms
Indicative content: longer chain → stronger intermolecular forces → higher boiling point, more viscous, less flammable
questions.tip: 'Condense', not 'evaporate', describes what happens as each fraction is collected.

questions.q: Explain why short-chain hydrocarbons such as petrol are more useful as fuels than long-chain hydrocarbons such as fuel oil.
questions.answer: Short-chain hydrocarbons are more flammable (ignite easily) and less viscous (flow easily), so they burn cleanly and are easy to use in engines.
ms: More flammable / easier to ignite (1 mark)
Less viscous / lower boiling point so easily vaporised (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the precise property words: flammability, viscosity, boiling point.

questions.q: Describe how bromine water can be used to tell an alkene from an alkane. Give the result for each.
questions.answer: Add bromine water and shake. The alkene decolourises it (orange to colourless); with the alkane it stays orange.
ms: Alkene: bromine water turns from orange to colourless (1 mark)
Alkane: no change / stays orange (1 mark). Do not accept 'clear' for colourless.
questions.tip: Give the colour change in full: 'orange to colourless'. 'Goes clear' scores zero.

questions.q: State the conditions needed for catalytic cracking.
questions.answer: Heat the hydrocarbon vapour and pass it over a hot catalyst.
ms: Vapour passed over hot catalyst (allow high temperature with catalyst) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Steam cracking: mix with steam at very high temperature. Learn both.

questions.q: A supply of crude oil produces 20% petrol fraction, but demand for petrol is 40%. Explain how cracking helps.
questions.answer: Cracking breaks down longer-chain fractions (in low demand) into shorter-chain alkanes such as petrol (in high demand), and alkenes for making polymers.
ms: Breaks down long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful ones (1 mark)
Converts low-demand fractions to meet the high demand for petrol / alkenes for polymers (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link supply and demand using the data given.

questions.q: Which test identifies chlorine gas?
options: Lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
ms: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper (it turns white). Blue litmus may turn red first.
questions.tip: The litmus paper must be DAMP.

questions.q: In a chromatogram the solvent front moved 6.0 cm. A spot has Rf 0.40. How far did the spot travel?
ms: Distance moved by spot = Rf × solvent distance = 0.40 × 6.0 = 2.4 cm.
questions.tip: Rf is always less than 1. If you get a distance bigger than the solvent front, you have divided the wrong way.

questions.q: A food colouring gives three spots in one solvent. In a second solvent, it gives four spots. What is the best conclusion?
options: The colouring contains at least four substances
One of the substances reacted with the solvent
The colouring contains exactly three substances
ms: Two substances with the same Rf in the first solvent may be separated by the second. So there are at least four.
questions.tip: Using more than one solvent is a check of purity: a pure substance gives one spot in all solvents.

questions.q: Which is NOT an example of a formulation?
ms: A formulation is a mixture designed as a useful product, with measured quantities of each component. Distilled water is a pure substance.
questions.tip: A formulation is a mixture made to a precise recipe.

questions.q: Describe the test for hydrogen and give the result.
questions.answer: Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the test tube; it burns with a squeaky pop.
ms: Lighted / burning splint (1 mark)
Squeaky pop (1 mark). Do not accept 'glowing splint' or 'pop' alone in strict marking.
questions.tip: Lighted splint for hydrogen, glowing splint for oxygen.

questions.q: In chromatography, explain why the start line is drawn in pencil and not ink.
questions.answer: Pencil (graphite) is insoluble in the solvent, so it will not move up the paper. Ink would dissolve and separate, interfering with the results.
ms: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent / will not move (1 mark)
Ink would dissolve and produce spots that confuse the chromatogram (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'insoluble in the solvent'.

questions.q: Explain how paper chromatography separates a mixture of dyes. Use the terms 'mobile phase' and 'stationary phase'.
questions.answer: The solvent is the mobile phase that moves up the paper; the paper is the stationary phase. Each dye is distributed between the two phases differently. Dyes more soluble in the solvent / less attracted to the paper spend more time in the mobile phase and travel further, so dyes separate and have different Rf values.
ms: Solvent = mobile phase; paper = stationary phase (1 mark)
Different substances have different attraction to / distribution between the phases (1 mark)
More soluble / less attracted to paper travels further, so they separate with different Rf values (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'distribution between the phases' or 'attraction to the paper versus solubility in the solvent'.

questions.q:
An unknown sample X is compared with substances P, Q and R using chromatography.
Substance | Rf values of spots
X | 0.25, 0.60
P | 0.25
Q | 0.45
R | 0.60, 0.80
Deduce which of P, Q and R could be in X. Explain your answer.
questions.answer: P is in X (both have a spot at 0.25). Q is not (no spot at 0.45). R is not, because R also produces a spot at 0.80 which is not in X; the 0.60 spot in X could be the same substance as one component of R but X does not contain all of R.
ms: P is present (same Rf 0.25) (1 mark)
Q is not present (no spot at 0.45) (1 mark)
R is not present (as a whole) because X has no spot at 0.80 / X contains the 0.60 substance but not all of R (1 mark)
questions.tip: Matching ONE spot of a mixture does not mean the whole mixture is present.

questions.q: A sample of water boils at 102 °C at normal pressure. What does this tell you about the sample? Explain.
questions.answer: It is impure. Pure water boils at exactly 100 °C; impurities raise the boiling point.
ms: Impure / a mixture (1 mark)
Pure water boils at 100 °C (exactly / sharp point); impurities change (raise) the boiling point (1 mark)
questions.tip: Pure substances have a fixed, sharp melting AND boiling point.

questions.q: Describe the test for oxygen.
questions.answer: Insert a glowing splint into the gas; it relights.
ms: Glowing splint relights (both needed) (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Burns brighter' is not 'relights'.

questions.q:
A student tests a gas using limewater.
(a) Name the gas tested for.
(b) Give the positive result.
(c) Explain why the result occurs.
questions.answer: (a) Carbon dioxide. (b) Limewater turns milky / cloudy. (c) CO₂ reacts with calcium hydroxide solution to form insoluble calcium carbonate.
ms: (a) Carbon dioxide (1 mark)
(b) Turns milky / cloudy (1 mark)
(c) Forms (insoluble) calcium carbonate precipitate (1 mark)
questions.tip: Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution.

questions.q:
A student uses chromatography to identify a dye. Her solvent front moved 9.0 cm. Her dye spot moved 5.4 cm. A book gives the Rf of dye Y as 0.60 in the same solvent.
(a) Calculate the Rf of her dye.
(b) Explain whether this proves the dye is Y.
(c) Suggest how she could make her identification more certain.
questions.answer: (a) 5.4 ÷ 9.0 = 0.60. (b) It suggests it could be Y but does not prove it; other substances can have the same Rf in this solvent. (c) Run a pure sample of Y on the same paper alongside, and repeat in a different solvent; matching Rf in both supports identification.
ms: (b) Same Rf so it could be Y (1 mark)
(b) but other substances may have same Rf value in this solvent, so not proof (1 mark)
(c) Run a known sample of Y alongside / use a different solvent and compare (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Proves' is almost never right in science. Discuss alternatives.

questions.q: Which gas made up most of the Earth's early atmosphere, according to one theory?
ms: The early atmosphere is thought to have been mainly carbon dioxide from volcanoes, with little or no oxygen (like Mars and Venus today).
questions.tip: Today it is mostly nitrogen; the early atmosphere was mostly CO₂.

questions.q: Which process removed carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere?
options: Dissolving in oceans and forming carbonate sediments
ms: CO₂ dissolved in oceans and formed carbonate precipitates (sediments), and algae and plants absorbed it by photosynthesis. Some was locked in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
questions.tip: Learn all routes: dissolving, photosynthesis, carbonate rocks, fossil fuels.

questions.q: Which statement best explains how greenhouse gases warm the Earth?
options: They absorb short-wavelength radiation from the Sun
They reflect long-wavelength radiation back to the Sun
They absorb long-wavelength (infrared) radiation emitted by the Earth and re-radiate it
ms: Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through. The Earth emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation, which greenhouse gases absorb and then re-emit in all directions, including back to Earth.
questions.tip: Short wavelength in, long wavelength out. Greenhouse gases absorb the long-wavelength radiation. Never mention ozone.

questions.q: How are oxides of nitrogen formed in a car engine?
options: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at high temperatures
ms: Oxides of nitrogen form when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the high temperatures inside an engine. The fuel itself contains almost no nitrogen.
questions.tip: Sulfur dioxide comes from sulfur in the fuel; NOx comes from the AIR.

questions.q: Name the gas produced by photosynthesis that increased in the atmosphere about 2.7 billion years ago, and name the organisms responsible.
questions.answer: Oxygen; algae.
ms: Oxygen (1 mark)
Algae (allow plants for later) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Algae first (2.7 billion years ago), then plants.

questions.q: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
questions.answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
ms: Correct formulae (1 mark)
Correctly balanced (1 mark)
questions.tip: Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆. Balance with 6s.

questions.q: Explain how the formation of the oceans and the evolution of algae reduced the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
questions.answer: As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and formed carbonate precipitates that became sediments (e.g. limestone). Algae and later plants used CO₂ in photosynthesis, producing oxygen.
ms: Water vapour condensed to form oceans (1 mark)
CO₂ dissolved in oceans / formed carbonate precipitates / sediments (1 mark)
Photosynthesis by algae/plants used up CO₂ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention 'condensed' for oceans and 'carbonate precipitates' for the higher-band phrasing.

questions.q: Describe one human activity that increases each of the following greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide, methane, and explain why water vapour is not normally considered a gas that humans increase significantly.
questions.answer: CO₂: burning fossil fuels / deforestation. Methane: cattle farming / rice fields / landfill. Water vapour levels are controlled by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle, so human activity has little direct effect.
ms: CO₂ activity (1 mark)
Methane activity (1 mark)
Water vapour amount determined by the water cycle / natural processes (1 mark)
questions.tip: Deforestation increases CO₂ because fewer trees photosynthesise AND burning releases CO₂.

questions.q: Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous and why it is hard to detect.
questions.answer: It combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells, reducing the capacity of blood to carry oxygen. It is colourless and odourless.
ms: Combines with haemoglobin / reduces oxygen-carrying capacity of blood (1 mark)
Colourless and odourless (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood'.

questions.q:
Global average temperatures have risen since 1900. Some people argue the rise is natural.
Evaluate the evidence that human activities are causing climate change.
questions.answer: Most scientists agree that human activities increase greenhouse gas levels, causing an increase in mean global temperature. Evidence: CO₂ levels have risen in step with fossil fuel use; peer-reviewed data and models show this. However, climate is complex; models involve simplifications, and there are natural variations. Uncertainty exists but the strong correlation and mechanism support the human cause.
ms: CO₂ concentration has increased with fossil fuel burning since the industrial revolution (1 mark)
Mechanism: greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation, so more gases → more warming (1 mark)
Uncertainty: climate is complex / models are simplified / natural variation (1 mark)
Conclusion: overwhelming peer-reviewed evidence supports human cause (1 mark)
questions.tip: Evaluation questions need both sides AND a conclusion.

questions.q: Give one effect of sulfur dioxide on the environment.
questions.answer: Acid rain (damages buildings, kills plants and aquatic life).
ms: Acid rain (1 mark). Allow respiratory problems in humans.
questions.tip: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain; particulates cause global dimming.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by a 'carbon footprint'.
questions.answer: The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
ms: Total amount of CO₂ and other greenhouse gases (1 mark)
emitted over the full life cycle of a product / service / event (1 mark)
questions.tip: Include 'full life cycle'.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of filtration in water treatment?
ms: Filtration (through filter beds) removes solid particles. Sterilising (chlorine, ozone or UV) kills microbes.
questions.tip: Two stages: filter (remove solids), sterilise (kill microbes).

questions.q: Why is desalination by distillation expensive?
options: It uses large amounts of energy to boil water
ms: Distillation and reverse osmosis both need large amounts of energy.
questions.tip: Desalination methods are energy-intensive.

questions.q: In bioleaching, what is produced?
ms: Bacteria produce leachate solutions containing metal compounds. The copper is then extracted by displacement (scrap iron) or electrolysis.
questions.tip: Bioleaching makes leachate; phytomining makes plant ash. Both need a final displacement or electrolysis step.

questions.q: Which is the best reason for recycling glass bottles instead of making new ones?
options: Less energy is needed to melt used glass than to make new glass from raw materials
ms: Crushing and melting recycled glass uses less energy and fewer raw materials (sand, limestone) than making new glass.
questions.tip: Recycling answers should mention energy, raw materials and waste.

questions.q: Give two stages of treating fresh water in the UK to make it potable.
questions.answer: Filtration (filter beds); sterilisation (chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light).
ms: Filtration / passing through filter beds (1 mark)
Sterilisation using chlorine / ozone / UV (1 mark)
questions.tip: Potable water is safe to drink; it is not pure.

questions.q: Describe how sewage is treated to make it safe to release into rivers.
questions.answer: Screening and grit removal; sedimentation produces sewage sludge and effluent; anaerobic digestion of sludge; aerobic biological treatment of effluent.
ms: Screening / removal of grit and large objects (1 mark)
Sedimentation to form sludge and effluent (1 mark)
Anaerobic digestion of sludge AND/OR aerobic biological treatment of effluent (1 mark)
questions.tip: Sludge is digested anaerobically; effluent is treated aerobically.

questions.q: Explain why a life cycle assessment (LCA) may not give a completely objective comparison of two products.
questions.answer: Values for energy, water use and some resources can be measured, but values for pollutant effects are harder to quantify and involve value judgements. LCAs can be shortened or selectively used to support claims, e.g. for advertising.
ms: Some values (e.g. pollution effects) are difficult to measure / quantify (1 mark)
Value judgements are needed / not objective (1 mark)
Can be selectively used / shortened to support claims (e.g. by companies) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'value judgement' and 'selective'.

questions.q: Copper is extracted from low-grade ore by phytomining. Describe the process and explain why it is used.
questions.answer: Plants absorb metal compounds from the soil. Plants are harvested and burned; the ash contains metal compounds. The ash is dissolved in acid and copper is obtained by displacement with scrap iron or electrolysis. Used because high-grade ores are running out, and it avoids digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
ms: Plants absorb metal compounds (1 mark)
Plants harvested and burned to produce ash containing metal compounds (1 mark)
Copper extracted by displacement (scrap iron) or electrolysis (1 mark)
High-grade ores limited / reduces environmental impact of mining (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention the ash and the final extraction step to score all marks.

questions.q: Explain why water is distilled in the required practical analysis of water samples, rather than just filtered.
questions.answer: Filtering only removes insoluble solids. Distillation removes dissolved substances (salts), as the water evaporates and condenses, leaving salts behind.
ms: Filtration removes only insoluble solids (1 mark)
Distillation separates water from dissolved salts (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dissolved salts pass through filter paper.

questions.q: Give one reason why seawater is not potable.
questions.answer: It contains high levels of dissolved salts.
ms: Too much dissolved salt (1 mark)
questions.tip: Salt content is the key issue.

questions.q: A company says its product is 'green' because it can be recycled. Explain why this claim might be misleading.
questions.answer: Recycling still requires energy; the LCA of the whole product may show high energy use in manufacture/transport.
ms: Recycling requires energy / not all products are actually recycled (1 mark)
Full life cycle impact may be high (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link to life cycle assessment.

questions.q: A spring has a spring constant of 120 N/m. It is stretched by 5.0 cm without passing its limit of proportionality. How much elastic potential energy is stored?
ms: Ee = ½ke² = 0.5 × 120 × 0.050² = 0.15 J. 150 J uses e = 5.0 (cm not m); 0.30 J drops the ½; 3.0 J uses e not e².
questions.tip: Convert cm to m before squaring the extension.

questions.q: A 250 g apple falls 1.8 m from a branch. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Ignoring air resistance, how much kinetic energy does it have just before hitting the ground?
ms: Ek gained = Ep lost = mgh = 0.25 × 9.8 × 1.8 = 4.41 J ≈ 4.4 J. 441 J comes from mixing up g and kg (25 × 9.8 × 1.8); 2.2 J wrongly halves the answer as if using ½mv²; 0.45 J forgets to multiply by g.
questions.tip: Ep lost = Ek gained only if no energy is transferred to the surroundings: say so if asked to state an assumption.

questions.q: Describe the energy transfer when a battery-powered fan is switched on. Name the energy store that decreases and the useful energy store that increases.
questions.answer: Chemical store of the battery decreases; energy transferred electrically to the motor; kinetic store of the fan blades increases (some wasted to thermal store of surroundings).
ms: Chemical (energy store of the battery) decreases (1 mark)
Kinetic (energy store of the fan blades) increases, energy transferred electrically (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the word 'store'. 'Electrical energy' is a transfer pathway, not a store: AQA won't credit 'electrical store'.

questions.q: A climber gains 3.5 kJ of gravitational potential energy when she climbs a vertical height of 12 m. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the mass of the climber. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
ms: Converts 3.5 kJ to 3500 J (1 mark)
m = Ep ÷ (g × h) seen or implied, e.g. 3500 ÷ 117.6 (1 mark)
30 kg to 2 s.f. (1 mark). Allow 29.8 kg for 2 marks only if s.f. instruction ignored.
questions.tip: Read the s.f. instruction again before writing the final line. 29.76 is not 2 s.f.

questions.q: A spring in a toy has a spring constant of 200 N/m. When compressed it stores 0.90 J of elastic potential energy. Calculate the compression of the spring in cm. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
ms: Rearranges to e² = 2Ee/k or e = √(2Ee/k) (1 mark)
e = 0.0949 m (allow 0.095 m) (1 mark)
9.5 cm (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two traps: forgetting the square root, and forgetting to convert m to cm at the end.

questions.q: A roller coaster car of mass 500 kg starts from rest at the top of a 20 m drop. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. As it descends to the bottom, 18 kJ of energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings by friction and air resistance. Calculate the speed of the car at the bottom of the drop.
ms: Ep = mgh = 98 000 J (1 mark)
v² = 2Ek ÷ m = 320 (1 mark)
v = 17.9 m/s, allow 18 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Subtract the wasted energy BEFORE using Ek = ½mv². Students who skip this get 19.8 m/s and lose 2 marks.

questions.q: A car's speed increases from 15 m/s to 30 m/s. A student says: 'The car's kinetic energy has doubled.' Explain whether the student is correct. Use the kinetic energy equation in your answer.
questions.answer: Incorrect. Ek = ½mv², so Ek is proportional to v². Doubling v multiplies Ek by 2² = 4. The kinetic energy is four times bigger.
ms: Student is incorrect (no mark on its own) and Ek ∝ v² / speed is squared in Ek = ½mv² (1 mark)
Speed doubles (×2) (1 mark)
So kinetic energy increases by a factor of 4 (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Doubles' and 'quadruples' are the key comparison. Show the factor 2² = 4 explicitly.

questions.q: A pole vaulter runs at 8.5 m/s. Assume all of the vaulter's kinetic energy is transferred to gravitational potential energy. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Show that the maximum height the vaulter's centre of mass could rise is about 3.7 m.
ms: Equates ½mv² = mgh (mass cancels) (1 mark)
h = v² ÷ 2g (1 mark)
h = 3.69 m (must show more s.f. than 3.7 for a 'show that') (1 mark)
questions.tip: In a 'show that' question, give your answer to one more s.f. than the value given, otherwise you have not shown it.

questions.q: A 200 g copper block absorbs 3600 J and its temperature rises by 45 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of copper?
ms: c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ) = 3600 ÷ (0.20 × 45) = 400 J/kg °C. 0.40 uses m = 200 g not 0.20 kg; 9.0 is just m × Δθ; 80 ignores the mass (3600 ÷ 45).
questions.tip: Convert grams to kilograms: c is per kilogram.

questions.q: Water has a much higher specific heat capacity than concrete. Equal masses of water and concrete receive the same amount of energy. Which statement is correct?
options: Both temperatures rise by the same amount
The water's internal energy increases more
ms: Δθ = ΔE ÷ (mc). With the same ΔE and m, the lower c (concrete) gives the bigger temperature rise. Internal energy increase is the same for both.
questions.tip: High specific heat capacity means it takes MORE energy per °C, so the temperature changes LESS.

questions.q: A 2.0 kW kettle heats 1.5 kg of water for 2.0 minutes. The water starts at 18 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Assume all the energy is transferred to the water. Calculate the final temperature of the water.
ms: E = Pt with t = 120 s and P = 2000 W (1 mark)
Final temperature = 56 °C (adds starting temperature) (1 mark)
questions.tip: The question asks for FINAL temperature: add the rise to 18 °C. Stopping at 38 °C loses the last mark.

questions.q: In the specific heat capacity practical, identify the independent variable and the dependent variable when a student records the temperature of the block every minute while it is heated by an immersion heater with a joulemeter.
questions.answer: Independent: energy transferred (joulemeter reading) or time. Dependent: temperature of the block.
ms: Independent variable: energy transferred / time of heating (1 mark)
Dependent variable: temperature (rise) of the block (1 mark)
questions.tip: The independent variable is the one YOU change or choose to record at; the dependent is what you measure in response.

questions.q:
A student heats a 1.0 kg aluminium block and plots temperature (y-axis, °C) against energy transferred (x-axis, J). The straight section of the graph rises from 20.0 °C at 0 J to 31.0 °C at 10 000 J.
(a) Calculate the gradient of the graph. (1 mark)
(b) Use the gradient to calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium. (2 marks)
questions.answer:
(a) gradient = 11.0 ÷ 10 000 = 0.0011 °C/J
(b) gradient = 1/(mc), so c = 1 ÷ (m × gradient) = 1 ÷ (1.0 × 0.0011) = 909 J/kg °C (allow 910)
ms: (b) c = 1 ÷ (m × gradient) seen (1 mark)
(b) 909 J/kg °C (allow 900 to 910) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Δθ = E/(mc) means θ against E has gradient 1/(mc). Many students write c = gradient and lose both marks.

questions.q: A night storage heater contains 120 kg of concrete bricks. Overnight the bricks are heated from 25 °C to 150 °C. Specific heat capacity of concrete = 880 J/kg °C. Calculate the energy stored in the bricks in MJ.
ms: Δθ = 125 °C (1 mark)
13.2 MJ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mega = 10⁶. Divide joules by 1 000 000 to get MJ.

questions.q: Suggest why a material with a high specific heat capacity is chosen for the bricks in a night storage heater.
questions.answer: It can store a large amount of energy for each degree of temperature rise, so it stores lots of energy overnight without getting dangerously hot, and releases it slowly as it cools.
ms: Stores a lot of energy per kg per °C / large energy for a small temperature change (1 mark)
So it can release energy over a long time / does not reach unsafe temperatures (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the definition: energy per kilogram per degree. That is what the mark scheme looks for.

questions.q:
Three groups measure the specific heat capacity of the same aluminium block. Their values are 880 J/kg °C, 920 J/kg °C and 1010 J/kg °C.
(a) Calculate the mean value. (1 mark)
(b) Estimate the uncertainty in the mean, using the range. (2 marks)
(c) The accepted value is 900 J/kg °C. Suggest why most values are higher than this. (1 mark)
questions.answer: (a) mean = 2810 ÷ 3 = 937 J/kg °C (b) range = 1010 − 880 = 130; uncertainty = ± half the range = ± 65 J/kg °C (c) Energy is dissipated to the surroundings, so the temperature rise is smaller than expected, making c = E/(mΔθ) too big.
ms: (a) 937 J/kg °C (allow 936.7 or 940) (1 mark)
(b) Range = 130 J/kg °C (1 mark)
(b) Uncertainty ± 65 J/kg °C (1 mark)
(c) Energy lost to surroundings so Δθ smaller / c too high (1 mark)
questions.tip: Uncertainty = half the range, written with ±.

questions.q: Two kettles boil the same mass of water from the same starting temperature. Kettle A takes 3 minutes. Kettle B takes 4 minutes. Which statement is correct?
options: Kettle A transfers more energy to the water
Kettle B has a higher power
Both kettles have the same power
Kettle A has a higher power
ms: Same energy needed; P = E/t, so the shorter time means higher power. Both transfer the same energy to the water.
questions.tip: Power is the RATE of energy transfer: same energy in less time means more power.

questions.q: A light bulb has an input power of 60 W and an efficiency of 15%. How much energy does it waste every second?
ms: Useful power = 0.15 × 60 = 9 W, so wasted = 60 − 9 = 51 W = 51 J every second. 9 J is the useful energy, not the wasted.
questions.tip: Read whether the question asks for useful or wasted energy.

questions.q: A student of mass 62 kg runs up a flight of stairs with a vertical height of 3.5 m in 4.2 s. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the student's useful power output.
ms: Ep = mgh = 2126.6 J (1 mark)
P = E ÷ t (1 mark)
506 W (allow 510 W) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the VERTICAL height, not the length of the stairs.

questions.q: An electric pump has an input power of 1.5 kW and an efficiency of 40%. It lifts 900 kg of water through a vertical height of 6.0 m. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the time taken.
ms: Useful power output = 600 W (1 mark)
Ep gained = mgh = 52 920 J (1 mark)
t = E ÷ P(useful) (1 mark)
88.2 s (allow 88 s) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Match like with like: useful energy with useful power. Using 1500 W gives 35 s and loses 2 marks.

questions.q: Give one way of reducing the unwanted energy transfer from a bicycle chain and gears, and explain how it reduces the energy wasted.
questions.answer: Lubricate the chain and gears with oil. This reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the chain and surroundings.
ms: Lubricate / oil the chain and gears (1 mark)
Reason: reduces friction so less energy dissipated to thermal store (1 mark)
questions.tip: Lubrication reduces FRICTION. Always link the method to what it reduces.

questions.q:
A student wraps three identical beakers of hot water in different materials and records the temperature after 10 minutes. Each starts at 80 °C.
Material | Temperature after 10 min (°C)
Bubble wrap | 68
Newspaper | 62
Cotton wool | 71
(a) Which material is the best insulator? Give a reason. (2 marks)
(b) Give one control variable. (1 mark)
questions.answer: (a) Cotton wool; it had the smallest temperature drop (9 °C), so the lowest rate of energy transfer. (b) Volume/mass of water, starting temperature, thickness/number of layers of material, same time, same beaker.
ms: (a) Cotton wool (1 mark)
(a) Smallest temperature decrease / smallest rate of cooling (1 mark)
(b) Any one: same volume/mass of water, same starting temperature, same thickness/number of layers, same type/size of beaker, lid or no lid on all (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Same amount of material' is vague. Say thickness or number of layers.

questions.q: A householder replaces a single-glazed window with a double-glazed window. Explain why this reduces the rate of energy transfer from the house.
questions.answer: Double glazing has a gap of air (or vacuum/gas) between two panes; air has a low thermal conductivity so the rate of energy transfer by conduction is reduced; the air is trapped so cannot form convection currents easily; so the house loses energy more slowly / cools down more slowly.
ms: Gap of air/gas (or vacuum) between two panes (1 mark)
Air/gas has low thermal conductivity / is a poor conductor (1 mark)
So a lower rate of energy transfer by conduction through the window (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'rate of energy transfer' and 'thermal conductivity'. 'Keeps heat in' scores nothing.

questions.q: An electric motor in a toy crane is supplied with 2.4 kW for 60 s. The useful energy output is 30 kJ. Calculate the efficiency of the motor as a percentage.
ms: Input energy E = Pt = 144 000 J (1 mark)
Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 30 000 ÷ 144 000 (1 mark)
21% (allow 20.8%) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Both energies must be in the same unit: convert kJ to J before dividing.

questions.q: Which energy resource is NOT renewable?
ms: Nuclear fuel (uranium/plutonium) will run out: it cannot be replenished as it is used. The others are renewable.
questions.tip: Renewable means replenished as it is used, not 'clean'. Nuclear is low-carbon but non-renewable.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why biofuels are described as carbon neutral?
options: Biofuels do not need land to grow
The carbon dioxide released when burned was absorbed by the plants as they grew
Burning biofuels releases no carbon dioxide
Biofuels are made from fossil fuels
ms: Biofuels do release CO₂ when burned, but this was taken in by photosynthesis as the plants grew, so overall there is (ideally) no net increase.
questions.tip: Never say biofuels release no CO₂. They release it; the plants absorbed it first.

questions.q: Give two reasons why solar cells are not a reliable way to generate electricity in the UK.
questions.answer: No electricity at night; output depends on cloud cover/weather; less in winter (shorter days, lower sun).
ms: No output at night (1 mark)
Output reduced on cloudy days / in winter / depends on weather (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Not reliable' means you cannot guarantee output when needed. Give reasons linked to time/weather.

questions.q: Explain why the UK still has gas-fired power stations even though it has many wind turbines.
questions.answer: Wind is unreliable: turbines produce no electricity when there is no wind (or too much wind). Demand can rise quickly (e.g. evenings). Gas power stations can be started up quickly and produce a reliable output to meet peaks in demand.
ms: Wind is unreliable / does not blow all the time (1 mark)
Demand for electricity varies / has peaks (1 mark)
Gas stations have a short start-up time / reliable so can meet demand when wind output is low (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention start-up time for gas. It is the key advantage AQA rewards over nuclear and coal.

questions.q: Give one environmental advantage and one environmental disadvantage of building a hydroelectric dam.
questions.answer: Advantage: no carbon dioxide/polluting gases produced when generating. Disadvantage: flooding a valley destroys habitats / rotting vegetation releases methane.
ms: Advantage: no CO₂ / no greenhouse gas / no air pollution while generating (1 mark)
Disadvantage: floods land / destroys habitats / affects river ecosystems (1 mark)
questions.tip: The question asks for ENVIRONMENTAL points. Cost and reliability are not environmental.

questions.q:
A country's wind turbines generated 8 TWh of electricity in 2012 and 36 TWh in 2024. Total electricity generated in 2024 was 300 TWh.
(a) Calculate the percentage of 2024 electricity generated by wind. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in wind generation from 2012 to 2024. (2 marks)
ms: (b) Increase = 36 − 8 = 28 TWh (1 mark)
questions.tip: Percentage increase = change ÷ ORIGINAL value × 100. Dividing by 36 gives 78%: wrong.

questions.q: A remote island currently generates all its electricity using diesel generators. The council is considering replacing them with a combination of wind turbines and tidal barrage. Evaluate this plan. Give a conclusion.
questions.answer: Wind and tidal are renewable, produce no CO₂ when generating, and remove the need to ship diesel. Tidal is predictable and reliable (tides twice a day) though output varies with tide; wind is unreliable. Together they partly cover each other. Disadvantages: high initial building costs, visual impact and noise from turbines, tidal barrage affects estuary habitats and shipping, need backup or storage when output is low. Conclusion: likely a good plan if some backup (e.g. keep a diesel generator or battery storage) is kept for times of low output.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Detailed, balanced evaluation covering advantages and disadvantages of both resources, comparing with diesel, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Some advantages and disadvantages, may focus on one resource; a conclusion may be stated but not fully justified.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple relevant points, e.g. wind is renewable, tidal is expensive.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: renewable vs diesel (finite fossil fuel); no CO₂/sulfur dioxide when generating; no fuel costs or transport; tidal is predictable and reliable; wind unreliable/variable; combination reduces gaps; high set-up costs; tidal barrage affects habitats, mud flats and boat access; wind turbines visual/noise; may still need diesel backup or energy storage; conclusion with reason.
questions.tip: 'Evaluate' needs both sides AND a conclusion. Without a conclusion you cannot reach Level 3.

questions.q: Suggest why the energy demand for heating in the UK is much higher in winter than in summer, and which energy resource is mainly used to meet it.
questions.answer: Colder outside temperatures in winter mean more energy needed to keep homes warm. Mostly met by burning natural gas (in boilers).
ms: Lower outside temperatures / colder so more heating needed (1 mark)
Natural gas (allow fossil fuels/electricity from gas) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Heating in UK homes is mainly from gas boilers, not electricity.

questions.q: A current of 0.80 A flows through a motor for 45 minutes. How much charge flows?
ms: Q = It = 0.80 × (45 × 60) = 0.80 × 2700 = 2160 C. 36 C forgets to convert minutes to seconds.
questions.tip: Time in Q = It must be in seconds.

questions.q: A 12 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel to a 6.0 V battery. What is the current from the battery?
ms: Current in 12 Ω = 6.0/12 = 0.50 A; in 6.0 Ω = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A; total = 1.5 A. 0.33 A wrongly adds resistances (18 Ω) as if in series.
questions.tip: In parallel each branch has the full supply pd. Find each branch current then add.

questions.q: Two resistors, 15 Ω and 25 Ω, are connected in series with a 12 V supply. Calculate the potential difference across the 25 Ω resistor.
ms: Total resistance = 40 Ω (1 mark)
I = V ÷ R = 0.30 A (1 mark)
V = 7.5 V (1 mark)
questions.tip: In series the pd splits in the ratio of the resistances: the bigger resistor gets the bigger share.

questions.q: A student wants to measure the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it. Describe how the ammeter and the voltmeter should be connected.
questions.answer: Ammeter in series with the lamp; voltmeter in parallel across the lamp.
ms: Ammeter in series (with the lamp) (1 mark)
Voltmeter in parallel (across the lamp) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Learn it as a pair: ammeter series, voltmeter parallel.

questions.q: A torch has two identical lamps connected in parallel to a battery. One lamp breaks. Explain what happens to the current from the battery and the brightness of the other lamp.
questions.answer: The other lamp stays lit at the same brightness, because it still has the full battery pd across it (each branch is independent). The total resistance of the circuit increases (only one branch), so the current from the battery decreases (halves).
ms: Other lamp stays the same brightness (1 mark)
Because pd across it is unchanged / still the full supply pd (1 mark)
Total current from battery decreases (because total resistance increases / one fewer branch) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Adding a branch in parallel decreases total resistance; removing one increases it.

questions.q: A 6.0 V battery drives a current of 1.5 A through a motor for 1.0 hour. Calculate the energy transferred by the battery.
ms: t = 3600 s (1 mark)
Q = 5400 C or E = VIt seen (1 mark)
questions.tip: Chain equations: Q = It then E = QV. Write each step: method marks come from the working.

questions.q:
A 9.0 V battery is connected in series with a 20 Ω resistor and a thermistor. The current is 250 mA.
(a) Calculate the resistance of the thermistor. (3 marks)
(b) The temperature of the thermistor increases. State and explain what happens to the current. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
(a) R total = 9.0 ÷ 0.250 = 36 Ω; thermistor = 36 − 20 = 16 Ω
(b) Current increases because thermistor resistance decreases as temperature rises, so total resistance decreases.
ms: (a) Converts 250 mA = 0.250 A (1 mark)
(a) Total R = V ÷ I = 36 Ω (1 mark)
(a) Thermistor = 16 Ω (1 mark)
(b) Current increases because thermistor resistance decreases (so total resistance decreases) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Find total resistance first, then subtract the known resistor.

questions.q: Explain why adding a resistor in parallel with another resistor decreases the total resistance of the circuit.
questions.answer: Adding a parallel branch gives the charge an extra path to flow through. Both branches have the same pd as the supply, so the total current from the supply increases. Since R = V ÷ I, with the same V and a bigger I, the total resistance is smaller.
ms: Extra path / more routes for current (charge) to flow (1 mark)
pd across each branch is the same / total current increases (1 mark)
R = V ÷ I so larger current with same pd means smaller total resistance (1 mark)
questions.tip: This is a spec 'explain' point. Mention both the extra path and the increase in total current.

questions.q: Which component's resistance decreases as light intensity increases?
ms: An LDR's resistance decreases as light intensity increases. A thermistor responds to temperature.
questions.tip: LDR: more Light, Less resistance. Thermistor: more heat, less resistance (for the type in the spec).

questions.q: The current-potential difference graph for a component is a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
options: Current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature
ms: A straight line through the origin shows I ∝ V, so resistance is constant: an ohmic conductor at constant temperature.
questions.tip: 'Directly proportional' needs a straight line AND through the origin.

questions.q: A filament lamp has a current of 0.40 A at 6.0 V and 0.60 A at 12.0 V. By how much does its resistance increase?
ms: R = V/I: 6.0/0.40 = 15 Ω; 12.0/0.60 = 20 Ω. Increase = 5 Ω. 30 Ω uses the gradient ΔV/ΔI = 6.0/0.20 (not valid for resistance at a point).
questions.tip: Resistance at a point is V ÷ I at that point, NOT the gradient of the graph.

questions.q: A student investigates how the resistance of a wire depends on its length. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and one control variable.
questions.answer: Independent: length of wire. Dependent: resistance (calculated from V and I). Control: material, diameter/thickness of wire, temperature, current/pd setting.
ms: Independent: length (1 mark)
Dependent: resistance (allow current/pd readings used to find it) (1 mark)
Control: any one of material, cross-sectional area/diameter, temperature (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Same wire' is not a control variable answer. Say same material and same diameter.

questions.q:
Results for the resistance of a wire:
Length (cm) | Resistance (Ω)
20 | 1.3
40 | 2.6
60 | 3.8
80 | 5.1
(a) Describe the relationship between length and resistance. (2 marks)
(b) A second student repeats the experiment with different leads and clips. Her line of best fit is parallel to this one but crosses the resistance axis at 0.2 Ω instead of passing through the origin. Suggest the cause and the type of error. (2 marks)
questions.answer:
(a) Resistance increases as length increases; directly proportional (roughly constant ratio R/L ≈ 0.064 Ω/cm, line through the origin).
(b) Resistance of the leads/crocodile clips is added to every reading, or the 0 cm clip is not lined up with zero on the ruler; systematic error (zero error).
ms: (a) As length increases, resistance increases (1 mark)
(a) (Directly) proportional / doubling length doubles resistance, with evidence e.g. 20 → 40 cm, 1.3 → 2.6 Ω (1 mark)
(b) Resistance of connecting leads/clips or clip not at zero on the ruler (1 mark)
(b) Systematic error / zero error (1 mark)
questions.tip: A constant offset in every reading is a systematic (zero) error. Random errors cause scatter, not an offset.

questions.q: Design a circuit that would make a lamp switch on automatically when it gets dark, using an LDR. Explain how the potential difference across the LDR changes when it gets dark.
questions.answer: LDR in series with a fixed resistor across a supply (potential divider); the lamp circuit (or switch) is controlled by the pd across the LDR. In the dark the LDR resistance increases, so it takes a larger share of the supply pd; the pd across the LDR increases, which switches the lamp on.
ms: LDR in series with a fixed resistor / potential divider (1 mark)
In the dark, LDR resistance increases (1 mark)
So pd across the LDR increases (larger share of the supply pd) and this switches on the lamp (1 mark)
questions.tip: In series, the component with the higher resistance gets the bigger share of the pd.

questions.q: Describe the current-potential difference graph for a diode.
questions.answer: In the forward direction the current is zero until a small pd is reached, then the current increases rapidly. In the reverse direction the current is (almost) zero because the resistance is very high.
ms: Forward: current increases steeply after a small threshold pd (1 mark)
Reverse: (almost) no current / very high resistance (1 mark)
questions.tip: A diode lets current flow in one direction only.

questions.q: Describe a method to investigate how the length of a wire affects its resistance. Include the circuit you would use and how you would make the results valid.
questions.answer: Tape a wire (e.g. constantan) along a metre ruler. Connect in series with a battery/low-voltage supply, switch and ammeter, with a voltmeter in parallel across the length being tested; one crocodile clip at 0 cm, the other moved to set lengths (e.g. 10, 20 … 80 cm). Record V and I for each length, calculate R = V/I. Keep current low and switch off between readings so the wire doesn't heat up. Repeat and calculate means. Plot R against length.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear, logically ordered method with correct circuit, range of lengths, R = V/I, and steps to make results valid (low current/temperature control, repeats).
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Correct circuit and method of changing length and finding resistance, but some steps missing.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple relevant statements, e.g. measure current for different lengths.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: wire attached to metre ruler; crocodile clips; ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel across test length; at least 5 lengths spread over range; R = V ÷ I; switch off between readings / low current to stop heating (temperature is a control variable); same material and diameter; repeat and mean; plot R (y) against length (x); expect straight line through origin.
questions.tip: Mention heating: a warm wire has a higher resistance, which spoils a fair test.

questions.q:
A student measures the resistance of a thermistor at different temperatures.
Temperature (°C) | Resistance (Ω)
10 | 1800
30 | 1100
50 | 650
70 | 400
90 | 280
(a) Describe the relationship. (2 marks)
(b) Suggest why this thermistor would be useful in a fire alarm. (1 mark)
questions.answer: (a) As temperature increases, resistance decreases. The decrease is non-linear: it drops quickly at low temperature and more slowly at high temperature (the rate of decrease gets smaller). (b) At high temperatures its resistance is low, so the current in the alarm circuit increases, which can trigger the alarm.
ms: (a) Resistance decreases as temperature increases (1 mark)
(a) Not proportional / rate of decrease gets smaller, with data, e.g. drop of 700 Ω from 10–30 °C but only 120 Ω from 70–90 °C (1 mark)
(b) Resistance falls / current rises when hot, triggering the alarm (1 mark)
questions.tip: For 'describe the relationship', give the trend AND the pattern (linear, proportional, or how the rate changes) using data.

questions.q: Which wire in a UK plug is brown and carries the alternating potential difference from the supply?
ms: The live wire is brown and is at 230 V. Neutral is blue (about 0 V); earth is green and yellow.
questions.tip: Colours: live brown, neutral blue, earth green/yellow.

questions.q: A 2.5 kW heater is used for 90 minutes. Electricity costs 28p per kWh. What is the cost?
questions.tip: Convert minutes to hours when using kWh: 90 min = 1.5 h, not 0.9 h.

questions.q: A 2.0 kW electric heater is connected to the 230 V mains supply. Calculate the resistance of its heating element. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
ms: I = P ÷ V = 8.7 A (1 mark)
R = V ÷ I (or P = I²R rearranged) (1 mark)
26 Ω to 2 s.f. (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two-step: find I with P = VI, then R with V = IR.

questions.q: A cable with a total resistance of 0.15 Ω carries a current of 13 A to an appliance. Calculate the power wasted heating the cable, and suggest why thicker cables are used for high-power appliances.
questions.answer: P = I²R = 13² × 0.15 = 25.35 W ≈ 25 W. Thicker cables have lower resistance, so less power is wasted and the cable doesn't overheat (fire risk).
ms: 25 W (allow 25.4 W) (1 mark)
Thicker cable has lower resistance so less energy dissipated / less heating / less fire risk (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use P = I²R for heating in wires: the current is squared, so doubling current quadruples the wasted power.

questions.q: State the function of the earth wire and explain when it carries a current.
questions.answer: It is a safety wire that stops the appliance's metal casing becoming live. It only carries a current if there is a fault (e.g. the live wire touches the casing).
ms: Safety wire / stops the casing becoming live (1 mark)
Only carries a current if there is a fault (1 mark)
questions.tip: The earth wire is at 0 V and normally carries NO current.

questions.q: The National Grid transmits electricity at 400 000 V. Explain how transmitting at high potential difference makes the system efficient. Refer to power equations in your answer.
questions.answer: For a given power, P = VI, so a high pd means a low current. Power lost heating the cables is P = I²R. A low current means much less energy wasted as heat in the cables, so transmission is efficient. Step-down transformers then reduce the pd to 230 V for safe use in homes.
ms: P = VI: for the same power, high pd means low current (1 mark)
Power loss in cables P = I²R (1 mark)
Lower current gives much less energy dissipated/heating in cables (1 mark)
So more efficient; step-down transformers reduce pd for safe use in homes (1 mark)
questions.tip: Quote both P = VI and P = I²R. That's what turns a 2-mark answer into 4.

questions.q: A kettle transfers 405 kJ of energy in 2.5 minutes from the 230 V mains. Calculate the power of the kettle in kW, and the current it draws to 2 significant figures.
ms: t = 150 s and P = E ÷ t (1 mark)
2.7 kW (1 mark)
I = 12 A (1 mark)
questions.tip: Convert kJ to J and minutes to seconds before dividing.

questions.q: A table lamp has a plastic case with no exposed metal parts. Its cable only has two wires: live and neutral. Suggest why the lamp is still safe without an earth wire.
questions.answer: The case is made of plastic, which is an electrical insulator. Even if the live wire came loose and touched the case, the case could not become live, so a person touching it would not get a shock.
ms: Plastic is an (electrical) insulator (1 mark)
So the case cannot become live / no current through a person touching it (1 mark)
questions.tip: The earth wire protects METAL cases. No metal case, no need for earth.

questions.q: A block of aluminium has a mass of 5.4 kg and a volume of 0.0020 m³. What is its density?
questions.tip: Density = mass ÷ volume. Check your answer is sensible: metals are thousands of kg/m³.

questions.q: During boiling, water stays at 100 °C even though it is still being heated. Where does the energy go?
options: It increases the kinetic energy of the particles
It breaks the bonds between particles, increasing the potential energy store
It increases the temperature of the steam
It is all lost to the surroundings
ms: During a change of state the energy breaks/weakens intermolecular forces, increasing the potential energy of particles, not their kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant.
questions.tip: Temperature is linked to kinetic energy. Flat section = potential energy increasing.

questions.q: A 1.2 kW kettle boils away 50 g of water. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg. Assuming all the energy goes into boiling the water, how long does this take?
questions.tip: Two steps: E = mL, then t = E/P. Convert grams to kg and kW to W.

questions.q: A student finds the density of a cork stopper. Its mass is 3.6 g. It has a volume of 15 cm³. Calculate the density in kg/m³.
ms: ρ = m ÷ V (1 mark)
0.24 g/cm³ (1 mark)
240 kg/m³ (× 1000 conversion) (1 mark)
questions.tip: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Water is 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³: use it as a check.

questions.q: 0.20 kg of ice at 0 °C is melted and the water is then warmed to 25 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the total energy needed.
ms: E = mL = 66 800 J (1 mark)
E = mcΔθ = 21 000 J (1 mark)
Adds both stages (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two stages need two equations: latent heat for the change of state, specific heat capacity for the temperature change.

questions.q: Describe the differences in the arrangement and motion of particles in a solid and a gas.
questions.answer: Solid: particles close together in a regular arrangement, vibrate about fixed positions. Gas: particles far apart, random arrangement, move quickly in random directions.
ms: Solid: close together, regular pattern (1 mark)
Gas: far apart / random arrangement (1 mark)
