Solid particles vibrate in fixed positions; gas particles move fast and randomly (1 mark)
questions.tip: Compare like with like: arrangement AND motion for both states.

questions.q: A 1500 W heater melts a 0.50 kg block of a solid wax. A temperature-time graph shows the temperature is constant at 62 °C between 3.0 minutes and 5.0 minutes. Assume all the heater's energy is transferred to the wax. Calculate the specific latent heat of fusion of the wax.
ms: Time at constant temperature = 120 s (1 mark)
E = Pt = 180 000 J (1 mark)
L = 3.6 × 10⁵ J/kg (1 mark)
questions.tip: The flat part of the graph is when the change of state happens. Use only that time.

questions.q: Explain why the density of a substance is usually lower as a gas than as a liquid.
questions.answer: Same mass of particles, but in a gas the particles are much further apart so they take up a much larger volume. ρ = m/V, so density is lower.
ms: Particles much further apart in a gas / larger volume for the same mass (1 mark)
Density = mass ÷ volume so lower density (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mass doesn't change when the state changes; only volume does.

questions.q:
A sealed 2.0 m³ container is full of air of density 1.2 kg/m³. A pump removes half of the mass of the air. The volume of the container does not change.
(a) Calculate the mass of air originally in the container. (1 mark)
(b) Determine the new density of the air. Explain your answer in terms of particles. (2 marks)
questions.answer: (a) m = ρV = 1.2 × 2.0 = 2.4 kg (b) 1.2 kg in 2.0 m³ gives 0.60 kg/m³. The remaining particles spread out to fill the same volume, so they are further apart on average.
ms: (a) 2.4 kg (1 mark)
(b) 0.60 kg/m³ (1 mark)
(b) Fewer particles fill the same volume / particles further apart (1 mark)
questions.tip: A gas always fills its container. Density changes if mass changes at fixed volume.

questions.q: Which particle is found orbiting the nucleus of an atom?
ms: Electrons are in energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.
questions.tip: Nucleus = protons + neutrons. Shells = electrons.

questions.q: An atom of chlorine-37 has an atomic number of 17. How many neutrons does it have?
ms: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 37 − 17 = 20.
questions.tip: Mass number is protons + neutrons. Subtract the atomic number.

questions.q: Why did scientists replace the plum pudding model with the nuclear model?
options: Neutrons were found in the nucleus
Atoms were found to be indivisible
Some alpha particles were deflected through large angles by a thin gold foil
ms: Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment showed large deflections, which the plum pudding model couldn't explain: positive charge and mass must be concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
questions.tip: Link each model change to the evidence that caused it.

questions.q: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
questions.answer: An atom has equal numbers of protons (+1 each) and electrons (−1 each), so the charges cancel.
ms: Number of protons = number of electrons (1 mark)
Protons positive and electrons negative / equal and opposite charges cancel (1 mark)
questions.tip: Neutrons have no charge, so they don't affect the overall charge.

questions.q:
Two atoms: atom X has 6 protons and 6 neutrons; atom Y has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.
(a) Explain why X and Y are isotopes of the same element. (2 marks)
(b) Give the mass number of Y. (1 mark)
questions.answer: (a) Same number of protons (6), so same element; different numbers of neutrons. (b) 14
ms: (a) Same number of protons / same atomic number (1 mark)
(a) Different number of neutrons / different mass number (1 mark)
(b) 14 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons. Both halves needed for 2 marks.

questions.q: The radius of a gold atom is about 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The radius of its nucleus is about 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Calculate how many times larger the radius of the atom is than the radius of the nucleus, and use your answer to explain why most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil.
questions.answer: 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 20 000 (2 × 10⁴). The nucleus is tiny compared to the atom, so the atom is mostly empty space; most alpha particles do not pass close to a nucleus.
ms: Correct division (1 mark)
Atom is mostly empty space, so most alpha particles don't come near the nucleus (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dividing standard form: divide the numbers, subtract the powers. −10 − (−15) = 5.

questions.q: Describe what Niels Bohr and James Chadwick each contributed to the model of the atom, and explain how scientific models are developed.
questions.answer: Bohr: electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances/energy levels; his calculations agreed with experimental observations. Chadwick: discovered the neutron in the nucleus (about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted). Models change when new experimental evidence cannot be explained by the existing model; ideas are tested and checked by other scientists.
ms: Bohr: electrons in fixed orbits/energy levels at specific distances (1 mark)
Bohr's theory agreed with experimental observations/calculations (1 mark)
Chadwick: provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus (1 mark)
Models are changed/replaced when new evidence doesn't fit the old model (1 mark)
questions.tip: Pair each scientist with the precise idea they added. Don't mix up Bohr and Rutherford.

questions.q: An atom loses an electron from its outer shell. What has it become, and what is its charge?
questions.answer: A positive ion with a charge of +1.
ms: Positive ion (1 mark)
Charge +1 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Losing negative charge makes the atom positive.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium but not by paper?
ms: Beta particles pass through paper but are absorbed by a few mm of aluminium. Alpha is stopped by paper; gamma needs thick lead or concrete.
questions.tip: Penetration: alpha (paper), beta (aluminium), gamma (lead/concrete).

questions.q: Polonium-210 (atomic number 84) decays by alpha emission. What are the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus?
ms: Alpha particle = ⁴₂He. Mass number 210 − 4 = 206; atomic number 84 − 2 = 82 (lead).
questions.tip: Alpha: mass number −4, atomic number −2. Beta: mass number unchanged, atomic number +1.

questions.q: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. What fraction of the original undecayed nuclei remain after 24 hours?
questions.tip: Count the half-lives first, then halve that many times.

questions.q: A radioactive source has a corrected count rate of 960 counts per minute. Its half-life is 10 minutes. Calculate the count rate after 40 minutes, and state what fraction of the original count rate this is.
ms: Number of half-lives = 4 (1 mark)
60 counts per minute (1 mark)
Fraction = 1/16 (allow (1/2)⁴) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Count the half-lives first, then halve that many times. Write each step so a slip still earns method marks.

questions.q:
(HT) A sample has an initial activity of 4800 Bq. After 15 days the activity is 600 Bq.
(a) Determine the half-life. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the net decline in activity as a ratio of the initial activity after 15 days. (2 marks)
questions.answer:
(a) 4800 → 2400 → 1200 → 600 = 3 half-lives in 15 days; half-life = 5 days.
(b) Net decline = 4800 − 600 = 4200 Bq; ratio = 4200 ÷ 4800 = 0.875 (7/8)
ms: (a) 3 half-lives seen (1 mark)
(a) 5 days (1 mark)
(b) Net decline = 4200 Bq (1 mark)
questions.tip: Net decline is how much it has DROPPED, not what is left.

questions.q: Write the nuclear equation for the beta decay of strontium-90 (atomic number 38) into yttrium (Y).
questions.answer: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e
ms: Yttrium has mass number 90 (1 mark)
Yttrium has atomic number 39 (1 mark)
Beta particle written as ⁰₋₁e (1 mark)
questions.tip: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron: atomic number goes UP by 1.

questions.q: A worker's hand is exposed to a gamma source held nearby. A second worker gets dust containing an alpha emitter on their skin. Explain the difference between irradiation and radioactive contamination, and suggest why swallowing the alpha-emitting dust would be especially dangerous.
questions.answer: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from a source outside the body; the hand does not become radioactive. Contamination is unwanted radioactive atoms getting on or into a material/the body, so exposure continues until they are removed. Swallowed alpha emitters are inside the body, and alpha is the most strongly ionising, so it damages nearby cells/DNA.
ms: Irradiation: exposure to radiation from an outside source, object does not become radioactive (1 mark)
Contamination: radioactive atoms/material get on or into the object/body (so it keeps being exposed) (1 mark)
Alpha is (very) strongly ionising so inside the body it damages cells / tissue / DNA (1 mark)
questions.tip: Outside the body alpha is stopped by skin. Inside the body it is the most dangerous because it is the most ionising.

questions.q: Give three precautions a scientist could take to reduce their exposure to a radioactive source in a laboratory.
questions.answer: Use tongs to handle the source; keep the source as far from the body as possible; minimise time of exposure; store in a lead-lined box; wear gloves/protective clothing; point the source away.
ms: Use tongs / keep at arm's length to increase distance (1 mark)
Reduce time of exposure / return to lead-lined box when not in use (1 mark)
Shielding, e.g. lead screen, or gloves to prevent contamination (1 mark)
questions.tip: Distance, time and shielding are the three main ideas.

questions.q: What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope? Explain why radioactive decay is described as random.
questions.answer: Half-life is the time it takes for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample (or the count rate) to halve. Decay is random because you cannot predict which nucleus will decay next or when a particular nucleus will decay.
ms: Time for the number of (undecayed) nuclei / count rate / activity to halve (1 mark)
Cannot predict which nucleus will decay or when (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'number of nuclei' or 'count rate' halves. 'Time for half the substance to disappear' does not get the mark.

questions.q: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
ms: Mass has magnitude only. Weight, velocity and momentum have direction too, so they are vectors.
questions.tip: Weight is a force, so it is a vector. Mass is not.

questions.q: A suitcase has a weight of 196 N on Earth. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. What is its mass?
ms: m = W ÷ g = 196 ÷ 9.8 = 20 kg. 1920 multiplies instead of dividing.
questions.tip: Mass in kg, weight in N. Check the direction of your rearrangement.

questions.q: A horse pulls a cart with a force of 450 N for a distance of 1.2 km. How much work is done?
ms: W = Fs = 450 × 1200 = 540 000 J = 540 kJ. 540 J forgets to convert km to m.
questions.tip: Distance must be in metres.

questions.q: (HT) Two forces act on a boat: 9.0 N east from the wind and 12 N north from the current. Calculate the size of the resultant force on the boat.
questions.answer: R = √(9.0² + 12²) = √225 = 15 N (direction north of east)
ms: Forces are perpendicular so use Pythagoras or a scale drawing (1 mark)
15 N (1 mark)
questions.tip: Only add forces directly if they act along the same line.

questions.q: A car moves at a steady speed on a flat road. The driving force is 1800 N. State the size of the resistive forces and explain your answer.
questions.answer: 1800 N. At steady speed the resultant force is zero, so the forces are balanced.
ms: 1800 N (1 mark)
Constant speed so resultant force is zero / forces balanced (1 mark)
questions.tip: Constant velocity = zero resultant force (Newton's first law).

questions.q: A cyclist and bike of total mass 80 kg are travelling at 6.0 m/s. The brakes are applied and the bike stops in 4.5 m. Calculate the average braking force. Use the idea of work done.
questions.answer: Ek = ½ × 80 × 6.0² = 1440 J; work done by brakes = Ek, F = W ÷ s = 1440 ÷ 4.5 = 320 N
ms: Ek = 1440 J (1 mark)
Work done = Ek lost and F = W ÷ s (1 mark)
320 N (1 mark)
questions.tip: Work done by the braking force = kinetic energy lost.

questions.q: (HT) A child pulls a sledge with a rope at 40° above the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 50 N. Determine the horizontal component of the force (by scale drawing or otherwise) and explain why only this component does work in moving the sledge forward.
questions.answer: Horizontal component ≈ 38 N (50 cos 40° = 38.3 N). The sledge moves horizontally, and work is done only by the force component along the direction of motion.
ms: Correct method (scale diagram with stated scale or trigonometry) (1 mark)
38 N (allow 37 to 39 N) (1 mark)
Work is done only by the component in the direction of movement (horizontal) (1 mark)
questions.tip: On a scale drawing always state your scale, e.g. 1 cm = 5 N.

questions.q: (HT) A book rests on a slope. Its weight is 12 N. Explain how the forces on the book can be in equilibrium.
questions.answer: Weight can be resolved into a component down the slope and one perpendicular to it. Friction up the slope balances the component down the slope, and the normal contact force balances the perpendicular component, so the resultant is zero.
ms: Weight resolved into components parallel and perpendicular to the slope (1 mark)
Friction balances the parallel component and normal reaction balances the perpendicular one, so resultant force is zero (1 mark)
questions.tip: Equilibrium means resultant force = 0. Show it by resolving or by drawing a closed triangle of forces.

questions.q: A satellite orbits the Earth. Name the force that acts on the satellite and say whether it is a contact or non-contact force.
questions.answer: Gravitational force (weight); non-contact.
ms: Gravity / gravitational force / weight (1 mark)
Non-contact (1 mark)
questions.tip: Gravitational, magnetic and electrostatic forces are the three non-contact forces in the spec.

questions.q: A spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m. What force is needed to stretch it by 8.0 cm?
questions.tip: Always convert extension to metres.

questions.q: A spring is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality. Which statement is correct?
options: The force-extension graph starts to curve
The spring has no elastic potential energy
Extension is still directly proportional to force
ms: Beyond the limit of proportionality, F = ke no longer applies and the graph curves.
questions.tip: Only use F = ke and ½ke² up to the limit of proportionality.

questions.q: A spring has an unstretched length of 15.0 cm. When a 3.0 N weight is attached its length becomes 20.5 cm. Calculate the spring constant. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
ms: Extension = 5.5 cm = 0.055 m (1 mark)
k = F ÷ e (1 mark)
55 N/m (1 mark)
questions.tip: Extension = new length − original length. Using 20.5 cm as the extension is the commonest mistake.

questions.q:
A student hangs masses from a spring and records extension. Mass of each slotted mass = 100 g. g = 9.8 N/kg.
Number of masses | Extension (cm)
1 | 2.0
2 | 3.9
3 | 6.1
4 | 8.0
5 | 11.5
(a) Calculate the force for 4 masses. (1 mark)
(b) Use the 4-mass result to calculate the spring constant. (2 marks)
(c) Suggest what happened at 5 masses. (1 mark)
questions.answer: (a) F = 0.40 × 9.8 = 3.92 N (b) k = 3.92 ÷ 0.080 = 49 N/m (c) Exceeded the limit of proportionality (extension not proportional).
ms: (a) 3.92 N (1 mark)
(b) k = F ÷ e with e = 0.080 m (1 mark)
(b) 49 N/m (1 mark)
(c) Passed the limit of proportionality / extension no longer proportional to force (1 mark)
questions.tip: Turn grams into newtons in two steps: g → kg, then × 9.8.

questions.q: Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in a spring with spring constant 49 N/m extended by 8.0 cm.
ms: Correct substitution with e = 0.080 m (1 mark)
0.16 J (allow 0.157 J) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Square the extension (in metres) before multiplying.

questions.q: In the force and extension practical, explain why the student should read the ruler at eye level and use a pointer attached to the bottom of the spring.
questions.answer: Reading at eye level avoids parallax error. A pointer gives a clear fixed point to read against the ruler. Both make the length measurements more accurate.
ms: Eye level avoids parallax error (1 mark)
Pointer gives a precise reference point on the scale (1 mark)
Improves accuracy of extension measurements (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Parallax' is the key word. Say it.

questions.q: Compare the behaviour of a spring and a rubber band when they are stretched by small forces and then released.
questions.answer: Spring (within limit of proportionality): extension proportional to force, linear graph; returns to original length (elastic). Rubber band: extension not proportional to force, graph curves; also returns to (near) original shape when released if not overstretched.
ms: Spring: extension directly proportional / obeys Hooke's law (1 mark)
Rubber band: extension not proportional / non-linear graph (1 mark)
Both deform elastically / return to original shape when forces removed (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Compare' needs a similarity or difference for both. Don't describe them separately without linking.

questions.q: A spring with spring constant 30 N/m is stretched by 12 cm. How much work is done stretching it, assuming it doesn't pass its limit of proportionality? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: Work done = elastic potential energy stored = ½ke² = ½ × 30 × 0.12² = 0.216 J ≈ 0.22 J
ms: Work done = Ee = ½ke² (1 mark)
0.22 J (allow 0.216 J) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Work done stretching a spring = Ee stored, provided it doesn't deform inelastically.

questions.q: A toy launcher contains a spring with spring constant 80 N/m. The spring is compressed by 5.0 cm and then released, firing a 20 g ball vertically upwards. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Assume all the elastic potential energy is transferred to the gravitational potential energy store of the ball. Calculate the maximum height the ball reaches.
ms: e = 0.050 m and m = 0.020 kg (1 mark)
Ee = 0.10 J (1 mark)
Ee = mgh rearranged: h = Ee ÷ (mg) (1 mark)
0.51 m (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two unit conversions here: cm to m AND g to kg. Missing either one is the commonest way to lose marks.

questions.q: A sprinter runs 100 m in 10.5 s. What is the average speed?
questions.tip: Check it's a sensible answer: about 10 m/s for a sprinter.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal line show?
ms: Horizontal line = zero gradient = speed of zero: the object is stationary.
questions.tip: Don't confuse with velocity-time graphs, where a horizontal line means constant velocity.

questions.q: A car slows from 25 m/s to rest in 5.0 s. What is its acceleration?
ms: a = (v − u) ÷ t = (0 − 25) ÷ 5.0 = −5.0 m/s². The negative sign shows deceleration.
questions.tip: a = Δv/t: final minus initial.

questions.q: A train accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m/s² over a distance of 100 m, reaching 20 m/s. Calculate its initial velocity.
ms: Uses v² − u² = 2as (1 mark)
u² = 100 (1 mark)
u = 10 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rearrange before substituting. The equation is on the equation sheet, but rearranging is not.

questions.q:
(HT) A velocity-time graph for a scooter: accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 8.0 s, travels at 12 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 4.0 s.
(a) Calculate the total distance travelled. (3 marks)
(b) Calculate the deceleration in the final stage. (1 mark)
ms: (a) Distance = area under the graph (1 mark)
(a) At least two correct areas (48, 120, 24 m) (1 mark)
(a) 192 m (1 mark)
(b) 3.0 m/s² (1 mark)
questions.tip: Split the area into triangles and rectangles. Label each part as you go.

questions.q: (HT) A distance-time graph for an accelerating car is a curve. A tangent drawn at t = 5.0 s passes through (2.0 s, 30 m) and (8.0 s, 90 m). Determine the speed of the car at t = 5.0 s, and explain your method.
questions.answer: Speed = gradient of tangent = (90 − 30) ÷ (8.0 − 2.0) = 60 ÷ 6.0 = 10 m/s
ms: The speed at a point is the gradient of the tangent to the curve (1 mark)
Change in distance ÷ change in time = 60 ÷ 6.0 (1 mark)
10 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Draw the tangent long: a big triangle reduces reading errors.

questions.q: A stone falls from rest from a cliff. Ignore air resistance; acceleration = 9.8 m/s². Calculate its speed after falling 30 m.
ms: u = 0 and v² = u² + 2as (1 mark)
v² = 588 (1 mark)
24 m/s (allow 24.2 m/s) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Falling from rest: u = 0. 'From rest' in the question is data.

questions.q: A ball is dropped and reaches terminal velocity. Explain why it stops accelerating.
questions.answer: As speed increases, air resistance increases until it equals the weight. The resultant force is then zero so acceleration is zero.
ms: Air resistance increases with speed until it equals weight (1 mark)
Resultant force zero so no acceleration / constant velocity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say what increases (air resistance), what it becomes equal to (weight) and the consequence (zero resultant force).

questions.q: A bus travels 18 km at an average speed of 40 km/h. Calculate the journey time in minutes, and the average speed in m/s.
ms: t = 0.45 h (1 mark)
27 minutes (1 mark)
11 m/s (allow 11.1 m/s) (1 mark)
questions.tip: To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6.

questions.q: A resultant force of 6.0 N acts on a 1.5 kg trolley. What is its acceleration?
ms: a = F ÷ m = 6.0 ÷ 1.5 = 4.0 m/s². 9.0 multiplies F by m.
questions.tip: Rearrange F = ma to a = F/m.

questions.q: A spacecraft in deep space, far from any planet, switches off its engines. What happens to its motion?
options: It continues at a constant velocity
ms: With no resultant force, Newton's first law says the velocity stays constant.
questions.tip: Objects don't need a force to keep moving. They need a force to CHANGE velocity.

questions.q: A student pushes on a wall with a force of 40 N. Which statement about the Newton's third law pair is correct?
options: The student's weight balances the 40 N push
Friction on the student's feet is the third law pair
The wall pushes back with less than 40 N because it doesn't move
The wall pushes on the student with 40 N in the opposite direction
ms: Third law pairs act on DIFFERENT objects, are the same type of force, equal in size and opposite in direction.
questions.tip: A third law pair never acts on the same object, so the forces never 'cancel' each other.

questions.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 3200 N. The resistive forces are 1400 N. Calculate the acceleration of the car.
ms: Resultant force = 1800 N (1 mark)
a = F ÷ m (1 mark)
1.5 m/s² (1 mark)
questions.tip: F in F = ma is the RESULTANT force. Using 3200 N gives 2.7 m/s²: wrong.

questions.q: A van of mass 850 kg accelerates at 2.0 m/s². The total resistive force is 600 N. Calculate the driving force provided by the engine.
questions.answer: Resultant = ma = 850 × 2.0 = 1700 N; driving force = 1700 + 600 = 2300 N
ms: Resultant = 1700 N (1 mark)
Driving force − resistance = resultant (1 mark)
2300 N (1 mark)
questions.tip: Work backwards: find resultant first, then add back the resistive force.

questions.q: In the acceleration practical, a light gate system records a trolley's speed as 0.20 m/s at the first gate and 0.62 m/s at the second gate. The time between gates is 0.70 s. Calculate the acceleration.
ms: Change in velocity = 0.42 m/s (1 mark)
a = Δv ÷ t (1 mark)
0.60 m/s² (1 mark)
questions.tip: Light gates reduce human reaction time errors. That's the usual 'why use light gates' answer.

questions.q:
In the acceleration practical, a student investigates the effect of mass. She adds masses to the trolley and keeps the hanging mass (accelerating force) the same.
Total accelerating mass (kg) | Acceleration (m/s²)
0.50 | 1.20
0.75 | 0.80
1.00 | 0.60
1.50 | 0.40
(a) Describe the relationship shown. (2 marks)
(b) Use one result to calculate the accelerating force. (2 marks)
questions.answer: (a) As mass increases, acceleration decreases; inversely proportional (mass × acceleration is constant: 0.60). (b) F = ma = 0.50 × 1.20 = 0.60 N.
ms: (a) As mass increases, acceleration decreases (1 mark)
(a) Inversely proportional with evidence, e.g. doubling mass from 0.50 to 1.00 kg halves a (1 mark)
(b) F = ma with one pair of data (1 mark)
(b) 0.60 N (1 mark)
questions.tip: To show inverse proportion, multiply the pairs: a constant product proves it.

questions.q: Explain why the hanging masses should be moved from the trolley to the hanger (rather than added from outside) when investigating the effect of force on acceleration.
questions.answer: This keeps the total mass of the system (trolley + hanging masses) constant, so mass is a control variable and only the force changes. So any change in acceleration is due to the change in force.
ms: Total mass of the system (accelerating mass) stays constant (1 mark)
Mass is a control variable / fair test (1 mark)
So changes in acceleration are only due to changes in force (1 mark)
questions.tip: The accelerating mass includes the hanging masses, not just the trolley.

questions.q: (HT) A full shopping trolley is harder to start moving than an empty one. Explain this using the idea of inertia.
questions.answer: The full trolley has a greater mass so greater inertia: a greater tendency to stay at rest. A larger force is needed to give it the same acceleration (a = F/m).
ms: Greater mass so greater inertia / greater inertial mass (1 mark)
Needs a bigger force for the same acceleration (1 mark)
questions.tip: Inertia is a tendency to remain at rest or in uniform motion.

questions.q: A driver's reaction time is 0.60 s. The car travels at 13 m/s. What is the thinking distance?
ms: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time = 13 × 0.60 = 7.8 m.
questions.tip: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time (no acceleration involved).

questions.q: Which of these increases braking distance but NOT thinking distance?
ms: Worn tyres reduce friction between tyres and road, so braking distance increases. The others affect the driver's reaction time.
questions.tip: Driver factors affect thinking distance; car and road factors affect braking distance. Speed affects both.

questions.q: A car travels at 22 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.75 s. The brakes give a deceleration of 6.5 m/s². Calculate the stopping distance.
questions.answer: Thinking = 22 × 0.75 = 16.5 m; braking: s = v² ÷ 2a = 22² ÷ (2 × 6.5) = 484 ÷ 13 = 37.2 m; stopping = 53.7 m (allow 54 m)
ms: Thinking distance = 16.5 m (1 mark)
Uses v² − u² = 2as for braking distance (1 mark)
Braking distance = 37.2 m (1 mark)
Stopping distance = 54 m (1 mark)
questions.tip: Stopping = thinking + braking. Find both and add them.

questions.q: In the ruler-drop test, a student catches a ruler after it falls 0.18 m. The student uses the equation: reaction time = √(2 × distance ÷ 9.8). Calculate the reaction time and comment on whether it is typical.
questions.answer: t = √(2 × 0.18 ÷ 9.8) = √0.0367 = 0.19 s. Typical range is 0.2 s to 0.9 s, so this is at the fast end (just below typical).
ms: Correct substitution (1 mark)
0.19 s (1 mark)
Compares to typical 0.2–0.9 s: fast/at the low end (1 mark)
questions.tip: Quote the typical range 0.2 s to 0.9 s from the spec when asked to comment.

questions.q: A driver is travelling along a wet road at night after a long day at work, and is listening to loud music. Explain how these conditions could affect the stopping distance of the car. Use your answer to suggest what the driver should do.
questions.answer: Tiredness and distraction (loud music) increase reaction time, so thinking distance increases. Wet road reduces friction between tyres and road, so braking distance increases. Night: harder to see hazards so reaction is slower. Overall stopping distance increases. Driver should slow down (both distances decrease with speed), leave a bigger gap, turn music down, take a break.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear explanation of factors affecting both thinking and braking distances, linked to reaction time and friction, with sensible suggestions.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Identifies factors affecting both thinking and braking distance with some explanation.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. a wet road makes stopping distance longer.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: tiredness increases reaction time; distraction from music increases reaction time; longer thinking distance = speed × reaction time; poor visibility at night delays noticing hazards; wet road reduces friction/grip so lower deceleration, longer braking distance; possible skidding; driver should reduce speed, increase gap, rest, reduce distractions.
questions.tip: Split your answer into thinking distance and braking distance. Examiners mark against both.

questions.q: (HT) A car of mass 1400 kg travelling at 25 m/s brakes and stops in a distance of 40 m. Calculate the average braking force, and explain why large decelerations are dangerous.
questions.answer: a = v² ÷ 2s = 625 ÷ 80 = 7.8 m/s²; F = ma = 1400 × 7.81 = 10 900 N (1.1 × 10⁴ N). Large decelerations need large forces which may cause brakes to overheat and/or the car to skid; large forces on passengers cause injury.
ms: a = 7.8 m/s² (1 mark)
F = ma (1 mark)
1.1 × 10⁴ N (allow 10 900 N) (1 mark)
Large forces cause brakes to overheat / skidding / injury (1 mark)
questions.tip: Alternative method: work done = Ek lost so F = ½mv² ÷ s. Both get full marks.

questions.q: Explain what happens to the kinetic energy of a car when the brakes are applied.
questions.answer: Work is done by the friction force between brakes and wheels, transferring kinetic energy to the thermal energy store of the brakes, so their temperature increases.
ms: Work done by friction between brake pads and disc/wheel (1 mark)
Kinetic energy transferred to thermal store of the brakes / brakes heat up (1 mark)
questions.tip: The spec phrase is 'work done by the friction force reduces the kinetic energy'.

questions.q:
Data for a car on a dry road:
Speed (m/s) | Thinking distance (m) | Braking distance (m)
10 | 7 | 6
20 | 14 | 24
30 | 21 | 54
Use the data to explain how thinking distance and braking distance depend on speed.
questions.answer: Thinking distance is directly proportional to speed (doubling 10 → 20 m/s doubles 7 → 14 m). Braking distance is proportional to speed squared (doubling speed multiplies braking distance by 4: 6 → 24 m; tripling multiplies by 9: 6 → 54 m), because kinetic energy ∝ v².
ms: Thinking distance directly proportional to speed, with data evidence (1 mark)
Braking distance increases by a factor of 4 when speed doubles / ∝ v², with data evidence (1 mark)
Because kinetic energy ∝ v² and work done by brakes (F × d) must equal Ek (1 mark)
questions.tip: Quote numbers from the table. Examiners want evidence, not just a description.

questions.q: (HT) A 160 g cricket ball moves at 25 m/s. What is its momentum?
ms: p = mv = 0.160 × 25 = 4.0 kg m/s. 4000 forgets to convert grams.
questions.tip: Mass in kilograms.

questions.q: (HT) A 3000 kg truck at 12 m/s collides with a stationary 1000 kg car. They move off together. What is their combined velocity?
ms: Momentum before = 3000 × 12 = 36 000 kg m/s; after: (3000 + 1000)v = 36 000; v = 9.0 m/s. 12 m/s ignores the car's mass; 36 m/s divides by 1000 only. 3.0 m/s divides the speed by 4.
questions.tip: Use the combined mass after a 'stick together' collision.

questions.q: (HT) A 50 kg student stands at rest on a skateboard (mass 2.0 kg) and throws a 4.0 kg ball forwards at 6.5 m/s. Calculate the velocity of the student and skateboard just after the throw.
questions.answer: Momentum before = 0; ball momentum = 4.0 × 6.5 = 26 kg m/s; student + board: 52 × v = −26; v = −0.50 m/s, i.e. 0.50 m/s backwards
ms: Total momentum before = 0 (1 mark)
Ball momentum = 26 kg m/s and student + board mass = 52 kg (1 mark)
0.50 m/s backwards / in opposite direction (1 mark)
questions.tip: In an 'explosion' from rest the two momenta are equal and opposite. Give the direction.

questions.q: (HT) Explain why the total momentum of a rocket and its exhaust gases is zero just before launch, and how the rocket moves upwards.
questions.answer: Before launch everything is at rest, so momentum = 0. Gases are pushed down with momentum downwards; to conserve momentum the rocket gains equal momentum upwards.
ms: At rest so velocity (and momentum) is zero (1 mark)
Gases gain downward momentum so rocket gains equal upward momentum (conservation) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Momentum is a vector: equal sizes in opposite directions sum to zero.

questions.q: (HT) Trolley A (mass 2.0 kg) moves right at 4.0 m/s. Trolley B (mass 3.0 kg) moves left at 1.0 m/s. They collide and stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision, including direction.
questions.answer: Taking right as positive: momentum before = 2.0 × 4.0 + 3.0 × (−1.0) = 8.0 − 3.0 = 5.0 kg m/s; after: 5.0 × v = 5.0; v = 1.0 m/s to the right
ms: Momentum of B is negative / opposite direction (−3.0 kg m/s) (1 mark)
Total momentum before = 5.0 kg m/s (1 mark)
Combined mass 5.0 kg used (1 mark)
1.0 m/s to the right (1 mark)
questions.tip: Choose a positive direction and stick to it. Adding 8.0 + 3.0 gets 2.2 m/s and loses most marks.

questions.q: (HT) A 0.20 kg ball moving at 3.0 m/s hits a wall and rebounds at 3.0 m/s. A student says the momentum has not changed. Explain why the student is wrong.
questions.answer: Momentum is a vector. Before: +0.60 kg m/s; after: −0.60 kg m/s. Change = 1.2 kg m/s, because the direction reversed.
ms: Momentum is a vector / direction has changed (1 mark)
Change in momentum = 1.2 kg m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Same speed but opposite direction means different velocity, so different momentum.

questions.q:
(HT) Data for a car and a bullet:
Object | Mass | Velocity
Car | 1500 kg | 20 m/s
Bullet | 60 g | 500 m/s
Compare their momenta, using calculations.
questions.answer: Car: 1500 × 20 = 30 000 kg m/s. Bullet: 0.060 × 500 = 30 kg m/s. Car's momentum is 1000 times bigger, even though the bullet is much faster.
ms: Car momentum = 30 000 kg m/s (1 mark)
Bullet momentum = 30 kg m/s (1 mark)
Comparison: car has 1000 times more momentum (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Compare' means give a statement linking both values, ideally a ratio.

questions.q:
(HT) A 0.45 kg football is at rest. A player kicks it and it leaves the foot at 28 m/s.
(a) Calculate the change in momentum of the ball. (2 marks)
(b) The foot is in contact with the ball for 0.015 s. Use F = ma and a = Δv/t to calculate the average force on the ball. (2 marks)
ms: (a) p = mv used (1 mark)
(a) 12.6 kg m/s (allow 13) (1 mark)
(b) a = 1870 m/s² (1 mark)
(b) 840 N (1 mark)
questions.tip: When starting from rest, the change in momentum equals the final momentum.

questions.q: A sound wave in air has a speed of 340 m/s and a frequency of 850 Hz. What is its wavelength?
questions.tip: Rearrange v = fλ for λ: divide speed by frequency.

questions.q: What does the frequency of a wave mean?
options: The time taken for one wave to pass
The number of waves passing a point each second
ms: Frequency is the number of waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
questions.tip: Learn the exact definition: 'number of waves passing a point each second'.

questions.q: A wave has a frequency of 2.5 kHz. What is its period?
questions.tip: kHz = × 1000. Convert before taking 1/f.

questions.q: A student stands 85 m from a tall wall and claps. The echo is heard 0.50 s after the clap. Calculate the speed of sound in air.
questions.answer: Total distance = 2 × 85 = 170 m; v = 170 ÷ 0.50 = 340 m/s
ms: Sound travels to the wall and back: distance = 170 m (1 mark)
v = s ÷ t (1 mark)
340 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: An echo travels there AND back. Double the distance.

questions.q:
In the waves on a string practical, a vibration generator at 120 Hz sets up a standing wave. The student measures the length of 4 half-wavelengths as 1.60 m.
(a) Calculate the wavelength. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the speed of the wave on the string. (2 marks)
questions.answer: (a) 4 half-wavelengths = 2 wavelengths = 1.60 m, so λ = 0.80 m. (b) v = fλ = 120 × 0.80 = 96 m/s
ms: (a) Recognises 4 half-wavelengths = 2 full wavelengths (1 mark)
(a) λ = 0.80 m (1 mark)
(b) v = fλ (1 mark)
(b) 96 m/s (1 mark)
questions.tip: Measuring across several half-wavelengths and dividing reduces the uncertainty.

questions.q: In the ripple tank practical, explain why the student measures the length of 10 waves and divides by 10, rather than measuring one wavelength directly.
questions.answer: One wavelength is small and hard to measure accurately. Measuring across 10 waves gives a bigger distance, so the uncertainty (percentage error) is smaller. Dividing by 10 gives a more accurate mean wavelength.
ms: One wavelength is very small / hard to measure (1 mark)
Measuring a larger distance reduces the (percentage) uncertainty (1 mark)
Gives a more accurate value of wavelength (1 mark)
questions.tip: Same idea as timing 10 oscillations: spreading the error over many waves.

questions.q: Describe a method to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones and an oscilloscope (or other suitable equipment). Explain how you would use the measurements.
questions.answer: Signal generator and loudspeaker produce a sound of known frequency (e.g. 2 kHz). Two microphones connected to a dual-trace oscilloscope. Start with microphones together so the traces line up. Move one microphone away until traces line up again: distance moved = one wavelength. Repeat for several wavelengths (e.g. move until 5 alignments), divide distance by number. v = fλ. Repeat and take a mean.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Coherent method that would give valid results, including measuring wavelength and frequency, using v = fλ, with repeats/reducing uncertainty.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): A method which measures wavelength or distance/time with some detail and identifies how to calculate speed.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements of relevant equipment or measurement.
0 marks: no relevant content.

Indicative content: signal generator connected to loudspeaker; frequency read from generator; two microphones to oscilloscope; traces in phase at start; move one mic until in phase again = 1 wavelength; measure distance with metre ruler; over several wavelengths for accuracy; v = fλ; repeat at different frequencies; alternative method: distance ÷ time with two people/clapping and timing echoes over a long distance.
questions.tip: Name the equation you use (v = fλ or v = s/t) and say how you get each quantity.

questions.q: Describe the motion of air particles when a sound wave passes through air.
questions.answer: They vibrate (oscillate) backwards and forwards, parallel to the direction the wave travels. They do not travel with the wave.
ms: Vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer (1 mark)
Do not move along with the wave / only energy is transferred (1 mark)
questions.tip: Longitudinal: vibrations PARALLEL to direction of energy transfer.

questions.q: Which list puts electromagnetic waves in order of increasing wavelength?
ms: Increasing wavelength goes from gamma (shortest) towards radio (longest): gamma, X-ray, UV, visible, IR, microwave, radio.
questions.tip: Increasing wavelength = decreasing frequency.

questions.q: Which type of electromagnetic radiation is used in fibre optic communications?
ms: Visible light (and infrared) travels along optical fibres by total internal reflection.
questions.tip: AQA lists visible light: fibre optic communications.

questions.q: Why are microwaves, rather than radio waves, used to communicate with satellites?
options: Microwaves can pass through the atmosphere/ionosphere
Microwaves are not absorbed by water
ms: Microwaves pass through the Earth's atmosphere to reach satellites. All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
questions.tip: Never say one EM wave travels faster than another in a vacuum.

questions.q: A microwave oven produces microwaves with a wavelength of 12 cm. The speed of electromagnetic waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the frequency in GHz.
ms: λ = 0.12 m (1 mark)
f = v ÷ λ = 2.5 × 10⁹ Hz (1 mark)
2.5 GHz (1 mark)
questions.tip: Giga = 10⁹.

questions.q: Explain why ultraviolet radiation is more harmful to the human body than visible light.
questions.answer: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency than visible light, so it transfers more energy. Skin cells absorb this energy, which can damage cells and their DNA, causing the skin to age prematurely and increasing the risk of skin cancer.
ms: UV has higher frequency / transfers more energy (1 mark)
Energy absorbed by skin cells damages cells / DNA (1 mark)
Causes premature ageing of skin / increased risk of skin cancer (1 mark)
questions.tip: Higher frequency = more energy = more harmful. Make the chain explicit.

questions.q:
In the infrared practical, a student fills a Leslie cube with hot water and measures the infrared emitted from each face using an infrared detector.
Face | Reading
Matt black | 9.6
Shiny black | 7.8
Matt white | 4.2
Shiny silver | 1.4
(a) Give two conclusions. (2 marks)
(b) Explain why the detector must be the same distance from each face. (2 marks)
questions.answer: (a) Matt black is the best emitter; shiny silver is the worst emitter. Dark surfaces emit more than light ones; matt more than shiny. (b) Infrared intensity decreases with distance, so a different distance would change the reading; distance is a control variable so the comparison is fair/valid.
ms: (a) Matt black emits the most / is the best emitter (1 mark)
(a) Matt surfaces emit more than shiny / dark more than light / shiny silver worst (1 mark)
(b) Reading depends on distance / intensity decreases with distance (1 mark)
(b) Control variable so only surface type affects the result / valid comparison (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'emitter' for this practical. Students often write 'absorber' and lose the mark.

questions.q: State what is meant by 'radiation dose' and give its unit.
questions.answer: A measure of the risk of harm from the body being exposed to radiation. Measured in sieverts (Sv) or millisieverts (mSv).
ms: Measure of risk of harm from exposure to radiation (1 mark)
Sievert / Sv (1 mark)
questions.tip: Don't confuse with activity (becquerel, Bq).

questions.q:
(HT) Light of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz travels from air into glass. Its speed in air is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and in glass is 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. The frequency does not change.
(a) Calculate the wavelength in air and in glass. (3 marks)
(b) Explain how the change in speed leads to refraction when light enters at an angle to the normal. (1 mark)
questions.answer: (a) λ = v ÷ f; air: 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m; glass: 2.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m (b) Light slows down; the part of the wavefront entering first slows first, so the wave changes direction (towards the normal).
ms: (a) λ = v ÷ f (1 mark)
(a) 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m in air (1 mark)
(a) 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m in glass (1 mark)
(b) Speed decreases, one side of wavefront slows first so direction changes (1 mark)
questions.tip: Frequency is set by the source and never changes on refraction. Speed and wavelength change together.

questions.q: Gamma rays are used to treat some cancers. Suggest why gamma rays are suitable, and explain why doctors must consider the radiation dose.
questions.answer: Gamma rays are highly penetrating so can reach tumours deep in the body, and are ionising so they can kill cancer cells. They can also damage healthy cells and cause mutations, so the dose must be high enough to treat the cancer but the risk of harm to healthy tissue must be weighed against the benefit.
ms: Gamma is penetrating / can reach tumours inside the body (1 mark)
Ionising so kills/damages (cancer) cells (1 mark)
Also damages healthy cells / risk of cancer, so benefit must outweigh risk (1 mark)
questions.tip: For risk vs benefit questions, state the benefit AND the risk, then say they are weighed up.

questions.q: Which material is magnetic?
ms: Iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are the magnetic materials. Copper and aluminium are not.
questions.tip: Only four: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt.

questions.q: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
options: In the middle of the magnet
ms: Field lines are closest together at the poles, showing the field is strongest there.
questions.tip: Field line spacing shows strength: closer lines = stronger field.

questions.q: (HT) A wire 15 cm long carries a current of 4.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.25 T. What is the force on it?
questions.tip: Length in metres.

questions.q: (HT) A wire of length 6.0 cm is at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.30 T. The force on it is 0.072 N. Calculate the current in the wire.
ms: l = 0.060 m (1 mark)
I = F ÷ (B × l) (1 mark)
4.0 A (1 mark)
questions.tip: Rearrange F = BIl by dividing both sides by Bl.

questions.q: Explain how an electromagnetic door lock works. When the switch is closed, a current flows through a coil, which attracts an iron bolt and unlocks the door. When the switch is opened the spring pushes the bolt back.
questions.answer: When the current flows the coil becomes an electromagnet, creating a magnetic field. The iron bolt becomes an induced magnet and is attracted into the coil, compressing the spring and unlocking the door. When the switch opens, the current stops, the magnetic field disappears, and the iron loses its magnetism quickly (soft iron). The spring pushes the bolt back to lock the door.
ms: Current produces a magnetic field / coil becomes an electromagnet (1 mark)
Iron bolt becomes an induced magnet and is attracted (1 mark)
Switch off: no current, so magnetic field disappears (1 mark)
Iron loses magnetism (is not a permanent magnet) so spring pushes bolt back (1 mark)
questions.tip: In unfamiliar-context questions, track the sequence: current → field → magnetism → movement.

questions.q: (HT) A wire carrying a current is placed parallel to a magnetic field. Explain why there is no force on the wire, and state what change would give the maximum force.
questions.answer: The motor effect force only acts when the current has a component at an angle to the field; when the wire is parallel, the force is zero. Maximum force when the wire is at right angles (90°) to the field.
ms: No force when the conductor is parallel to the field (1 mark)
Force depends on the angle between wire and field (1 mark)
Maximum force when wire is perpendicular / at 90° to the field (1 mark)
questions.tip: F = BIl only applies when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

questions.q: (HT) Using Fleming's left-hand rule, state what each finger represents.
questions.answer: First finger: magnetic field (N to S). Second finger: current (conventional, + to −). Thumb: force/motion (thrust).
ms: First finger = field; second finger = current (1 mark)
Thumb = force / motion (1 mark)
questions.tip: FBI: F (thumb) force, B (first finger) field, I (second finger) current.

questions.q: Describe the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
questions.answer: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time. An induced magnet becomes magnetic only when placed in a magnetic field and loses most/all magnetism when removed.
ms: Permanent magnet produces its own field (1 mark)
Induced magnet only magnetic when in a magnetic field, loses it when removed (1 mark)
questions.tip: Induced magnetism always causes attraction.

questions.q: Describe how a plotting compass could be used to show that a current-carrying straight wire produces a magnetic field, and describe how the field changes with distance from the wire and size of current.
questions.answer: Pass the wire vertically through a horizontal card. Place a plotting compass on the card near the wire; with the current on, the needle points in a circle around the wire (it changes direction when the current is switched on). The field is weaker further from the wire and stronger for a larger current.
ms: Compass placed near wire deflects when current switched on / points in circles around the wire (1 mark)
Field gets weaker with distance from the wire (1 mark)
Field gets stronger with a larger current (1 mark)
questions.tip: Field lines around a straight wire are concentric circles.

questions.q: A student has a solution of salt in water. Which method gives a sample of pure water from it?
ms: Simple distillation boils the water off and condenses the vapour, leaving the salt behind. Filtration cannot remove a dissolved solid, crystallisation keeps the salt and loses the water, chromatography separates dyes.
questions.tip: Ask yourself which part you want to keep. Want the solvent: distillation. Want the dissolved solid: crystallisation.

questions.q: Which statement about an atom of chlorine-35 and an atom of chlorine-37 is correct? (Atomic number of chlorine = 17)
options: They both have 17 protons, but chlorine-37 has 20 neutrons and chlorine-35 has 18
They have different numbers of electrons in the outer shell
They have different numbers of protons
They have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of electrons
ms: Isotopes have the same number of protons (17) but different numbers of neutrons: 35 − 17 = 18 and 37 − 17 = 20. Electron numbers (and so outer shells) are the same.
questions.tip: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Isotopes never differ in protons or electrons.

questions.q: A sample of magnesium contains 79% magnesium-24, 10% magnesium-25 and 11% magnesium-26. What is the relative atomic mass of magnesium to 1 decimal place?
ms: Ar = (79 × 24 + 10 × 25 + 11 × 26) ÷ 100 = 2432 ÷ 100 = 24.32, so 24.3. 25.0 is the simple average of 24, 25 and 26, which ignores abundance.
questions.tip: With three isotopes, multiply every mass by its own abundance. Never just average the mass numbers.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a compound and a mixture. Use iron sulfide and a mixture of iron and sulfur powders as examples.
questions.answer: In a compound (iron sulfide) iron and sulfur atoms are chemically bonded in fixed proportions and can only be separated by chemical reactions. In a mixture the iron and sulfur are not chemically combined, so they can be separated by physical methods (e.g. a magnet removes the iron).
ms: Compound: two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions, e.g. iron sulfide, which can only be separated by a chemical reaction (1 mark)

Mixture: elements/compounds not chemically combined, so can be separated by physical methods, e.g. a magnet attracts iron out of the iron and sulfur mixture (1 mark). Allow filtration/crystallisation/distillation/chromatography as named physical methods.
questions.tip: 'Chemically combined' or 'chemically bonded' is the phrase the examiner looks for. 'Joined together' or 'mixed together' is too vague.

questions.q: Copper has two isotopes. 69.2% of copper atoms are copper-63 and 30.8% are copper-65. Calculate the relative atomic mass of copper. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
ms: A1: ÷ 100 to give 63.6 (1 mark). 63.616 not rounded to 1 d.p. scores M1 only; do not accept 64.
questions.tip: Check your answer lies between the two mass numbers and closer to the more common isotope. If it doesn't, you've mixed up the percentages.

questions.q: Boron has two isotopes, boron-10 and boron-11. The relative atomic mass of boron is 10.8. Calculate the percentage abundance of boron-10. Show your working.
ms: M1: sets up an equation using x and (100 − x), e.g. 10x + 11(100 − x) = 10.8 × 100 (1 mark)
M1: correct rearrangement, e.g. 1100 − x = 1080 (1 mark)
A1: boron-10 = 20% (1 mark). Allow trial and improvement that is shown and reaches 20%. Do not accept 80% given as the answer for boron-10.
questions.tip: Ar 10.8 is closer to 11, so boron-11 must be the common one. Use that as a sense check before you write 80% for the wrong isotope.

questions.q: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom and give two ways it is different from the nuclear model.
questions.answer: Plum pudding: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it. Differences: the nuclear model has the positive charge (and almost all the mass) concentrated in a tiny central nucleus; the nuclear model is mostly empty space; in the nuclear model the electrons are outside the nucleus (in shells, after Bohr).
ms: Plum pudding: a ball/sphere of positive charge with (negative) electrons embedded/spread through it (1 mark)
Difference 1: nuclear model has the positive charge in a small central nucleus (1 mark)
Difference 2: nuclear model is mostly empty space / mass concentrated in the nucleus / electrons orbit outside the nucleus at set distances (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'ball of positive charge'. Writing 'a pudding with electrons in' describes the name, not the model.

questions.q: Scientists' ideas about the structure of the atom have changed over time as new evidence was found. Describe how the model of the atom developed from the idea of tiny spheres to the modern model. Include the evidence that caused each change.
questions.answer: Atoms were first thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided. The discovery of the electron (J.J. Thomson) led to the plum pudding model: a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it. Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden's alpha scattering experiment showed most alpha particles passed straight through gold foil, a few were deflected and a very small number bounced back. This meant the atom is mostly empty space with mass and positive charge concentrated in a tiny nucleus: the nuclear model. Bohr's calculations, which agreed with experimental observations, showed electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (shells). Later experiments showed the positive charge of the nucleus is made of smaller particles, protons. Chadwick provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A detailed, logically ordered account of at least four models/stages in the correct sequence, each linked to the evidence that caused the change, including the alpha scattering results and the conclusions drawn from them.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Describes at least three models in a sensible order with some evidence linked, e.g. alpha scattering linked to the nucleus.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Names or describes one or two models, or gives some evidence, without clear links between evidence and change.
Indicative content: Early model: atoms as tiny spheres that cannot be divided
Indicative content: Discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model: ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded

Indicative content: Alpha scattering: most alpha particles passed straight through (atom mostly empty space), some deflected (positive centre repels them), a few bounced back (mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus)
Indicative content: Nuclear model replaced plum pudding: positive charge and mass in a small nucleus
Indicative content: Bohr: electrons orbit in shells at specific distances, theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations
Indicative content: Later: positive charge of nucleus subdivided into protons
Indicative content: Chadwick: evidence for neutrons in the nucleus (about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted)
questions.tip: A list of names and dates caps you at Level 1 or 2. Every model needs its evidence, and alpha scattering needs results AND what each result shows.

questions.q: Rock salt is a mixture of salt (sodium chloride) and sand. Salt dissolves in water but sand does not. Describe how you would obtain pure, dry salt crystals from rock salt.
questions.answer: Grind the rock salt, add water and stir (warm it) so the salt dissolves. Filter: the sand stays on the filter paper and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate. Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin until crystals start to form, then leave it to cool so the salt crystallises. Pat the crystals dry with filter paper or leave in a warm oven.
ms: Add (warm) water and stir to dissolve the salt (1 mark)
Filter to remove the sand / sand left as residue on filter paper (1 mark)
Heat the filtrate (salt solution) to evaporate some of the water (1 mark)
Leave to cool/crystallise, then dry the crystals with filter paper or in a warm place (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the residue and filtrate correctly. The salt is in the filtrate, not on the filter paper.

questions.q: Helium has the electronic structure 2. Explain why helium is placed in Group 0 and not in Group 2.
questions.answer: Helium's outer (first) shell is full with 2 electrons, so it is stable and unreactive like the other noble gases. Its properties match Group 0, not the reactive metals in Group 2.
ms: Helium's outer shell is full / it has a stable arrangement (the first shell holds only 2 electrons) (1 mark)
So it is unreactive / does not form ions or bonds, like the other noble gases; Group 2 elements are reactive metals that lose 2 electrons (1 mark)
questions.tip: Group number equals outer electrons for Groups 1 to 7 only. The key word for Group 0 is a FULL outer shell, not 'eight electrons'.

questions.q: A calcium ion, Ca²⁺, and a chloride ion, Cl⁻, both have the electronic structure 2,8,8. Calcium has atomic number 20 and chlorine has atomic number 17. (a) Explain how each ion forms from its atom. (b) Explain why the two ions have different charges even though they have the same electronic structure.
questions.answer: (a) Calcium atom (2,8,8,2) loses its 2 outer electrons to form Ca²⁺. Chlorine atom (2,8,7) gains 1 electron to form Cl⁻. (b) Ca²⁺ has 20 protons and 18 electrons, so its charge is +2. Cl⁻ has 17 protons and 18 electrons, so its charge is −1. The charge depends on protons as well as electrons.
ms: (a) Calcium (2,8,8,2) loses 2 electrons (1 mark)
(a) Chlorine (2,8,7) gains 1 electron (1 mark)
(b) Different numbers of protons: Ca²⁺ has 20 protons and 18 electrons, Cl⁻ has 17 protons and 18 electrons (1 mark)
questions.tip: Charge = protons − electrons. Quote both numbers for each ion, not just 'they have different protons'.

questions.q: Which method would you use to separate the different coloured dyes in a sample of black ink?
ms: Paper chromatography separates soluble substances (dyes) because they move different distances up the paper with the solvent.
questions.tip: Chromatography is for separating dissolved substances that are all mixed in one solution, like dyes in ink.

questions.q: Mendeleev's periodic table of 1869 did not include the noble gases. Suggest why, and explain how the later discovery of the noble gases supported his table.
questions.answer: The noble gases had not been discovered because they are unreactive and do not form compounds, so they were hard to detect. When they were discovered they fitted neatly as a whole new group (Group 0) between the halogens and the alkali metals, without disturbing the pattern of his table.
ms: Noble gases had not been discovered (yet) because they are unreactive / do not form compounds (1 mark)
They fitted into the table as a new group (Group 0) with no change to the existing pattern / order (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link 'not discovered' to the reason: unreactive. 'They didn't exist' scores 0.

questions.q: A student adds bromine water to sodium chloride solution. (a) Predict whether a reaction happens. (b) Explain your answer in terms of the electronic structure of the halogen atoms.
questions.answer: (a) No reaction / no colour change (solution stays orange). (b) Bromine is less reactive than chlorine so cannot displace it. A bromine atom has more electron shells than a chlorine atom, so its outer shell is further from the nucleus and there is more shielding. The attraction for an extra electron is weaker, so bromine gains an electron less easily than chlorine.
ms: (a) No reaction / no colour change / stays orange-yellow (1 mark)
(b) Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so cannot displace chlorine (1 mark)
(b) Bromine's outer shell is further from the nucleus / more shells, so weaker attraction to gain an electron (1 mark). Do not accept 'bromine loses electrons less easily'.
questions.tip: Halogens GAIN electrons. Writing 'loses electrons' (Group 1 wording) in a halogen answer throws away the explanation mark.

questions.q: Which pair of elements would react to form an ionic compound?
ms: Ionic bonding happens between a metal and a non-metal. Potassium is a metal and fluorine is a non-metal. Carbon/oxygen and hydrogen/chlorine are two non-metals (covalent); copper and zinc are two metals (they form an alloy).
questions.tip: Metal + non-metal = ionic. Non-metal + non-metal = covalent. Metal + metal = metallic.

questions.q: The ammonium ion is NH₄⁺ and the carbonate ion is CO₃²⁻. What is the formula of ammonium carbonate?
ms: Two NH₄⁺ ions (total +2) balance one CO₃²⁻ ion (−2), giving (NH₄)₂CO₃.
questions.tip: Brackets go round a molecular ion when you need more than one of it. NH₄₂ is not a formula.

questions.q: Which statement best describes what happens when solid sodium chloride melts?
options: Covalent bonds between sodium and chlorine atoms break
Weak intermolecular forces between NaCl molecules are overcome
Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions are overcome and the ions become free to move
Electrons become delocalised so the liquid can conduct
ms: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice. Melting overcomes the strong electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, so the ions can move. There are no NaCl molecules and no covalent bonds.
questions.tip: Never write 'molecules' or 'intermolecular forces' for an ionic compound. It is a lattice of ions.

questions.q: Mercury has a melting point of −39 °C and a boiling point of 357 °C. Give the state of mercury at: (a) 25 °C (b) 400 °C
questions.answer: (a) Liquid (b) Gas
ms: (a) Liquid: 25 °C is above the melting point but below the boiling point (1 mark)
(b) Gas: 400 °C is above the boiling point (1 mark)
questions.tip: Put the temperature on a number line between the melting and boiling points before you answer. Negative melting points catch people out.

questions.q: Calcium (electronic structure 2,8,8,2) reacts with chlorine (2,8,7) to form calcium chloride. Describe what happens to the electrons when calcium chloride forms. Give the formula and the charges of the ions formed.
questions.answer: Each calcium atom loses its two outer electrons, one to each of two chlorine atoms. Each chlorine atom gains one electron. This forms Ca²⁺ (2,8,8) and two Cl⁻ ions (2,8,8). Formula CaCl₂.
ms: Calcium atom loses 2 electrons / one electron to each of two chlorine atoms (1 mark)
Each chlorine atom gains 1 electron (1 mark)
Ions Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ and formula CaCl₂ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say electrons are TRANSFERRED from calcium to chlorine. 'Shared' turns it into covalent bonding and loses marks.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is a gas at room temperature. (a) Describe the bonding in a carbon dioxide molecule. (b) Explain why carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature.
questions.answer: (a) Covalent bonding: the carbon atom forms a double covalent bond with each oxygen atom, sharing two pairs of electrons with each (four shared pairs in total). (b) CO₂ is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them. Little energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the boiling point is low (below room temperature).
ms: (a) Covalent bonds / shared pairs of electrons (1 mark)
(a) Two double bonds, i.e. two shared pairs between C and each O (1 mark)
(b) Small molecules with weak intermolecular forces, little energy needed to overcome them (1 mark). Do not accept 'weak covalent bonds'.
questions.tip: Covalent bonds are strong. A gas has weak forces BETWEEN molecules. Mixing these up is the most common bonding mistake.

questions.q: Carbon and silicon are both in Group 4. Carbon dioxide, CO₂, turns into a gas at −78 °C. Silicon dioxide, SiO₂, melts at about 1710 °C. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding.
questions.answer: CO₂ is a simple molecular substance: small molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces, which need little energy to overcome, so it becomes a gas at a low temperature. SiO₂ has a giant covalent structure: every atom is joined to others by strong covalent bonds in a huge lattice. Melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds, which needs a lot of energy, so its melting point is very high.
ms: CO₂ has a simple molecular structure / small molecules (1 mark)
Weak intermolecular forces in CO₂ that need little energy to overcome (1 mark)
SiO₂ has a giant covalent structure / lattice (1 mark)
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken in SiO₂, needing a lot of energy (1 mark)
questions.tip: For a 4-mark compare question, give structure AND what is overcome for BOTH substances. One side only caps you at 2.

questions.q: Metals such as iron are used to make bridges, wires and pans. Explain why metals have high melting points, conduct electricity and heat, and can be bent into shape. Then explain why steel, an alloy of iron, is harder than pure iron.
questions.answer: Metals have a giant structure of positive metal ions arranged in regular layers, surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons. A lot of energy is needed to overcome these strong forces throughout the giant structure, so melting points are high. The delocalised electrons can move through the metal, carrying charge (electric current) and transferring thermal energy. The layers of ions can slide over each other while the bonding is kept, so metals are malleable. In steel, other atoms (e.g. carbon) are a different size, which distorts the layers, making it harder for them to slide, so steel is harder.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Clear explanation of all three properties linked to the structure and bonding, plus a correct explanation of alloy hardness using distorted layers. Uses scientific terms (delocalised electrons, positive ions, electrostatic attraction, layers) accurately.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Explains two or three properties with some reference to structure, or explains properties with a weak alloy explanation.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements about metal properties with little explanation, e.g. 'metals have free electrons so conduct'.
Indicative content: Giant structure of positive ions in regular layers
Indicative content: Sea of delocalised electrons
Indicative content: Metallic bonding: strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
Indicative content: High melting point: lots of energy needed to overcome strong metallic bonding
Indicative content: Conduct electricity: delocalised electrons move through the structure carrying charge
Indicative content: Conduct heat: delocalised electrons transfer thermal energy
Indicative content: Malleable: layers of ions can slide over each other
Indicative content: Alloy: atoms of different sizes distort the layers so they cannot slide as easily, so harder
questions.tip: Say 'positive metal ions', not 'atoms', and 'delocalised electrons', not 'free ions'. The alloy part needs 'different sized atoms distort the layers'.

questions.q: Dot and cross diagrams and ball and stick models are both used to represent molecules. Give one limitation of each.
questions.answer: Dot and cross: does not show the shape of the molecule / relative sizes of atoms. Ball and stick: shows bonds as sticks with gaps between atoms, when atoms are really touching; does not show which atom the electrons came from.
ms: Dot and cross: does not show the 3D shape / relative sizes of atoms / how atoms are arranged in space (1 mark)
Ball and stick: bonds are not physical sticks / atoms shown far apart when they are touching / does not show electrons or where they came from (1 mark)
questions.tip: Each limitation must be about THAT model. 'It's not accurate' or 'it's 2D' with no detail scores nothing.

questions.q: Diamond and buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) are both made only of carbon atoms. Diamond has a very high melting point, but C₆₀ turns into a gas at a much lower temperature. Explain why.
questions.answer: Diamond is a giant covalent structure: each carbon is bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds, so melting means breaking many strong bonds, which needs a lot of energy. C₆₀ is made of separate molecules. The covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong but do not break; only the weak intermolecular forces between C₆₀ molecules are overcome, which needs much less energy.
ms: Diamond: giant covalent / each C bonded to 4 others, many strong covalent bonds to break (1 mark)
C₆₀ is a simple molecule / exists as separate molecules (1 mark)
Only weak intermolecular forces between C₆₀ molecules are overcome, needing less energy (covalent bonds in the molecule do not break) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Same element, different structure. Point out that C₆₀'s covalent bonds stay intact. That is the Level 3 detail.

questions.q: Add the correct state symbols to this equation for magnesium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg( ) + 2HCl( ) → MgCl₂( ) + H₂( )
questions.answer: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
ms: All four correct: Mg(s), HCl(aq), MgCl₂(aq), H₂(g) (2 marks)
Two or three correct (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dilute acids and dissolved salts are (aq), not (l). (l) is only for a pure liquid like water or a molten substance.

questions.q: A solution of sugar in water does not conduct electricity. A solution of sodium chloride in water does. Explain why.
questions.answer: Sugar is a covalent (simple molecular) substance: its molecules have no overall charge, so there are no charged particles to carry current. Sodium chloride is ionic: when dissolved, its ions are free to move and carry charge.
ms: Sugar is made of molecules / covalent, with no charged particles (no ions or delocalised electrons) (1 mark)
Sodium chloride solution contains ions that are free to move and carry charge (1 mark). Do not accept 'electrons move' for NaCl solution.
questions.tip: In solutions it is the IONS that move, never electrons. 'Free electrons' is only for metals and graphite.

questions.q: In graphite, how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom covalently bonded to?
ms: Each carbon in graphite forms three covalent bonds within its layer, leaving one electron per atom delocalised. Four is diamond.
questions.tip: Three bonds in graphite (spare electron delocalised) and four in diamond (no spare electrons). This explains conduction.

questions.q: Substance Y is a black solid that sublimes at about 3650 °C. It conducts electricity as a solid. It is soft and slippery. Identify substance Y and explain each of these three properties using its structure.
questions.answer: Y is graphite. Very high sublimation point: giant covalent structure, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Conducts: each carbon forms three bonds, so one electron per atom is delocalised and can move through the structure. Soft and slippery: layers of hexagonal rings with weak forces between them, so the layers slide over each other.
ms: Identifies Y as graphite (1 mark)
High melting/sublimation point: giant covalent, many strong covalent bonds to break (1 mark)
Conducts: one delocalised electron per carbon atom (each C forms 3 bonds) that can move (1 mark)
Soft/slippery: layers with weak forces between them that can slide (1 mark). Do not accept 'weak covalent bonds between layers'.
questions.tip: The forces between graphite layers are weak, but they are not covalent bonds. 'Weak bonds between layers' is risky; say 'weak forces between layers'.

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃? Ar: Al = 27, S = 32, O = 16
ms: Mr = (2 × 27) + 3 × (32 + 4 × 16) = 54 + 3 × 96 = 54 + 288 = 342. 150 forgets to multiply by 3 for the bracket; 123 is Al + S + 4O with no multipliers.
questions.tip: The number after a bracket multiplies EVERYTHING inside it. Work out the bracket first, then multiply.

questions.q: 6.0 g of copper sulfate is dissolved in water to make 500 cm³ of solution. What is the concentration in g/dm³?
ms: 500 cm³ = 0.500 dm³. Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 6.0 ÷ 0.500 = 12 g/dm³. 3.0 multiplies instead of dividing; 0.012 uses cm³.
questions.tip: Convert cm³ to dm³ (÷ 1000) BEFORE dividing. A concentration smaller than the mass you dissolved in under 1 dm³ is a warning sign.

questions.q: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of: (a) potassium carbonate, K₂CO₃ (b) copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NO₃)₂. Ar: K = 39, C = 12, O = 16, Cu = 63.5, N = 14
ms: (b) 187.5 (1 mark). Do not accept 188 (rounding Ar values of Cu).
questions.tip: Keep Cu as 63.5. Rounding it to 64 changes the answer and loses the mark.

questions.q: Sodium reacts with chlorine: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. Calculate the mass of sodium chloride produced when 4.6 g of sodium reacts completely. Ar: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5
questions.answer: Moles Na = 4.6 ÷ 23 = 0.20 mol. Ratio Na : NaCl = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1, so 0.20 mol NaCl. Mr NaCl = 58.5. Mass = 0.20 × 58.5 = 11.7 g
ms: M1: moles of Na = 4.6 ÷ 23 = 0.20 (1 mark)
M1: moles NaCl = 0.20 using the 2 : 2 ratio and Mr NaCl = 58.5 (1 mark)
A1: 11.7 g (1 mark). Correct answer with no working scores 3.
questions.tip: Show the mole ratio step even when it is 1 : 1. If you slip later, that is the method mark you keep.

questions.q: Propane burns in oxygen: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 4.4 g of propane burns completely. Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16
questions.answer: Mr C₃H₈ = 44, moles = 4.4 ÷ 44 = 0.10 mol. Ratio C₃H₈ : CO₂ = 1 : 3, so 0.30 mol CO₂. Mr CO₂ = 44. Mass = 0.30 × 44 = 13.2 g
ms: M1: Mr propane = 44 and moles = 4.4 ÷ 44 = 0.10 (1 mark)
M1: moles CO₂ = 0.10 × 3 = 0.30 (1 mark)
A1: 13.2 g (1 mark). 4.4 g (ignoring the ratio) scores M1 only.
questions.tip: Propane and CO₂ both have Mr 44. That is a trap: the ratio is 1 : 3, so the mass of CO₂ is three times bigger.

questions.q: Methane burns in oxygen: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. 8.0 g of methane is mixed with 16.0 g of oxygen and ignited. (a) Identify the limiting reactant. Show your working. (b) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced. Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16
questions.answer: (a) Moles CH₄ = 8.0 ÷ 16 = 0.50 mol. Moles O₂ = 16.0 ÷ 32 = 0.50 mol. 0.50 mol CH₄ needs 1.0 mol O₂, but only 0.50 mol is present, so oxygen is the limiting reactant. (b) 0.50 mol O₂ gives 0.50 ÷ 2 = 0.25 mol CO₂. Mass = 0.25 × 44 = 11 g
ms: (a) M1: moles CH₄ = 0.50 and moles O₂ = 0.50 (1 mark)
(a) A1: oxygen is limiting because 0.50 mol CH₄ needs 1.0 mol O₂ (1 mark). Do not accept 'oxygen' with no comparison using the ratio.
(b) M1: moles CO₂ = 0.25 (from O₂ using 2 : 1 ratio) (1 mark)
(b) A1: 11 g (1 mark). Allow error carried forward: if methane was wrongly chosen as limiting, 22 g scores (b) M1 only.
questions.tip: Equal moles does not mean neither is limiting. Compare with the RATIO in the equation, then work out the product from the limiting reactant only.

questions.q: 5.6 g of iron reacts completely with 10.65 g of chlorine, Cl₂, to form 16.25 g of iron chloride, FeCl₃. Use these masses to work out the balanced symbol equation for the reaction. Ar: Fe = 56, Cl = 35.5
ms: M1: moles Fe = 0.10 and moles Cl₂ = 0.15 (using Mr Cl₂ = 71) (1 mark)
M1: Mr FeCl₃ = 162.5 and moles FeCl₃ = 0.10 (1 mark)
M1: divides by smallest to get 1 : 1.5 : 1 and scales to 2 : 3 : 2 (1 mark)
A1: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ (1 mark)
questions.tip: Chlorine is Cl₂, so use Mr 71, not 35.5. Using 35.5 gives 0.30 mol and the wrong ratio.

questions.q: A student mixes 100 cm³ of sodium chloride solution with a concentration of 20 g/dm³ and 150 cm³ of sodium chloride solution with a concentration of 10 g/dm³. Calculate the concentration of the mixture in g/dm³.
questions.answer: Mass in first = 20 × 0.100 = 2.0 g. Mass in second = 10 × 0.150 = 1.5 g. Total mass = 3.5 g. Total volume = 250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³. Concentration = 3.5 ÷ 0.250 = 14 g/dm³
ms: M1: mass of solute in each solution: 2.0 g and 1.5 g (1 mark)
M1: total mass 3.5 g ÷ total volume 0.250 dm³ (1 mark)
A1: 14 g/dm³ (1 mark). Do not accept 15 g/dm³ (simple average of the two concentrations).
questions.tip: You cannot average concentrations when the volumes differ. Work out the mass of solute in each, add, then divide by total volume.

questions.q: How many ions are in 0.20 mol of calcium chloride, CaCl₂? (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ per mole)
ms: Each CaCl₂ contains 3 ions (one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻). Moles of ions = 0.20 × 3 = 0.60 mol. Number = 0.60 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.61 × 10²³. 1.20 × 10²³ counts formula units only.
questions.tip: Read whether the question asks for formula units, molecules, atoms or ions. Then multiply by how many of those are in one formula.

questions.q: A student heats 5.0 g of calcium carbonate in an open crucible. After heating, the mass of solid left is 2.8 g. The equation is CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. (a) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced. (b) Explain why the mass of solid decreases even though mass is conserved.
questions.answer: (a) 5.0 − 2.8 = 2.2 g (b) Carbon dioxide is a gas that escapes from the open crucible into the air, so it is not weighed. The total mass of products (CaO + CO₂) still equals the mass of reactant.
ms: (a) 2.2 g (1 mark)
(b) CO₂ is a gas that escapes / leaves the crucible, so its mass is not measured (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mass is never 'lost' or 'destroyed'. Say the gas escaped and so is not included in the measurement.

questions.q: Calculate the number of moles in 1.0 kg of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16
questions.answer: Mr CaCO₃ = 100. 1.0 kg = 1000 g. Moles = 1000 ÷ 100 = 10 mol
ms: A1: 1.0 kg converted to 1000 g and 1000 ÷ 100 = 10 mol (1 mark). 0.01 mol (using 1.0 kg as 1 g) scores M1 only.
questions.tip: Moles equation uses grams. Convert kg to g (× 1000) first.

questions.q: Hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. What mass of water forms when 1.0 g of hydrogen burns completely? Ar: H = 1, O = 16
ms: Moles H₂ = 1.0 ÷ 2 = 0.50 mol. Ratio H₂ : H₂O = 2 : 2, so 0.50 mol H₂O. Mass = 0.50 × 18 = 9.0 g. 18 g uses 1.0 ÷ 1 (treating hydrogen as atoms).
questions.tip: Hydrogen gas is H₂ with Mr 2. Using Ar 1 doubles your answer.

questions.q: A student adds a large excess of magnesium ribbon to 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the hydrogen. She repeats the experiment with 50 cm³ of the same acid and the same excess of magnesium. Predict how the mass of hydrogen produced changes, and explain your answer using the idea of a limiting reactant.
questions.answer: The mass of hydrogen doubles. The acid is the limiting reactant because the magnesium is in excess. The amount of product depends on the amount of limiting reactant, and doubling the volume of acid doubles the amount of acid.
ms: Hydrogen produced doubles (1 mark)
Acid is the limiting reactant (magnesium in excess), and the amount of product is proportional to the amount of limiting reactant (1 mark)
questions.tip: The reactant in excess has NO effect on how much product forms. Only the limiting reactant controls the amount of product.

questions.q: In the thermite reaction, aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. (a) Calculate the mass of aluminium needed to react completely with 40 g of iron(III) oxide. (b) Calculate the mass of iron produced. Ar: Al = 27, Fe = 56, O = 16
