questions.answer: (a) Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160. Moles = 40 ÷ 160 = 0.25 mol. Al needed = 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 mol. Mass Al = 0.50 × 27 = 13.5 g. (b) Fe formed = 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 mol. Mass = 0.50 × 56 = 28 g
ms: (a) M1: Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160 and moles = 0.25 (1 mark)
(a) A1: 13.5 g aluminium (1 mark)
(b) M1: moles Fe = 0.50 (using 1 : 2 ratio) (1 mark)
(b) A1: 28 g (1 mark)
questions.tip: Fe₂O₃ has TWO iron atoms. Its Mr is 2 × 56 + 3 × 16 = 160, not 56 + 48.

questions.q: What are the products when magnesium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
ms: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Sulfuric acid makes sulfates, so the products are magnesium sulfate and hydrogen. Water forms with oxides, hydroxides and carbonates, not metals.
questions.tip: Sulfuric acid makes a sulfATE. Sulfide is the ion S²⁻ and is a different thing.

questions.q: Which is the correct ionic equation for the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid?
ms: Chloride ions are spectator ions, so they are left out. Magnesium atoms lose 2 electrons to form Mg²⁺ and hydrogen ions gain electrons to form H₂ molecules.
questions.tip: Cancel spectator ions and check both charge and atoms balance. Hydrogen gas is H₂, never H.

questions.q: Complete the word equations. (a) sulfuric acid + zinc carbonate → (b) nitric acid + calcium hydroxide →
questions.answer: (a) zinc sulfate + water + carbon dioxide (b) calcium nitrate + water
ms: (a) zinc sulfate + water + carbon dioxide, all three needed (1 mark)
(b) calcium nitrate + water (1 mark)
questions.tip: Carbonates give THREE products. Forgetting carbon dioxide is the usual slip.

questions.q: A student makes magnesium sulfate crystals by adding magnesium oxide powder to warm dilute sulfuric acid. (a) Why is the acid warmed? (b) How can the student tell when the magnesium oxide is in excess? (c) Give one hazard in this practical and a precaution to reduce the risk. (d) Why should the student not heat the solution until all the water has evaporated?
questions.answer: (a) To increase the rate of reaction. (b) Solid magnesium oxide remains / no more dissolves (stays cloudy) even after stirring. (c) Sulfuric acid is an irritant/corrosive: wear eye protection (goggles). Or hot apparatus: handle the evaporating basin with tongs. (d) Heating to dryness gives a powder rather than crystals and may decompose the salt / water of crystallisation is lost / spitting.
ms: (a) Speeds up the reaction (1 mark)
(b) Unreacted solid is left / no more magnesium oxide dissolves (1 mark)
(c) A hazard with a matching precaution, e.g. acid irritant → wear goggles; hot basin → use tongs/let cool; spitting solution → goggles (1 mark)
(d) Would form powder not crystals / the salt may decompose / solution spits (1 mark)
questions.tip: Hazard and precaution must match. 'Acid is dangerous, so be careful' scores 0.

questions.q: A student makes copper sulfate crystals from excess copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Her crystals are small, and some contain a black powder. Explain the cause of each problem and suggest how she should change her method.
questions.answer: Black powder: unreacted copper oxide got into the solution because she did not filter, or the filter paper was torn/she poured round it. Fix: filter the mixture to remove excess copper oxide before heating, and check the filtrate is clear blue. Small crystals: the solution was cooled too quickly or evaporated too far. Fix: heat only until crystals start to form (e.g. on a cold glass rod), then leave to cool slowly at room temperature.
ms: Black powder is excess / unreacted copper oxide (1 mark)
Filter (carefully) to remove excess copper oxide before crystallising (1 mark)
Small crystals from cooling too fast / evaporating too much: heat until crystals just start to form, then cool slowly (1 mark)
questions.tip: Identify the black solid as copper oxide by name. Then give a fix that matches each problem.

questions.q: Metals are extracted from their ores in different ways. Gold is found as the metal. Iron is extracted by heating its oxide with carbon. Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis. Explain why different methods are used for these three metals. Refer to the reactivity series and to oxidation and reduction in your answer.
questions.answer: The method depends on the metal's position in the reactivity series. Gold is very unreactive, so it does not react with other elements and is found uncombined as the native metal; it is extracted by physical means. Iron is less reactive than carbon. When iron oxide is heated with carbon, carbon displaces the iron: carbon removes the oxygen. Iron oxide is reduced (loses oxygen) and carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen) to carbon dioxide. This is relatively cheap. Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove oxygen from aluminium oxide. Aluminium has to be extracted by electrolysis of the molten oxide, where aluminium ions gain electrons (reduction) at the cathode. Electrolysis uses a lot of electricity, so it is expensive.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Explains all three methods linked clearly to reactivity relative to carbon, with correct use of oxidation and reduction (in terms of oxygen and/or electrons) and some reference to cost.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Explains two methods linked to reactivity, or all three with weak links, with some correct use of oxidation or reduction.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. gold is unreactive, aluminium uses electrolysis, with little explanation.
Indicative content: Gold is very unreactive, so found native / uncombined as the metal
Indicative content: Gold separated by physical methods
Indicative content: Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon can displace it from its oxide
Indicative content: Iron oxide is reduced (loses oxygen); carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen) to CO₂
Indicative content: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide
Indicative content: Aluminium extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide; Al³⁺ gains electrons (reduction) at the cathode
Indicative content: Electrolysis needs a lot of electrical energy so is more expensive than reduction with carbon
questions.tip: Compare each metal to CARBON, not just 'more reactive'. 'More reactive than carbon' is the phrase the mark scheme wants for aluminium.

questions.q: A student adds three metals, P, Q and R, to solutions of each other's sulfates. Results: P in Q sulfate: no reaction. P in R sulfate: coating forms. Q in P sulfate: coating forms. Q in R sulfate: coating forms. R in P sulfate: no reaction. R in Q sulfate: no reaction. Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first, and explain how the results show this.
questions.answer: Q, P, R. Q displaces both P and R, so it is the most reactive. P displaces R but not Q. R displaces neither, so it is the least reactive.
ms: Correct order: Q > P > R (1 mark)
Q displaces both P and R (from their sulfate solutions) (1 mark)
R displaces neither / P displaces only R (1 mark)
questions.tip: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one. The metal that causes most coatings is the most reactive.

questions.q: Copper reacts with silver nitrate solution. Silver crystals form and the solution turns blue. (a) Write the ionic equation for this reaction. (b) Write the two half equations. (c) Identify which species is oxidised.
questions.answer: (a) Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag (b) Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (allow 2Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Ag) (c) Copper (atoms) is oxidised because it loses electrons.
ms: (a) Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag, balanced (1 mark). State symbols not needed.
(b) Both half equations correct (1 mark). Allow Cu − 2e⁻ → Cu²⁺.
(c) Copper is oxidised, because it loses electrons (1 mark)
questions.tip: Silver ions are Ag⁺, so you need 2 of them for each copper atom. Unbalanced charge is the common error.

questions.q: A solution of a weak acid has a pH of 4. A solution of a strong acid of the same concentration has a pH of 1. (a) How many times greater is the hydrogen ion concentration in the strong acid? (b) Explain why the two acids have different pH values even though their concentrations are the same.
questions.answer: (a) 3 pH units difference, so 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 times greater. (b) The strong acid is completely ionised in solution, so it releases all its hydrogen ions. The weak acid is only partially ionised, so fewer H⁺ ions are released and the H⁺ concentration is lower.
ms: (a) 1000 times (1 mark). Do not accept 3 times.
(b) Strong acid completely / fully ionised in solution (1 mark)
(b) Weak acid only partially ionised, so lower H⁺ concentration (1 mark)
questions.tip: Each pH unit is a factor of 10. And 'ionised' is the key word: 'dissociated' is allowed, 'dissolved' is not.

questions.q: Which substance is a base but NOT an alkali?
ms: A base neutralises an acid to form a salt and water. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to form OH⁻ ions. Copper(II) oxide is insoluble, so it is a base but not an alkali.
questions.tip: All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis. Insoluble metal oxides are the classic example.

questions.q: Copper oxide is heated with carbon: 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂. Identify the substance that is oxidised and the substance that is reduced. Explain your answer in terms of oxygen.
questions.answer: Carbon is oxidised because it gains oxygen (forms CO₂). Copper oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen (forms copper).
ms: Carbon oxidised because it gains oxygen (1 mark)
Copper oxide reduced because it loses oxygen (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the substance AND give the reason. 'Carbon is oxidised' alone does not get the explain mark.

questions.q: The half equation Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ shows:
ms: Electrons appear on the products side, so iron atoms lose electrons. Loss of electrons is oxidation (OIL RIG).
questions.tip: Look at which side the e⁻ is on. Electrons as a product means they are lost: oxidation.

questions.q: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution a little at a time to dilute hydrochloric acid containing universal indicator. Describe how the pH and the colour of the indicator change as more sodium hydroxide is added until it is in excess.
questions.answer: At the start the pH is low (about 1) and the indicator is red. As sodium hydroxide is added, the acid is neutralised and the pH rises. At neutral (pH 7) the indicator is green. When excess sodium hydroxide is added the solution becomes alkaline, pH rises above 7 (up to about 13 or 14) and the colour goes blue then purple.
ms: Starts at low pH / red (allow orange/yellow as it rises) (1 mark)
pH increases to 7, green, when neutral (1 mark)
pH above 7 with excess alkali, blue/purple (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give both pH AND colour at each stage. The question asks for two things.

questions.q: Calcium reacts vigorously with dilute hydrochloric acid, but copper does not react at all. Explain these observations in terms of the reactivity series and the formation of ions.
questions.answer: Calcium is high in the reactivity series: its atoms lose electrons easily to form Ca²⁺ ions, so it reacts quickly with the H⁺ ions in the acid to give hydrogen. Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series: copper atoms do not form positive ions as easily as hydrogen does, so copper cannot displace hydrogen from the acid.
ms: Calcium is very reactive / high in the reactivity series (1 mark)
Reactivity linked to how easily the metal forms positive ions (loses electrons): calcium loses electrons easily (1 mark)
Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so cannot displace hydrogen from the acid (1 mark)
questions.tip: The reactivity of a metal is linked to how easily it forms positive ions. Use that idea, not just 'calcium is more reactive'.

questions.q: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. What forms at each electrode?
ms: A molten compound only contains its own ions. Positive Na⁺ ions go to the cathode and form sodium; negative Cl⁻ ions go to the anode and form chlorine. Hydrogen only forms when water is present.
questions.tip: Molten = only two ions, so the metal and the non-metal. Aqueous = water ions too, so check the rules.

questions.q: Potassium nitrate solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What forms at each electrode?
ms: Potassium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms at the cathode. Nitrate is not a halide, so oxygen forms at the anode (from hydroxide ions/water).
questions.tip: Reactive metal in solution → hydrogen. No halide in solution → oxygen.

questions.q: Copper(II) chloride solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which half equation happens at the cathode?
ms: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are discharged at the cathode. They gain 2 electrons (reduction). 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ happens at the anode.
questions.tip: Cathode = reduction = electrons on the LEFT of the arrow.

questions.q: Molten zinc bromide, ZnBr₂, is electrolysed. State which ions move to each electrode and explain why.
questions.answer: Zinc ions, Zn²⁺, move to the cathode (negative electrode) because they are positive and are attracted to the opposite charge. Bromide ions, Br⁻, move to the anode (positive electrode) because they are negative.
ms: Zn²⁺ (positive) ions move to the cathode / negative electrode (1 mark)
Br⁻ (negative) ions move to the anode / positive electrode; opposite charges attract (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'ions', not 'atoms', and give the reason: opposite charges attract.

questions.q: Silver nitrate solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the product at each electrode and explain each choice.
questions.answer: Cathode: silver, because silver is less reactive than hydrogen, so silver ions are discharged instead of hydrogen ions. Anode: oxygen, because nitrate is not a halide ion, so hydroxide ions (from water) are discharged.
ms: Cathode: silver (1 mark)
Silver is less reactive than hydrogen (1 mark)
Anode: oxygen, because no halide ions present / nitrate ions not discharged (1 mark)
questions.tip: The comparison for the cathode is always with HYDROGEN, not with carbon.

questions.q: Sodium iodide solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Write the half equation at each electrode and state which electrode reaction is oxidation.
questions.answer: Cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Anode: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻. The anode reaction is oxidation because iodide ions lose electrons.
ms: Cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (1 mark). Allow 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻.
Anode: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (1 mark). Allow 2I⁻ − 2e⁻ → I₂.
Anode reaction is oxidation, because electrons are lost (1 mark)
questions.tip: Iodine is diatomic, so you need 2I⁻ to make I₂. Sodium is too reactive to form at the cathode.

questions.q: Concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine) is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Explain what is produced at each electrode and why the solution left at the end is alkaline. Include half equations.
questions.answer: The solution contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from the salt, and H⁺ and OH⁻ from water. At the cathode, sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions gain electrons and hydrogen gas forms: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (reduction). At the anode, chloride is a halide ion, so Cl⁻ ions lose electrons and chlorine gas forms: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation). Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions are left in the solution, which is sodium hydroxide solution, so it is alkaline.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): Identifies all four ions, gives both products with correct reasons, both correct half equations, and explains the alkaline solution in terms of Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remaining.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Gives both products with some reasons and at least one correct half equation, or explains the alkaline solution with only partly explained products.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Names one or two products, or makes simple statements, with little explanation.
Indicative content: Ions present: Na⁺, Cl⁻ (from salt), H⁺, OH⁻ (from water)
Indicative content: Cathode: hydrogen, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
Indicative content: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, reduction
Indicative content: Anode: chlorine, because chloride is a halide ion
Indicative content: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻, oxidation
Indicative content: Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remain in solution: sodium hydroxide
Indicative content: OH⁻ ions make the solution alkaline
questions.tip: For the alkaline part, name the IONS left over (Na⁺ and OH⁻). Just saying 'sodium hydroxide forms' is weaker.

questions.q: A student uses inert electrodes to investigate the products formed when different aqueous solutions are electrolysed. (a) Name the independent variable. (b) Give one control variable. (c) Describe how she can collect any gas formed at an electrode. (d) Electrolysis of chloride solutions produces chlorine. Give one precaution to reduce the risk from chlorine.
questions.answer: (a) The solution (salt) being electrolysed. (b) Any one: voltage/current of the power supply, concentration of solution, volume of solution, type of electrode, time. (c) Fill a small test tube with the solution and place it upside down over the electrode so gas displaces the liquid. (d) Work in a well-ventilated room or fume cupboard / use low voltage and switch off once a small amount of gas is collected.
ms: (a) The type of solution / salt used (1 mark)
(b) One valid control variable, e.g. voltage, concentration, volume, electrode material, time (1 mark)
(c) Inverted test tube filled with the solution over the electrode (1 mark)
(d) Ventilation / fume cupboard / small amounts / switch off soon (1 mark). Do not accept 'wear goggles' alone for chlorine.
questions.tip: Chlorine is toxic to breathe. Goggles do not protect your lungs, so give ventilation or a fume cupboard.

questions.q: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed in a fume cupboard. (a) Give one observation at each electrode. (b) Explain why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.
questions.answer: (a) Cathode: a silvery liquid / bead of lead forms (collects at the bottom). Anode: brown/orange-brown gas (bromine) forms. (b) Bromine vapour is toxic, and lead compounds are toxic, so the fumes must be removed.
ms: (a) Cathode: silver/grey (liquid) metal or bead of lead (1 mark)
(a) Anode: brown / red-brown gas or vapour (1 mark)
(b) Bromine (vapour) is toxic (1 mark)
questions.tip: An observation is what you SEE. 'Lead forms' is a product, not an observation. Give colour and state.

questions.q: Which ions are present in copper(II) sulfate solution?
options: Cu²⁺, S²⁻, O²⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻
ms: The salt gives Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻. Water also ionises slightly, giving H⁺ and OH⁻. All four are present in an aqueous solution.
questions.tip: Any aqueous solution also contains H⁺ and OH⁻ from water. That is why hydrogen or oxygen can form.

questions.q: What is meant by an electrolyte? Give one example.
questions.answer: An electrolyte is an ionic compound that is molten or dissolved in water, so that its ions are free to move and conduct electricity. Example: molten lead bromide, or sodium chloride solution.
ms: Molten or dissolved ionic compound / liquid or solution containing ions that are free to move (1 mark)
Valid example, e.g. molten lead bromide, copper sulfate solution, brine (1 mark). Do not accept solid sodium chloride.
questions.tip: The ions must be free to move. A solid ionic compound is not an electrolyte.

questions.q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using inert electrodes. The solution contains H⁺, SO₄²⁻ and OH⁻ ions. (a) Name the product at each electrode. (b) Write the half equation for each electrode. (c) The volume of gas at the cathode is twice the volume at the anode. Use your half equations to explain why.
questions.answer: (a) Cathode: hydrogen. Anode: oxygen. (b) Cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻. (c) To transfer 4 electrons, 2 molecules of H₂ form at the cathode (4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂) but only 1 molecule of O₂ forms at the anode, so twice as much hydrogen is produced.
ms: (a) Cathode hydrogen and anode oxygen (1 mark)
(b) 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (1 mark)
(b) 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ (1 mark)
(c) Same number of electrons transferred: 4 electrons make 2H₂ but only 1O₂, so 2 : 1 (1 mark)
questions.tip: To compare gases, make the electrons equal in both half equations first. Then compare molecules of gas.

questions.q: Pure water is a very poor conductor of electricity. When a little sodium sulfate is dissolved in the water, electrolysis produces hydrogen and oxygen. Explain why adding sodium sulfate allows the electrolysis to happen, and why sodium is not produced.
questions.answer: Sodium sulfate provides many more ions that are free to move, so the solution conducts. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms at the cathode instead of sodium.
ms: Sodium sulfate adds (many) ions that can move and carry charge (1 mark)
Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is discharged instead (1 mark)
questions.tip: Pure water has very few ions. The added salt is there to carry the current, not to be discharged.

questions.q: Explain why sodium is produced at the cathode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed, but hydrogen is produced at the cathode when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed.
questions.answer: Molten sodium chloride contains only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, so Na⁺ is the only positive ion and is discharged. In solution, H⁺ ions from water are also present. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead.
ms: Molten: Na⁺ is the only positive ion present (1 mark)
Solution: H⁺ ions from water also present, and sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so H⁺ is discharged (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention where the H⁺ comes from (water). Without that, the comparison is incomplete.

questions.q: What happens to the temperature of the surroundings during an endothermic reaction?
ms: An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
questions.tip: Endothermic = energy goes IN to the reaction, so the surroundings (and the thermometer) get colder.

questions.q: A reaction profile shows the reactants at an energy of 120 kJ/mol, the products at 40 kJ/mol and the highest point of the curve at 230 kJ/mol. What is the overall energy change for the reaction?
ms: Overall energy change = products − reactants = 40 − 120 = −80 kJ/mol (exothermic, products lower). 110 is the activation energy (230 − 120). 190 is 230 − 40.
questions.tip: Energy change = products − reactants. Products below reactants means the answer is negative.

questions.q: Hydrogen reacts with fluorine: H₂ + F₂ → 2HF. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H = 436, F–F = 158, H–F = 568. What is the energy change for the reaction?
ms: Energy to break bonds = 436 + 158 = 594. Energy released making bonds = 2 × 568 = 1136. Change = 594 − 1136 = −542 kJ/mol. +26 uses only one H–F bond (594 − 568).
questions.tip: Count bonds in the products: 2HF means TWO H–F bonds. Then do broken − made.

questions.q: A student mixes citric acid solution with sodium hydrogencarbonate. The temperature falls from 20.5 °C to 14.0 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature change. (b) State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
questions.answer: (a) 14.0 − 20.5 = −6.5 °C (a fall of 6.5 °C) (b) Endothermic
ms: (a) 6.5 °C fall / −6.5 °C (1 mark)
(b) Endothermic, because the temperature decreased (1 mark)
questions.tip: Show it is a decrease: write −6.5 °C or 'a fall of 6.5 °C'. A bare '6.5' can look like a rise.

questions.q: A student investigates how the type of metal affects the temperature rise when a metal powder is added to copper sulfate solution. (a) State the independent variable and the dependent variable. (b) Give two control variables. (c) Explain why the student uses a polystyrene cup with a lid instead of a glass beaker.
questions.answer: (a) IV: the type of metal. DV: the temperature change (rise). (b) Any two: mass of metal powder, volume of copper sulfate solution, concentration of copper sulfate, starting temperature, particle size of metal. (c) Polystyrene is a good insulator and the lid stops heat escaping, so less energy is lost to the surroundings and the temperature change measured is more accurate.
ms: (a) IV type of metal and DV temperature change, both needed (1 mark)
(b) First valid control variable, e.g. mass of metal powder, volume of copper sulfate solution, concentration of copper sulfate, starting temperature, particle size of metal (1 mark)
(b) Second valid control variable (1 mark). Do not accept 'amount' without saying mass or volume.
(c) Reduces energy/heat loss to surroundings because polystyrene is an insulator / lid reduces loss (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Amount of solution' is too vague for a control variable. Say volume (in cm³) or concentration.

questions.q: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution, 5 cm³ at a time, to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature rise. Results (volume of NaOH added in cm³ : temperature rise in °C): 5 : 2.8, 10 : 5.5, 15 : 8.2, 20 : 10.9, 25 : 12.6, 30 : 11.5, 35 : 10.4. Explain the pattern in these results.
questions.answer: From 5 to 25 cm³ the temperature rise increases because more neutralisation happens as more sodium hydroxide reacts with the acid, so more energy is released. The maximum is at about 25 cm³ because at this point all the acid has been neutralised. After this, no more reaction happens. The extra sodium hydroxide added is cooler than the mixture, and the same energy is spread through a larger volume, so the temperature rise falls.
ms: Rise increases up to about 25 cm³ because more acid reacts / more energy released (1 mark)
Maximum at about 25 cm³ when all the acid has been neutralised / reaction complete (1 mark)
After 25 cm³, no further reaction; excess (cooler) alkali absorbs energy / same energy in a larger volume, so rise decreases (1 mark)
questions.tip: Explain the fall as well as the rise. 'The reaction stops' needs a reason: the acid has run out.

questions.q: Ethene burns in oxygen: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. Each ethene molecule has one C=C bond and four C–H bonds. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C=C = 614, C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 805, O–H = 464. Calculate the overall energy change for the reaction.
ms: M1: energy to break bonds = 3760 kJ/mol (1 mark)
M1: energy released making bonds = 5076 kJ/mol (2 CO₂ has four C=O; 2 H₂O has four O–H) (1 mark)
M1: broken − made (1 mark)
A1: −1316 kJ/mol, with negative sign (1 mark). +1316 scores 3.
questions.tip: Count the bonds in 2CO₂ and 2H₂O carefully: four C=O and four O–H. Then keep the minus sign: it is exothermic.

questions.q: A reaction profile shows the reactants at 0 kJ/mol, the top of the curve at 175 kJ/mol and the products at 62 kJ/mol. (a) State the activation energy. (b) Calculate the overall energy change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. (c) Explain, in terms of bonds, why the reaction has this sign of energy change.
questions.answer: (a) 175 kJ/mol (b) 62 − 0 = +62 kJ/mol, endothermic (c) More energy is needed to break the bonds in the reactants than is released when new bonds form in the products.
ms: (a) Activation energy = 175 kJ/mol (1 mark)
(b) +62 kJ/mol and endothermic (1 mark)
(c) Energy needed to break bonds is greater than energy released making bonds (1 mark)
questions.tip: Activation energy is measured from the REACTANTS to the peak, not from the products.

questions.q: Compare exothermic and endothermic reactions. In your answer, refer to energy transfer to or from the surroundings, temperature changes, reaction profiles and bond breaking and bond making. Give an example of each.
questions.answer: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. Examples: combustion, neutralisation, most oxidation reactions. On a reaction profile the products are at a lower energy than the reactants, and the energy change is negative. Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature decreases. Examples: thermal decomposition, citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate. On a reaction profile the products are higher in energy than the reactants and the energy change is positive. Both need activation energy, the minimum energy for particles to react, shown as the rise from reactants to the peak. Breaking bonds is endothermic and making bonds is exothermic. A reaction is exothermic if more energy is released making new bonds than is needed to break existing bonds, and endothermic if more energy is needed to break bonds than is released making them.
ms: Level 3 (5-6 marks): A detailed comparison covering energy transfer, temperature change, reaction profiles (relative levels of reactants and products, activation energy) and bond breaking/making for both types, with a correct example of each.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Compares the two types on at least two aspects with an example, or covers bond breaking/making correctly with some profile detail.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Simple statements, e.g. exothermic gives out heat, endothermic takes in heat, with little comparison.
Indicative content: Exothermic: energy transferred to surroundings, temperature of surroundings increases
Indicative content: Endothermic: energy taken in from surroundings, temperature decreases
Indicative content: Examples: combustion/neutralisation (exo); thermal decomposition/citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate (endo)
Indicative content: Profiles: exothermic products lower than reactants; endothermic products higher
Indicative content: Both have an activation energy: minimum energy needed for particles to react
Indicative content: Bond breaking takes in energy; bond making releases energy
Indicative content: Exothermic: energy released making bonds > energy needed to break bonds
Indicative content: Endothermic: energy needed to break bonds > energy released making bonds
questions.tip: 'Bond making releases energy' is a fact. A lot of students write that breaking bonds releases energy and lose the bond marks.

questions.q: Which statement explains why a reaction is exothermic?
options: The products have more energy than the reactants
Breaking bonds releases more energy than making bonds takes in
The activation energy is greater than the energy released
The energy released when new bonds form is greater than the energy needed to break the bonds
ms: Bond making releases energy and bond breaking takes in energy. If more is released forming bonds than is taken in breaking them, the overall change is negative (exothermic).
questions.tip: Breaking bonds always takes IN energy. Any option that says breaking releases energy is wrong.

questions.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Each H₂O₂ molecule has two O–H bonds and one O–O bond. Bond energies (kJ/mol): O–H = 464, O–O = 146, O=O = 498. Calculate the overall energy change for the reaction.
ms: M1: bonds broken = 2148 kJ/mol (1 mark)
M1: bonds made = 2354 kJ/mol (1 mark)
A1: −206 kJ/mol (1 mark)
questions.tip: Don't mix up O–O (single, 146) in H₂O₂ with O=O (double, 498) in oxygen gas. They are different bonds.

questions.q: In a temperature change practical, a student uses a thermometer that reads to the nearest 1 °C, and records the temperature only once, 5 minutes after mixing. Suggest two improvements to her method and explain each.
questions.answer: Use a digital thermometer / temperature probe reading to 0.1 °C, which gives a more precise reading of a small change. Record the highest (maximum) temperature reached, or take readings every 15 to 30 s, because after 5 minutes the mixture may already have cooled. Also allow: stir the mixture so the temperature is even.
ms: Use a thermometer with a higher resolution (e.g. 0.1 °C / digital probe) to measure the change more precisely (1 mark)
Record the maximum/minimum temperature or take readings at regular intervals, because energy is lost to the surroundings over time (1 mark). Allow: stir to make the temperature even throughout.
questions.tip: Each improvement needs a reason. 'Use a better thermometer' scores nothing without saying why it is better.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate only decomposes into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide while it is being heated strongly. State whether this reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain how you know.
questions.answer: Endothermic. It needs a continuous supply of energy (heat) taken in from the surroundings to keep the reaction going.
ms: Endothermic (1 mark)
It takes in energy / needs continuous heating to keep going (1 mark)
questions.tip: Many reactions need heat to START (activation energy). Needing heat the WHOLE time is what shows it is endothermic.

questions.q: Two reactions are being considered for use in a self-heating can of soup. Reaction A has an activation energy of 30 kJ/mol and an overall energy change of −400 kJ/mol. Reaction B has an activation energy of 250 kJ/mol and an overall energy change of −50 kJ/mol. Which reaction is more suitable? Explain your answer using both values.
questions.answer: Reaction A. Its overall energy change is much more negative, so it releases much more energy to heat the soup. Its activation energy is low, so it starts easily at room temperature without needing much energy to get going. Reaction B releases little energy and needs a lot of energy to start.
ms: Reaction A (1 mark)
A releases more energy (more negative energy change: −400 compared with −50) (1 mark)
A has a lower activation energy so it starts easily / needs less energy to start (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use BOTH numbers in your answer. Choosing A for only one reason loses a mark.
